text:
The company launches a competitive bidding process for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan solar energy.

Get Solar Panels

DTE Energy has announced plans to add up to 150 megawatts of new solar energy in Michigan, creating construction jobs, supporting local communities, and saving customers money on fuel costs.

Get Solar Panels

Because solar generation does not require fuel, the new projects will help reduce the company’s exposure to changing fuel prices over their operating lives. The projects will also support DTE’s work to provide customers with energy that is reliable, increasingly clean, and affordable.

“These projects are an investment in Michigan and the communities we’re proud to serve. By producing more Michigan-made energy that doesn’t require us to purchase fuel, we can help lower energy costs for our customers and reduce our reliance on fuel from outside our state. At the same time, these projects will create good jobs and bring new investment and tax revenue into local communities, providing more resources for schools, first responders and the services Michigan families count on every day.”

Project and bidding details

DTE is seeking competitive proposals for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan-based solar generation. The procurement supports the requirements of the settlement agreement in Michigan Public Service Commission Case No. U-21662, approved May 15, 2025.

Get Solar Panels

Projects must achieve commercial operation by June 30, 2030, be located in Michigan and connect to either the MISO transmission system or DTE’s distribution system. Interested bidders can register and obtain additional information through PowerAdvocate. Proposals are due Jan. 19, 2027, and DTE expects to execute contracts in the second or third quarter of 2027.

title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America - TechCrunch
description:
Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched.
The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall.
EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market.
Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027.
The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.
text:
Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding new life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com.

The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place.

According to , the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average.

Karl Brauer, executive analyst at , told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue.

Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer said.

“The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he said, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP.

The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.

“The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer said. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.”

Brauer said that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again.

“When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he said.

text:
Ineos has expressed its intention of building the Grenadier SUV and Quartermaster pickup variant within the United States as soon as possible. However, this has required that the automaker sell off its main production facility in France.

On the surface, this announcement seems like a good deal for the brand. Ineos has been building the Grenadier to effectively cater to the kind of people who want mechanically simple vehicles with serious off-road potential and traditional controls. The model is basically an homage to the classic Land Rover Defender that was built from 1990-2016, as well as the Land Rover 90 and 110 models that preceded it.

It fills a similar niche as the Toyota Land Cruiser 70 Series, which has been in continuous production since roughly 1984. The big difference is that the Ineos Grenadier is a wholly unique model that was inspired by the beloved British SUV and is actually available on our market.

Since Ineos does a significant amount of business inside North America, it makes sense to relocate to the United States to help avoid tariffs. Some of the reasons we don’t get the Land Cruiser 70 Series is because it’s based on an older model that would likely have trouble passing the modern U.S. safety and emissions regulations.

The Toyota would also be subject to the current tariffs, with pickup variants falling prey to the dreaded chicken tax that adds 25 percent. The classic Land Rover would likewise steal sales from other Toyota models. Plenty of Tacoma or 4Runner buyers would gladly pivot to the 70 Series were it ever made available here.

Ineos plans on getting around all of the above by simply building its vehicles stateside. It also doesn’t have to worry about the Grenadier or Quartermaster stealing sales from other models.

Despite promoting itself as a British company that only exists because of its affinity for iconic vehicles originating from the United Kingdom, Ineos does the brunt of its business on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean and has its main production facility based in Hambach, France.

That facility was a former Mercedes-Benz site, responsible for the Smart ForTwo, and will reportedly be sold to China’s BYD and is assumed to be repurposed to build all-electric vehicles sold on the European market.

The big question is what will happen in the interim period. Ineos needs a place to build its vehicles and is reportedly targeting U.S. production for 2028. That almost assuredly means that it will be buying a preexisting facility that it can retool, rather than building something from the ground up. We’re assuming Ineos won’t be handing over the keys to BYD until after it has things up and running in the United States, unless it’s fine with an extended period of not selling anything.

Details on the arrangement haven’t yet been finalized. We haven’t heard anything on where Ineos wants to set up shop in the United States, nor when the Chinese brand expects to move into France. But the deal with BYD sounds like it’s been solidified and the British company has certainly already been browsing American real estate.

This is a massive undertaking for what is effectively a very small automaker. Ineos has only sold about 35,000 vehicles since commencing production three years ago. But volumes have been increasing and the brand estimates that about 70 percent of those sales went to people living in North America.

That alone probably makes moving to the U.S. a foregone conclusion. Continuing to eat the cost of international shipping and regional tariffs makes little sense when you can just relocate to your core market. Ineos has suggested that the scheme will also help keep prices on the Grenadier and Quartermaster lower — which presently start around $73,000 and $84,000, respectively.

Assuming Ineos could bring those figures down by a few thousand dollars, it’s possible that the Grenadier could see more mass appeal. But they are likely to remain niche products. Due to boasting extremely traditional architecture, these models lack most modern convenience features and tend to drive like classic off-road vehicles.

That said, buyers' growing disdain for connectivity features and electronic gatekeeping could play into Ineos’ hands. Despite your author’s belief that modern pickups and SUVs have received some of the most useful tech features in recent years, that’s still accompanied by plenty of invasive boatware nobody really wants.

The Grenadier simply existing as an alternative to that, while still offering serious off-road performance reliant on mechanical hardware, could result in a sales boom for the brand. Ineos products don’t even come with an internal modem that can do more than send out an emergency signal, requiring customers to pair vehicles to their phone if they want to use the internet. There are no over-the-air updates, telemetry data, or in-car apps to speak of — which is something Ineos seems rather proud of.

Expect more information about the company’s relocation plans as they surface.

description:
NYLCV and a group of two dozen environmental, labor, clean energy, and community organizations are urging Governor Kathy Hochul to deploy previously committed Sustainable Future Program funds and invest another $3 billion dollars in the FY28 budget.
The Sustainable Future Program allocations in the FY 2026 and FY 2027 budgets are the largest climate investments in New York’s history.

text:
NYLCV and a group of two dozen environmental, labor, clean energy, and community organizations are urging Governor Kathy Hochul to deploy previously committed Sustainable Future Program funds and invest another $3 billion dollars in the FY28 budget.

In a letter sent last week, the groups thanked the governor for championing the $1 billion SFP in the FY27 State Budget and applauded her Climate Week announcement to allocate that funding to key areas of the state’s climate plan to help make the energy cleaner and more affordable for all New Yorkers — from no-cost energy efficiency upgrades for low- to moderate-income households, to union job-creating thermal energy networks, to cleaner, healthier schools.

These investments are vital and come at a moment that calls for bold action on energy security and affordability, a healthier environment, and climate change mitigation. Advancing these projects and programs quickly is critical for delivering cleaner air, union jobs, improved public health, energy bill savings, stronger communities, and investments in disadvantaged communities for New Yorkers.

The Sustainable Future Program allocations in the FY 2026 and FY 2027 budgets are the largest climate investments in New York’s history. With this precedent set, the geopolitical energy landscape and the rapidly worsening climate crisis demand that we accelerate our commitment to clean energy and clean air investments that deliver immediate and long-term health, affordability, job, and economic benefits to New Yorkers.

“We urge you to deploy the past years’ funding commitments as quickly as possible and double down on these commitments by including a $3 billion allocation for the Sustainable Future Program in your FY 2028 Executive Budget as the state works towards sustained funding with labor standards for these projects,” the letter stated.

The groups also requested that the funding be directed through the Climate Action Fund, with all funding subject to the same public reporting requirements included in the Clean Water, Clean Air and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act.

The Sustainable Future Program is a critical down payment for the kinds of investments that can be scaled and sustained through the Clean Air Initiative — New York’s emerging cap-and-invest program — once it is operational. The Clean Air Initiative could initially generate $3 billion each year from polluters, and this number should grow over time.

This program would provide urgently needed funding to directly support household energy affordability — for example, through electricity bill credits — and scale programs like those funded by the SFP that would help New Yorkers access energy efficiency, clean energy upgrades, and clean, affordable transportation, further driving down household energy costs across the state.

New York has laid the groundwork for a cleaner, healthier, and more affordable energy future. Now is the time to build on that progress by getting committed dollars out the door, scaling up investments in the coming budget, and establishing an ongoing source of funding that will deliver benefits to New Yorkers for generations to come.

text:
On November 19, 2026, the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) as a substitute amendment to H.R. 2347. BAAJA would amend several federal statutes that govern the permitting of infrastructure, energy, and development projects, including the Clean Water Act (CWA), 33 U.S.C. § 1251 et seq.; the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. § 4321 et seq.; the Endangered Species Act (ESA), 16 U.S.C. § 1531 et seq.; and the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), 54 U.S.C. § 300101 et seq. BAAJA would also impose new agency deadlines and limit how and when project approvals may be challenged in court. BAAJA is not yet law; the House must still act on the Senate’s version, which it could amend further, and the President must sign the final bill to become law.

BAAJA’s Key Elements

Section 401 water quality certification would be subject to a clear and convincing evidence standard and firm deadlines.

An applicant for a federal permit or license for an activity that would result in a discharge into “waters of the United States” (WOTUS), such as a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) dredge-and-fill permit under CWA § 404, 33 U.S.C. § 1344, must first obtain under CWA § 401, 33 U.S.C. § 1341, a certification that the discharge will comply with water quality requirements from the “certifying authority,” which BAAJA would define as the state or interstate agency to which the application is submitted (including a tribe treated as a state under 40 C.F.R. § 131.8) or, where none has authority, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). A denial generally prevents the federal permit from being issued. Under BAAJA, review would be limited to water quality requirements, and the certifying authority could deny certification only if it determines, by clear and convincing evidence, that no modification or reasonable condition would allow the project to comply, or that the application remains incomplete after the applicant has had a reasonable opportunity to supply missing materials. Each condition would have to meet the same standard and be the least burdensome necessary to ensure compliance with water quality requirements. If a denial or condition is litigated, the certifying authority, rather than the applicant, would bear that burden of proof. The federal licensing or permitting agency, in consultation with the certifying authority, would set a reasonable period for final action on the application (grant, grant with conditions, deny, or waive) of no more than one year from receipt (nine months for direct point source discharges from Natural Gas Act § 7 pipelines and bulk-power system transmission projects). If the certifying authority fails to act within that period, certification would be waived unless the applicant requests, and the certifying authority agrees in writing to, an extension.

CWA § 402 NPDES permits could last up to ten years, and WOTUS rules would be reviewed directly in the court of appeals with jurisdiction.

Pursuant to CWA § 301, a facility that discharges pollutants from a point source (such as a pipe or outfall) into WOTUS generally must obtain a CWA § 402 National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit. NPDES permits have a maximum five-year term; BAAJA would extend that maximum term to ten years. BAAJA would also require EPA to adopt water quality criteria through notice-and-comment rulemaking and would send challenges to those criteria, and to EPA rules defining WOTUS, directly to the federal court of appeals with jurisdiction. BAAJA would not itself change the WOTUS definition, which has been the subject of varying and confusing rulemakings and litigation for decades.

Section 404 permits would provide longer and more secure coverage.

CWA § 404 requires a USACE permit to discharge dredged or fill material into WOTUS, including many wetlands and streams. Smaller scale impacts often associated with certain designated development or infrastructure projects and activities may proceed under general permits, including nationwide permits (NWPs), rather than individual permits. BAAJA would extend Section 404 general permit terms from five to ten years, deem discharges into less than two acres as having only minimal effects, and require USACE to maintain NWPs 12, 14, 27, 43, 57, and 58 for discharges into less than two acres per project. For applications submitted after enactment, EPA could exercise its Section 404(c) “veto” authority to prohibit or restrict a dredge spoils disposal site only between submission of a complete application and permit issuance, foreclosing such veto after permit issuance.

Section 404 challenges would be subject to a 150-day deadline and limited remedies.

Challenges to Section 404 permits and general-permit verifications generally would have to be filed within 150 days. Where a draft permit is published in the Federal Register with a comment period of at least 30 days occurring after enactment, only parties that raised the issue in sufficiently detailed comments on the proposed permit could sue. That limitation would not apply to NWP coverage determinations that are not subject to such a public-comment period, but the 150-day deadline would still apply. A court could not vacate, enjoin, or otherwise limit a permit or verified activity unless the permitted activity would present an imminent and substantial danger to human health or the environment for which no other equitable remedy is available.

NEPA would be confirmed as procedural and subject to firm review deadlines

NEPA requires federal agencies to evaluate the environmental effects of major federal actions, including many permits, through an environmental assessment (EA) or a more detailed environmental impact statement (EIS). BAAJA would provide that NEPA establishes a procedure and does not mandate any particular outcome. At a project sponsor’s request, agencies would have to consider relying on existing federal, state, or tribal analyses, and no NEPA document would be required where the lead agency determines that a state or tribal review, or compliance with another federal law, serves a similar function. Lead agencies would have one year to complete an EA and two years to complete an EIS. After an EIS is published, the lead agency would have 45 days to issue a record of decision, and other agencies would have 90 to 120 days to act on remaining approvals.

NEPA challenges would be subject to a 150-day deadline, direct appellate review, and limited remedies.

NEPA claims generally would have to be filed within 150 days by parties that submitted sufficiently detailed comments on the issue (where the comment period occurs after enactment), and most would proceed directly in the federal court of appeals for the circuit where the project is located. If a court finds a violation, it generally could only remand the approval for correction within 180 days, and the project could proceed during remand. Preliminary injunctions would be available only in limited circumstances and only for violations of laws other than NEPA and the NHPA.

ESA Section 7 consultation would be shorter and aligned with NEPA.

A federal agency that permits, funds, or carries out an action that may affect a threatened or endangered species must consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Marine Fisheries Service, a process that concludes with a biological opinion. BAAJA would shorten formal consultation from 90 to 60 days and allow applicants to seek judicial relief if an extension would exceed 145 days without a written statement to the applicant or the applicant’s consent. Where an EA or EIS is required, BAAJA would generally require consultation to be completed by the NEPA completion deadline for that document—that is, by the date the EA is completed and made public or, for an EIS, the date the final EIS is published. It would also exempt certain transportation projects in operational rights-of-way, and challenges to biological opinions generally would have to be filed in the D.C. Circuit within 150 days after the opinion is made public.

NHPA Section 106 review would be narrower and tied to the NEPA schedule.

Section 106 requires federal agencies to consider the effects of their permits, funding, and actions on historic properties and resources. BAAJA would exclude several categories of activities from review, including certain financial-assistance-only projects and minor or routine repair and maintenance, and would limit review to historic properties within the area of potential effects identified by the permitting agency. For projects requiring an EA or EIS, consultation would have to begin when NEPA review begins and would generally have to be completed when the EA is completed and made public or the final EIS is published. As under NEPA, a court finding a violation generally could only remand the matter for correction within 180 days. Federal agencies would remain obligated under the Section 106 process to consult with tribes as to the potential impacts on historic resources.

Do Not Forget About State/Local Programs

Regulated parties should keep in mind that most states, and some regional and local jurisdictions, administer the CWA § 402 NPDES program under EPA authorization. These programs must be at least as stringent as the federal program, and the CWA and NPDES regulations allow them to be more stringent. In addition, certain states (like Virginia) have their own state-law permitting programs for impacts to surface waters, including wetlands, that overlap with or are more stringent than the USACE and EPA § 404 program, or that reach waters beyond WOTUS. So, while BAAJA may provide welcome relief at the federal level, state programs may not necessarily follow suit. Regulated parties should therefore track applicable state permitting and water quality standards programs regardless of BAAJA and, where needed, be prepared to pursue a parallel state permitting track for the same activity, with potentially different procedures and outcomes.

Looking Forward

If enacted as currently passed by the Senate, BAAJA would require each federal agency to revise its NEPA regulations and procedures within 180 days, and, beginning December 31, 2027, a certifying authority that has not adopted rules specifying additional Section 401 application materials would have to treat an application as complete if it contains the basic information BAAJA specifies. BAAJA could shorten permitting timelines and reduce litigation risk for many projects, but, because the final legislation may differ, developers, utilities, and other permittees should monitor its fate closely and consult legal counsel regarding how it may affect their pending or planned projects.

Robinson Meyer:

Hello, it’s Wednesday, November 25, and the House of Representatives is due to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, also known as the Permitting Reform Bill. I think it’s fair to say it’s divided climate, clean energy folks, and the broader Democratic coalition more than any other policy or decision I can think of. A few weeks ago, we had on Lena Moffitt and Pete Wyckoff from Evergreen Action to discuss why that relatively new climate and clean energy focused organization was supporting the bill, why they were one of the few environmental groups that was not just, opposing it or sitting on the sidelines, but affirmatively saying, yes, it should pass. It was a great conversation. But of course, you can’t just talk to the supporters. You have to talk to the opponents as well. And so for this show, I wanted to get one of the most respected opponents of them all. My guest today is Abbie Dillen. She’s an environmental lawyer and the president of Earthjustice, the world’s largest nonprofit environmental law firm. She’s been at Earthjustice since 2000, where she was previously vice president of litigation for climate and energy and involved in that organization’s work to shut down coal plants. We had a great conversation. It is very long, as you can tell from the runtime. We talked about the part of the bill that Abby is most worried about, where she stands now on the National Environmental Policy Act, how we got here politically, and where the climate movement goes from here. I’m Robinson Meyer, the founding executive editor of Heatmap News, and all that more. It’s all coming up on this special episode of Shift Key.

Robinson Meyer:

Abbie Dillen, welcome to ShiftKey.

Abbie Dillen:

Thank you. I’m glad to be here.

Robinson Meyer:

It’s great to have you. I mean, we’ve talked in the past, but it’s so great to have you here, and I appreciate you coming on. I mean, first of all, what a few months it has been, and we have all been very busy working on or around this bill. And so we had evergreen action on ShiftKey a few weeks ago, and they are endorsing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which I’m interested to hear what your pronunciation for the initials are, because at this point, I feel like I’ve heard every variation. And so I started off that conversation by asking them, why are you supporting this bill?

Robinson Meyer:

So let me now start off this conversation with you by asking you, Abbie, why is Earthjustice opposing the bipartisan permitting bill that’s just passed the Senate and is now facing a vote in the House?

Abbie Dillen:

Well, I like how you got me to introduce my pronunciation of the acronym. It’s gone through some iterations, but I’ve landed at Baja. So as you know, Earthjustice has this gigantic clean energy program, and we have made our biggest bet on deploying clean energy. And so I can’t help but start with the real sentiment that this is the first time we’ve ever seen a true transmission package that’s well-designed to unleash clean energy, pass any House of Congress. So that’s a big deal. And I want to make clear that we don’t oppose everything about this bill. The red line for me and for Earthjustice is that it gives this president so much more power over the next two years to do his worst. And by that, I mean corrupt deals that he could monetize and projects that will be inordinately harmful. And while much of the debate about Baja is about what it does in the sphere of energy regulation, these provisions around project certainty, and I know we’ll get more into the details, are about every kind of thing that a developer could do that requires some kind of federal authorization. And as thrilled as I am, and we are about these election results and all the possibilities that they unleash, we also know that these are going to be two extraordinarily scary years. This president doesn’t obey the law, and his White House is making it clear that they want to find all the ways they can to stretch the law and to insulate themselves from court review. And for all of the kind of issues that we work on, this bill gives them that. And then in addition, does things to our bedrock environmental laws within the energy sphere, which is a big enough scope all by itself, but again, across the board. And so as much as I’ve spent my professional career working on climate, we know that there are other dials on the dashboard blinking red, whether it’s water or a crisis for species. And this bill takes away so many protections that we desperately need and that I think would be very difficult politically to ever win back in the foreseeable future.

Robinson Meyer:

I want to get one more philosophical kind of high-level view from you, which is one argument that supporters of the bill have made, and that I think I find to be true, is that, the status quo for energy permitting is very bad. And under the status quo, it is already much easier to build fossil fuels than it is to build clean. And we can get into the various ramifications of this. But I just want to get your sense at a high level. Do you think today’s permitting system helps or hurts clean energy more than it does fossil?

Abbie Dillen:

Here’s how I frame that for myself. We need transmission to get clean energy online at the scale that’s needed to decarbonize everything. So we have to have an expanded grid. We need more transmission and we need different rules about who has access to it. So that’s, I think, uncontroversial and non-negotiable. And then the question is, are we building enough transmission? Are we building that fast enough? Are we reforming our energy regulatory system fast enough? No, on all three. And so what Earthjustice has been focusing on for the last several years is creating more understanding of what transformative regulation of the transmission system could be. You just need to get over all of the vetoes that are currently in the system and have better planning,

Abbie Dillen:

Better siting, with a federal backstop, and also answer the question of who’s going to pay for all this expensive new infrastructure. That’s what this bill does. And I think it’s uncontroversial that, or at least I think it is, that it would help us unleash the transmission that we absolutely need. Can we talk about how the politics have evolved here? Because I think even if the Congress were to pass a bill next year, the president would still need to sign it and you would still need multiple votes, multiple additional votes in the Senate. And every previous permitting reform bill has been foiled by the party that just won the election saying, you know, let’s get to this next time. We’re going to be in a better position to get this done in two years. So there will need to be some trade for the transmission section i think that is absolutely the case because right now, transmission is at such a disadvantage compared to everything else and especially in the political environment that would develop if this were to become an issue next year, transmission would be seen as the democratic demand so what like what what do you give up for that, for the transmission provision.

Abbie Dillen:

And I will answer your question, but what I think has changed really quite profoundly over the last even three or four years where a gas rush has been ascending and the industry has become so consolidated so that so many of the developers do both gas and renewables. There are very few companies left that are doing just renewables, for example, at scale. So what that means is it used to be transmission is a gift to Democrats and clean energy and maybe the Republicans who quietly like it. And now transmission helps everyone. And arguably, I think we’ll do more for clean over time just because clean should be able to outcompete. But at this moment where there’s a perfect storm of intentional and atmospheric pressures, upward pressures on the price of clean, I think the gas industry is making the bet that they’ll take just as much or more advantage of this And that their companies, they’re sort of all of the above companies anymore. So I think that is very different. And I think this hyperscaler dimension is very, very different. Another way to ask the question is what concessions can be gotten from this industry and the gas industry that wants to make a lot of money right now. Will there be concessions to environmental protections or things that matter to earth justice? I would assume so. full stop. But it would be shocking to me if you couldn’t have a deal that does not toss out the ESA, by the way, in ways that make a more complicated permitting system, we should talk about that, that don’t dismantle Clean Water Act provisions for everything, that don’t have cross-cutting ways of rejiggering how the courts work, I think there’s a better deal to be had because these pipeline provisions are not just status quo. They really matter to the most powerful industries in this country that the president listens to. And I think the president could sign anything that API and the people who are funding his ballroom support. And let’s not bet against ourselves. you could imagine a next president that builds on the momentum of this election and is able to deliver an even better holistic package if it can’t get done with Trump, because you can never bet on him.

Robinson Meyer:

That’s a very reasonable point of view. I guess what I would observe is that the politics of this issue over the past four years have not been reasonable. And the setup into to this current moment where Democrats who support permitting reform are trying, especially in the Senate, wanted to get it done before the lame duck ends. That has happened against a backdrop where folks, including me, have been begging for a kind of progressive permitting reform proposal, a progressive actually like, what would be acceptable here? What are the things not to touch?

Abbie Dillen:

You want someone to write a paper on here’s all the environmental laws to take down?

Robinson Meyer:

I want a paper that says here are the obstacles to why the IRA didn’t work. Not that the IRA didn’t work, but here’s the obstacles that held up IRA implementation. I trust that Earthjustice has been involved on this. What I will say is that this hasn’t stopped people from arguing, for instance, that Sunzia, obviously a very famous anecdote in this story, but I think an important one, was not a policy problem. It was not a policy problem that it took 18 years. This hasn’t stopped people from arguing that any kind of suggestion of permitting reform is deregulatory and kind of kowtowing to fossil fuel interests. But there has been a long policy, and it is not the earth justices of the world necessarily. It is other groups that also use the legal system to slow down projects.

Abbie Dillen:

Well, what I can—

Robinson Meyer:

Say is— Don’t give an inch.

Abbie Dillen:

Yeah.

Robinson Meyer:

And it seems to me like those politics have backfired in this moment and are backfiring now.

Abbie Dillen:

I mean, I can only speak for the work that we have been doing with many partners across the clean energy and environmental space, which sometimes feel separate, but are mostly not in my experience. And, you know, like today you have Mike Levin, Representative Levin and Representative Kasten recommitting to getting the Energy Bill Relief Act move forward. We’ve been working with many of our colleagues to whip up sponsorship for that. I think it has 163 sponsors. Leader Jeffries, you know, before the election, we haven’t spoken to him since, has said that can be an H.R. 1 through 10 bill. Like, we’re just in a different place, and not least through your efforts, to make this issue one that people cannot look away from. This whole community has changed so much the understanding of how energy policy works, why transmission is needed. It’s different in kind. And I think... I think there’s space on the legislative agenda for it. The need to bring down bills and create a solution that gets us off of the most expensive energy is felt. More people get it. But there’s also never been a good transmission package before. That’s what really makes this different and what puts us on a different footing.

Robinson Meyer:

I hear that. I think what I am analyzing here is that if you’re a lawmaker and you’re looking at this situation. Voters just voted for a lot of things, but one of them was cheaper energy. And unfortunately, I’m not happy about this, but many of the new senators who won ran on an all-of-the-above policy. We’re explicitly like, we want everything. We want it all to be cheap. We are going to give you the cheapest energy we can. Annie Andrews ran explicitly on passing permitting reform. And it seems to me that you have climate organizations. And let me cite a specific example here. The Sunrise Movement put out a video last week of activists haranguing Senator Ossoff. And they said in the video, it was they were trying to get him to vote for Van Hollen as Senate Majority Leader. I don’t have a view on this. One of the things they were kind of yelling at him about was that Chuck Schumer has done nothing to stop the climate crisis. Now, I don’t have a view on Schumer versus Van Hollen, but it is just not true that Chuck Schumer has done nothing to stop the climate crisis. He passed the IRA through the Senate. His team wrote a lot of the bill. And I think where a lot of this has wound up is that there are a lot of lawmakers who are trying to weigh cutting costs and cutting energy costs for an electorate that, cares about climate change, but not in a very salient way. And getting slimed on social media for supporting policy that’s good for data centers or bad for the climate, being attacked is not a true climate person. And they look at Chuck Schumer, for instance, being attacked. And they go, well, Well, if Chuck Schumer is getting attacked or if John Ossoff is getting attacked, John Ossoff wrote the solar manufacturing law that’s part of the IRA. Like, why should I? I’m just going to be attacked by this fringe no matter what. And I should focus on what will actually I can actually bring back to voters, which is making costs cheap. And that, to me, feels like the political setup for why then Democrats are like, let’s just get this done now, because it’s not earth justice that’s going to be attacking us in next term. But it is maybe sunrise. It is maybe, any of the environmental litigant groups that tried to stop the Champlain-Hudson, transmission line or are still litigating against Sunzia. And so let’s just get this done now, because we’re going to get attacked by kind of highly viral social media folks, no matter what, who describe themselves as climate advocates. So we might as well just focus on making sure that we can do stuff the next time we have the presidency and trying to reduce costs as much as we can now?

Abbie Dillen:

I don’t know. I mean, there’s a lot of slime going around, but I’m going to try to dodge it completely because I think it’s terrible. I just think that the structural forces, the structural need to do something on permitting and the amount of money involved will keep this in the sights of legislators. It’s not going away. And I’ve been talking to legislators across the spectrum about this. And I, of anything I’m saying, I feel confident that permitting is not going away. I don’t have a crystal ball to say what could pass. I understand my friends who say, I think this might be now or never, or now or a long time from now. I would like to, as Senator Whitehouse has, you know, keep this bird in the hand. And I don’t know when this will happen again. And I hear it. I understand the argument. And I have wrestled enormously, just speaking for myself. What I feel very certain about is what happens over the next two years. And I think we would regret it. I think it would hurt a lot of people, a lot of people in communities where I am accountable and know what that would look like. And I think we would come to regret it for this harm that can never be repaired and also for what it does politically. And so we just may disagree on that calculus.

Robinson Meyer:

Why is that different next year? Because if this passes in late 27.

Abbie Dillen:

Because what it would allow this president to do.

Robinson Meyer:

But it would allow, but any time that they, if it were to happen in the next Congress, then it would allow the president to do this.

Abbie Dillen:

It would not be this deal. This Congress would never have these provisions that would unleash the president to do his worst. I can’t believe that that would be part of the deal again. The biggest thing facing this Congress is how to deal with the AI industry. And that will be a major focus no matter what. There is some leverage around access to energy and what kind of deal that could elicit when you have Senator Heinrich having a different negotiating partner with Senator McCormick, what that could agenda when Josh Hawley is just as accountable to Senator Jeff Merkley about addressing voter concerns about transparency water. I just think it would be a different deal. I think it would certainly have concessions to the fossil fuels industry if you wanted to get this president to sign it. I don’t think it would... Create forever permitting. I don’t think it would weaken the Clean Water Act across the board. I don’t think it would turn over implementation of the ESA to states and fall away on the best available science for species protection. So that’s how I make my calculus.

Robinson Meyer:

You’re willing to bet that. And let me just say, because it seems to me that this is still going to divide the Democratic caucus no matter what next year, because we’ve seen in the politics of the data center provisions, for instance, that, or in the politics of even the transmission provisions, that there is nothing you can do on transmission that will not prevent an influential group of actors, of commentators from saying, this is good for data centers. You want to build more electricity? This is good for data centers.

Abbie Dillen:

It would help if it weren’t. I mean, you know, it would help if the bill didn’t have so many poison pills. And I haven’t even mentioned what it does to preservation of culture and history and the ability of tribes to protect their sovereign interests. There are so many poison pills in this bill as it stands that are correctly poisonous. They’re intolerable. We could do better than this. That’s my point. If your point is someone will always have a problem with it, I’m sure that’s the case. I’m sure that’s the case.

Robinson Meyer:

My point is it divides the Democratic coalition in a way that would make it, rapidly have it fall out of consideration next year. And it requires a lot of folks in Congress to suddenly take positions that they have opposed in the past.

Abbie Dillen:

What do you think are the provisions that would have to be part of this that would inherently make it impossible to keep Democrats together, at least in numbers that you couldn’t compensate for?

Robinson Meyer:

I think transmission is extremely divisive. I think transmissions would prove to be divisive again.

Abbie Dillen:

More so on the Republican side.

Robinson Meyer:

But I think it would be as soon as Democrats are in charge of it, this is a giveaway to the big tech. They need more energy. They’re going to eminent domain property through the back of your land, through the back of your house to feed data centers. And what we’ve seen on this bill is that even with the data with the ratepayer protection provisions, it’s like people see those as bad, too, because they help solve the problem. The data centers need electricity.

Abbie Dillen:

I’m not sure I’m following because I didn’t hear a single Democrat in the Senate base their opposition or concerns on the transmission provisions. Of course, there were Hawley and Co. Who had theirs on the Republican side, and that is a dynamic. And then there’s, of course, the Duke and Southern Company issue, which I think watered down this package. But on the Democratic side, I didn’t see that in the Senate. And I do think there’s a danger. I think there’s a danger of ramming through a bill that is so harmful in so many ways, because right now you and I both know this. You cover it exceptionally well on Heatmap. There is a well-funded, organized effort to try to brand clean energy as a problem.

Robinson Meyer:

Yes, totally. I agree.

Abbie Dillen:

And so we don’t want clean energy to have the taint of a bill that’s doing so many unpopular things. Why not position it in a bill that is not so unpopular with so many people?

Robinson Meyer:

But I think that that is going to be the issue of bringing it up in a next Congress.

Abbie Dillen:

So just jam it through now, notwithstanding all of the problems.

Robinson Meyer:

That it creates? No, but I think that that is what is driving some of the kind of bird in the hand thinking here. And I think that the... And perhaps you’re right on NEPA. Maybe NEPA is a solved problem, so to speak. I guess I would say, I think the six-year statute of limitations requires a statutory remedy. And I would say what I’ve seen. Well, what I’ve seen from the Democrats who are about to lead negotiations on this, including Representative Huffman, who would lead negotiations in a future Congress, are a sense that only understaffed agencies and inadequate reviews are the problems, that cause NEPA to hamstring major federal initiatives. I don’t agree with that. And I think people who believe that, for instance, there needs to be a statutory remedy on NEPA, who believe the next Democratic president should be, more empowered to build infrastructure of the type that I think we both think the country needs, look at kind of the set the lineup of principles and their what they’ve said historically and go.

Abbie Dillen:

So I disagree. I disagree. I mean, I’ve spent a lot of time with the players on the Democrat side. And I think there is a seriousness about this that the situation warrants. And I think part of what we’re dealing with is the sense that this is a gigantic overhaul. Can we please think about the unintended consequences of this? And so I understand that the political calculus is difficult. It’s difficult to do anything. That’s not through reconciliation with 51 people. Anything durable is difficult. I get it. But when we look at, I mean, you and I have both lived through the last two years. Everything I imagined when I read Project 2025, I was like, they can’t really do that. They’re doing it. They’re doing it. And so what I’m asking you to hear me on today. Can we not do something that hasn’t been thought through, I think that has predictable consequences, however unintended, of empowering someone who will abuse this extra power and I think leave all of us much worse off?

This conversation becomes so abstract. But what I’m hearing from clients, whether it’s, you know, in the Gulf South or Appalachia is, oh, my goodness, the wave of new development that’s coming. Or we work on deep seabed mining. How many leases could you give out? The president just sold two, even though a court had already found the ESA analysis was invalid. That’s what we’re going to have to be dealing with. And as someone who’s been dealing with it for the last two years, I want you to hear me that the next two will be worse. The next two will be worse because there’s no prospect of an election to restrain anyone. It makes a difference that someone like Stephen Miller is the chief of staff. I just think, you know, Mike Levin said this well in his remarks today, and I think it captured it. He says there’s real promise on costs and clean energy, but taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that are not guaranteed. And when you add that dimension to who is president now, that’s why I am where I am.

Robinson Meyer:

Isn’t the challenge here that we never know who will be president in the future and you could roll back? I mean, you do it in a year and oopsie daisy, you have empowered people. A president, you know, Tucker Carlson or someone else.

Abbie Dillen:

Even a president Vance.

Robinson Meyer:

Right. And so it just seems to me that as long as the fear, is of what a future president could do, we’re never going to allow what needs to happen on the Democratic side or on the decarbonization side because there will always be. And in fact, Democrats will continue to govern basically at a disadvantage because Republicans won’t care. Whoever the next Republican president after Trump is will have no problem doing all the things they’ve done the first two years of this. But the next Democrat comes in, well, first they have to staff the full Department of Energy, and they have to staff all the permitting agencies, and then they have to kind of cross their T’s and dot their I’s. And what it means is that the status quo, as long as we’re scared of what a future president or a current president could do, The status quo will create speed limits that only apply to Democrats.

Abbie Dillen:

We have to bet on ourselves, but I’m talking about the project certainty provisions that allow bad things to happen now. That’s not just fear. And then either it allows bad things to continue under a Vance administration or it prevents a better president of either party from repairing the damage. So I don’t think that sort of just take the risk that on the future applies in this context, because I think it’s like a lose lose whoever the next president is.

Robinson Meyer:

But then that president gets to lock in there.

Abbie Dillen:

I guess, but they’re already locked into the Trump world. That’s a carry forward problem. And then they can’t fix the problems that they probably ran and won on. If they’re a good president and if they’re a bad president, it’s just compounds. I think these provisions were well intended, but they’re really, really problematic.

Robinson Meyer:

And so it’s really just so if you were to pick this up next year, it’s you take out that. Yeah.

Abbie Dillen:

If you want to figure out how to make developers who’ve gotten skittish about expensive projects that have run into permitting barriers, let’s do that. And if there’s something in addition, let’s just really think it through. This is the problem with very closed door negotiations. And so I feel skeptical about it getting fixed. We will continue to try. We will leave no stone unturned. But if we’re starting over in a next Congress, I think it’s very hard to do this well.

Robinson Meyer:

So I asked the Evergreen folks, what keeps you up at night about the bill? I feel like we’ve been talking about this, so I’m not going to. Let me ask you, last question. What is the outcome for this bill that you would look at it and say, you know, this was actually worth it?

Abbie Dillen:

The whole project of our work at Earthjustice for all the clients that we represent, whether it’s the 80 tribes or the many community-based groups or big national groups, is to find a way. We’ll always work and find a way. Yeah. If this bill were to pass without significant improvements for tribal sovereignty, for the president’s unleashed power, for protection of water and endangered species, I know that our job would get so much harder. And I would just have to hope that we could summon the political will to get reforms for the future, and that we could do our very best to stop the worst and surprise ourselves. I went into this administration feeling that we would lose many more cases given the Supreme Court and the composition of the courts. And so far, we’ve been winning much more than I even would have expected. And so it’s possible that we surprise ourselves. This election surprised me. I would love, okay, I would love nothing more than you forgive me for being such a contentious guest. And you bring me back two years from now. And I say you were right. This is great.

Robinson Meyer:

My view on this bill is, let me put it this way. I think that the dynamic on this bill has been that there has a lot of folks who are very skeptical of changing any aspect of the status quo. I’m not putting earth justice in this bucket. Suddenly got religion on transmission really fast after the bill text came out, and suddenly kind of got religion on some aspects of, how the existing kind of permitting status quo benefits private developers on private land in a way that it discourages public development on public land, or the federal government actually building things. And I would say as someone who I have never, i mean obviously i think my work stands for itself but i haven’t said congress should do this on this bill i have been like we need permitting reform for a long time and as someone interested in that line i think, there’s a lot of groups that are opposed to anything that looks like this, and I think a lot of lawmakers basically feel that the contours of the issue are dominated by one fringe here or one kind of side here and.

Robinson Meyer:

Means that they’re just kind of more willing to take the plunge. And I think the politics of saying, hey, these laws don’t work has been very unpleasant for, and I realize it’s now unpleasant for everyone, but has been really unpleasant for a long time. And I think that has led to the moment that we’re in now. I’m just not convinced that after Jan 1, if this bill dies, we don’t immediately go back to having the same transmission fights we were in May or June. Maybe I’m wrong.

Abbie Dillen:

I see it differently.

Robinson Meyer:

Okay. Listen, if Baja now doesn’t pass in the House, there’s got to be a transmission bill next year. So I am doubtful the politics of it will be favorable, and I expect it to be dropped relatively quickly, but I would love to be wrong.

Abbie Dillen:

Okay. Well, let’s remember.

Robinson Meyer:

Let’s end it there.

Abbie Dillen:

11/23 next year. We’ll see where we are. Exactly.

Robinson Meyer:

Thank you. Abby, thank you so much for joining us.

Abbie Dillen:

Thanks for having me, Rob.

Robinson Meyer:

And thank you for being here.

title: Will permitting reform be the first casualty of the blue wave? - Washington Examiner

text:
The bill would make it easier to build transmission lines that carry electricity from wind and solar farms to customers. Federal regulators could approve qualifying interstate lines when states reject them or fail to act. Neighboring grid regions would plan new connections together, and developers would connect their projects to the grid faster.

For Democrats, the changes to the Federal Power Act would make it easier to build transmission lines and connect wind and solar projects to the grid, while Republicans would get limits on environmental reviews and lawsuits that have delayed pipelines, wells, and other infrastructure.

The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act by a seemingly strong 62-33 vote last Thursday night, but procedural maneuvering by the bill’s most determined opponents prevented a vote on a key amendment that could have secured more Democratic support.

The four bipartisan sponsors of the bill had come to an agreement on a manager’s amendment that would have narrowed exemptions to the National Historic Preservation Act, increased spending on the Historic Preservation Fund, and made it harder for states to use eminent domain for transmission projects.

But Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) and Ron Wyden (D-OR) refused to consent to a time agreement that would have allowed votes on up to a dozen amendments, including the bipartisan manager’s amendment, thus blocking changes to the legislation on the floor. This meant that while 21 Democrats voted to end a filibuster and move on to the bill, just 14 voted for final passage. Those who switched from yes to no included two possible presidential candidates, Sens. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and Raphael Warnock (D-GA).

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act now moves to the House, where the chamber’s lame-duck status will complicate efforts by Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) to get it across the finish line. In theory, Johnson should have the votes to move the bill to the floor and pass it as is, but he can’t force his members to show up, especially those who lost and have no reason to come back other than the quaint, old-fashioned idea of doing their jobs and serving their country. Republicans were missing an average of 30 members per vote last week.

While much of the language in the Senate bill is taken from the bipartisan work of Reps. Bruce Westerman (R-AR) and Jared Golden (D-ME), Democratic opposition to the latest Senate version of the bill has grown thanks in part to the Democratic Party’s overwhelming victory earlier this month.

“From what I’ve seen, Sens. Whitehouse and Heinrich have done some good work, but they’ve been negotiating from a position of weakness,” future House Natural Resources Committee Chairman Jared Huffman (D-CA) said of the bill. “Folding our hand now or in the lame duck makes no sense when we can keep working on this and, in a few more months, have a much better deal that works for everyone.”

EDITORIAL: TRUMP DIDN’T GET THE CORRUPTION MESSAGE

Huffman is not alone. He is joined by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), an array of green activist organizations (such as Defenders of Wildlife, Earthjustice Action, Friends of the Earth, the Natural Resources Defense Council, and the Sierra Club), and Democratic attorneys general from 15 states, including California, New York, and Massachusetts. It is hard to see how House Democrats would be willing to give President Donald Trump such a policy victory after soundly beating him at the polls when they are set to take power in two months.

Democrats want to make it easier to build infrastructure, but only infrastructure they like. That is the problem with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act from their perspective. It makes it easier to build transmission lines to solar projects, but it also makes it easier to build natural gas pipelines and data centers. Democratic states have an abysmal track record of building homes, pipelines, and high-speed rail projects. Now voters have handed that party control of Congress. If House Democrats run out the clock on permitting reform, Americans will start getting the anti-growth policies they voted for before the new majority is even sworn in.

title: BAAJA would deliver affordable energy and cleaner air for California families
description:
OPINION — Year after year, California families face impossible choices.
BAAJA would institute real deadlines and rules for every stage of permitting and every type of project, including clean energy.
Clean energy, like wind and solar, offers a way to get cheaper energy onto the grid.
California families, particularly those from already marginalized and climate-impacted communities, would feel that most acutely.
They must do it once more and help pass BAAJA this year, so California can build the clean energy our neighborhoods were promised.
text:
Capitol Weekly welcomes Opinions on California public policy or politics. Please read our guidelines for opinion pieces before submitting an Op-Ed. Submissions that do not adhere to our guidelines will not be considered for publication.

OPINION — Year after year, California families face impossible choices. Utility bills keep rising, with rates up by almost 40% between 2019 and 2025. And in the summer, when demand peaks, the options shrink. This comes at a time where families can no longer withstand added pressure on household budgets.

As a pastor and civil rights advocate in Sacramento, I believe energy policy must be measured by its impact on working families. Households can run their air conditioner almost 24/7 and risk a bill they can’t cover. Or they can suffer as temperatures reach triple digits and hope there aren’t any health impacts. Families in Sacramento and across the state make these choices every week, and I’ve seen them firsthand.

Climate change has added another strain. It has meant a longer, smokier wildfire season, which brings its own challenges, including that families are forced to run air purifiers around the clock. To power those systems adds another expense to California’s already soaring cost of living.

Many Californians are struggling with rising costs and the dirty air they’ve breathed for generations. The families I work with in South Sacramento know this better than most, having lived for decades in the shadow of gas power plants, industrial sites that release fossil fuel emissions into the air, and recurring wildfire smoke as temperatures rise. While clean energy was supposed to help on these fronts, it hasn’t arrived quickly enough.

California has led the nation on climate law, including 100% clean electricity and carbon neutrality by 2045. But those are just targets, and without the corresponding clean energy infrastructure, they can’t be met. Right now, too many of the projects that make those goals a reality are stuck waiting on Washington.

That’s why Congress must pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) before this session ends, ensuring its final provisions protect public health and encourage community participation.

Federal permitting is the bottleneck that stops new clean energy projects from being built. BAAJA would change the process to fix that. California’s attorney general and other state leaders have raised concerns about provisions affecting environmental protections and state and tribal authority. Congress should address those concerns so that faster decisions also preserve meaningful safeguards for the communities most affected by new infrastructure.

Families in our state deserve a permitting process that is timely and responsive to their health and economic needs. BAAJA would institute real deadlines and rules for every stage of permitting and every type of project, including clean energy. That includes transmission lines, environmental reviews under NEPA, lawsuit filings, and consultations under the National Historic Preservation Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act.

The bill would not remove these laws. Projects would still be required to meet their requirements. The difference is a deadline that would give project developers the certainty to invest and build.

California families already face sky-high rates. Couple that with rising demand, and it’s an untenable situation. If new supply doesn’t keep up, prices go up, as does the risk of rolling outages or other electricity issues. Clean energy, like wind and solar, offers a way to get cheaper energy onto the grid. That lowers costs for families.

And clean power means cleaner air. Clean energy projects that go unbuilt can’t cut carbon emissions. Meanwhile, the gas plants that would be replaced stay online, and those emissions continue. Passing BAAJA would fight back against this. The Solar Energy Industries Association estimates the bill would cut power sector carbon emissions by about 20% from 2028 to 2035, compared with current law.

That reduction in emissions is also projected to avoid $54 billion in public health damages. That means fewer trips to the hospital, less asthma and fewer lung issues, and better outcomes. California families, particularly those from already marginalized and climate-impacted communities, would feel that most acutely.

Working families can’t afford another decade of waiting. Neither can our climate or our health.

The California delegation has long stood with the communities I represent. They must do it once more and help pass BAAJA this year, so California can build the clean energy our neighborhoods were promised.

Dr. Tecoy M. Porter Sr. is President and Executive Director of the National Action Network Sacramento Chapter and Senior Pastor of Genesis Church Sacramento.

text:
Georgia communities have paid a steep price for decades of reliance on coal, and the bill keeps growing with no end in sight. Plant Bowen and Plant Scherer have polluted surrounding communities for decades, threatening Georgia families with higher electricity bills and deadly public health hazards.

On Wednesday, Nov. 18, the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy joined the Climate Action Campaign (CAC) and community leaders in Decatur, Ga., to speak out against the state’s continued reliance on coal. Speakers called on the Public Service Commission (PSC), state officials, and federal leaders to chart a path toward clean energy.

Data Center Demand

Plant Bowen, owned and operated by Georgia Power, spans more than 3,000 acres and has a capacity of roughly 3,499 megawatts across four coal-fired units.

“Coal power plants are inefficient and expensive to run,” said SACE Climate Advocacy Director Chris Carnevale. “That’s why, four years ago, Georgia Power themselves chose to close half of Plant Bowen’s units, stating at the time that continued operation is not economic or in the best interest of customers.”

Georgia Power had initially planned to end coal operations at the plant by 2035, but rising grid demand driven by data centers, along with federal regulatory changes, has pushed that timeline back several years; closure is now estimated for 2038 or 2039.

“Big tech is abandoning net zero goals to cash in on the AI boom. I hope and pray that our newly elected officials won’t let them get away with it. I hope they will adopt policies and regulations that put our people and our planet ahead of obscene company profits,” Lisa Coronado, co-founder of Decatur Cares About Climate, said.

DeKalb County was among the first counties in the state to enact a moratorium on new data center developments. In September, SACE announced a call for an 18-month moratorium on new large data centers across Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida.

Sign on to SACE’s call for a data center moratorium in Georgia

The Cost to Ratepayers

According to the Southern Environmental Law Center, Georgia Power customers have seen six bill increases in the past three years and now pay nearly $500 more per year.

“For over three years it has been proven that continuing to operate existing coal plants costs more than building new, local renewable resources such as solar and battery backup,” DeKalb County Super District 6 Commissioner Ted Terry said. “Our residents spoke loud and clear this November; DeKalb residents want clean energy now. DeKalb residents want affordable solutions.”

Terry also described Georgia Power’s choice to keep operating coal units it had previously planned to retire as disappointing, citing its effect on both the environment and household costs. He urged stakeholders with decision-making power to “end the costly polluting coal plants” and expand clean energy resources across the state.

Coronado widened the cost discussion beyond the monthly bill. She cited health care costs, coal ash cleanup, the water use of coal and gas plants, and the billions of dollars spent importing coal into a state with no coal mining or drilling.

Meanwhile, she said, many Georgians are forced to choose between keeping the lights on and buying food or medicine. Some Georgians’ utility bills, she noted, are now as large as a mortgage payment.

“Georgia could have thriving rooftop solar and battery installation industries, creating thousands of jobs,” Coronado said. “Schools, churches, hospitals, and local governments could afford solar and storage, lowering utility bills and freeing up money for teachers and community services.”

Coronado also pointed out that solar and battery storage are more resilient and can keep homes and community buildings powered during outages.

“Georgia Power spent a billion dollars repairing Hurricane Helene’s damage, a storm made far more destructive by record warm ocean waters,” Coronado said. “[Georgia Power] passed nearly all of that cost onto us.”

The Health Toll

Dr. Anne Mellinger-Birdsong, a pediatrician and medical and health advisor for Mothers & Others For Clean Air, focused on how coal pollution affects human health, particularly for children.

Children, she said, are “more vulnerable because they are still growing and every organ in their body is still developing, and because they breathe more air for their size than adults.” They also spend more time outdoors. She cited damage to lung growth, asthma, effects on cognitive development, and mental health problems. In adults, she said, exposure can contribute to lung disease, heart attacks, heart failure, strokes, and dementia.

“Plant Bowen is one of the deadliest coal power plants in the country, and it is still causing deaths today,” Mellinger-Birdsong said.

Plant Bowen ranks second-deadliest among 480 plants nationwide, with Scherer also in the top 25. An estimated 7,500 deaths in the region between 1999 and 2019 can be attributed to climate pollution from Bowen alone. And the metro Atlanta area ranks 43rd worst in the nation for smog, according to the American Lung Association’s 2026 report.

“It baffles me why we continue to allow power plants that cause so much health and economic damage to operate when less expensive and healthier alternatives are available,” Dr. Mellinger-Birdsong said.

Federal Policy and Local Goals

At the local level, DeKalb County committed in 2021 to powering its needs with 100% clean energy and clean transportation by 2050. On Earth Day 2025, the county approved a transition plan laying out how to reach that goal.

“It’s very clear that since we’ve passed that plan, we cannot reach it simply by ourselves. We are part of the Georgia Power Utility Network, and so even if we choose as the government to electrify, have more electric vehicles, the utility and the regulatory sector ultimately determine what that greenhouse gas content will be for most of our community’s power bills,” Terry said.

Terry called on local, state, and federal leaders, including the PSC, to work with community partners and commit to clean energy. Carnevale also emphasized the state and federal government’s responsibility to listen to constituents.

In recent years, the Trump administration has made costly energy decisions with lasting repercussions for both the climate and utility bills. Rollbacks of environmental protections allowed coal and gas plants to pollute the climate without limits, while the administration illegally withheld grant money that would have given 16,000 Georgia households low-cost solar, cutting their electric bills by 20% or more.

“This isn’t just another debate about clean energy,” Carnevale said. “This is about whether the people who live near these plants and pay electricity bills actually have a seat at the table when it comes to the energy decisions that will impact them for years.”

Looking ahead, Terry recommended the PSC advocate for affordable, clean energy in the long-range planning process with Georgia Power, noting that the next two Integrated Resource Planning (IRP) processes will be crucial for getting the state back on track. Terry also pointed to residential and community solar programs as additional tools for speeding up Georgia’s clean energy transition.

“Georgia is one of the best states for solar. I would love to see solar on our rec centers, on our tennis courts, on our parking lots, and all throughout Georgia, spreading the wealth that comes with producing our own domestically sourced energy,” Terry said.

text:
Three buildings, together the size of 28 football fields, are rising on what was farmland in Saline Township. It is Michigan’s first hyperscale data center.

Just east, in Van Buren Township, Wayne County has ordered a halt to construction on a second massive data center, this one for Google. The county says the developer did work without the permits it needed and violated the county’s stormwater rules. The developer, Panattoni, says it’s working with the county.

Data centers like these need enormous amounts of power, and DTE Energy has agreed to supply both. Getting that power to them takes new power plants, power lines and pipelines.

A bill in Congress would change how the country approves big energy projects: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

The bill is built on a trade. It promises faster, more certain approval of energy projects. In return, communities get less time to weigh in and fewer ways to stop a project they believe will harm them, from solar farms to gas pipelines.

The Senate passed it on Nov. 19, and Michigan’s two Democratic senators, Elissa Slotkin and Gary Peters, voted yes. The House still has to approve it.

Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib represents Detroit, Dearborn and Southfield. Her caucus has called the bill a gift to Big Oil and Big Tech. She joined The Metro’s Robyn Sfeir-Vincent to talk about what the bill would mean for data center opposition in Michigan and what she would pass instead.

text:
Last week, a Trump-backed bill that could speed up energy projects advanced out of the U.S. Senate with some bipartisan support. The controversial federal permitting reform proposal now sits with lawmakers inside the House, where a vote looms before the lame-duck session on Capitol Hill ends next month.

Arizona Democratic Congresswoman Adelita Grijalva is alarmed by how the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, better known as BAAJA, would effectively strip tribal consultation from Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act.

Tribes have long relied on it as a legal defense to save sacred sites.

“I was really disappointed,” she told KJZZ, stressing that her dad, the late Congressman Raúl Grijalva, would be, too. “He would hate every bit of it — would be as vocal, if not more than I’m being, just because he was a part of helping to create so much of the protections that were all thrown out.”

Senator Ruben Gallego had served alongside the elder Grijalva in the U.S. House and, in 2019, became the inaugural chair of the Subcommittee for Indigenous Peoples, part of the House Committee on Natural Resources.

More recently, Gallego was among 14 Democratic senators who broke party lines by backing BAAJA. Arizona’s senior Senator Mark Kelly voted against it.

Congresswoman Grijalva had this to say about their votes: “I’m very glad that Sen. Kelly was able to see through all of that. I’ve been texting concerns to both senators and I unfortunately didn’t hear back with Gallego’s team.”

In a statement explaining last week’s vote from the Senate floor, Gallego admitted “there is still work to be done” to address tribal concerns, but argued the overall bill “is an important step forward” for creating new jobs, lowering energy costs and speeding up permits to accelerate the clean energy transition.

title: These Maine heat-pump owners will get discounted power this winter - Canary Media
description:
A discount electricity rate for heat pump owners in Maine seemed dead earlier this year.
Essentially, the heat pump rate is just more likely to drive heat pump adoption at this point than during the pilot, supporters argued during the approval process.
So making heat pump owners pay more when they aren’t adding cost makes no sense, Lopez said.
