“Heat pump rates are a tool that will help us through that transition,” he said.
text:
A discount electricity rate for heat pump owners in Maine seemed dead earlier this year. Now, it’s been revived as regulators look for ways to encourage households to ditch increasingly pricey heating oil and make winter warming more affordable for those already using the electric systems.

The Maine Public Utilities Commission last week approved the rate structure proposed by the state’s top electric utility, Central Maine Power, which serves more than 670,000 households across most of the western half of the state. CMP expects the voluntary program, which kicks in Dec. 1, to save participating customers hundreds of dollars annually compared to default rates.

The heat pump rate eliminates transmission and distribution charges during the winter, leaving customers to pay for their electric supply — 13.63 cents per kilowatt-hour as of the new year — and a monthly fee of about $41 (somewhat higher than the $27 monthly fee paid by standard-rate households). Customers who opt into this rate will then see a higher rate during the summer months: 25 cents per kWh, as opposed to the standard rate’s 12 cents per kWh.

The idea is that the savings from winter operations will be greater than the additional summer costs, giving customers a net financial advantage. A customer who uses 500 kWh per month in the summer and 1,200 kWh per month in the winter would save $211 per year, compared to standard rates, according to CMP’s calculations. Use less in the summer and more in the winter and the savings go up.

Now, however, circumstances have changed. The price of heating oil — used by roughly half the homes in Maine — has spiked as a result of the ongoing war in the Middle East, lingering just below $6 per gallon in recent weeks. Heat pumps and the accompanying discount rates could offer much-needed savings this winter, regulators reasoned in their decision approving the new pricing structure. Essentially, the heat pump rate is just more likely to drive heat pump adoption at this point than during the pilot, supporters argued during the approval process.

“The cost of delivered fuels is incredibly high right now,” said Alex Lopez, senior manager of regulatory policy at electrification nonprofit Rewiring America, which was not directly involved in the Maine decision. ​“Heat pumps represent an opportunity to upgrade heating systems with a fuel that is less volatile, more efficient, provides healthier indoor air quality … there’s just so many benefits.”

Heat pump rates are gaining traction in other cold-winter places as well. Massachusetts requires all three of its major electric utilities to offer a lower seasonal rate for heat pump users, which took effect last winter. In that first season, the rates saved customers more than $37 million, an average of more than $250 per household. In Minnesota, Xcel Energy offers a program that lowers seasonal rates for homes with electric heat — both heat pumps and resistance. Colorado utilities will be required to consider heat pump discounts in future rate requests, and New York is looking at whether it can alter its current time-of-use rates to create more savings for heat pump users.

Supporters of heat pump rates emphasize that these are not a handout or subsidy, but instead a fair way of charging for the infrastructure these systems use. The electric grid is built to carry all the power needed when demand is highest, which generally happens on hot summer days. In the winter, therefore, there’s plenty of room on the system to carry electricity to heat pumps without spending money on improvements. So making heat pump owners pay more when they aren’t adding cost makes no sense, Lopez said.

As more heat pumps hook up to the grid, a time will come when demand peaks in winter instead of summer. At that point, new rate-setting approaches will be needed. In the meantime, though, heat pump rates are an appropriate way to encourage electrification and make the system more fair, Lopez said.

“Heat pump rates are a tool that will help us through that transition,” he said. ​“They are a bridge solution.”

text:
RICHMOND, Va. — After a week of testimony over the proposed $67 billion Dominion Energy-NextEra Energy merger, NextEra CEO John Ketchum took the stand one final time, addressing a controversy that began on the first day of the hearings before making his case for what the deal could deliver for Virginians.

A viral photo captured by Mike Kropf of the Richmond Times-Dispatch showed a NextEra employee laughing at a picture taken in front of protesters.

Ketchum said Tuesday that two employees involved in the incident are no longer with the company.

“As soon as I learned the photo, I was beyond upset. As soon as I found out about it, I immediately went to the hallway, sent those two individuals home, and those two individuals are no longer with the company.”

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger also weighed in, calling the behavior disrespectful.

“There’s folks flying in from Florida, and not only are they saying that they are going to buy up Dominion, we are going to do this, we are going to do that, but then they come and mock the Virginians who aren’t yet convinced this deal is good for them,” Spanberger said.

Beyond the controversy, Ketchum used his final testimony to reinforce what he says the merger could deliver for Virginians.

Ketchum backed the companies’ revised $2 billion bill credit proposal announced Monday. Under the proposal, typical residential customers would receive a $15 monthly credit for the first two years, followed by $10 per month in the third year and $5 per month in the fourth year.

Ketchum also addressed protections for customers facing disconnection. He said the combined company would adopt Dominion Energy’s existing disconnection policy, including its 30-day policy and weather-related restrictions.

That policy differs from the one used by Florida Power & Light, a NextEra Energy subsidiary.

Watch Related Coverage: SCC keeps controversial Robo Memo sealed

SCC keeps controversial Robo Memo sealed, calls for more transparency in $67B merger

Growing electricity demand was also a major focus of Ketchum’s testimony.

With data centers driving increased demand, Dominion is already purchasing 25% of its power from other sources.

Ketchum acknowledged Dominion could handle that growth on its own but argued the two companies could meet the demand at a lower cost together.

He also said the combined company would comply with the Virginia Clean Economy Act, pointing to NextEra’s renewable energy and battery-storage capabilities. Ketchum said he was surprised he had been questioned about whether NextEra could meet Virginia’s clean energy goals.

“We're you know by far the world's leader in renewables and in battery storage because that that is what we do. And I don't say this to be boastful. Please don't take it that way. But I truly do believe if NextEra can't do it, I'm not sure who else could,” Ketchum said.

Tuesday marks the sixth day of evidentiary hearings on the proposed merger.

The commission has until Jan. 11 to decide whether the merger will move forward.

text:
Hyperscalers face a big question: How do you feed power-hungry data centers while working toward net-zero carbon emissions? Amazon(NASDAQ:AMZN) is betting nuclear energy can help bridge that gap. The company is backing 5 gigawatts of new nuclear power by 2039, with small modular reactor developer X-energy (NASDAQ:XE) playing a key role.

With projects in the pipeline, Amazon's partnership gives X-energy a powerful backer and an opportunity to prove its nuclear technology can deliver. Could the artificial intelligence (AI) boom help turn this next-generation nuclear stock into a major growth opportunity?

Nuclear energy is crucial for next-gen data centers

In 2019, Amazon co-founded The Climate Pledge, which calls on signatories to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040. More recently, Amazon laid out plans to cut the carbon intensity of operations by 65% compared with 2019 levels.

A major component of Amazon's carbon-reduction goals involves nuclear energy, which provides carbon-free, reliable, 24/7 baseload power that data centers desperately need. Nuclear energy complements intermittent renewables, like wind and solar power, and numerous hyperscalers, including Microsoft, Meta Platforms, and Alphabet, are signing agreements for nuclear power.

How SMR developer X-energy got a leg up from Amazon

Amazon launched its $2 billion Climate Pledge Fund in 2020, and it used some of those funds to become an early investor in X-energy in October 2024 during its Series C-1 financing round. Amazon provided much-needed project and development funds, and has been central in helping X-energy with the design, licensing, and build-out of its nuclear fuel facility.

X-energy develops the Xe-100 SMR, a high-temperature, gas-cooled nuclear reactor. The Xe-100 uses small graphite pebbles packed with uranium particles and coated in a high-temperature ceramic, and it uses helium gas for cooling. The reactor uses its core physics and heat-resistant fuel to naturally shut down the nuclear reaction and passively dissipate heat without pumps or human intervention.

SMRs are appealing because they are manufactured in modular factory units and can be linked together. For example, each Xe-100 produces 80 megawatts (MW) of electricity and can be linked together, like the 12-unit, 960 MW project planned in Indiana.

Amazon has been crucial for X-energy, helping it fund a four-unit project totaling 320 MW with Energy Northwest in central Washington. It has also committed funding to develop the 12-unit project with American Electric Power at the former coal plant in Indiana. Meanwhile, X-energy's project with Dow in Texas has cleared regulatory review for construction and hopes to deliver power by the early 2030s.

Is X-energy stock a buy?

SMRs could completely change how we think about and deploy nuclear energy, and X-energy is one of many start-ups in the space. Amazon has helped X-energy clear regulatory hurdles and secure commercial agreements, giving it a massive leg up on competitors that lack similar backing.

X-energy could be a massive winner over the next decade as the nuclear renaissance unfolds. That said, X-energy's story is still being written, and it will be several years before it deploys its first reactors commercially, making the stock best suited for your watch list for now.

text:
This past election, Americans across the country rejected data centers, voting to restrict new projects in their communities. As voters push back against data centers, a new study out of Harvard reveals startling revelations about the severity of the pollution they create.

Pollution from data centers is three times higher than previously estimated, according to a new study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

The study examined 403 "hyperscale" data centers and found that emissions from these facilities were underestimated. In fact, the lead author Gianluca Guidi believes that their research only provides a "floor estimate." When factoring in the thousands of data centers across the country, many of which were not included in the study, the energy use is likely much higher.

The study found that the largest data centers in the U.S. use as much energy in a single year as the state of Michigan does. Carbon emissions from these data centers surpassed those of entire countries.

Researchers found that 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. during the study period came from data centers. A single data center included in the study consumed as much energy as 30,000 homes on average.

Certain U.S. states are worse off than others in terms of climate pollution from data centers, according to Harvard researchers. For example, Virginia has the most data centers, and fossil fuel-burning power plants are most common there. Other states, such as Oregon, have green-friendly, eclectic grids, so data centers residing there are likely emitting less pollution.

Data centers have become a controversial topic across the U.S. Thanks to the AI boom, the tech industry is looking to build more data centers in the U.S. to provide compute for AI models and research. However, data centers are proving unpopular in many communities. Some state legislatures have taken action to restrict data center buildouts and stiffen regulations around the industry. As previously mentioned, 44 ballot measures to restrict data center buildout were passed by voters during the midterm elections.

And the movement against AI data centers appears to only be growing. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich launched her own data center tracking initiative earlier this year.

The tech and AI industries are currently struggling with a series of other issues. However, based on what studies are finding, it seems the anti-data-center movement will continue to be a thorn in the side of big tech and AI.

ABBEVILLE — Louisiana regulators have stopped their review of coastal development for SpaceX's proposed facility in Vermilion Parish due to missing environmental information and concerns about the impact on coastal wetlands.
The department cannot continue processing SpaceX's permit application until more information is submitted.
In late October, residents of Vermilion Parish filed a lawsuit against the Vermilion Parish Police Jury and Industrial Development Board, accusing the groups of having illegal meetings about SpaceX.
The lawsuit alleges eight violations involving government meetings, public notices and decisions tied to SpaceX.
SpaceX, headquartered in Texas, must now address the state's concerns before regulators continue processing the application.
text:
ABBEVILLE — Louisiana regulators have stopped their review of coastal development for SpaceX's proposed facility in Vermilion Parish due to missing environmental information and concerns about the impact on coastal wetlands.

A letter sent to SpaceX on Monday by the Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy states that the application does not provide enough information for the Office of Permitting and Compliance to complete a review for inconsistencies with the Louisiana Coastal Resources Program. The department cannot continue processing SpaceX's permit application until more information is submitted.

The letter also states that if the issues with the application are not fixed within six months of when the letter was sent, the project will be deemed inconsistent with Louisiana's approved Coastal Management Program. It's not immediately clear if there is an appeals process for the project to move forward if it is deemed inconsistent.

In a separate seven-page letter, the Department of Conservation and Energy has asked SpaceX to include more information on the acreage of impact by specific impacted habitat type for both temporary and permanent impacts, a proposed restoration plan, marsh creation and canal dredging, as well as several other environmental concerns.

The $100 billion investment—which SpaceX bills as the largest capital investment project in Louisiana history—is expected to begin in next year, with the first launch planned for as early as 2029.

When the project was first announced in August, Elon Musk compared it to something that previously "has only existed in science fiction." However, residents of the area have had concerns about the project from the beginning.

In late October, residents of Vermilion Parish filed a lawsuit against the Vermilion Parish Police Jury and Industrial Development Board, accusing the groups of having illegal meetings about SpaceX. The lawsuit alleges eight violations involving government meetings, public notices and decisions tied to SpaceX.

SpaceX, headquartered in Texas, must now address the state's concerns before regulators continue processing the application.

title: BAAJA Permitting Reform: Key Changes For Energy, Infrastructure And Data Center Projects
description:
According to the bill’s sponsors, BAAJA will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.
How BAAJA Could Accelerate Energy Infrastructure Development For energy infrastructure, BAAJA would facilitate grid expansion and modernization.
The bill would expand the permitting authority of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) over qualifying interstate transmission facilities and strengthen coordinated transmission and generation-interconnection planning.
What to Watch as BAAJA Moves to the House Despite levels of bipartisan support, approval of BAAJA by the House is not guaranteed.
FOOTNOTES [1] Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA): Resource Hub, Bipartisan Pol’y Ctr.
text:
Last week, the U.S. Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (“BAAJA”), setting the stage for a consequential vote in the U.S. House of Representatives after the Thanksgiving recess. Heralded as “the most comprehensive permitting bill to date,”[1] BAAJA would reform key provisions of several federal laws that are critical for infrastructure development, namely, the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”), Clean Water Act (“CWA”), Endangered Species Act (“ESA”), Federal Power Act (“FPA”) and National Historic Preservation Act (“NHPA”). BAAJA is poised to make meaningful changes to the legislative framework related to project development and, in so doing, reshape how federal agencies evaluate and approve projects.

Introduced by a bipartisan coalition of four senators on September 30, 2026, BAAJA marks the culmination of a decades-long effort to reform the federal environmental review and permitting processes. According to the bill’s sponsors, BAAJA will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.[2] On the environmental review and permitting front, the bill’s NEPA amendments would set one- or two-year deadlines for environmental reviews and deadlines for the permitting decisions that follow. The amendments would also limit the alternatives agencies must consider to those that meet both the project’s purpose and need and the non-Federal sponsor’s goals, while retaining the option of taking no action. The bill would also extend maximum CWA permit terms from five to 10 years, shorten the ordinary ESA consultation period from 90 to 60 days, and narrow the activities and effects subject to historic-preservation review. These changes are expected to make development schedules far more predictable.

How BAAJA Could Accelerate Energy Infrastructure Development

For energy infrastructure, BAAJA would facilitate grid expansion and modernization. The bill would expand the permitting authority of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) over qualifying interstate transmission facilities and strengthen coordinated transmission and generation-interconnection planning. Additionally, certain grid upgrades and natural gas pipeline improvements within existing corridors would be exempt from NEPA and NHPA review.

Data Centers: New Rules for Power Costs, Grid Interconnection and Financial Assurance

For data centers, BAAJA would place greater emphasis on infrastructure-cost responsibility. The bill would direct FERC to revise transmission-pricing policies to reflect embedded costs and a reasonable assessment of incremental costs, while prohibiting utilities from shifting retail incremental costs to other customers. For newly interconnecting data centers, utilities would require financial assurances or contributions before building necessary infrastructure, and service arrangements would provide for continued cost recovery even if the customer exits. The bill also recognizes the authority of states to condition service on procuring new generation or accepting limits on grid withdrawals, while generally preserving previously approved arrangements. For developers and investors, these provisions would make power procurement, financial security, and infrastructure-cost allocation central diligence considerations.

Permitting Litigation: Shorter Deadlines and New Limits on Project Challenges

To bring more certainty as to whether an approval is final and non-appealable, which is critical to financing projects, BAAJA would also generally impose 150-day filing windows for specified challenges under NEPA, NHPA, CWA and ESA, with differing triggers and exceptions. This is a dramatic improvement from the existing six-year Administrative Procedure Act statute of limitations. For NEPA and NHPA violations, the ordinary remedy would be remand without vacating approvals or enjoining projects, while preserving preliminary relief for qualifying violations of other laws. Separately, the bill would give qualifying developers additional remedies for federal interference and intentional patterns of disparate treatment, alongside judicial enforcement of certain permitting deadlines. This would provide more stability for both renewable and non-renewable energy projects when administrations change.

What to Watch as BAAJA Moves to the House

Despite levels of bipartisan support, approval of BAAJA by the House is not guaranteed. While the future of BAAJA remains uncertain, the legislative efforts being undertaken show that Congress is taking active steps to improve the legal framework to allow for a more efficient delivery of much-needed infrastructure improvements.

Sheppard is closely monitoring BAAJA’s fate in the House. Stay tuned for updates examining the potential implications for renewable energy, fossil fuels, digital infrastructure and related industries if the bill passes.

FOOTNOTES

[1] Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA): Resource Hub, Bipartisan Pol’y Ctr. (Oct. 30, 2026), https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-baaja-resource-hub/.

text:
—

A federal court today denied the Trump administration’s second request to pause enforcement of Senate Bill 1137, California’s landmark oil and gas health buffer law, during its legal challenge. The court’s denial means the state’s 3,200-foot health protection zones between new oil drilling and communities, established by the law, will remain in effect while the lawsuit proceeds.

Today’s decision is consistent with the Bureau of Land Management’s own regulations, which say that operators must follow state laws that are more protective of the environment than federal laws.

“For the second time this year, the court has refused to let the Trump administration override California’s health protections so it can lease land next to homes, schools, and parks,” said Jeff Kuyper, executive director of Los Padres ForestWatch. “The BLM tried to invent an emergency out of a lease sale that no oil company asked for, and the court saw right through it. These buffer zones protect families and the public lands they love, and we’ll keep defending them for as long as this fight lasts.”

The BLM cited its planned Dec. 1 California oil and gas lease sale as evidence that the court needed to revisit its previous decision and quickly deny the injunction. Nineteen of the 43 parcels the BLM plans to lease in Kern, Kings, San Luis Obispo and Fresno counties are in health protection zones.

“The Trump administration tried to create a fake emergency to run roughshod over California’s health and environmental protections. Thankfully the court saw through this second attempt to block a critically important state law,” said Victoria Bogdan Tejeda, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute. “This charade is another example of the Trump administration jumping at the chance to make life easier for Big Oil and worse for everyday Americans.”

In January, Trump’s BLM sued California, claiming that federal laws override the state’s buffer law on federal land or leases. Enacted in 2022, S.B. 1137 prohibits new oil and gas drilling within 3,200 feet of homes, schools, hospitals and other sensitive places where science shows increased health and safety risks. The goal of the law is to improve public health by reducing exposure to pollution. The court denied the administration’s first preliminary injunction request in March.

Environmental groups have challenged this lease sale in a protest letter submitted to the BLM. The BLM’s own lease sale documents recognize the permitting authority of state regulators over oil and gas companies seeking federal leases, including a state’s ability to prohibit oil and gas activity near homes and other locations.

A coalition of advocacy groups joined the state in opposing this second preliminary injunction request, including Food & Water Watch, Friends of the Earth, Los Padres ForestWatch, and Sierra Club, represented by Earthjustice, and the Center for Biological Diversity representing itself.

In its first decision to preserve S.B. 1137 during the lawsuit, the court characterized the law as a “reasonable environmental regulation” with an “obvious and important purpose” of protecting people from adverse health effects that is backed by science. In denying the BLM’s second request for a preliminary injunction, the court found no basis for a new decision, calling the rehashed arguments “akin to a second bite at the apple.” The ruling noted that the court had previously considered the fact that the BLM would resume lease sales.

“Today’s ruling continues to show the Trump administration that it cannot bulldoze over a state’s policies simply because it disagrees with them,” said Hallie Templeton, legal director at Friends of the Earth. “California’s buffer zones are reasonable and clearly tied to protecting public health and safety. Whether Trump likes it or not, these issues should receive priority over Big Oil’s profit margins.”

“The millions of Californians who work and live near dangerous wells have shouldered the burden of unsafe air and water for far too long, and the Trump Administration’s repeated efforts to override these hard-won health protections is unconscionable,” said Tomás Rebecchi, organizing manager at Food & Water Watch. “We are pleased that the court once again allowed this vital, common-sense law that protects millions of Californians to remain in effect.”

“It is disheartening that the federal government continues to pander to the oil and gas industry over protecting public health,” said Elizabeth Fisher, an attorney at Earthjustice. “We hope the Trump administration will stop wasting taxpayer dollars on its anti-California crusade and leave the health protections that community members and the public fought hard to secure alone.”

California’s buffer law is based on a growing body of scientific evidence showing that close proximity to oil and gas activity likely causes a host of serious health and safety harms including adverse birth outcomes, respiratory illness, and higher rates of cancer.

text:
As American developers and manufacturers move closer to implementing broader supply practices around Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) restrictions, companies like Pantheon Electric are unveiling domestic supply plans for utilities and grid equipment makers to increase reliability.

The copper supplier is helping power providers get ahead of the FEOC order this month by securing U.S.-made copper components before the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) finalizes its nationwide bulk-power system security rules between late December and January 2027. The rules stem from Executive Order 14421, in which President Donald Trump declared a “national emergency” in August over security, foreign policy and economic risks from certain foreign actors “increasingly creating and exploiting vulnerabilities” in the U.S.

To ensure reliable electricity for the nation’s defense system, emergency services and other related infrastructure, critical resources such as copper have become increasingly vital amid the rapid growth of manufacturing, data centers and artificial intelligence. Without copper, traditional power plants could not function, and the electricity that travels from them to homes and businesses would not be produced.

But the federal ruling will bar access to grid equipment and critical components made by select foreign nations that include China, Russia, Iran and North Korea.

AI data center demand tests Pantheon’s merged copper hub for grid equipment

Currently, Pantheon Electric, one of North America’s largest copper component manufacturers, reportedly processes more than 1 million pounds of copper a day across 14 U.S. plants out of 21 globally. Pantheon supplies copper components to equipment and cable makers, including Schneider Electric, Eaton and Prysmian Group, among its base of more than 2,500 customers.

However, limiting these components to domestic supply to carry out this massive hyperscaler buildout alone is raising some industry concern about keeping pace. A next-gen hyperscale facility can reportedly consume 50,000 tons of the metal.

A Nov. 17 study by Johns Hopkins University researchers in Cell Reports Sustainability also indicates that data center transformers require more than four times as much copper compared to conventional ones. Researchers noted that this increased demand could trigger copper-driven grid equipment shortages as early as 2027.

“Whatever form the final rules take, utilities need a supply chain they can count on,” said Pantheon Electric CEO Gregory J. Smith in a statement. “As data centers push power demand higher, the grid can’t afford to depend on materials that swing with tariffs and global events. Copper made and sourced at home gives utilities one less thing outside their control.”

The U.S. grid today is growing faster than its supply chain. Utilities and manufacturers scramble to reinforce an already tight market amid S&P Global projections of a 10 million metric ton copper shortfall by 2040. Meanwhile, federal review of grid equipment sourcing brings the spotlight onto Pantheon’s domestic recycling and repurposing methods.

The company noted that it is on pace to hit $2 billion in revenue this year, as reported by Bloomberg earlier in the year, scaling its domestic operations to help secure copper supply for the U.S. power grid.

While EnergyTech covered the official unified manufacturing push in July, the private-equity merger of four companies, International Wire Group, Hussey Copper, EMS and Special Corde, launched Pantheon Electric as a company in January. It highlights the consolidation of a fragmented supply chain into a "single-sourced" hub for busbars, conductors and recycled scrap processing.

Pantheon Electric acts as a single commercial point of contact across its independent operating plants, which do not supply one another. The newly unified platform aligns with the DOE’s new $237 million Grid SCALED initiative, which aims to cut costs and bolster domestic energy reliability while keeping contracts away from FEOC suppliers.

Pantheon states it is working directly with utilities and the equipment makers to close the supply gap and secure the copper behind their grid upgrades while DOE rules are finalized.

Domestic copper scrap recycling aims to ease refining bottleneck

While the majority of this copper refinement has historically happened overseas, Pantheon Electric keeps component manufacturing stateside across plants in New York, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, South Carolina and Texas.

A third of Pantheon’s copper now comes from recycled scrap. This includes scrap from its factory floor, anchored by its Pennsylvania facility, which processes more than 100 million pounds of scrap a year into grid components.

text:
This story was originally published by Canary Media.

Mitch Hall and his wife, Lori, live in one of the most sustainable communities in the United States. Their town house is among a few dozen residences constructed so far at Veridian at County Farm, a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes here make about as much solar energy as they consume, with the help of batteries that save solar power for use in the evenings.

Now, the couple is eager to share the benefits of their clean energy infrastructure with the wider grid.

In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in Michigan’s first residential pilot of a virtual power plant; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy will then be able to remotely control the network of residents’ home batteries to inject their stored solar power onto the grid when operators need it most.

“This pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,” Joi Harris, president and chief executive officer of DTE Energy, said in a statement. VPPs can smooth out demand peaks, reducing the utility’s need to invest in grid-infrastructure upgrades and generate kilowatt-hours with expensive fossil-fuel peaker plants, both of which would pile costs on consumers.

The initiative ​“should work well for the residents, too,” Hall said. ​“DTE will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.” Because the utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and electricity prices are likely to be highest, ​“a neat part about the virtual power plant is you don’t have to spend a lot of time learning and trying to optimize,” he noted. ​“DTE will manage that battery for you.” (DTE did not respond to Canary Media’s request for exact figures on how much it would compensate customers in time for publication.)

VPPs have existed for years but have been slow to gain widespread traction because of a host of factors. Utilities often haven’t been incentivized to embrace the approach, while home solar and batteries remain too expensive for many households in the U.S. But as electrification and the data center rush spur unprecedented demand, VPPs are taking off as a fast way to get power on the grid. Earlier this month, the Brattle Group estimated that 524 gigawatts of distributed energy resources harnessed in VPPs could save households on average $122 per year by 2050.

Currently, ​“there’s immense untapped capacity,” said Kevin Brehm, manager in the carbon-free electricity practice at clean energy think tank RMI.

Matt Grocoff, the founder of Thrive Collaborative, started to consider a VPP pilot at Veridian in 2019. He wanted the neighbourhood to mimic an ecosystem—a resilient web of relationships in which individual organisms do more than just extract resources. For example, a tree in a forest turns sunlight into nutrients and shares them symbiotically with a vast, interconnected underground web of fungi.

Likewise, with a VPP, each Veridian home ​“can be producing energy that it needs and mutually beneficially sharing it across a network of energy rather than a linear grid that flows in only one direction,” Grocoff said.

DTE expects nearly 100 battery-equipped Veridian homes to ultimately participate in the pilot. So far, 44 market-rate homes with solar and batteries have been built, out of 120 planned, as have 50 affordable housing units that don’t have batteries yet, according to Thrive Collaborative. Battery manufacturer Sonnen USA, maker of the home storage systems installed at Veridian, is helping DTE operate the pilot using Sonnen’s proprietary software.

“Veridian is a test bed,” said Geoff Ferrell, executive vice president of Sonnen USA’s VPP business unit. The initiative, which is expected to be able to deliver up to about 300 kilowatts for three hours, will give DTE a clearer picture of how much power the home battery fleet can actually generate and when, providing ​“a really great basis” for a scaled-up program, he noted.

Ferrell points to another Sonnen-facilitated VPP that also sprang up as a humble pilot project, but rapidly mushroomed into a full-scale program because of early positive results. That initiative started in 2017 with a new apartment building topped with solar, Soleil Lofts outside Salt Lake City.

Sonnen hadn’t even finished installing batteries in each of the development’s 600 units when the utility Rocky Mountain Power and the state utility commission decided that the initial data was promising enough to merit extending the program to every residential customer in the utility’s territory, Ferrell said. Today, about 7,900 homes and businesses participate in the program, now called Wattsmart Battery, in Utah, Wyoming, and Idaho.

Given the success of that VPP and many others, Brehm would like to see more utilities go full throttle at the outset.

“Do you need another pilot?” he asked, noting that numerous VPP programs exist for utilities to model their own programs after.

But for utilities that do approach VPPs with caution, Rocky Mountain Power’s pilot is a good model, according to Brehm. The utility’s employees were able to rapidly understand how the residential battery fleet worked and how to deploy it, he said, ​“so that they could integrate these batteries into their operations initially, and subsequently [into their resource-capacity] planning.” He’d like to see DTE do the same.

The VPP pilot at Veridian is already starting to inspire developers and utilities outside Michigan, including the development Peace Hill in Townsend, Washington, said Grocoff of Thrive Collaborative.

“We’re getting calls from all over the country,” Grocoff said. ​“It’s really exciting.”

text:
After canceling a year of solar bidding, North Carolina regulators approved a Duke Energy plan that includes one of the nation's largest natural gas expansions.

Here's what to know

While the state still was projected to expand its solar generation in the coming years, the canceled year of solar bidding left over 1 gigawatt of planned solar capacity unprocured, according to Canary Media. Solar additions under the state's 2021 legislation would total 6.4 gigawatts following the Utilities Commission's rulings, including 2.3 gigawatts Duke Energy plans to add by 2034.

"We just completely skipped a year of solar procurement in the state," said Nick Jimenez, a senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center, which challenged the cancellation on behalf of three environmental organizations. "That's a huge missed opportunity in terms of bringing low-cost generation online in North Carolina."

Duke's approved long-term carbon reduction plan also included leaving expensive coal plants operating longer. Meanwhile, the commission refused requests to revisit its chair's decision to cancel the solar bidding.

More background

Under state law, Duke Energy must explain how it will reach zero carbon by 2050 in a plan it is required to update every two years. As part of the 2050 goal, Duke Energy was required to cut carbon pollution 70% by 2030, but North Carolina's Republican-led legislature removed that benchmark. Commissioners noted that change when citing a "reduced near-term need for solar" and arguing that tariffs were driving up the cost of solar, according to Canary Media.

Carson Harkrader, who develops solar projects and chairs the Carolinas Clean Energy Business Association, also raised concerns about solar costs. Harkrader, however, argued that the rising expenses meant the state should invest in solar now to head off future increases.

"We can no longer expect that the price of solar is going to go down every year," Harkrader said, per Canary Media. "So when solar procurements are pushed out, we lose the opportunity to lock in our prices as early as possible and deliver lower-priced solar energy for ratepayers."

For households facing rising electricity prices, rooftop solar panels are the most effective solution. Solar leases may offer savings of hundreds of dollars per month with no upfront costs.

What's being done?

The Southern Environmental Law Center appealed the cancellation on behalf of Vote Solar, the Sierra Club, and the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, according to Canary Media. Harkrader's trade group also challenged the decision. An expert testifying for the group urged the procurement of up to 1,200 megawatts of solar annually over two years, compared to Duke Energy's proposed 770.

Duke Energy, meanwhile, testified that procuring 2.3 gigawatts by the end of 2028 remained achievable. The commission gave the company 10 days to explain its approach, with spokesperson Bill Norton identifying Thanksgiving Day as the deadline for the update.

"The best ways that our companies can bring lower prices for consumers is through business certainty and clear annual procurements that we can plan towards," Harkrader said. "That helps us bring down costs because we know that our investments will lead to real projects, and that leads to more competition."

title: Recycled power is the new Normal for Rivian - Automotive Manufacturing Solutions
description:
Battery reuse Rivian is now capable of providing 10MWh of energy to the Normal plant with the energy storage system of repurposed batteries provided by Redwood.
The batteries deemed suitable for energy storage are integrated into the Redwood Energy system and supported by Redwood Pack Manager technology (see box).
Recycling for independence Batteries recovered that are not useful for battery storage are being recycled by Redwood Materials for their critical minerals.
Redwood’s Battery Materials Campus in Nevada, is the only calcining facility for battery recycling in North America.
This expanded partnership with Redwood Materials reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power.
text:
Rivian is advancing the circular economy of its plant in Normal, Illinois with its energy technology partner Redwood Materials by reusing end-of-life batteries for energy storage, as well as recycling batteries and production scrap. Redwood can recycle battery scrap generated at Rivian's manufacturing operations and recovering critical minerals such as lithium, nickel, cobalt and copper at rates exceeding 95%. It is helping Rivian to close the loop on the battery supply chain.

BASF takes a mass-balance approach to Toyota’s truck bed

Toyota’s Tacoma short-bed pickup is now fitted with a sustainable thermoplastic truck bed made from an innovative material from BASF

Rivian produced 19,751 vehicles at its Normal plant between January and the end of September this year. It currently makes the R1S, R1T and R2 crossover at the plant. The company ramped up production of the R2 in the third quarter and has raised its delivery guidance for 2026 to between 67,000-70,000 vehicles.

At the same time, it assembles the battery modules on site at Normal with battery cells supplied by Samsung SDI in South Korea for the R1S and R1T, and from LG Energy Solution in Queen Creek, Arizona for the R2.

Currently, Rivian is already using renewable energy sources to support energy demand at Normal, and thanks to the expanded collaboration with Redwood Materials, it is supporting this with energy from vehicle batteries recovered for storage.

Battery reuse

Rivian is now capable of providing 10MWh of energy to the Normal plant with the energy storage system of repurposed batteries provided by Redwood. The system comprises of 100 former R1 battery packs, mostly sourced from Rivian’s engineering test fleet. They are being used to reduce peak energy costs and relieve the strain on the local energy grid.

"Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials," according to JB Straubel, founder and CEO of Redwood Materials. In a statement last month, he said his company’s ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries was an opportunity to enable fast, flexible and more cost-efficient energy storage. “As the demand and cost for energy keeps rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges,” he said in October.

Redwood is collecting used Rivian EV battery packs that are no longer suitable for in-vehicle use. It evaluates each battery pack to determine best use case – whether to repurpose it for energy storage at the Normal plant or to recycle it. The company is collecting the batteries through three channels. The first is from what Rivian calls manufacturing fallout – batteries from the production process that cannot be used in vehicles yet remain ideal for second-life stationary energy storage. Secondly, it is recovering batteries directly from Rivian’s service network that are no longer suitable for EV remanufacturing. Finally, it is looking to end-of-life vehicle recovery, where packs are salvaged post-vehicle retirement that retain adequate state-of-health for repurposed stationary storage uses.

The batteries deemed suitable for energy storage are integrated into the Redwood Energy system and supported by Redwood Pack Manager technology (see box). The system is scalable and enables faster, more flexible deployment of energy capacity directly where demand is high, according to Redwood. Rivian’s CEO RJ Scaringe has previously stated that, as the company’s energy needs grow, it will need an energy grid that is flexible, secure and affordable.

“The project will help avoid an estimated 600+ metric tons CO2e each year by reducing load during peak events, times when the grid is typically run on fossil fuel peaking generators,” confirms a spokesperson for Rivian.

Charge down on production

The battery system is helping control high energy costs in manufacturing at the Normal plant by lowering operational expenditure. “By lowering Rivian's electricity demand during periods of high grid stress, the battery energy storage system assists in managing and minimising our demand charges,” adds Rivian’s spokesperson.

72% have Circularity targets. Only 20% have closed the loop

As assembly lines evolve into closed-loop ecosystems, vehicle manufacturers across Europe are redefining sustainability through advanced recycling, low-carbon steel adoption and radical factory overhauls.

During periods of low demand or when low-cost renewable energy is most productive, the packs can store electricity for easy dispatch during periods of higher demand. According to Redwood, when paired with Rivian EV battery packs, Redwood's proprietary technology architecture offers an integrated system that can respond intelligently to the needs of the facility it is serving.

Rivian says that saving a few dollars in cost of goods sold represents a significant achievement in automotive manufacturing.

“A key differentiator of Redwood's proprietary pack manager technology is its capability to blend diverse battery chemistries and makes into a single, cohesive stationary storage system,” says the spokesperson.

That stimulates the development of a circular, domestic supply chain for battery materials in the US, something of note given the anticipated energy demands over the next five years. Redwood Materials cites estimates that more than 600 GWh of energy storage will be needed to meet demand by 2030, as well as stabilise peaks and power technology innovation as time goes on.

Recycling for independence

Batteries recovered that are not useful for battery storage are being recycled by Redwood Materials for their critical minerals. “Once a battery has truly exhausted its useful life, it enters a third phase that further secures American energy independence,” says Rivian’s spokesperson. As mentioned, through advanced recycling, critical minerals such as lithium, nickel, cobalt and copper can be recovered at rates exceeding 95%.

The company’s proprietary hydrometallurgy process purifies the recovered materials into intermediates – partially processed materials – or converts them into chemicals to produce high-grade cathode-active materials to minimise environmental impact and bolster domestic supply.

Redwood Materials is also recycling battery scrap produced from Rivian's manufacturing operations. Using battery scrap for remanufacturing involves strict technical, economic, safety and regulatory requirements. Rivian says that working with Redwood it has developed visual and functional inspections, as well other technical criteria, including ISO standards, to ensure the packs can be used effectively.

Digital product passports move from compliance to production tool

The Digital Product Passport is intended to ensure transparency, sustainability and quality throughout the entire vehicle life cycle. Will the DPP become a gamechanger for quality, warranty and remanufacturing or a bureaucratic monster?

Redwood’s Battery Materials Campus in Nevada, is the only calcining facility for battery recycling in North America. Calcination is a controlled thermal process that heats battery materials (or black mass) below their melting point. The process drives off volatile components, burns or vaporises organic binders and electrolytes, and prepares metals or active materials for recovery. According to Redwood, it is used for processing all types of live battery feedstocks efficiently and enables it to handle live battery cells, consumer electronics, and electric vehicle modules. The Nevada campus can process over 40,000 metric tons (about 15-20 GWh) annually.

R2 recycled interior

Looking beyond the repurposing or recycling of batteries and the recycling of manufacturing scrap, Rivian is looking more extensively into what goes into its vehicles, as well as what comes out.

“R2 reached a milestone with 25% of its materials coming from recycled or bio-based sources,” says Rivian’s spokesperson. “This required developing supply chains for many different materials, including those for steel, aluminium and polymers.”

Rivian is sourcing over 550kg of recycled and bio-based materials in every vehicle. Among the recycled materials in the R2 are interior textiles using Nordic paper-industry waste and floor mats made from 99% ocean waste. The frunk and trim are 85% post-consumer recycled material, and the resin cell trays are 100% recycled.

This expanded partnership with Redwood Materials reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power. Rivian says that as grid connections take years to secure and the supply of conventional infrastructure remains constrained, companies are increasingly looking for partners who can recover materials, manage recycling and rollout battery storage as a single system. Rivian says its work with Redwood is a model for that approach – a partnership spanning the full lifecycle of a battery.

text:
A new study from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) finds that the expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence (AI) has had substantial negative health and air quality impacts — not just in the areas where most of these centers are being built, but also in regions far away from them.

As a result, hundreds of people across the U.S. are dying annually, the study suggests, with researchers finding that pollution from electricity demands of data centers resulted in around 650 premature deaths in 2023 alone. Considering the rapid expansion of data centers since that time, the number could be even higher.

“States hosting the largest data center loads do not necessarily experience the highest attributable mortality rates, while some states with little data center demand bear substantial burdens,” a summary of the study states.

Researchers compared electricity that was generated from areas with data centers and those without them. They then modeled the electrical output increase due to data centers in both areas, monitoring air pollution rates in various areas of the country.

Because the U.S. grid is interconnected, data center electricity demand is more spread out than many people realize. Different types of power plants also emit different amounts of pollution. So, while more data centers are being constructed in states like Virginia and Texas, Midwestern states, including Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas, are seeing higher per capita rates of death as a result of pollution from data centers.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors,” said Noelle Selin, senior author of the study. “But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region.”

“Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” Selin added.

In their findings for 2023, researchers found that data centers likely accounted for 513 premature deaths from fine particulate matter, while 137 deaths were associated with increases in ozone or fog that the data centers helped to create.

A separate study published earlier this month also demonstrated the enormous output of electricity — and pollution — due to the explosive growth of data centers in the U.S.

In that Harvard-based study, it was determined that data centers across the country emitted a total of 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year. That number is equivalent to the output of some countries, including Bolivia and Denmark.

Much of the research amounted to “detective work,” the authors of the study said, due to lax federal requirements on public disclosure.

title: Inside Toyota's New Forklift Factory - Assembly Magazine
description:
Electric forklifts, tuggers and other devices are in big demand in factories, warehouses and distribution centers.
One of the companies leading the charge to electric forklifts is Toyota Material Handling North America (TMHNA).

text:
Electrification is transforming airplanes, boats, buses, cars, motorcycles, tractors, trucks and other forms of transportation. The material handling industry has also been adopting battery-powered vehicles. Electric forklifts, tuggers and other devices are in big demand in factories, warehouses and distribution centers.

Many companies are transitioning away from gas, diesel and propane-powered material handling equipment toward electric alternatives. In fact, some projections predict the market for environmentally friendly products will grow more than 12 percent annually between now and 2033.

The transition is fueled by stricter emissions standards, rising fossil fuel costs and an increasing commitment to sustainability. Forklifts equipped with lithium-ion batteries offer numerous advantages, including reduced maintenance and longer operational cycles.

Electric models also enhance safety and precision with features like smooth acceleration, optimized torque control, reduced exhaust emissions and quieter operation indoors.

One of the companies leading the charge to electric forklifts is Toyota Material Handling North America (TMHNA). It recently opened a state-of-the-art factory in Columbus, IN, devoted to battery-powered equipment.

The 295,000-square-foot facility is located just north of the company’s 36-year-old flagship factory along I-65, a busy thoroughfare that links Indianapolis and Louisville. The new plant expands TMHNA’s local footprint to 1.9 million square feet.

“Electric forklifts make up 65 percent of the North American market and this trend toward electrification in the material handling industry will continue to grow,” says Brett Wood, president and CEO of TMHNA and senior executive officer at parent company Toyota Industries Corp. (TICO).

He sees no end in sight for continued growth. In fact, within the next decade, electric models are expected to account for up to 80 percent of the forklift market.

“We hope this announcement shows our customers that we are a proactive company, not a reactive one,” explains Wood. “We do not just plan for next week or next year. We’re preparing for the next decade, and this new initiative perfectly represents our commitment to that strategy.”

“We are excited about this significant strategic expansion to our Columbus campus,” adds Tony Miller, senior vice president of engineering, operations and strategic planning at TMHNA. “At Toyota, we will always be driven by what is best for our customers.

“Electric products are more popular than ever, and we are committed to doing whatever it takes to keep up with increased demand,” claims Miller. “This new factory will allow us to deliver those electric units to customers faster than we can today.

“We made a decision to do some things differently than in the older facility,” Miller points out. “For instance, the flow in the new plant is very simple and easy to follow.

“The building is expandable to the north, south and east, because we don’t want to repeat the same kind of growth challenges that we have experienced in the older factory,” says Miller. “If we need to expand welding, for instance, we’ll build an addition on the south side.”

The new $100 million factory has several other unique design features. For instance, the roof can accommodate multiple solar panels. The electrical infrastructure is also designed to use battery packs for energy storage and can be easily tied into switchgear.

Hoosier Roots Run Deep

TICO has a long heritage and traces its roots back to 1926, when it was established to manufacture an automatic loom invented by Sakichi Toyoda. It branched into automobiles in the mid-1930s. Today, TICO is part of the Toyota Group, which includes the Toyota Motor Corp.

Toyota has been active in the material handling industry for 70 years. Its first lift truck was built in 1956, followed by a tow tractor in 1957. Ten years later, Toyota sold its first forklift in the United States.

The company opened a state-of-the-art assembly plant in Columbus in 1990. It was expanded 14 times over the next 20 years to keep up with growing demand.

Along the way, the company focused on just-in-time delivery and waste elimination as it implemented key principles of the Toyota Production System, such as heijunka, jidoka, kaizen, kanban and poka yoke. It’s one reason why TMHNA excels at quality and continues to rank No. 1 in a competitive industry.

Today, the facility, which is referred to as Plant 1, encompasses more than 1 million square feet and recently produced its 750,000th vehicle.

The high-mix, high-volume factory assembles a wide range of industrial equipment, including three- and four-wheel lift trucks with various capacities. Options include battery-, diesel-, gasoline- and compressed natural gas-powered drivetrains. The factory typically builds more than 160 vehicles a day and exports to 20 countries.

Just about every machine moving down the assembly line features a different configuration. Products vary by engine size, lifting capacity, maximum lift speed and turning radius. Lifting capacity determines the type of mast and counterweights that are used on each product. For instance, two-, three- and four-rail masts are available.

Other variables include various front and rear axles, fuel tanks, hydraulic cylinders and transmissions. More than 12 different varieties of seats that can be installed in any vehicle. And, depending on the application, forklifts are equipped with either solid rubber, cushion or pneumatic tires.

The vertically integrated plant builds a wide variety of subassemblies internally, such as front and rear axles, fuel tanks, hydraulic cylinders and overhead guards, which vary from vehicle to vehicle.

Toyota acquired the Raymond Corp. in 2001, but operated it as a separate subsidiary under the TICO umbrella for 24 years. Both operations were integrated in 2025 when TMHNA was formed. While the brands share flexible assembly plants in Columbus, IN, and Greene, NY, each maintains a separate identity and dealer network in the marketplace.

Electrified Products

Toyota unveiled its first electric forklift, the 7FBEU, in 2003. Since then, it has continued to innovate and develop new products. In fact, the company shocked the material handling world in 2021 by launching 22 electric models.

Today, it offers more than 80 products powered by either lithium-ion or thin-plate pure lead batteries, which also act as counterweights. The lineup includes both three- and four-wheel configurations, with payload capacities range from 3,000 to 17,500 pounds.

Beyond sit-down and stand-up rider forklifts, Toyota also offers electric reach trucks, order pickers, electric pallet jacks, walkie stackers, tow tractors and automated guided vehicles (AGVs).

According to Miller, battery-powered forklifts are less complex that traditional gas- or propane-powered machines. “That’s because there’s no transmission and there’s just an electric motor mounted to a relatively simple gearbox,” he explains. “There is no drivetrain connection between wheels, so that entire axle assemble is eliminated. It is a significantly simpler product to build.”

Advanced AC drive and lift motor systems deliver energy efficiency, while providing responsive acceleration and supporting precise load control. Energy efficiency is also a core outcome of regenerative plugging, which returns energy to the battery, increasing runtime.

Many of TMHNA’s electric models feature the company’s new 5/35 lithium-ion batteries. The devices are available in multiple configurations, including 24-, 36- and 48-volt power capacities, to fit various customer needs and enhance operational productivity. Batteries are made at the company’s two-year-old Energy Solutions Center of Excellence in Kirkwood, NY.

The new assembly plant in Columbus currently produces electric Class 1 stand-up counterbalanced forklifts, which until recently were only built at Raymond’s state-of-the-art factory in Greene.

“However, in the future, additional products will be added to the mix, such as three-wheel sit-down models,” says Miller. “The move will enable Raymond to focus on other material handling devices, such as order pickers and reach trucks.”

Unlike traditional sit-down forklifts, stand-up models typically use padded backrests and lean pads rather than seats. They offer several advantages, including better line-of-sight vision for drivers and enhanced maneuverability in tight indoor spaces. Their compact footprint, with three- and four-stage mast options and a lift height of 270 inches, navigates narrow aisles easily.

Lean Plant Layout

The new TMHNA plant will enable the company to leverage cutting-edge manufacturing processes to produce electric products much more quickly. The facility is laid out to maximize efficiency, while addressing ergonomics, flexibility, lean manufacturing, productivity and safety. For example, the entire facility is climate controlled.

All weld fumes in the fabrication department are confined to each weld gun source. There’s also a solid wall to contain any weld smoke that escapes and prevent it from reaching other parts of the factory.

Electric forklifts are built to order, based on unique customer needs. They are assembled on AGVs at workstations equipped with digital work instructions.

“The AGVs are height adjustable, because our goal is to not lift anything with cranes,” explains Miller. “We minimized the use of cranes and hoists in the factory through a variety of lift-assist devices.

“Unlike Plant 1, where we primarily use paper work-instructions, instructions are integrated digitally into each operator’s work process at the new facility,” says Miller. “When a lift truck is ready to enter a production area, the person at the first workstation selects the next unit from an electronic schedule fed by the plant’s manufacturing execution system (MES) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) system.

“Based on each product’s bill of materials, the systems provide configuration-specific instructions to the assembler,” explains Miller. “The MES also indexes critical process information down the line so that equipment parameters can be adjusted for each truck at each stage of production.

“It records data such as torque results, component serial numbers, equipment faults and problems identified during the assembly process,” Miller points out. “We use this data to support continuous improvement efforts and help prevent issues from recurring.

“Nearly all of our fastening tools are electric, with pneumatic tools used only for a small number of high-torque applications,” says Miller. “During the line-design process, we identified joints that are critical to the safety or functionality of the lift truck.

“For those joints, we incorporate torque monitoring and poka yoke error-proofing controls to help ensure that each fastening operation is completed to specification within the process,” explains Miller. “This monitoring is tied to the assembly line through our MES. The line will stop if the torque requirements are not met within the takt time.

“We have used Atlas Copco tools successfully for critical joints in Plant 1 for many years,” adds Miller. “However, for the new plant, we chose Desoutter transducerized battery tools because they have a lower reaction force and improved ergonomics. In addition, we continue to use battery-powered Makita tools for noncritical fastening applications.”

Most fastening tools are attached to balancers to improve ergonomics and counter the downside of performing repetitive tasks. “They’re mounted from the top down on movable rails so that as processes change or production volumes increase, we can easily move lift-assist devices from workstation to workstation,” notes Miller.

Sequential Parts Delivery

Many parts are delivered in sequence to the assembly line, which is balanced based on workload. Products that require a specific option or configurations requiring higher labor content are spaced in between to level the amount of work and not overburden operators.

Subassembly processes are grouped in a common area, which enables operators to support one or multiple processes depending on the amount of work required for each task.

“This layout allows us to adjust staffing more efficiently as capacity requirements change, while also minimizing the amount of walking between subassembly stations,” says Miller. “We eventually plan to use an autonomous mobile robot to deliver kits from the subassembly area to line-side workstations.”

The plant currently uses a CB18 automated guided forklift from Toyota Automated Logistics to move the overhead guards and frames from welding through paint and into assembly.

“Most of our other AGVs move loads either by pulling them or by carrying them on top of a load-handling frame,” explains Miller. “Because the CB18 can pick up, lift, transport and lower the load itself, it requires less auxiliary material-handling equipment.”

The mast assembly line uses two conveyor systems that work together. The first provides stationary work positions for the initial three processes, which supports the safe assembly and shimming of the mast sections. The remaining nine processes use continuous motion to maintain a consistent production flow.

“Designed and built by Toyota Automated Logistics, the system combines the safety benefits of stationary work with the efficiency of continuous movement,” says Miller. “It also includes multiple fail-safe features to ensure that the two conveyors operate in unison and maintain consistent flow.

“The mast and lift-truck assembly lines are coordinated through our MES and ERP systems,” Miller points out. “The mast line feeds three different truck assembly lines—one in the new factory and two in the older, main plant. The MES and ERP connection helps us maintain the planned level of work-in-process inventory between the lines.”

While various levels of automation are used throughout in the factory, only a handful of six-axis robots are currently in operation. For instance, the majority of each frame is robotically welded. There are two cells in the fabrication department, with three robots in each cell.

“In the near future, we plan to robotically weld the mast,” says Miller. “We also use robots in our paint shop to powder coat the frame.

“Welding is an excellent application for robotics,” notes Miller. “Over the next decade, demand for welders will continue to outpace supply and we are focused on overcoming this challenge with robotics.

“However, much of the type of assembly tasks we do in our factories is very difficult to automate,” explains Miller. “The conveyor is constantly indexing forward, so the location is not as repeatable as welding. Some smaller subassembly processes can be automated in fixed positions, and we focus our automation efforts on assembly elements that are ergonomically challenging for humans.

“We believe that humans are inherently very good at complex and detail-oriented work,” says Miller. “Assembly of a truck moving down an assembly line is complicated and detail-oriented work. The other challenge we are faced with is that 70 percent of our production includes a special design. This introduces a very high level of variability where automation is not effective.”

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Late last month, Ford confirmed that its midsize electric pickup, Fathom, will be able to deliver more than 10 kW of alternating-current power to a home when it hits the market next year.

Though it’s the sort of technical detail that may be lost on drivers more concerned with sticker price, styling or battery range, experts say it’s potentially game-changing for utilities hoping to harness the vast quantities of energy stored in hundreds of thousands of bidirectional-capable EVs on U.S. roads.

Drivers of EVs that can discharge AC power don’t need to install pricey, code-sensitive inverter equipment to back up their homes or send power back into the grid, said David Almeida, director of clean energy transportation at Pacific Gas & Electric Co. A Ford spokesperson told Utility Dive that the automaker’s pre-Fathom vehicle-to-home backup package retails for more than $5,000, not including professional installation. The Fathom’s package will cost up to about 60% less, they said.

“You take that cost from the customer [and reduce the] complexity of installation, and you make it a lot easier for them to take this option and … for the utility to tap into that,” Almeida said.

More accessible equipment is not the only precondition for bidirectional-capable EVs to realize their full potential, however. Utilities, regulators and automakers will also need to coordinate on enabling regulation, utility program design, product development and customer education, experts tell Utility Dive.

High cost holds back bidirectional charging, for now

Automakers sell more than 20 bidirectional-capable light-duty EV models in the United States. Nearly all are “grid-parallel,” meaning they have the technical capability to both back up a home and export power to the grid, said Zach Woogen, executive director of the Vehicle-Grid Integration Council.

Some of these can be described as mass-market rides. The Chevrolet Equinox EV’s base trim retails for just over $35,000, about $16,000 less than the average cost of a new vehicle in 2026.

But nearly all require external inverters to convert their batteries’ direct-current power to AC flows that homes can use, Almeida said. Before this fall, the slow-selling Tesla Cybertruck — with a sticker price north of $80,000 — was the only AC-capable bidirectional EV on U.S. roads. Tesla began accepting orders in October for AC-capable versions of its more affordable Model 3 and Y vehicles, but drivers will still need a Powerwall home backup battery at an installed cost of around $12,000.

Low AC-capable vehicle stock is one reason why PG&E, which has more EVs than any other U.S. utility in its Northern California territory and aims to support 2 million bidirectional-capable vehicles by 2030, has seen limited uptake so far for its vehicle-to-everything program, Almeida said.

“We are still in the hundreds” of enrolled vehicles, including commercial vans, trucks and buses, he said.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

PG&E provides up to $3,000 in upfront incentives for eligible residential customers to install bidirectional charging equipment at home, thousands less than the full cost of a DC-to-AC conversion package with installation.

Another reason is that, cost aside, installing a home DC-to-AC inverter is not as simple as mounting and wiring a new light fixture.

Some inverter models “take up quite a bit of space on the wall” and, at least in PG&E’s territory, must meet building codes requiring minimum setbacks from a home’s gas meter, Almeida said. That gives a homeowner with a tight garage or carport the difficult choice of moving their gas meter — if that’s even possible — or forgoing vehicle-to-home capability, he said.

“It’s not just that it’s costly,” Almeida said. “Any time you add more complexity, it’s going to make it that much less likely that the customer is going to do it.”

While disclaiming inside knowledge of automakers’ plans, Almeida said Tesla’s and Ford’s recent moves suggest other automakers are working on designs for AC-capable vehicles. New car designs can take five years or longer to move from concept to showroom, he said.

Ford and Tesla offer “a good signal of what the market is going to be,” he said. “I’d imagine that … other major automakers have [onboard AC capabilities] in the plan and they’re just not ready to share with us.”

At Ford’s invitation, PG&E in July teamed up with American Electric Power, BC Hydro, Consumers Energy and Exelon to develop what Dave McCreadie, Ford’s director of energy and grid services, called “scalable interconnection processes” ahead of Fathom’s 2027 release.

Read More in Building & Transportation Electrification

In an October blog post, McCreadie said the five utilities aligned on three key principles: clarifying when interconnection regulations should apply to bidirectional EVs, and specifically to require interconnection only for customers operating a vehicle in parallel with the grid rather than for charging or “isolated backup power;” updating interconnection procedures and/or regulations to accommodate newer standards, such as AC-capable vehicles; and maintaining collaboration between utilities, regulators and equipment manufacturers to reduce barriers to interconnection.

The working group was “a head start” for electric utilities in places where it expects the Fathom to sell well, Almeida said. After the midsize truck arrives, “it’s totally possible that we will see thousands of vehicles that have this kind of capability” on PG&E’s system, he added.

“We’ve been kind of in the ‘crawl’ stage. In the next year or two we’re going to be in the ‘walk’ stage before we run,” he said.

Bidirectional EVs can be worth a lot — to utilities and consumers

Bidirectional charging is one component of a portfolio of distributed resources that PG&E, with encouragement from state regulators, can use to get more value from an increasingly constrained grid, Almeida said.

“How can we tap into this technology to mitigate the need for us to build infrastructure to help save all of our customers money,” he said, paraphrasing a question PG&E has kicked around internally and in regulatory filings for years.

Electric vehicles play into other PG&E flexibility initiatives. Most customers participating in Flex Connect, its flexible interconnection program for larger distribution-connected loads, are commercial EV-charging sites, a PG&E manager responsible for the program told Utility Dive earlier this year. PG&E also serves more than 70 bidirectional-capable electric school buses in Oakland, California, which has one of the country’s biggest fleets today. It plans to add infrastructure for more than 230 electric buses over the next two years across three sites in San Francisco, a particularly constrained load pocket.

Utilities, regulators and state energy offices elsewhere see value in private and commercial EVs.

Read More in Building & Transportation Electrification

In New England, residential and business customers with enrolled thermostats or stationary batteries have for years taken advantage of the region’s ConnectedSolutions virtual power plant program, which pays battery owners upwards of $200/kW-year to participate in both traditional peak-shaving and more targeted local events. This year, the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center deployed dozens of fully subsidized bidirectional chargers to bring electric vehicles into the fold. One Highland Electric Fleets bus earned nearly $12,000 per summer in a two-year pilot earlier this decade, though “more like $6,000 per year is the norm” moving forward, company CEO Duncan McIntyre told Utility Dive.

Still, even after accounting for equipment installation costs, “that is not hard to make pencil — it is a lot of money if you’re able to show up” for called events, Woogen said.

Regional regulators keep upping the ante. Next month, the Connecticut Public Utilities Regulatory Authority is set to expand the state’s energy storage compensation framework to include commercial EV charging sites. The program would pay $325/kW-year for the first five years of enrollment and $175/kW-year for the next five.

The proposed decision would also clarify bidirectional EV interconnection standards, including for residential customers. But residential EVs aren’t yet eligible for demand-response compensation in Connecticut, highlighting the challenge of bringing regulation in line with technical capability, Woogen said.

In fact, only California and Maryland have adopted vehicle-to-grid interconnection standards for AC-capable EVs, according to Woogen’s group.

“In some cases, technology and customer interest are ahead of the market and regulatory capability to support [them]. That is the long pole in the tent — it’s very fragmented, and that tends to slow things down,” said Greg Guthridge, global power and utilities customer experience transformation leader for EY.

Program design will be key to uptake

That said, utilities and their partners may also need to work on “consumer interest” through education, incentives and innovative program design, Guthridge said. Recent EY market research found that only 18% of U.S. customers have an “immediate interest” in energy-flexibility services, a broad category that includes bidirectional EV charging, he said.

“We have a bit of a challenge here. … We need to convince consumers that there’s value. Either they don’t understand that or they’re not buying into [it] just yet,” Guthridge said.

EY’s research suggests customers will be more receptive to “packaged” bidirectional charging programs that meet certain criteria, Guthridge said.

One is financial benefit: generous compensation for participation, ideally with an upfront component so customers feel they’re benefiting early. Control over or at least visibility into a program is another. Customers want to understand what’s happening in their home — and in this case, to their vehicle — and be looped into the process, Guthridge said. They also want participation that isn’t inconvenient or otherwise detrimental to their lifestyle or business activities, he said.

For inspiration, utilities and their automaker partners can look to companies like Rheem, which sells water heaters that play a significant role in some utilities’ distributed resource portfolios and has a reputation for “working with the utility closely to allow a seamless, effortless adoption process,” Guthridge said.

In that light, Ford seems to be making a shrewd move to get key utility partners onboard before Fathom hits the road.
