title: US governors seek relief from 2027 biofuel mandates as biodiesel producers resume operations
description:
If the EPA approves the request and reduces the 2027 requirements, refiners and fuel importers would need fewer compliance credits.
The RFS is a federal programme that sets annual targets for the use of renewable fuels in the US transport sector.
Companies meet these obligations by purchasing and retiring Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs), which are tradable credits generated by qualifying renewable fuels.
In August, the EPA granted exemptions to small refineries for 2025, removing more renewable fuel obligations than initially projected.
The Renewable Fuels Association, however, has cited wholesale ethanol prices being lower than wholesale gasoline prices in opposing the state waiver requests.
text:
US biodiesel producers are bringing idle plants back into operation even as governors of Alabama and Louisiana have asked the federal government to ease biofuel blending requirements for 2027, raising uncertainty over future demand for renewable fuels, ResourceWise reported.

Alabama Governor Kay Ivey and Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry have asked the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to grant a partial waiver from the 2027 Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) volume requirements. They argue that the cost of complying with the mandates could increase fuel prices and cause serious economic harm in their states and across the southeastern United States.

If the EPA approves the request and reduces the 2027 requirements, refiners and fuel importers would need fewer compliance credits. This could weaken demand for biodiesel and renewable diesel at a time when producers are deciding whether to restart operations, increase output and purchase feedstock.

The RFS is a federal programme that sets annual targets for the use of renewable fuels in the US transport sector. The EPA converts these targets into percentage-based standards, which refiners and fuel importers use to calculate their individual Renewable Volume Obligations (RVOs) based on the volume of petrol and diesel they produce or import.

Companies meet these obligations by purchasing and retiring Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs), which are tradable credits generated by qualifying renewable fuels. Higher blending requirements generally increase demand for these credits and the fuels that generate them.

The EPA’s decision to increase the biomass-based diesel requirement for 2027 had provided a positive signal to biodiesel and renewable diesel producers by indicating that the market could absorb higher volumes.

However, the agency is also considering how to compensate for volumes removed from the programme through small refinery exemptions. In August, the EPA granted exemptions to small refineries for 2025, removing more renewable fuel obligations than initially projected.

In October, the agency proposed two options to make up for the shortfall: distributing the additional volume equally between 2026 and 2027, or assigning the entire volume to 2027. The decision will determine when refiners and importers will have to meet the additional credit requirements.

The governors’ petition seeks a waiver for fuel produced or consumed in Alabama and Louisiana, along with corresponding changes to the 2027 percentage standards. If the EPA reduces the national requirement, the move could offset some of the additional demand that the agency is considering restoring through the small refinery exemption reallocation.

To approve an economic hardship waiver, the EPA would have to determine that implementing the requirements would cause severe economic harm. The agency must also provide an opportunity for public comment before making its decision.

The impact of the biofuel requirements on retail fuel prices remains disputed. The governors argue that higher RIN compliance costs are passed on to consumers. The Renewable Fuels Association, however, has cited wholesale ethanol prices being lower than wholesale gasoline prices in opposing the state waiver requests.

The EPA’s decision on the waiver petition and its approach to reallocating exempted volumes will be important for the 2027 compliance market and demand prospects for US biodiesel and renewable diesel producers.

Regulatory Developments Strengthen the Battery Circular Economy Government regulations are becoming an important driver of the global EV battery recycling market.
Outlook: Building a Circular and Sustainable EV Battery Ecosystem The EV battery recycling market is expected to become an increasingly important part of the global electric mobility value chain.
text:
The rapid expansion of electric vehicle (EV) adoption worldwide is creating a significant opportunity for the battery recycling industry. As automakers increase electric vehicle production and battery manufacturers expand manufacturing capacity, the need for sustainable battery disposal, material recovery, and circular supply chains is becoming increasingly important.

According to Cervicorn Consulting, the global EV battery recycling market was valued at USD 5.73 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow from USD 7.56 billion in 2026 to approximately USD 92.16 billion by 2035, registering a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 32% during 2026–2035.

The market’s expansion is being supported by rising demand for lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese, increasing volumes of end-of-life electric vehicle batteries, and stricter government regulations concerning battery waste management. Technological advancements in hydrometallurgical processing, direct recycling, and battery material recovery are further strengthening the industry’s growth prospects.

Battery Recycling Becomes Critical to the Global EV Supply Chain

Electric vehicle batteries contain valuable materials that can be recovered and reused in the production of new battery cells. Recycling helps reduce dependence on virgin mineral extraction, improves resource efficiency, and supports the development of a circular battery economy.

As the global EV fleet expands, battery manufacturers and recyclers are increasingly focusing on recovering high-value materials from manufacturing scrap, damaged batteries, and retired EV battery packs.

Lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, and graphite are among the major materials targeted through recycling processes. Their recovery can help strengthen supply chain security while reducing the environmental impact associated with conventional mining and mineral processing.

Automotive OEMs, battery manufacturers, and recycling companies are also developing strategic partnerships to establish closed-loop recycling systems. These arrangements enable recovered materials to re-enter battery manufacturing, creating a more integrated and sustainable supply chain.

Advanced Recycling Technologies Transform Battery Material Recovery

Technological innovation is playing a major role in improving the efficiency, economics, and sustainability of EV battery recycling.

1. Hydrometallurgical Recycling

Hydrometallurgical recycling uses chemical solutions to extract valuable metals from used batteries. The process can achieve high recovery rates and produce materials with the purity required for battery manufacturing. Its relatively lower energy requirements compared with conventional high-temperature processing make it an important technology for the recycling industry.

2. Direct Battery Recycling

Direct recycling is gaining attention because it aims to preserve and restore the structure of battery cathode materials instead of completely breaking them down into individual metals. This approach can reduce material losses, energy consumption, and processing requirements.

The technology is particularly relevant for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, where recovering and restoring cathode functionality can improve recycling economics.

3. Pyrometallurgical Recycling

Pyrometallurgical recycling uses high-temperature processes to recover valuable metals from battery waste. It is an established recycling method, although energy consumption and the recovery of certain materials remain important considerations.

4. Mechanical Recycling

Mechanical recycling involves the physical dismantling, separation, crushing, and sorting of battery components. It is frequently used as an initial processing stage before advanced material recovery technologies are applied.

The development of automated dismantling, artificial intelligence based sorting, and digital battery tracking is expected to improve operational efficiency and worker safety.

Asia Pacific Dominates the EV Battery Recycling Market

Asia Pacific accounted for approximately 50% of global EV battery recycling market revenue in 2025, supported by its strong electric vehicle manufacturing ecosystem, battery production capacity, and growing investments in recycling infrastructure.

The regional market was valued at USD 2.87 billion in 2025 and is projected to exceed USD 46.08 billion by 2035.

China remains a major contributor due to its extensive EV production base, battery manufacturing capabilities, and regulatory focus on battery lifecycle management. The country’s battery recycling ecosystem is increasingly emphasizing traceability, material recovery, and integration between battery manufacturers and recyclers.

India is also emerging as an important market as electric mobility adoption increases and the country seeks to strengthen domestic access to critical battery materials.

India’s dependence on imported lithium, cobalt, nickel, and other battery minerals is creating opportunities for domestic recycling companies to recover valuable materials from manufacturing scrap and end-of-life batteries. Investments in hydrometallurgical processing, direct recycling, and battery-grade material refining can support the development of a stronger domestic battery supply chain.

North America Emerging as a High-Growth Recycling Market

North America is expected to experience significant growth during the forecast period, with the regional EV battery recycling market projected to increase from USD 1.09 billion in 2025 to approximately USD 17.51 billion by 2035.

The expansion of EV manufacturing, investments in battery gigafactories, government incentives, and increasing focus on domestic critical mineral supply chains are supporting regional growth.

The United States is witnessing growing collaboration between automotive manufacturers and battery recycling companies to establish closed-loop material recovery systems. Companies such as Redwood Materials, Li-Cycle, Cirba Solutions, and Ascend Elements are contributing to the development of the domestic battery recycling ecosystem.

These initiatives are intended to improve access to recovered lithium, nickel, cobalt, and other materials while reducing dependence on international mineral supply chains.

NMC and LFP Battery Chemistries Create Different Recycling Opportunities

By battery chemistry, lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) accounted for approximately 40% of the EV battery recycling market in 2025.

NMC batteries contain valuable nickel and cobalt, making material recovery economically attractive. Their use in electric vehicles requiring higher energy density and longer driving ranges is supporting demand for specialized recycling processes.

Meanwhile, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries are expected to witness rapid growth in recycling demand. Their increasing adoption in electric passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles, and energy storage applications is creating a future stream of recyclable battery materials.

Although LFP batteries do not contain the same quantities of high-value nickel and cobalt as NMC batteries, improvements in direct recycling and material recovery technologies are expected to strengthen their recycling economics.

Manufacturing Scrap Creates Immediate Recycling Opportunities

Battery manufacturing scrap represented approximately 60% of the EV battery recycling market by battery source in 2025.

The rapid expansion of battery manufacturing facilities is generating substantial quantities of production waste, including defective cells, electrode materials, and other manufacturing residues.

Unlike end-of-life EV batteries, manufacturing scrap can often be collected and processed through more predictable supply chains. Its relatively consistent composition and availability make it an attractive source of recyclable materials.

However, end-of-life EV batteries are expected to become an increasingly important growth segment as the number of electric vehicles reaching retirement increases over the coming years.

Second-Life Batteries Open New Business Opportunities

Battery recycling is not limited to recovering raw materials. Retired EV batteries can also create value through second-life applications.

Many EV batteries retain approximately 70%–80% of their original capacity when removed from vehicles, depending on their age, usage patterns, chemistry, and operating conditions.

After appropriate testing, grading, and safety assessment, these batteries may be repurposed for stationary energy storage applications, including renewable energy integration, commercial backup power, and grid-support systems.

Second-life battery applications can extend battery utilization before final material recovery, improving resource efficiency and creating additional business opportunities for battery manufacturers, energy storage developers, and recycling companies.

Regulatory Developments Strengthen the Battery Circular Economy

Government regulations are becoming an important driver of the global EV battery recycling market.

The European Union’s Battery Regulation establishes requirements relating to battery sustainability, collection, recycling efficiency, material recovery, and recycled content.

In India, the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, provide an extended producer responsibility framework for battery manufacturers and producers, supporting organized collection, recycling, and environmentally responsible battery disposal.

China is also strengthening battery lifecycle management and traceability requirements to improve the collection and recovery of used EV batteries.

These regulatory developments are encouraging automotive OEMs, battery manufacturers, and recycling companies to invest in compliant recycling infrastructure and sustainable material recovery technologies.

Leading Companies Strengthen Their Competitive Positions

The global EV battery recycling industry includes battery manufacturers, material technology companies, specialist recyclers, and resource recovery businesses.

Some of the prominent companies operating in the market include:

CATL

GEM Co., Ltd.

Umicore

Li-Cycle Corp.

Glencore

Attero Recycling

Redwood Materials

Cirba Solutions

Ecobat

LOHUM

These companies are focusing on recycling capacity expansion, advanced material recovery technologies, strategic partnerships, and closed-loop battery supply chains.

Competition is increasingly shaped by recovery efficiency, processing costs, access to battery feedstock, recovered material quality, and long-term agreements with automotive and battery manufacturers.

Challenges That Could Influence Market Expansion

Despite strong growth prospects, the EV battery recycling industry faces several operational and economic challenges.

The high capital investment required to establish advanced recycling facilities can limit market entry for smaller companies. Recycling economics are also influenced by fluctuations in lithium, nickel, and cobalt prices, which affect the commercial value of recovered materials.

Battery pack designs, cell formats, and chemistries vary across manufacturers, making automated dismantling and standardized recycling processes difficult.

Additionally, damaged or improperly handled lithium-ion batteries can create thermal runaway and fire risks during transportation, storage, and processing. Companies must therefore invest in specialized safety systems, battery discharge technologies, and trained personnel.

Outlook: Building a Circular and Sustainable EV Battery Ecosystem

The EV battery recycling market is expected to become an increasingly important part of the global electric mobility value chain. Rising EV adoption, expanding battery manufacturing capacity, growing demand for critical minerals, and stricter environmental regulations will create long-term opportunities for recycling technology developers and material recovery companies.

Advancements in direct recycling, hydrometallurgical processing, automated battery dismantling, and second-life battery applications are expected to reshape the competitive landscape.

For automotive OEMs, battery manufacturers, investors, and recycling companies, developing reliable access to recyclable battery materials and establishing closed-loop supply chains will become essential to long-term competitiveness.

text:
American car manufacturer Ford has begun delivering the first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells for the prototypes of its Fathom battery electric pickup truck, and has reported significant cost improvements in its first venture into the battery business.

Ford president David Carroll announced on November 19 that the company would branch out into battery manufacturing, and its first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery plant is up and running at BlueOval Battery Park in Michigan.

Batteries rolling off the production line are being delivered to Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant where they will be powering the prototypes of the Ford Fathom, the carmaker’s latest battery electric pickup that was announced in August which will be the first car to be built on its new Universal Electric Vehicle platform.

Ford is building the battery pack into the structure of the vehicle, designing it to serve as a structural component and using prismatic, or rectangular, cells because they fit directly into the chassis, helping to cut costs.

The milestone is an important one for Ford, following several years of false starts in the electric vehicle space, including the much hyped but ultimately unsuccessful Ford F-150 Lightning which was eventually scrapped at the end of 2025 as part of the company’s larger pivot away from EVs which forced it to take a massive $US19.5 billion hit to profits.

Driven in part by the unsettled environment of an America once again under the leadership of Donald Trump, Ford nevertheless maintained its battery manufacturing capabilities.

This included the BlueOval Battery Park Michigan facility where it is making its LFP prismatic battery cells based on technology licensed from Chinese battery manufacturing giant CATL, as well as at a facility in Kentucky, which it retained after the dissolution of its battery joint venture, BlueOval SK, with South Korean company SK On.

Billed as a “mile-long gigafactory with state-of-the-art advanced manufacturing technology,” the Kentucky facility is now the home for Ford Energy, the company’s new battery energy storage systems (BESS) manufacturing site.

Not only is the company delivering battery cells at a plant it owns and operates, then, but with the delivery of its first LFP prismatic cells, it becomes the first company in the United States to deliver LFP batteries for mainstream consumer automotive use.

The assembly lines at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it one of the fast LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China, helping to drive down battery costs.

With cells already being delivered for the Ford Fathom prototypes, the next step for BlueOval Battery Park Michigan is to have its battery pack plant operational next year ahead of the launch of the Ford Fathom.

Meanwhile, at the Louisville Assembly Plant, Ford has already produced more than 5,000 large aluminium unicastings for the Ford Fathom to support process testing and prototype assembly.

According to Ford, the Fathom will feature a pair of large unicastings that reduce mass by simplifying construction, reducing 146 structural parts to just two, while also improving overall energy efficiency.

As federal protections are rolled back, state governments are advancing climate policies, often linking emissions cuts to lower energy bills, greater reliability and job creation.

text:
The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) is currently taking place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9–20. Governments meeting under the UN climate framework will continue the lengthy discussion on how to advance global climate action and implement existing commitments, amid ever-growing climate disasters and the breaking of planetary limits.

The summit comes as the United States faces a widening divide between federal climate policy and state-level efforts to reduce emissions. At the same time, the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing is driving up electricity demand, raising questions about how the country can meet its energy needs while staying on track with climate goals.

Over the past decade, US greenhouse gas emissions averaged 6.59 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) equivalent annually from 2017 to 2019, during President Donald Trump’s first term, before falling to 5.98 billion tons in 2020, according to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The drop coincided with COVID-19’s effects on travel and economic activity. Under President Joe Biden, annual gross emissions were about 6.2–6.4 billion tons, peaking in 2022 before declining to 5.91 billion in 2024.

Since Trump returned to office, the federal government has used executive and legislative actions to hinder the energy transition and promote fossil fuel production and use. A preliminary estimate shows emissions rose 2.4% in 2025. The EPA’s 2025 inventory is not expected until 2027, reflecting the administration’s disregard for climate-policy disclosure. The EPA also revoked the Endangerment Finding, the legal basis for regulating greenhouse gases, and eliminated federal minimum emissions standards for power plants and automobiles.

A widening gap between Washington and the states

Both international and domestic action under the second Trump administration has shifted sharply, as the US federal government stepped back from the Paris Agreement and other federal commitments to renewable energy policies and financing. The move reversed Biden’s re-entry and echoed Trump’s decision during his first term.

The federal retreat has left states and cities to shoulder more of the climate-policy burden. The US Climate Alliance — a bipartisan coalition of 24 governors formed in response to the first withdrawal in 2017 — has become a prominent vehicle for state-level action. As federal protections are rolled back, state governments are advancing climate policies, often linking emissions cuts to lower energy bills, greater reliability and job creation.

The US Climate Alliance reports that its member states have reduced net greenhouse gas emissions by 24% below 2005 levels while growing their combined GDP by 34%. Illinois, for example, enacted a law to expand battery storage, helping stabilize electricity prices and support a cleaner grid. Massachusetts has announced plans to procure additional clean energy and storage, while New Jersey has expanded community solar, offering bill discounts to participating low-income households. In Washington, a new state authority will help plan and finance transmission infrastructure, and Virginia is advancing measures to expand solar, storage and virtual power plants.

States are also targeting emissions from transportation, buildings and industry. Texas is expanding its electric vehicle fast-charging network, while California and New York are considering rules to curb truck pollution linked to large warehouses. Maryland and Washington are weighing transportation plans that would account for greenhouse gas emissions and promote alternatives to highway expansion. In buildings, Maine has expanded heat-pump use to reduce reliance on heating oil, and Virginia is piloting programs to help households make energy-saving upgrades. Pennsylvania is directing grants toward industrial decarbonization, while Washington, California and other states are supporting cleaner manufacturing.

Many of these measures remain proposals or are still being implemented, but together they show how states are pursuing emissions reductions alongside economic and public-health benefits.

States seek a role at COP31

The federal government’s retreat and the technology sector’s rapid growth are shaping the US presence at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. The federal government has a limited role, focusing on monitoring discussions that affect US commercial interests rather than joining international climate-finance commitments.

Democratic members of Congress participate separately, along with state officials, positioning themselves through the US Climate Alliance, highlighting state and local climate action, and engaging with international partners; however, they cannot vote on behalf of the United States or sign treaties for the federal government.

The states’ alliance teams its efforts with America Is All In — the largest US subnational climate coalition — which unites states, cities, businesses and institutions representing 63% of the population and 74% of the country’s GDP.

Overall, according to Climate Action Tracker projections, US emissions could be about 14% lower by 2030 under pro-climate federal policies similar to those Biden considered in his last year in office. Among the top contributors to US emissions are the booming data center installations.

AI’s growing footprint: energy, water, copper and concrete

The rapid expansion of data centers for AI and cloud computing is making future energy and water use hard to predict. One concern is already clear: Facilities can be built faster than the power plants and transmission networks needed to serve them. Some have extended coal-plant operations or relied more on natural gas, while renewable projects face permitting and grid delays. It is a big issue. The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects that data centers could account for 11.8% of US electricity consumption by 2030.

Northern Virginia, one of the world’s largest data-center hubs, is already straining its power infrastructure. In response, states are considering or adopting a range of measures. New York has paused new data center projects pending environmental reviews; Texas has temporarily frozen new grid permits; and Colorado and Minnesota are requiring companies to secure new clean-energy supplies and limit drinking-water use for cooling. Georgia, Virginia and South Carolina have also changed electricity-rate rules to prevent households from bearing the cost of infrastructure built for major technology companies. Some of these measures include surcharges of up to 15% for technology firms.

Beyond energy issues, the expansion also carries a high cost. Data centers consume hundreds of thousands of tons of copper, which is becoming increasingly difficult to extract: the amount found in a ton of mined rock has fallen from about 50 kilograms to less than 10, and new mines can take more than two decades to become productive. The result could be a widening gap between demand and supply, along with greater environmental damage from mining.

Construction adds another burden, particularly through the concrete used to build these facilities. Solutions include AI-assisted concrete design, which could cut emissions by up to 40%, and companies developing lower-carbon or carbon-free cement. These advances are promising, but they do not address the central concern: Environmental impacts are already growing, while many remedies are still being tested.

Big Tech turns to nuclear power

Technology companies are seeking reliable, low-carbon electricity to meet the rising demand. Google has partnered with Kairos Power to support small modular reactors, with commercial deployment expected starting in 2030. Meta aims to secure up to 6.6 gigawatts of reliable, carbon-free power by 2035 through companies such as TerraPower and Oklo, and has supported efforts to keep Illinois’s Clinton nuclear plant open. Amazon acquired infrastructure tied to Pennsylvania’s Susquehanna nuclear plant to power its data centers. Microsoft backed a 20-year deal to restart Three Mile Island to supply its data centers. Nuclear power could ease supply shortages, but raises safety concerns.

Nuclear plants can be operated under stringent safety standards, but no reactor is risk-free. The key question is whether each new or remodeled plant meets its specific safety review, inspection, and operating requirements. The answer requires determining whether a permit or environmental finding constitutes approval to operate. Regulators must confirm that each plant is fit to operate despite pressure from a Big Tech company with a signed contract to buy its energy. Nuclear power avoids the air pollution and carbon emissions associated with fossil-fuel generation, but accident risks, radioactive waste, security, aging equipment and emergency preparedness still require oversight.

Water use becomes a central concern

African and Latin American countries, including Uruguay and Chile, are urging limits on using drinking water to cool AI infrastructure amid drought and water competition. The United Nations warns that, by 2030, global data centers could use as much water as the annual basic needs of 1.3 billion people in sub-Saharan Africa. It also cites a World Economic Forum estimate that a quarter of data centers already operate in areas under severe water stress.

Proposals would restrict aquifer and drinking-water use for evaporative cooling, favoring closed-loop air cooling or treated wastewater. Underwater data centers, inspired by Microsoft experiments, use seawater to cool servers and wind power for electricity. The source claims they can cut freshwater use by over 90% and energy use by more than 20%, but they account for little global data center energy use.

New and sustainable technologies are exciting, but AI (and cryptocurrency mining) follow a familiar Anthropocene pattern: Impacts arrive first, followed by efforts to contain them. The question is whether solutions can be deployed at the speed and scale required, or whether they will again come too late. Regulations, at the state, national or global level, always come after the damage.

Proposals to regulate data centers

Proposals to regulate data centers

Data centers are becoming part of international climate discussions; however, at a slower pace given their environmental impact. Proposals include energy-efficiency standards based on power usage effectiveness (PUE) and restrictions on using drinking water for evaporative cooling in water-scarce regions.

The emissions challenge is already substantial. A Harvard study of 403 large US data centers estimated that their electricity use produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 between May 2024 and April 2025, with more than half of their electricity coming from fossil fuels. The estimate relies on available data and modeling, underscoring a central problem: Companies’ limited disclosure makes it difficult to measure the sector’s footprint consistently. After all, there is no clear access to sustainability indicators for Big Tech’s fast-growing operations.

Other proposals would require companies to recycle servers, semiconductors and rare metals, reducing e-waste from frequently replaced equipment. Some policymakers have proposed carbon-pricing or cross-border measures that could affect high-emission digital services, but no such measure for data centers has been established as a COP31 negotiating proposal. Regulation may need to keep pace with the industry’s rapid growth.

The climate agenda at COP31 is late to the data centers issue. We are far from answering key questions, such as whether international rules will be cross-border and enforceable under US state and local laws, or remain voluntary. Voluntary targets risk weak annual reviews that encourage better practices without requiring emissions cuts. As UN Executive Secretary for Climate Change, Simon Stiell, put it, “Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now.” Credibility will depend on transparency, measurable reductions and, eventually, enforceable rules.

COP31’s best outcome

As the US climate debate is increasingly defined by a split between federal policy and state action, State governments are pushing ahead with clean-energy initiatives, but rising fossil-fuel production and the electricity needs of AI data centers are putting those gains under pressure. As international discussions turn to the energy and water demands of digital infrastructure, the challenge will be to align technological growth with climate targets and local resource limits.

The best outcome at COP31 would be practical safeguards for data centers, including clearer reporting of energy and water use, stronger efficiency standards and cleaner power for new facilities. Governments could also protect households from unfair grid costs and communities from water shortages. By aligning technological growth with climate goals, COP31 can encourage progress through cooperation among national and local governments, businesses and international partners.

COP31 cannot bridge Washington-state divides, but it can set shared expectations for technological growth to advance a cleaner, more reliable, equitable energy transition.

title: Farm Bureau Warns Farmers Could Lose Land Protections Under New Federal Transmission Rules
description:

The legislation would also allow federal permitting authority to come into play when a state fails to approve a qualifying transmission project within one year.
Farm Bureau recognizes permitting reforms but wants stronger protections Despite its objections to the transmission provisions, AFBF is not opposing permitting reform altogether.
That means the fight over private property rights and federal transmission authority is far from over.
As demand for electricity increases and the nation’s energy infrastructure expands, more transmission projects could mean more competition for agricultural land.
text:
A sweeping federal permitting reform package designed to accelerate energy and infrastructure development is drawing criticism from the American Farm Bureau Federation (AFBF), which warns that provisions involving high-voltage transmission lines could leave farmers and ranchers with insufficient protections when projects cross privately owned agricultural land.

The Senate’s failure to consider additional landowner protections in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) has left Farm Bureau leaders concerned about the potential expansion of federal authority to approve transmission projects and exercise eminent domain.

AFBF President Zippy Duvall acknowledged improvements in the legislation’s environmental review provisions but expressed disappointment that lawmakers did not address two significant concerns: federal backstop authority and the government’s ability to use eminent domain.

“We appreciate the improvements in environmental review reforms included in BAAJA, but we are disappointed the Senate did not take up additional amendments that would have addressed concerns farmers had about federal backstop authority and granting the government too much authority to use eminent domain,” Duvall said.

“These amendments, offered after careful consideration, presented an opportunity to strengthen protections for farmers and ranchers and would have provided greater certainty for the families and communities whose property could be affected by transmission development.”

Transmission provisions raise concern over farmland and eminent domain

At the center of Farm Bureau’s concerns is the bill’s proposed overhaul of federal electric transmission permitting, particularly changes to Section 216 of the Federal Power Act.

Historically, states have played the primary role in determining where transmission lines are built, with state utility commissions reviewing proposed routes and state laws governing the use of eminent domain.

BAAJA would significantly expand the federal government’s role by activating previously unused authority held by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).

Under the proposed changes, the federal backstop authority could apply to a much broader range of transmission projects, including lines operating at 230 kilovolts or higher. The legislation would also allow federal permitting authority to come into play when a state fails to approve a qualifying transmission project within one year.

For projects involving transmission lines of 345 kilovolts or greater, developers could submit applications to FERC and state regulators simultaneously.

AFBF argues that these changes could shift substantial decision-making authority away from state regulators and create new pathways for federal involvement in acquiring private farmland for transmission infrastructure.

The implications for agricultural operations extend well beyond the loss of a few acres.

Transmission-line construction can permanently remove productive ground from farming, compact soils, damage subsurface drainage tile and interfere with field access, livestock operations and future land improvements.

Easement agreements can also create restrictions that remain attached to a property when it is sold or inherited, potentially affecting generations of landowners.

Farm Bureau is particularly concerned that the legislation does not provide sufficient safeguards to ensure landowners receive adequate notice, compensation and opportunities to challenge proposed projects.

Although BAAJA establishes a 45-day public comment period and directs FERC to consider landowner feedback, AFBF says the legislation does not require direct written notification to individual landowners or provide assistance with legal representation and independent appraisal expenses.

The bill also would shorten the deadline for challenging environmental reviews in court to 150 days, compared with the current six-year period identified in Farm Bureau’s analysis.

For farmers whose property could be affected by a transmission project, those provisions raise questions about whether they will have sufficient time and resources to protect their property rights.

Farm Bureau recognizes permitting reforms but wants stronger protections

Despite its objections to the transmission provisions, AFBF is not opposing permitting reform altogether.

The organization recognizes that lengthy federal reviews and regulatory uncertainty can delay infrastructure investments, increase project costs and create obstacles for agricultural businesses.

The legislation includes several provisions Farm Bureau considers beneficial to agriculture.

Among them are changes to environmental review requirements that would exempt USDA farm loans and certain cost-share projects from historic preservation reviews. The legislation also extends the duration of certain Clean Water Act Section 404 permits from five years to 10 years.

However, Farm Bureau argues that lawmakers missed an opportunity to address additional regulatory concerns.

The organization has also called for reforms involving Waters of the United States (WOTUS) and greater clarity surrounding the Clean Water Act’s agricultural stormwater exemption.

In its analysis of the legislation, AFBF emphasized that Congress should build on the bill’s progress while ensuring permitting reform works for the farmers and ranchers whose land it affects.

Industry groups welcome Senate action

Farm Bureau’s concerns stand in contrast to the largely favorable response from several major agricultural and business organizations that support the broader permitting reforms.

The Association of Equipment Manufacturers and The Fertilizer Institute praised the legislation’s potential to accelerate infrastructure investments and reduce regulatory uncertainty.

The Association of Equipment Manufacturers welcomed the Senate’s action, arguing that a more predictable permitting system could help move infrastructure projects from planning to construction faster, unlock investment and strengthen America’s economic competitiveness.

For agricultural equipment manufacturers and their customers, the organization said infrastructure investment creates opportunities for growth, but permitting reform is necessary to turn those opportunities into results.

The Fertilizer Institute also endorsed the reforms, noting that fertilizer manufacturers depend on significant long-term investments in domestic production, transportation infrastructure and energy supplies.

The organization said streamlined permitting could help advance projects ranging from new mines to expanded nitrogen fertilizer manufacturing facilities while maintaining important environmental protections.

The differing perspectives underscore the challenge facing lawmakers: balancing the need for modern energy infrastructure and economic growth with the property rights of the farmers and ranchers whose land may be affected.

House consideration puts landowner protections back in focus

The Senate approved BAAJA on November 19 by a 62-33 vote, sending the legislation to the U.S. House of Representatives for consideration. The Senate’s action came without adoption of the additional landowner-protection amendments Farm Bureau had sought.

That means the fight over private property rights and federal transmission authority is far from over.

AFBF President Duvall said the organization intends to continue working with lawmakers as Congress tackles its remaining priorities before the end of the year.

“Protecting private property rights and ensuring farmers and landowners have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their property must remain at the forefront as Congress moves forward on its end-of-year priorities,” Duvall said.

He also identified three other major agricultural priorities requiring congressional attention: completing a farm bill, securing year-round E15 availability and delivering additional economic assistance to farmers.

For agricultural producers, the permitting debate carries implications that reach well beyond Washington’s regulatory process.

As demand for electricity increases and the nation’s energy infrastructure expands, more transmission projects could mean more competition for agricultural land.

Farm Bureau’s message to Congress is that modernizing America’s permitting system should not come at the expense of the property rights, productive farmland and long-term economic security of farm families.

The challenge now is whether House lawmakers will address those concerns before the legislation advances any further.

text:
Forum Mobility has opened two v4 Megawatt Charging Standard chargers at FM Harbor, its electric truck depot in the Port of Long Beach, and says they can recover up to 60 percent of a Tesla Semi’s range in 30 minutes. Another 30 megawatts of charging is under construction.

The release, as issued by Forum Mobility

Forum Mobility, one of the nation’s leading zero-emission trucking solutions providers, held a ribbon-cutting event for the addition of two new v4 Megawatt Charging Standard (MCS) chargers at FM Harbor, its flagship electric truck charging depot in the Port of Long Beach on November 5. The event also featured an inaugural charge sessions of a customer’s new production-model Tesla Semi.

The MCS chargers are Tesla Semi compatible and can recover up to 60% of range in 30 minutes, allowing for a fueling experience that does not disrupt carrier operations.

“We can fuel with electrons 40% cheaper than diesel, and these are the first of 30 megawatts of MCS chargers we have coming online in the coming months. We are providing a platform for our customers to go further, charge faster, and reduce their cost per mile in a challenging freight environment,” said Matt LeDucq, CEO and co-founder of Forum Mobility.

Forum Mobility is currently under construction on an additional 30 MW of charging infrastructure across four new charging depots (in Rancho Dominguez, CA; Ontario, CA; and two in Oakland, CA) and developing its next tranche of depots, including more in the Inland Empire and Central Valley in California, Las Vegas, Phoenix, Houston, Dallas, Seattle/Tacoma, and Chicago.

“Long range electric trucks and ultra-fast charging is the next step in zero emission freight. We are proud to partner with Forum Mobility in putting this advanced technology to work for the benefit of our customers. Together, we are delivering lower costs, and lower emissions,” said Jim Gillis, President, Pacific Division, IMC Logistics.

With a customer list of 25 carriers with contracted capacity, customer reservations for over 330 Tesla Semis, and a total of over 40 MW of CCS and MCS charging online and under construction, Forum Mobility is helping usher in the next generation of freight technology.

text:
Algeria has officially launched a project to build a lithium battery plant with a production capacity of 5 gigawatt-hours (GWh), targeting electric vehicles and energy storage systems.

President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has tasked Algerian-Canadian battery expert Karim Zaghib with overseeing the project's technical and technological development, under the supervision of Sonelgaz International.

Algeria aims to leverage its domestic mineral resources to develop a battery industry and serve local and export markets, although the country has yet to establish commercial lithium mining operations.

The Algerian government announced the official launch of a project to build a lithium battery manufacturing plant with a production capacity of 5 gigawatt-hours (GWh) on Monday, November 23.

The project featured prominently during a working session chaired by President Abdelmadjid Tebboune. During the meeting, the government tasked Algerian-Canadian lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery expert Karim Zaghib with "studying and monitoring the plant's implementation phases from a technical and technological perspective." The Ministry of Energy, Mines and Renewable Energies will oversee the project through Sonelgaz International, according to a statement from the Algerian presidency.

The planned facility will manufacture batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage systems, aiming to meet domestic demand while exporting part of its output to international markets.

"We need to consider the prospects of these projects, which hold great promise for Algeria, to meet domestic needs and also expand exports to African, European, North American and Asian markets, including China," Zaghib said after the meeting. He added that Algeria "has an integrated and exceptional ecosystem and possesses critical metals."

Algeria holds significant iron ore deposits, particularly at Gara Djebilet in the southwest, and phosphate deposits in Tebessa in the east. Domestic LFP battery production could allow the country to add value to its mineral resources through local manufacturing. However, Algeria does not currently operate a commercial lithium mine, although it has deposits undergoing exploration and assessment.

An Industrial Ambition Dating Back to 2023

Geological surveys by the National Mining Research and Exploitation Company (SONAREM) and the National Office for Geological and Mining Research (ORGM) have identified promising indications of lithium and other critical minerals, mainly in the southern provinces of Tamanrasset and In Guezzam, according to official data. Algeria is already working with Chinese mining giant Ganfeng Lithium to conduct field studies, assess the country's mineral potential and evaluate opportunities to develop its lithium industry.

Algeria's ambitions to establish an electric battery manufacturing industry date back to 2023. Officials first discussed a potential project during President Tebboune's visit to China in July 2023. At the time, Chinese President Xi Jinping expressed Beijing's intention to establish "one of the largest lithium battery factories" in Algeria. The initiative subsequently took a more domestically driven direction when the Algerian government decided to enlist Karim Zaghib's expertise. At this stage, the government has not announced any potential partnerships with foreign companies for the project.

Zaghib is a professor of chemical and materials engineering at Concordia University in Montreal, Canada. He previously served as director general of Hydro-Québec's Center of Excellence in Transportation Electrification and Energy Storage. Hydro-Québec is the state-owned company responsible for electricity generation, transmission and distribution in Quebec. Zaghib also worked as a strategic adviser at Investissement Québec, the Quebec government's financial institution responsible for attracting investment and financing businesses, where he helped structure the province's battery industry.

The ministry opposed including EVs in a proposed domestic production tax credit scheme at a parliamentary tax subcommittee meeting this week, the Maeil Business Newspaper reported on Tuesday, citing concerns over administrative inefficiencies and the potential for the scope to become too broad. The report added that the ministry said it saw little need for additional tax incentives for EVs, arguing that locally made models remain competitively priced against Chinese and other imports and that South Korea already had a well-established EV manufacturing base.

title: Kia Plans Electric Pickup Truck for America by 2030 With 90000 Annual Sales Target
description:
Its latest 2026 strategy points to hybrid and extended-range electric models, whereas an earlier announcement outlined plans for a fully electric pickup.
Kia Targets the American Midsize Pickup Market The U.S. pickup market represents a major opportunity for Kia, which has traditionally focused on passenger cars, crossovers, and SUVs in North America.
The company’s 2026 CEO Investor Day strategy identifies a new body-on-frame pickup for North America by 2030.
The company is targeting approximately 90,000 annual sales for the North American pickup program.
Kia’s earlier 2025 business strategy described a new electric pickup for North America, based on a dedicated EV platform.
text:
Kia is preparing to enter one of the most competitive parts of the American automotive market with a new midsize pickup planned for North America by 2030. The upcoming truck is expected to use a traditional body-on-frame construction, putting it in a different category from car-based pickups and many electric lifestyle trucks.

Kia has discussed a long-term annual sales target of approximately 90,000 units, showing the importance it places on this new segment.

The company’s plans for its powertrains have also changed over time. Its latest 2026 strategy points to hybrid and extended-range electric models, whereas an earlier announcement outlined plans for a fully electric pickup. This difference will be important as further information about the vehicle becomes available.

Kia Targets the American Midsize Pickup Market

The U.S. pickup market represents a major opportunity for Kia, which has traditionally focused on passenger cars, crossovers, and SUVs in North America.

The company already sells the Tasman in selected international markets, but that truck is not intended to serve as its main entry into the American market. Instead, Kia is developing a separate North American pickup with a body-on-frame platform.

The company’s 2026 CEO Investor Day strategy identifies a new body-on-frame pickup for North America by 2030. Kia’s presentation describes the project as part of its plan to enter the pickup segment and broaden its U.S. customer base.

The company is targeting approximately 90,000 annual sales for the North American pickup program.

That figure is a long-term target, not a production forecast or a confirmed first-year sales commitment. Kia has not announced a specific launch month, final model name, or complete production schedule. The target nevertheless indicates that the company expects the truck to become a meaningful part of its American lineup rather than a low-volume specialty product.

A body-on-frame construction is a significant choice. Unlike unibody SUVs and crossovers, this arrangement uses a separate frame to support the vehicle’s body and major mechanical components. It is commonly used in pickups because it can accommodate demanding workloads, towing requirements, and off-road use.

The platform should also give Kia flexibility to develop different powertrain configurations and equipment packages.

However, the company has not disclosed the truck’s dimensions, wheelbase, payload capacity, towing rating, suspension design, or off-road hardware. Those specifications will determine how closely it competes with established midsize pickups.

Kia’s strategy reflects the size of the American truck market. Pickups remain an important vehicle category for private buyers, contractors, businesses, and outdoor enthusiasts. Entering this segment gives the company access to customers who may not consider a conventional crossover or SUV.

Hybrid and Extended-Range Electric Powertrains Are Now Part of the Plan

The most important development concerns the pickup’s powertrain. Kia’s earlier 2025 business strategy described a new electric pickup for North America, based on a dedicated EV platform.

The company set the same long-term target of approximately 90,000 annual sales and highlighted the need for cargo space, towing capability, and off-road performance.

However, Kia’s more recent 2026 CEO Investor Day presentation identifies a body-on-frame pickup with hybrid electric vehicle (HEV) and extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) variants by 2030.

text:
Texas A&M University says the U.S. is falling behind in nuclear technology, comparing the three reactors China turns on each year with the three reactors the U.S. has turned on in total over the last 30 years.

However, a small nuclear reactor is taking shape on the University's RELLIS campus in Bryan, Texas, about a mile from an existing reactor.

Here's what to know

Before a reactor can begin a sustained nuclear reaction — known as reaching criticality — it needs Department of Energy authorization. For Last Energy, the reactor building is already complete. In September, it was just waiting on that authorization, according to The Eagle.

Last Energy is building the reactor in partnership with the University. By late August, work on the building was complete, after starting in January.

Designed for commercial and industrial applications, Last Energy's PWR 20 has a smaller counterpart in the PWR 5. The demonstration reactor will be housed below ground inside a hermetically sealed steel container.

Installation of a larger PWR 20 alongside the smaller unit is planned to follow the PWR 5's initial role as a proving ground.

If the PWR 5 reaches criticality, it would mark the first campus reactor construction in more than three decades.

More background

Adam Lenarz, the company's vice president of development, said that the ideas that work on paper and what works in real-life operation are not the same: "What we discovered was that the problem wasn't with the reactor, it was with the business model."

"So what we decided to do is take the existing fleet of operating nuclear reactors, or what's called pressurized water reactors — just means that you operate under fairly high pressures, water that moves around in the circuit," Lenarz continued. "Shrink that size to the same exact process conditions and just make it smaller, more manufacturable, more deliverable."

Parallel or sequential operation of multiple PWR 20 units is possible. The potential benefits include power for homes, businesses, and industrial development with substantial electricity needs.

Nuclear projects, however, also require careful safety oversight and long-term waste management. The coverage did not detail waste handling.

What's being done?

Microreactors, small modular reactors, and commercial reactors are the focus of agreements Texas A&M reached with Kairos Power, Natura Resources, Terrestrial Energy, and Aalo Atomics.

Longer-term commercial operations are also under consideration, said David Staack, Texas A&M's deputy vice chancellor overseeing research. He said the university has an agreement with Terrestrial Energy for a comparable pilot initiative under Department of Energy oversight.

A&M researchers help review the work on campus, while the Department of Energy is responsible for safety oversight.

Nuclear engineering students could gain hands-on experience through the Last Energy project, including internships and research opportunities. Those possibilities come alongside the project's potential to supply electricity.

Training would become the PWR 5's role in the proposed second phase, Lenarz said, with the larger PWR 20 supplying electricity to homes and businesses.

"We really want to be a place where the future happens. And so whether it's hypersonics or energy or space, we're building the infrastructure and working with the companies to really make it happen."

In October, Last Energy announced that it had received Documented Safety Analysis from the DOE, per Business Wire. Next is a readiness review, which the company said is "the final step before DOE can issue startup authorization for criticality and reactor operations."

name: Clean Energy
title: BAAJA Is a Clean Energy Affordability Bill, Not a Pro Data Center Bill - Evergreen Action
description:
BAAJA doesn’t open federal land to data centers—it makes them less likely Some worry this bill could open federal land to data centers.
But we need huge amounts of new clean energy to power and heat our homes, electrify buildings, clean up factories.
Data center developers will have to prove they can cover the cost of new infrastructure before it’s built.
Empowers local governments Communities facing a data center proposal often have to evaluate it with little information and no expert help.
The bottom line: Passing BAAJA will rein in data centers and unlock clean energy
text:
Data centers are driving the fastest growth in electricity demand in decades, and right now most of that demand is being met with gas. Some opponents of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) worry that faster permitting will only feed that boom. We see it the other way around.

BAAJA is a hard fought compromise, and it isn’t perfect. But after decades of failed fights over transmission and permitting reform, it finally clears the way for clean energy at scale. And it checks data center development in three key ways that today’s status quo does not:

It opens the grid bottleneck that pushes data centers toward gas. Instead, transmission will be built faster and bring more clean power on the grid, helping avoid the rush to dirty, behind-the-meter gas.

It makes data centers pay their full share, and then some. And the extra money goes to lowering everyone else’s bills.

It keeps families from getting stuck with the bill if a data center shuts down or doesn’t get built, and gives communities the tools to evaluate proposals before they say yes.

BAAJA fights a gas boom

Right now, data center developers are creating a demand for power not seen in decades, and today gas is the fastest power to permit. BAAJA changes that math.

The grid is the bottleneck. BAAJA will open it up.

To build a gas pipeline, a developer currently only needs federal approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and federal environmental reviews are already fairly streamlined for pipelines. To build a high-voltage transmission line, they need approval from every state it crosses, and the federal environmental review process currently takes much longer for transmission lines than pipelines. That’s why transmission lines can take up to 17 years to permit, compared to under 3 years for pipelines.

We need roughly 5,000 miles of new high-voltage transmission lines every year to clean up our power grid. In 2024, we only built about 300 miles. Without new lines, wind and solar projects sit in line waiting to connect, while utilities and data centers turn to gas.

BAAJA speeds up permitting for transmission, so more clean energy can reach the grid, for data centers or anyone else wanting to connect.

With abundant clean power on the grid, data center developers won’t have to turn to off-grid gas.

When data centers can’t get power from the grid, many build their own gas plants on site, often called “behind-the-meter” power. Data center developers have proposed about 90 GWs of these plants, most using extremely polluting generators like jet engines that are much worse for both the climate and local air quality, and can even drive up energy costs for everyone else despite being off the grid.

BAAJA doesn’t open federal land to data centers—it makes them less likely

Some worry this bill could open federal land to data centers. That’s a fair concern, but it describes the reality as it exists today. The federal government has approved a data center on federal land in Ohio powered by more than nine GWs of new gas. Current permitting law didn’t stop it. Cheap, plentiful clean electricity is the only long-term solution to prevent projects like this from coming to fruition.

Holding back clean energy won’t hold back data centers—it will just make cutting climate pollution impossible

It’s true that a faster permitting system means more things get built faster—data centers included. But we need huge amounts of new clean energy to power and heat our homes, electrify buildings, clean up factories. Without that, the country cannot cut climate pollution at all.

Slowing down clean energy won’t stop data centers. It will just guarantee they run on gas.

BAAJA makes data centers pay up

BAAJA creates the first nationwide mandate requiring data centers to pay for the costs they put on the grid, and opens other revenue opportunities that would reduce other ratepayers’ bills. It does this in three ways.

Data centers pay the full cost (and more) of grid upgrades needed to serve them, including transmission. Today, large customers like data centers usually only have to pay for one of these categories, not both. BAAJA makes data centers pay both, and requires the extra revenue to directly lower household electric bills. GridStrategies estimates this could transfer $35 billion in wealth over the next 10 years from hyperscalers to American ratepayers.

States can charge data centers more for new power and power lines. BAAJA lets states charge above cost for new generation, storage, and distribution lines built to serve data centers. States can use that money to cut ratepayer bills directly or to build or bolster community energy systems that make the grid more reliable and cheaper.

Utilities can auction unused grid space. BAAJA lets utilities offer spare grid capacity to data centers through a bidding process, raising additional revenue to lower bills even more. And because most grid costs are fixed, utilizing the grid more spreads costs across more customers, which lowers costs for everyone.

BAAJA protects ratepayers and empowers communities

BAAJA sets a national floor of ratepayer protections that goes further than what many states do today.

Strong Safeguards for Ratepayers

BAAJA establishes strong exit fee mandates. If a new power plant or transmission line is built to serve a data center, the data center pays for it—even if it shuts down early or never opens at all—so other ratepayers aren’t left holding the bill.

BAAJA also establishes financial collateral mandates. Data center developers will have to prove they can cover the cost of new infrastructure before it’s built. That helps weed out speculative projects, makes grid planning more accurate, and keeps ratepayers from paying for infrastructure built for demand that never materializes.

Empowers local governments

Communities facing a data center proposal often have to evaluate it with little information and no expert help. BAAJA changes that in two ways:

It requires the Department of Energy (DOE) to create a Data Center Community Assistance Program that provides local, state, and Tribal governments technical assistance, resources, and data needed to properly evaluate proposals.

It requires DOE to publish a Data Center Community Toolkit to help local communities gather and understand a project’s impact on electricity costs, water use, and the local economy, and learn about best practices.

The bottom line: Passing BAAJA will rein in data centers and unlock clean energy

title: NYPA Advances Energy Storage System Demonstration Project
description:

In the meantime, UEP is finalizing the system design and will begin fabrication of the energy storage system in early 2027.

text:
The New York Power Authority and Urban Electric Power are advancing a demonstration project with the State University of New York at Oneonta to deploy and illustrate the efficacy of a novel energy storage system to help power the campus increasing reliability and resiliency, NYPA said on Nov. 18.

The storage system will be able to provide stable power for the campus during high demand periods and in extreme weather conditions.

“Advancing next-generation energy storage technology is essential to New York’s all-of-the-above approach to building a cleaner, more resilient electric grid, ”said NYPA President and CEO Justin Driscoll. “With this promising energy storage technology demonstration, we can increase consumer confidence in new storage solutions, expand our use of renewable power and deliver more reliable, affordable electricity to communities across the state.”

The Power Authority is currently working with its energy service providers to select a contractor for engineering and construction services for the project. Engineering in support of installation will begin later this year with construction anticipated to start in 2027. In the meantime, UEP is finalizing the system design and will begin fabrication of the energy storage system in early 2027.

UEP’s energy storage system will involve a rechargeable zinc-manganese dioxide (Zn-MnO₂) technology with a power rating of 600 kW and energy capacity of 3,600 kWh. The alternative storage chemistry is similar to household AA batteries.

The technology can reduce the campus’ peak demand during high-demand events and provide backup electricity during power interruptions.

“Campuses, hospitals and other critical facilities need energy storage they can place near the buildings they serve, ”said UEP CEO Gabriel Cowles. “Our batteries use the same basic chemistry as everyday alkaline batteries, are made rechargeable, and our systems are manufactured in Pearl River, New York. We’re grateful to NYPA, SUNY Oneonta and NYSERDA for keeping this project moving after the loss of federal funding, and we look forward to showing what safe, New York-made storage can do for SUNY Oneonta’s campus and the grid.”

Improved energy storage technologies can strengthen grid reliability and enable better peak load management, which helps utilities avoid costly transmission upgrades that can drive energy prices up, NYPA noted in a news release. Advanced energy storage systems also can enable greater use of renewable resources like wind and solar and ensure clean energy is available when it is needed most.

"Partnering with energy leaders across New York State on this groundbreaking project will benefit our students, campus and surrounding community, "said SUNY Oneonta President Alberto Cardelle. "This initiative will create valuable opportunities for hands-on learning, research, internships and workforce training beyond the classroom. As one of Otsego County’s largest electricity consumers and an institution committed to sustainability, SUNY Oneonta is dedicated to investing in innovative energy solutions that strengthen campus operations, benefit our local community, and help build a more sustainable future for generations to come."

The project leverages low cost, abundant materials sourced from the U.S. and allied countries to reduce technology risk and ease pressure on grid infrastructure by lowering peak demand, NYPA said.

The technology is designed and manufactured in New York, has been deployed at customer sites across the U.S., uses recyclable raw materials, and requires fewer greenhouse gas emissions to produce than other widely used battery technologies.

NYPA and UEP will fund approximately $5.5 million of the $6.5 million project. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority is supporting nearly $1 million in project-related costs.

The project was initially announced in 2024 as a dual-site demonstration to be partially funded by the U.S. Department of Energy. NYPA said the DOE later withdrew from the project due to changing priorities. NYPA and UEP re-scoped the effort and advanced it as a single-site project.

As part of this re-scoping, the project team, including SUNY Oneonta stakeholders, reassessed system requirements and increased the power rating from 300kW to 600kW to improve short duration peak shaving capability, while maintaining the originally planned 3,600kWh of usable energy for long-duration emergency response.

At reduced loads, the system is estimated to be able to support critical campus buildings well beyond six hours during an outage.

During the demonstration phase the team aims to assess the system’s ability to reduce campus demand by up to 600 kW during peak events, enhance resilience by connecting to the campus radial feeder for improved building protection during extended outage and participate in demand reduction programs.

UEP is a New York-based energy storage company specializing in zinc aqueous battery chemistries, with patented technology in rechargeable zinc-manganese dioxide and nickel-zinc.

UEP manufactures its zinc-manganese dioxide batteries at its plant in Pearl River, New York, delivering energy storage that uses a non-flammable, water-based electrolyte, and is made from abundant, recyclable materials.

text:
With a newly divided Washington taking shape following the midterm elections, solar and storage executives at RE+ 2026 framed the next phase of U.S. clean energy manufacturing around a single imperative: ending the policy whiplash that stalls multi-year factory investments.

Speaking at an on-the-record media roundtable hosted by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and attended by pv magazine USA, SEIA president and chief executive officer Tim Pawlenty joined Qcells vice president of market strategy and public affairs Scott Moskowitz, Enphase Energy chief product officer Raghu Belur, Shoals Technologies senior vice president of Sales Karen Bazela, and SEIA senior vice president of supply chain and trade Stacy Ettinger to outline how domestic manufacturing is expanding beyond solar modules and what policy tools are needed to sustain it.

Making policy “purple” to stabilize capital

Asked how he plans to make SEIA’s advocacy more bipartisan, Pawlenty argued that shifting the industry’s political posture is less about optics and more about protecting long-term capital deployment from two-year election cycles.

“The goal here isn’t just, let’s make SEIA purple because we think it’s fun to make SEIA purple,” said Pawlenty, adding a nod to his home state of Minnesota and Prince’s Purple Rain. “The goal is to try to minimize the whiplash the industry experiences. You get people aggregating and deploying huge sums of capital, trying to have bigger, bolder plans for the future of solar and storage in America. You can’t do that when you get whipsawed every 24 months.”

He described the push for bipartisanship as “a policy, economic development, durability goal masquerading as a political objective,” noting that companies cannot plan capital-intensive factory expansions if incentives shift every two years.

With Democrats taking control of Congress while facing a Republican White House, Pawlenty noted that any legislation enacted over the next two years will be bipartisan by necessity. While SEIA’s board will formally set its 2027 legislative priorities at its December meeting, Pawlenty highlighted extending the Section 45X manufacturing tax credit beyond its current 2032 expiration as a top conceptual priority, arguing that multi-year factory construction requires long-range certainty well ahead of deadlines.

From near extinction to global export ambitions

Moskowitz, who also chairs SEIA’s board, offered a broader strategic framework for how the U.S. solar supply chain has evolved and what it will take to close remaining upstream gaps. Ten years ago, he noted, the industry’s central question was simply how to scale enough to compete on cost with conventional power sources. Following pandemic-era supply disruptions and geopolitical shifts, that question has changed to how the U.S. builds and sustains an end-to-end domestic industrial base.

“Energy security is national security,” Moskowitz said. “And if this is the technology that is gonna be the leading source of energy in America, adding year after year after year, it’s really important that we make it here.”

He laid out a four-stage progression for domestic clean energy manufacturing: moving from near extinction in critical upstream segments, to scaling initial capacity, to achieving domestic self-sufficiency across the U.S. market, and ultimately building enough scale and cost competitiveness to export American-made solar products globally. While U.S. capacity in polysilicon, module assembly, inverters, and racking has reached substantial scale, Moskowitz pointed out that ingot, wafer, and cell production remain the hardest gaps to fill against entrenched global scale in China. Even so, every link of the crystalline silicon supply chain is now being produced at some volume in the United States.

He pointed to Qcells’ footprint in northwest Georgia as a real-world test case for both vertical integration and bipartisan durability. Operating in a historically conservative region once known as the carpet manufacturing capital of the world, Qcells now runs roughly 8.4 GW of annual module capacity across two Georgia plants employing about 4,000 workers, including its Cartersville facility, which integrates ingot, wafer, cell, and module manufacturing under one roof. Opened initially in 2018 with backing from Republican Governor Brian Kemp and expanded alongside federal policies championed by Democratic Senators Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, the facilities have created multigenerational manufacturing jobs and maintained support across party lines, including preserving Section 45X value and duration in recent federal legislation.

To replicate that model and close remaining upstream gaps in both solar and battery cells, Moskowitz argued that policymakers must deploy “all of the tools in the toolbox” rather than relying on any single mechanism. That means pairing Section 45X production credits and Investment Tax Credit (ITC) domestic content bonuses, energy community adders, and prevailing wage rules with targeted trade enforcement, state-level economic development incentives, and federal permitting reform so projects can actually get built and absorb domestic factory output.

Navigating polysilicon Section 232 and upstream bottlenecks

When pressed on whether upcoming Section 232 trade actions on polysilicon and derivatives could inadvertently inflate input costs for domestic module assemblers that still rely on imported cells, Moskowitz noted that trade measures must be balanced with policies that keep deployment moving quickly while manufacturers focus on driving down costs through scale and innovation.

Ettinger added that the Section 232 measures do not take effect until December 4 and include an administration-backed investment incentive mechanism. Under that program, manufacturers expanding or standing up U.S. production lines can negotiate agreements with the Commerce Department to waive tariffs on imported manufacturing equipment and upstream inputs not yet available domestically.

“They’ve taken a tailored approach, working with manufacturers with the objective of helping support manufacturing facilities,” Ettinger said, noting that policymakers have paired tariff enforcement with targeted incentives to bring production onshore.

Solid-state transformers and the grid-edge expansion

Beyond panels and batteries, executives emphasized that the domestic clean energy supply chain is increasingly converging with grid modernization and data center load growth.

“It’s no longer solar and batteries anymore,” said Belur, whose company reshored manufacturing to the U.S. starting in 2023, primarily in Dallas, after producing zero units domestically from 2008 to 2023. “You’re starting to see a much broader ecosystem of players here: switchgear, transformers, distribution devices.”

Enphase is leveraging its power-electronics platform to build solid-state transformers (SSTs) for data centers and grid infrastructure. Noting an 85% supply chain overlap between Enphase’s solar and battery inverters and its SST architecture, Belur argued that traditional copper-and-iron transformers face lead times of 52 weeks or longer and rely heavily on overseas materials.

“There’s nothing wrong with horses and buggies, but we moved away from them,” Belur said of legacy 140-year-old transformer designs. “The grid needs to modernize, and part of the biggest thing about upgrading the grid is making it more electronic and software-driven.”

Belur also highlighted speed to power as a decisive advantage as data centers and industrial reshoring accelerate electricity demand, noting that distributed and utility-scale solar and storage can interconnect far faster than multi-decade gas or nuclear projects. To ease local pushback around data center power consumption, he pointed to behind-the-meter residential solar and storage deployments in surrounding communities as a model that benefits homeowners, utilities, and data center operators alike

Both Belur and Bazela advocated for broadening Section 45X eligibility to cover critical grid hardware like solid-state transformers and electrical balance-of-systems (eBOS) components. Bazela noted that Shoals recently opened a 647,000-square-foot eBOS manufacturing plant in Portland, Tennessee, adding nearly 500 workers year to date alongside its existing Muscle Shoals, Alabama operations.
