text:
A group of more than 120 climate scientists have urged US lawmakers to not pass contentious legislation to speed up the building of energy projects, datacenters and other infrastructure, amid a growing backlash to the sweeping permitting bill.

In an open letter to members of the House of Representatives, the collection of Earth and social sciences researchers expressed “deep concern” that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or Baaja) weakens environmental laws, locks in new fossil fuel projects without recourse and delivers only minor cuts to planet-heating emissions.

“We understand the need for trade-offs and compromise when passing bipartisan legislation,” they wrote. “But as scientists we feel strongly that the costs of this bill to the climate are too high.”

Last week, the US Senate rapidly passed Baaja, a bill co-written by two Democratic and two Republican senators but one that has bitterly divided Democrats and environmentalists. The House is set to vote on the bill next week, where it will be signed by Donald Trump into law if passed.

Michael Mann, a climate scientist who helped arrange the open letter, said that he did so because Baaja is a “deeply problematic bill” that is “backed by a veritable who’s who of bad fossil fuel and dark money actors”.

Mann said that Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, should “scrap Baaja, which in the end only takes us further down the dangerous fossil fuel pathway, and put a sensible, popular datacenter bill on Trump’s desk and force him to veto it. And force Republicans to defend sustaining that veto.”

Timmons Roberts, a Brown University academic and letter co-signatory, said the bill is “very worrisome, it has felt very rushed and there is grave potential for damage that can’t be done any time soon”.

“We are in a broken system, and it’s hard to build anything, but there has to be a better way to do this,” Roberts added. “In some ways it feels like we are being held hostage. If you want more renewables you have to also see the lock-in of fossil fuels and the devastating gutting of core legislation that has allowed the US to improve its natural environment.”

Mann said that Sheldon Whitehouse, the Democratic senator and longtime champion of climate action who has co-sponsored Baaja, has “long been one of my heroes, and nothing pains me to find him not only in support of the bill but in fact one of its principal backers”.

Asked for his response to the letter, Whitehouse said: “I have great respect for these climate scientists, and I am sorry to disagree with them here. The important takeaways about this bill are the gigaton-scale emissions reductions, the freed-up clean power, the $10bn in annual consumer electricity savings, and the $35bn whack at datacenters.”

Supporters of Baaja, who include some Democrats, a minority of green groups and other climate scientists, point to the laborious, sometimes terminal wait for clean energy projects to be approved and come online, as well as the lack of integrated power lines to take solar or wind-generated electrons to where it is needed.

Baaja would slash the barriers to new transmission lines and shrink the role of statutes such as the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act in scrutinizing various projects, aiding their rapid approval and making them virtually immune from being overturned by any future administration or the courts.

This should unleash much of the clean energy waiting to be connected to the grid but will also sideline legal challenges to new oil pipelines, datacenters and other infrastructure, such as ICE detention centers. This has raised alarm over a potential surge in fossil fuel activity and datacenters sited on public lands, with little community or tribal input.

“Congress must reject Baaja in its entirety,” the National Congress of American Indians said in a statement. “Native sovereignty, sacred places, and cultural heritage are not negotiable.”

The varied coalition of opponents, including former vice-president Al Gore, also argue that Trump will not faithfully execute the law. The president, a major backer of the artificial intelligence industry, has said Baaja result in a “tremendous amounts of new building” for dat centers but has insisted that he will still not allow the permitting of new wind power, which he has called a “major loser”.

“Democrats, what is the matter with you? Don’t you know better than to trust Trump?” the actor Mark Ruffalo, an environmental advocate, said in a widely-viewed social media post.

Unusually for a major, 500-page piece of legislation, Baaja has been pushed through Congress without a hearing. The pace of its ascension increases its chance of getting needed Republican support, including Trump’s, to pass, with no guarantee of such backing should Democrats write their own, revised version from January.

Faced with this dilemma, some Democrats in the House opposed to Baaja have set about trying to amend it rather than immediately kill it. This may succeed given that Republicans’ already slender hold on the House has been largely erased, with many Republicans now not in Washington for the lame-duck session after losing in the midterm elections.

“There are amendments to fix this bil that would hacve broad bipartisan support but we are about to find out if this is a ‘take it or leave it’ jam job,” Jared Huffman, a California Democrat, told the Guardian. “The Republicans will push for Democrats to abstain or not show up, that power play will come next week.”

Huffman, who is set to chair the House’s natural resources committee when Democrats take control of the chamber, has proposed five amendments to Baaja. These include more consultation with tribes and legal recourse for communities, as well as full reviews fore data centers and ending the “forever permit” provisions that ensure projects can continue even if they are shown to be destructive or unlawful.

“Look how thrilled the White House, the fossil fuel industry and big AI and datacenter interests are with this bill. They want what it gives and they aren’t going to stop wanting that six weeks from now,” Huffman said.

“We will be able to cut a deal on better terms then; we need to be better negotiators. This episode shows the dangers of not acting because you get something like Baaja, which is extremely destructive. If we go the next two to four years without legislating on a permitting deal, then shame on us.”

text:
by Alison F. Takemura

Nov. 18, 2026

Mitch Hall and his wife, Lori, live in one of the most sustainable communities in the U.S. Their town house is among a few dozen residences constructed so far at Veridian at County Farm, a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes here make about as much solar energy as they consume, with the help of batteries that save solar power for use in the evenings.

Now, the couple is eager to share the benefits of their clean energy infrastructure with the wider grid.

In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in Michigan’s first residential pilot of a virtual power plant; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy will then be able to remotely control the network of residents’ home batteries to inject their stored solar power onto the grid when operators need it most.

“This pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,” Joi Harris, president and chief executive officer of DTE Energy, said in a statement. VPPs can smooth out demand peaks, reducing the utility’s need to invest in grid-infrastructure upgrades and generate kilowatt-hours with expensive fossil-fuel peaker plants, both of which would pile costs on consumers.

The initiative ​“should work well for the residents, too,” Hall said. ​“DTE will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.” Because the utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and electricity prices are likely to be highest, ​“a neat part about the virtual power plant is you don’t have to spend a lot of time learning and trying to optimize,” he noted. ​“DTE will manage that battery for you.” (DTE did not respond to Canary Media’s request for exact figures on how much it would compensate customers in time for publication.)

VPPs have existed for years but have been slow to gain widespread traction because of a host of factors. Utilities often haven’t been incentivized to embrace the approach, while home solar and batteries remain too expensive for many households in the U.S. But as electrification and the data center rush spur unprecedented demand, VPPs are taking off as a fast way to get power on the grid. Earlier this month, the Brattle Group estimated that 524 gigawatts of distributed energy resources harnessed in VPPs could save households on average $122 per year by 2050.

Currently, ​“there’s immense untapped capacity,” said Kevin Brehm, manager in the carbon-free electricity practice at clean energy think tank RMI.

Matt Grocoff, the founder of Thrive Collaborative, started to consider a VPP pilot at Veridian in 2019. He wanted the neighborhood to mimic an ecosystem — a resilient web of relationships in which individual organisms do more than just extract resources. For example, a tree in a forest turns sunlight into nutrients and shares them symbiotically with a vast, interconnected underground web of fungi.

Likewise, with a VPP, each Veridian home ​“can be producing energy that it needs and mutually beneficially sharing it across a network of energy rather than a linear grid that flows in only one direction,” Grocoff said.

DTE expects nearly 100 battery-equipped Veridian homes to ultimately participate in the pilot. So far, 44 market-rate homes with solar and batteries have been built, out of 120 planned, as have 50 affordable housing units that don’t have batteries yet, according to Thrive Collaborative. Battery manufacturer Sonnen USA, maker of the home storage systems installed at Veridian, is helping DTE operate the pilot using Sonnen’s proprietary software.

“Veridian is a test bed,” said Geoff Ferrell, executive vice president of Sonnen USA’s VPP business unit. The initiative, which is expected to be able to deliver up to about 300 kilowatts for three hours, will give DTE a clearer picture of how much power the home battery fleet can actually generate and when, providing ​“a really great basis” for a scaled-up program, he noted.

Ferrell points to another Sonnen-facilitated VPP that also sprang up as a humble pilot project, but rapidly mushroomed into a full-scale program because of early positive results. That initiative started in 2017 with a new apartment building topped with solar, Soleil Lofts outside Salt Lake City.

Sonnen hadn’t even finished installing batteries in each of the development’s 600 units when the utility Rocky Mountain Power and the state utility commission decided that the initial data was promising enough to merit extending the program to every residential customer in the utility’s territory, Ferrell said. Today, about 7,900 homes and businesses participate in the program, now called Wattsmart Battery, in Utah, Wyoming, and Idaho.

Given the success of that VPP and many others, Brehm would like to see more utilities go full throttle at the outset.

“Do you need another pilot?” he asked, noting that numerous VPP programs exist for utilities to model their own programs after.

But for utilities that do approach VPPs with caution, Rocky Mountain Power’s pilot is a good model, according to Brehm. The utility’s employees were able to rapidly understand how the residential battery fleet worked and how to deploy it, he said, ​“so that they could integrate these batteries into their operations initially, and subsequently [into their resource-capacity] planning.” He’d like to see DTE do the same.

The VPP pilot at Veridian is already starting to inspire developers and utilities outside Michigan, including the development Peace Hill in Townsend, Washington, said Grocoff of Thrive Collaborative.

“We’re getting calls from all over the country,” Grocoff said. ​“It’s really exciting.”

description:

This extreme concentration presents a huge and growing problem for global energy security.
Jon Evans, Chief Executive Officer for Lithium Americas, also indicated that Trump-era immigration policy played a notable role in ramping up the project’s challenges.

When the firm announced the change in budget, stock market shares of Lithium Americas plunged to a record low.
text:
The Trump administration is making a push to reestablish the United States as a major global producer of critical minerals. The federal government is eager to challenge China’s dominance in the sector, as demand for these essential ingredients for clean energy and manufacturing grows exponentially against the backdrop of the global energy transition. But while the establishment of domestic critical mineral supply chains makes sense from an energy security standpoint, industry insiders are sounding the alarm that the expensive endeavor could be a major flop from an economic point of view.

Catalyzed by energy market volatility driven by the United States and Israel’s war in Iran, the world is electrifying faster than ever before. Sky-high fossil fuel prices have pushed countries around the world to invest in homegrown renewable energies as a more reliable and affordable alternative to oil and natural gas imports. As a result, COP31’s previously unthinkable goal of 35 percent electrification by 2035 is now squarely within striking distance.

This transition represents a huge uptick in demand for materials like lithium, nickel, cobalt, and magnesium, and therefore a major economic windfall for Beijing. At present, China supplies approximately 85-95 percent of the world’s refined rare earth minerals, and is home to 85-90 percent of the world’s rare earth mine-to-metal refining. This includes 68 percent of the world’s cobalt, 65 percent of nickel, and 60 percent of EV-battery-grade lithium. This extreme concentration presents a huge and growing problem for global energy security.

“If producers of these substances decide to restrict access to their customers as a political lever, if prices shoot up, or if more industries develop an appetite for them and eat into the supply,” Vox reports, “companies could go bankrupt and efforts to limit climate change could slow down.”

In response, the United States has funded a major effort to increase its presence in global critical mineral markets, particularly for lithium. This effort centers around a massive initiative called the Thacker Pass project in northern Nevada, which aims to produce 40,000 metric tons of lithium annually after wrapping up construction in 2027 and beginning operations in 2028.

Thacker Pass was initially supported and funded through considerable loans under the Biden administration, which were then continued under the Trump administration, albeit with an equity stake in return – 5 percent in the project and 5 percent in the project developer, Lithium Americas.

But now insiders warn that costs of the project are spiraling out of control, thanks to labor shortages, rising wages, tariffs and blistering inflation rates driven by the war in Iran. Jon Evans, Chief Executive Officer for Lithium Americas, also indicated that Trump-era immigration policy played a notable role in ramping up the project’s challenges.

“We’re in a situation where you already have a stressed shortage of craft labor in the US, now compounded by the fact that, for folks who want to come work in the US, that route isn’t readily available to them,” Evans said.

Together, these factors have caused the construction costs of the Thacker Pass project to balloon by approximately 31 percent, or nearly $900 million. When the firm announced the change in budget, stock market shares of Lithium Americas plunged to a record low. This development could have potentially disastrous consequences for Lithium Americas as well as “the dozens of mining projects the Trump administration is trying to coax into existence” as part of its critical minerals push, according to recent reporting from Bloomberg.

“For the companies behind us right now, it’s going to be tough — very tough,” Evans went on to say. “We’re just a barometer for what happens if you want to build power lines, or new power plants, or even a hospital. It requires a lot of specialized skill sets, and these are areas we need to focus on or else it’s going to bite us in the butt.”

By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

title: 970 Patents, 35000 Citations: Algerian Scientist Karim Zaghib to Lead Lithium Battery Project
description: From research laboratories in France and Japan to the technology industry in Canada, Algerian scientist Karim Zaghib has built an international reputation as one of the leading figures in lithium batteries and energy storage.
text:
From research laboratories in France and Japan to the technology industry in Canada, Algerian scientist Karim Zaghib has built an international reputation as one of the leading figures in lithium batteries and energy storage.

After more than three decades of professional experience, Zaghib has returned to the spotlight in Algeria following his appointment by President Abdelmadjid Tebboune to lead the lithium battery manufacturing plant project , with the aim of leveraging his international expertise to transfer technology and develop a domestic industry in one of the sectors most closely tied to the future of energy and manufacturing.

The Algerian professor’s scientific record includes more than 450 research papers and publications, contributions to the development of more than 970 patents, and significant achievements in battery technologies and energy storage systems. These accomplishments are detailed in his official biography and a 2024 announcement by MDPI concerning his appointment as editor-in-chief of the scientific journal Batteries .

Notably, Zaghib’s work has extended beyond academia. He has helped develop technologies that have reached commercial applications, contributing to Hydro-Québec’s standing in the field of battery technology.

Karim Zaghib was born in Constantine in 1963 and grew up in Setif. He later moved to France to pursue postgraduate studies in electrochemistry, earning a Diplôme d’Études Approfondies (DEA) in 1987, followed by a PhD in 1990 from the Grenoble Institute of Technology. In 2002, he obtained his habilitation in physics from Pierre and Marie Curie University in Paris .

His academic qualifications and professional background are documented in his official biography .

He began his career in 1990 as a researcher at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and battery manufacturer Saft, where his work focused on carbon materials and lithium-related reactions. In 1992, he moved to Japan as a visiting researcher at the National Institute of Industrial Research in Osaka, working on lithium-ion battery research.

The year 1995 marked a turning point in his career when he joined the research institute of Canadian utility Hydro-Québec. This began a 28-year career during which he became one of the key figures in developing materials and technologies used in rechargeable batteries.

Zaghib’s contributions have not been confined to theoretical research. They have extended to the development of technologies that helped bring lithium batteries from laboratories into industrial applications, particularly lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which have become an important option for electric vehicles and electricity storage systems.

During his time at Hydro-Québec, he held research management responsibilities in the development of materials for lithium-ion batteries. He contributed to the development of lithium iron phosphate-based electrodes, as well as technologies involving natural graphite anodes and lithium titanate nanomaterials. His contributions to battery research and materials development are also highlighted in MDPI’s profile of Zaghib .

He also led research initiatives and scientific and industrial collaborations aimed at developing large-scale electricity storage systems. These included projects involving Hydro-Québec and Sony, as well as research into solid-state batteries, ionic liquids, and advanced carbon materials.

His professional record indicates that technologies he helped develop have made their way into industrial applications benefiting major companies across the automotive and battery sectors, including Tesla, Ford, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, and BYD, highlighting the reach of his research across the global manufacturing supply chain.

Zaghib is regarded as one of the most prolific researchers in his field. According to his official biography , his achievements include:

More than 450 scientific publications.

Contributions to the development of more than 970 patents.

62 technology and patent licensing agreements.

An h-index of 100.

More than 35,000 citations of his scientific work.

Contributions to 22 books and scientific reference works.

His scientific achievements are also documented in MDPI’s June 2024 announcement of his appointment as editor-in-chief of Batteries . The publication provides additional recognition of his research career and patent portfolio. Its reported figures reflect an earlier reporting period and may differ from those in his more recent biography.

He also co-authored Lithium Batteries: Science and Technology , a reference book published by Springer in 2016 and translated into Chinese.

These figures reflect his considerable influence in battery research. The Royal Society of Canada also notes that his patents have been licensed to 62 companies worldwide.

After 28 years at Hydro-Québec, Zaghib joined Concordia University in Canada in 2022, where he serves as a professor of chemical and materials engineering and leads collaborative centres focused on energy and the energy transition.

In 2023, he was appointed chief executive officer of Volt-Age , a research initiative led by Concordia University that focuses on electrifying society and reducing carbon emissions. The programme brings together researchers and institutions from various disciplines to develop solutions for transportation, energy, and smart buildings.

The initiative received C$123 million in research funding from the federal government, one of the largest research grants in the university’s history. The funding and programme objectives were outlined in Concordia University’s announcement of Volt-Age’s launch .

Zaghib has also served as a strategic adviser to Investissement Québec and as a professor of practice at McGill University, where he contributed to efforts to develop Quebec’s battery industry supply chain, from mining to electric vehicles.

Throughout his career, Zaghib has received recognition from prestigious academic and industrial institutions, in addition to his patents and scientific publications. These honours include:

The 2019 Lionel Boulet Award, presented by the Government of Quebec in recognition of his contributions to industrial research and development.

Election to the Canadian Academy of Engineering in 2017.

Election to the Royal Society of Canada in 2021.

The 2022 Kalev Pugi Award from the Society of Chemical Industry.

The 2024 Research Award from the Battery Division of the Electrochemical Society.

Appointment as an Officer of the Order of Canada on April 17, 2025. ( Official Order of Canada record ).

The Canadian magazine L’actualité also named Zaghib its Personality of the Year on November 29, 2023 , in recognition of his contribution to the development of Quebec’s electric battery industry.

In the latest chapter of his career, Karim Zaghib has once again come into the spotlight in Algeria after President Abdelmadjid Tebboune appointed him on November 23, 2026, to head the project to establish a lithium battery manufacturing plant . He has been tasked with overseeing studies and monitoring the technical and technological aspects of the project at every stage of its development.

The project falls under the supervision of the Ministry of Energy and Renewable Energy, through Sonelgaz International, and aims to establish a plant with an annual production capacity of up to 5 gigawatt-hours (GWh). The facility will focus primarily on lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology, with production intended for both electric vehicle batteries and energy storage systems. Further details about the project’s objectives and technical specifications were also outlined following the presidential meeting.

He further noted that Algeria has significant potential in critical minerals, particularly iron and phosphate, which could be used to develop materials for battery electrodes. This would make it possible to establish a domestic manufacturing value chain rather than relying solely on imports of finished products.

The project is not intended to serve the Algerian market alone. Zaghib also spoke of the possibility of targeting international markets, including those in Africa, Europe, Asia, and North America.

name: EPA
title: Distran obtains first US EPA approval for acoustic technology for methane leak detection
description:
US federal rules require oil and gas operators to inspect their facilities regularly for methane leaks.
Most of these inspections are done with infrared cameras (optical gas imaging, OGI) or handheld gas analyzers (Method 21), which are slow and labor-intensive.
Distran’s Ulta Pro X Emission uses ultrasound cameras that detect the sound of gas escaping from pressurized equipment and show the leak on screen.
The newly obtained EPA approval allows operators to use Ultra Pro X Emissions for regular leak screening under the EPA’s methane rules for new and existing oil and gas facilities (NSPS OOOOa, OOOOb and EG OOOOc).
The EPA approval will further boost growth especially in the US where the largest market for methane leak detection is.
text:
Methane is the main component of natural gas and a potent greenhouse gas, with more than 80 times the warming effect of carbon dioxide over 20 years. US federal rules require oil and gas operators to inspect their facilities regularly for methane leaks. Most of these inspections are done with infrared cameras (optical gas imaging, OGI) or handheld gas analyzers (Method 21), which are slow and labor-intensive.

Distran’s Ulta Pro X Emission uses ultrasound cameras that detect the sound of gas escaping from pressurized equipment and show the leak on screen. The camera is easy to use and requires minimal training. Its performance was confirmed in independent blind tests at METEC, Colorado State University’s methane testing center. It is also certified for use in hazardous areas.

The newly obtained EPA approval allows operators to use Ultra Pro X Emissions for regular leak screening under the EPA’s methane rules for new and existing oil and gas facilities (NSPS OOOOa, OOOOb and EG OOOOc). It applies across the sector to pressurized equipment and locates leaks down to the individual component. The EPA approved it at the most demanding sensitivity level its rules set for this type of screening.

“US customers used our cameras alongside their compliance method; now the camera can be the compliance method itself”, says Florian Perrodin, CEO and Co-founder of Distran. Using only the Ultra Ori Emissions will lower the cost of compliance. For a modeled US midstream operator with 75 facilities, Distran estimates first-year savings of up to 73% compared with infrared cameras, including equipment and inspection labor.

This approval is an addition to the recently obtained ATEX and IECEx certification for Distran’s new fixed sensor, the SonicView X, which monitors hazardous areas around the clock and detects leaks of hydrogen, oxygen and flammable gases as soon as they occur. The company was also awarded with the 2026 Robert Zalosh Hydrogen Safety Excellence Award in the Organizational Category, recognizing its outstanding contributions to advancing hydrogen safety and excellence within the industry.

Distran was founded in 2013 and today serves more than 500 customers in the US and Europe. According to the CEO, demand has continued to grow as new customers request for Distran’s solutions, while existing ones expand their camera fleets across their sites. The EPA approval will further boost growth especially in the US where the largest market for methane leak detection is.

text:
CHILGOK, South Korea — TAGO EV, the electric low-speed vehicle (LSV) brand of South Korea's SD Nexphere Group and a partner member of the International Luxury Hotel Association (ILHA), announced that it has completed preparations to supply and operate rental cart fleets for hotels and resorts across the U.S. Southeast.

With roughly 300 vehicles already shipped to the U.S. and a logistics and assembly hub in Fountain Inn, South Carolina, TAGO EV is offering hotel operators a turnkey fleet package that bundles vehicles, financing, telematics and nationwide battery service into a single program.

Under the TAGO EV Fleet Partnership Program, hotels, resorts and rental operators build a cart fleet on a three-year contract with no upfront investment.

Vehicles are delivered from Fountain Inn with a lithium battery and charger installed and a pre-delivery inspection (PDI) completed, and a telematics-based rental solution — app reservations, remote locking, real-time location and battery monitoring — lets operators run guest rentals without adding staff.

"Hotels do not want to own carts. They want a fleet that is always charged, always located and always under warranty," a TAGO EV spokesperson said. "Through ILHA we have been talking directly with resort executives for the past year, and this program is built around exactly what they asked for."

TAGO EV is currently running a cart rental pilot in Florida's Gulf Coast resort region and will present the program, with test drives for hotel executives, at the ILHA INSPIRE conference in Orlando, Florida, on December 15–16, 2026.

The vehicles were engineered to passenger-car standards by a team drawn from Korea's major automakers. Rack-and-pinion steering, MacPherson independent front suspension, four-wheel hydraulic disc brakes and a powder-coated welded steel frame keep braking and steering stable with every seat occupied.

The platform has been in service on Korean golf courses for more than a decade with no vehicle retired for frame or chassis failure — the reason operators who run carts all day choose TAGO EV.

The lineup consists of the Islander, the rear-facing-seat Kiawah, the Sun Cruiser, the Zephyr and Venture VIP limousines and the two-seat Tasker utility vehicle, all rated at 25 mph.

The 2027 model year adds an exterior facelift and rental-fleet specifications.

Fleet-grade service is anchored by TAGO EV's supply partnership with Eco Battery, a Utah-based lithium battery manufacturer.

Every TAGO EV ships with an Eco Battery 51V LiFePO4 pack, backed by Eco Battery's warranty and nationwide dealer service network, with EB Trace remote monitoring of battery status and location.

"Hotels will not commit a fleet to a brand unless the battery and the service network are local. Eco Battery solved that for us," the spokesperson added.

LONGi Aims to Become A Solar-Storage Technology Company Making Green Energy Accessible to All

ANTALYA, Türkiye , Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At COP31 on Nov. 16 local time, LONGi outlined its next-phase strategy in the UN's official livestream and presented a new vision: To Be a Global Leader in Solar and Energy Storage Technology, Making Clean Energy Accessible to All .



This year's COP31 focuses on three main tracks: implementing emission-reduction targets, climate finance, and adaptation and resilience—with an emphasis on delivering real climate results. The UN climate chief said global climate action remains "far from fast enough, and far from fair enough." Renewable energy is now globally accepted, but the real gap is no longer whether to develop clean energy. It is how to make power stable, affordable and accessible to all.

Energy and climate issues reinforce each other. Over the past decade, the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) from PV has fallen by more than 95%, making it the world's most cost-competitive green power source. Yet PV intermittency, O&M barriers in some regions, and limited energy access in weak-grid areas are slowing clean energy's rise as a primary power source and delaying the global "35 by 35" goal—raising electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035.

Li Zhenguo, LONGi founder and Chief Technology Officer, has said on several occasions: "Benefiting the world means enabling any region and any user to access stable, affordable and clean electricity. This cannot be done with a single module, inverter or storage cabinet alone. It requires a complete technology system and ecosystem capabilities. The ultimate product of PV is not just electricity; it is people's ownership of energy."

Floria Wang, Head of Global Branding at LONGi, and Leon Zhang, Overseas Managing Director of LONGi, presented the new vision and explained its logic.

"A solar-storage technology company" means the business is no longer simply "solar plus storage" bolted together. Instead, it promotes native, deep integration of solar and storage. At the heart of "benefiting the world" is not just delivering power to more places, but giving ordinary people the right to use clean energy conveniently and earn a return from it. LONGi believes that through continuous innovation, we make clean energy more affordable, reliable and accessible. With every step forward, we help build a better world.

"Technology only matters when it truly benefits people," Leon Zhang said. About 600 million people in Africa still lack grid access. "If Africa is left behind, the energy transition cannot be truly global." Integrated solar-storage systems are a key lever for bridging the energy divide and strengthening climate resilience, he said. As AI power demand surges, LONGi ONE will also explore new ways to coordinate generation, storage and computing.

Since proposing "Solar for Solar" at COP24 in 2018, LONGi has taken part in successive UN Climate Conferences and has prioritized real project results over vague pledges. As of the third quarter of 2026, LONGi's solar-storage strategy is accelerating: module shipments have returned to No. 1, cumulative storage orders exceed 3 GWh, and projects are in more than 160 countries and regions across Europe, Australia, Africa and Latin America.

"Technological innovation makes clean energy within reach; open cooperation lets sustainable development take root." LONGi said it will continue to innovate in solar-storage technology and expand global green-energy cooperation, working with governments, development agencies and local partners to tackle financing, O&M and talent bottlenecks—so that stable, reliable green energy can truly benefit more ordinary people and help build a fairer, more sustainable global energy future.

text:
The Orlando Utilities Commission on Nov. 11 released management’s recommendations for the utility’s Electric Integrated Resource Plan, a long-term roadmap for meeting Central Florida’s future energy needs.

OUC noted that the EIRP reflects changing fuel markets, technology, customer demand, and generation resources.

The recommended portfolio supports OUC’s priorities by improving reliability, maintaining affordability, advancing clean energy goals, and strengthening resiliency through a more diverse energy mix.

The Florida public power utility also said that the recommended portfolio supports OUC’s long-term CO2 reduction goals through investments in solar energy, battery storage, energy efficiency, conservation programs, demand-side management, and emerging technologies. It also preserves flexibility to adopt future carbon-free technologies as they become available.

In addition, as fuel markets, technology, customer demand, and economic conditions continue to evolve, the recommended portfolio provides the flexibility needed to adapt while maintaining reliable, affordable, and sustainable service.

Meanwhile, analysis showed that upgrading Stanton Units 1 and 2 to operate fully on either coal or natural gas is more cost-effective than building new power plants or converting the units entirely to natural gas. This flexibility helps manage fuel price fluctuations and supply disruptions, supporting long-term affordability for customers, OUC noted.

More Extreme Weather Is Increasing the Focus on Resiliency

Recent winter and summer weather events have increased peak energy demand and challenged utilities across Florida.

Combined with expected growth in large electrical loads, these trends highlight the need for greater resiliency.

As a result, OUC is increasing its reserve margin from 15% to 20% to help ensure reliable service during periods of high demand.

Stakeholder and Community Input Helped Shape the Recommended Plan

Stakeholder engagement was a key part of the EIRP process, OUC noted.

Feedback from the 2025 and 2026 OUC Voice of the Customer surveys, ongoing Community Working Group discussions, and a public workshop informed the recommended portfolio and reinforced OUC’s commitment to transparency and meaningful community involvement, it said.

The final portfolio will be presented to the OUC Board for consideration on December 15, 2026.

The Donald Trump administration is pushing to limit ESG (Environmental, Responsibility, and Transparent Management) funds in investment products of retirement pensions. President Donald Trump is controversial as he continues his anti-environmental policy move to abolish the previous administration's eco-friendly policies not only in the first but also in the second term. Conflicts with President Trump are expected to be inevitable as the Democratic Party, which dominated the House and Senate through the midterm elections, is foreshadowing an eco-friendly stance.

According to CNBC on the 23rd (local time), the U.S. Department of Labor announced a regulatory reform plan to limit ESG fund investment in retirement pension products such as 401k. ESG funds consist of companies that are active in responding to climate change. It is also called a sustainable fund, an impact fund, etc.

Currently, 401k operators are allowed to choose ESG funds for social benefit reasons if the general fund and ESG fund are tied as a result of financial comparisons when choosing retirement pension products. Under the amendment, the return on investment funds becomes a top consideration.

"The rule reaffirms the principle that those who choose retirement pension investment products should make decisions only for the financial interests of workers and retirees, not to pursue a political and social agenda," said Labor Minister Keith Sonderling. An official from the Ministry of Labor said, "All trustees will determine whether impact funds or ESG funds are suitable for retirement pensions, but I think there will be few." In fact, he hinted at excluding ESG funds.

According to the retirement pension council (PSCA), only 5% of 401k products provide ESG funds as of last year. ESG funds account for 1% of all 401k investment assets. Preference for pension investment products is already low due to the uncertainty that policies on ESG funds have changed rapidly with each regime change.

Therefore, it is analyzed that this move is actually part of the former Joe Biden administration's eco-friendly policy 'erase'. Previously, during the first Trump administration in 2020, ESG investment restrictions were introduced, and when the Biden administration eased them in 2022, it will revert this time. CNBC analyzed, "This revision is an attack on ESG and other work policies in the Trump administration's push to make it easier to incorporate alternative investments such as private equity funds into retirement pensions."

However, some predict that the return on ESG funds may be higher than that of general funds. According to Morgan Stanley, the average return on ESG funds in the first half of this year is 4.9%, higher than that of general funds (4%).

President Trump has been abolishing eco-friendly policies since he took office last year. After taking office, he announced his withdrawal from the Paris Climate Agreement, a global climate agreement, and made it a reality in January this year. The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), a representative eco-friendly policy of the Biden administration, has actually become a piece of paper under the Trump administration. With the aim of reducing greenhouse gases, the main contents include wind and solar support and tax credits of up to $7,500 for electric vehicles.

Electric vehicle subsidies were abolished in October last year, and vehicle sales plunged due to soaring prices. President Trump also suspended large-scale wind and solar projects with executive orders, sparking controversy. Since then, the court has invalidated it, leading to a conflict. Through the 'One Big and Beautiful Act (OBBBA), a large-scale tax cut bill, tax credits for solar power projects were drastically reduced.

"A few days after taking office last year, President Trump announced his withdrawal from the Paris Climate Agreement, blocked subsidies for electric vehicles, pushed for fossil fuel production, and is fighting back against the previous administration's diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) policies," said Diana Iovernell, chief economist at Capital Economics.

As the Democratic Party of Korea takes control of the upper and lower houses, it is a variable that the situation of the women's and women's parties will unfold from January next year. The Democratic Party is already signaling a revival of various systems that the Trump administration has suspended or abolished, including eco-friendly policies. The Democratic Party has already proposed a bill that doubled subsidies from $7,500 to $15,000 when purchasing new electric vehicles.

However, there are concerns that uncertainty will increase if there is a series of policy conflicts with the Democratic Party as President Trump is in a position to actively exercise his veto power to confront the Democratic Party's superior Congress.

text:
By Noah Haggerty

A sweeping bipartisan bill that seeks to prevent catastrophic wildfires and restore fire-ravaged forests has revealed a schism in the nation’s environmental movement as some conservation advocates find themselves allied with a longtime foe: loggers.

The Fix Our Forests Act, which Congress is close to passing, aims to speed up forest management projects on public and tribal lands by reducing regulatory and legal hurdles.

The proposed legislation comes at a time of increasingly devastating wildfires and has garnered wide support among Republicans and the timber industry.

However, the traditional Democratic coalition of environmental groups is split over the role humanity has to play in forest management. Some argue ecosystems are best protected when humans leave them alone — a view that dominated during the timber wars of the ’80s and ’90s. Others argue that humans have a responsibility to intervene — an increasingly popular idea as climate change threatens ecosystems around the world.

Among the major environmental groups that oppose the legislation are the Sierra Club and Center for Biological Diversity. They worry that limiting environmental review and litigation will allow timber companies to heavily log these areas instead of gently thinning them. Meanwhile, some Southern California groups worry the bill would allow well-meaning land managers to approve misguided projects that ultimately harm local shrublands, which have a very different relationship with fire than the bill’s namesake, forests.

“It’s really handing the keys to the Trump administration to be able to push forward a lot of their timber agenda,” said Anna Medema, deputy legislative director for forests and public lands at the Sierra Club.

But the Nature Conservancy and other groups have voiced support for the bill, citing the constant and imminent threat that increasingly severe wildfires pose to communities and ecosystems.

“We do advocacy at a twofold level. We are doing defensive work to fight back against bad things, and we’re also trying to promote the good things that are happening on the ground,” said Morgan Cashwell, North America director of legislative affairs for the Nature Conservancy. Right now, that good work needs to “meet the moment in the current wildfire crisis.”

That sentiment appears to have motivated Western lawmakers in particular.

In the House of Representatives, roughly half of the Democrats from Western states voted for the bill, compared to about a quarter of Democrats from elsewhere in the country. Republicans voted overwhelmingly in favor. The legislation is now awaiting a final vote in the Senate. Congress has until Jan. 3, 2027, to pass it.

“Wildfires today are very different than wildfires from a generation ago,” said Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), who co-introduced the Senate version of the bill. “Oftentimes, they’re irreversibly devastating ecosystems and watersheds.”

“So,” he said, “ the status quo is clearly not working.”

The act was born when Rep. Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.), a former forester, stole a seat on a plane next to Rep. Scott Peters (D-San Diego). He used the opportunity to talk Peters’ ear off about a beloved species of tree that is under threat from worsening wildfires: the giant sequoia.

The two introduced a bill to protect them, called the Save Our Sequoias Act, and quickly saw an opportunity for something bigger.

“I knew right away that this could be a gateway to talking about permit reform,” Peters said. So, “we started working on a bigger, nationwide reform of forestry practices which have been really, really clogged up.”

While California grasslands, shrublands and woodlands are adapted to different frequencies and intensities of wildfire, research has found that high-severity fires — which kill the vast majority of trees in their path — are scorching 30 times more land area than in the 1980s.

The result: California is losing, on average, more than 200,000 acres of forest every year — or roughly 2.5% of all woodlands in the state every decade. U.S. Forest Service efforts to resuscitate these ecosystems have failed to keep pace. In recent years, the agency has reforested only about 1% of woodlands that are unlikely to recover on their own.

Californian supporters of the Fix Our Forests Act argue the problem has more to do with permitting delays than finances.

Rep. George Whitesides (D-Santa Clarita), who co-sponsored the Fix Our Forests Act, pointed to nonpartisan research that found it takes the Forest Service more than five years on average to complete a full environmental review and begin work on forest thinning projects that use mechanical equipment like bulldozers and wood chippers. For prescribed burns, it takes more than seven years on average.

“That’s insane,” he said, that it “takes as long as a kid growing up to be a first grader to be able to move on this.”

The Fix Our Forests Act would exempt projects from the full permitting process if they were in areas with the most extreme fire risk and would expand existing exemptions for projects under 3,000 acres to cover projects up to 10,000 acres. It also would limit the window during which environmental groups can sue over project approvals.

These projects tend to employ a combination of harvesting timber and thinning smaller trees and plants with heavy machinery (often the favored tools of Republicans and the timber industry) and using prescribed fire to clear out the forest floor (often favored by environmental groups).

The “environmental left” has “made it endlessly time-consuming and ultimately cost prohibitive to maintain our forests, all with the promise that this would improve the forest environment,” said Rep. Tom McClintock (R-Elk Grove), a co-sponsor who authored some of the permitting exclusions. “Well, after 50 years, I think we’re entitled to ask, how’s the forest environment doing?”

In March 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that blamed “our inability to fully exploit our domestic timber supply” as a contributor to disastrous wildfires. In response, the U.S. Forest Service set a goal to increase the amount of timber open to logging by 25% nationwide over five years.

Scott Dane, executive director of the American Loggers Council, argued the nightmare scenarios of expansive clear-cutting from the timber wars are not on the table for America’s public lands.

“It’s a boogeyman position that they love to take from 100 years ago,” he said. “It’s not, in reality, in modern forest management at all.”

Watchdogs in Southern California have a different concern: While research shows forest thinning is an effective tool in overgrown Sierra Nevada woodlands, the state’s coastal shrublands are not denser than they historically have been. Consequently, the type of projects the Fix Our Forests Act would expedite are far more controversial and contested in shrublands. Local advocates fear the act would undermine their ability to push back on proposals with questionable scientific backing.

In contrast to projects in conifer forests that aim to decrease the density of trees and vegetation across the landscape, shrubland projects are typically centered on creating a network of corridors hundreds of feet wide with no vegetation throughout the wildlands and clearing plants away from existing buildings.

While firefighters rely on these networks of fuel breaks to access the wildlands during fires and build containment lines, research has found that when firefighters cannot reach the fuel breaks — which is often the case during extreme winds — the lines only stop fires about 13% of the time. If they are not routinely maintained, they also risk supporting the growth of flammable invasive grasses.

In Los Padres National Forest, near Santa Barbara, officials proposed in 2022 creating roughly 187,000 acres of fuel breaks and structure defense zones. After organizations like Los Padres ForestWatch pushed back on the plan through the environmental review process, the national forest ultimately scaled the proposal down to about 22,000 acres this July.

“You had community input, and you had the federal government incorporating that input into a plan that is grossly improved,” said Benjamin Pitterle, director of advocacy and field operations at Los Padres ForestWatch. “It’s arguably a perfect example of how the process should work.”

title: North Carolina households face higher Duke Energy bills starting in 2027 - Yahoo
description:
Stock_Market_Visuals/Depositphotos Duke Energy changes start in 2027 North Carolina households served by Duke Energy will face higher electricity rates beginning Jan. 1, 2027.
Depositphotos Progress customers face the biggest jump Duke Energy Progress customers will see the larger first-year increase in monthly bills.
Over the two-year period, Duke Energy Progress residential rates will increase by an average of about 4.7% annually, compared with 4.8% for Duke Energy Carolinas.
Depositphotos Two utilities become one Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress are scheduled to operate as one combined utility beginning Jan. 1, 2027.
Depositphotos North Carolina growth adds demand North Carolina's continued population and business growth is increasing electricity demand across Duke Energy's system.
text:
Stock_Market_Visuals/Depositphotos

Duke Energy changes start in 2027

North Carolina households served by Duke Energy will face higher electricity rates beginning Jan. 1, 2027. The North Carolina Utilities Commission approved the increases on Nov. 16, 2026, covering both of Duke Energy's major service territories.

The adjustment will not happen all at once, because another increase takes effect Jan. 1, 2028. That two-step schedule gives customers separate rate changes over two years rather than a single, larger adjustment immediately.

Depositphotos

Progress customers face the biggest jump

Duke Energy Progress customers will see the larger first-year increase in monthly bills. A typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours each month is projected to pay $9.62 more starting Jan. 1, 2027.

The next increase arrives Jan. 1, 2028, adding another $5.89 to that example. Together, the increases amount to an additional $15.51 per month by 2028, the larger of the two utilities' projected monthly bill increases for the same electricity usage.

Depositphotos

Carolinas customers see a smaller rise

The increase for Duke Energy Carolinas customers is lower in dollar terms. A household using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month is projected to pay an additional $6.53 beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

Starting Jan. 1, 2028, another $4.66 will be added under the approved plan. That brings the combined monthly increase to $11.19 by 2028, meaning Duke Energy Carolinas customers will face a smaller dollar increase than Progress customers using the same amount of electricity.

Depositphotos

Percentages show the broader picture

The approved orders also outline average annual rate increases for residential customers. Over the two-year period, Duke Energy Progress residential rates will increase by an average of about 4.7% annually, compared with 4.8% for Duke Energy Carolinas.

These percentages differ from the specific dollar amounts based on 1,000 kilowatt-hours. They provide a broader view of the approved residential rate changes rather than predicting the exact increase for every individual household.

Depositphotos

Bills were already a household concern

Electricity costs were already a significant monthly expense for many North Carolina households before these new rates were approved. Federal data show the state's average residential electric bill was about $143.50 per month in 2024.

That statewide average includes customers served by multiple electricity providers, not just Duke Energy. Higher electricity bills could place additional pressure on household budgets already stretched by housing, groceries, transportation, insurance, and other everyday expenses.

Fun fact: North Carolina ranks fourth nationwide in total residential-sector electricity use, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

MauriceNorbert/Depositphotos

The original request was much higher

The final increases are substantially lower than the amounts Duke Energy initially proposed. The earlier request projected a $23.11 monthly first-year increase for a typical Progress customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity.

For a comparable Carolinas customer, the original first-year increase was projected at $17.22. Negotiations with the North Carolina Public Staff and other stakeholders helped reduce the proposed increases before the commission approved the final rate plans.

Depositphotos

Two utilities become one

Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress are scheduled to operate as one combined utility beginning Jan. 1, 2027. Regulators previously approved the combination, which the company says should reduce duplicated costs over time.

The merger does not immediately erase the two existing retail rate structures. Instead, rates are expected to gradually blend through future rate cases and rider filings, meaning customers in different service areas may continue to pay different prices for some time.

Depositphotos

North Carolina growth adds demand

North Carolina's continued population and business growth is increasing electricity demand across Duke Energy's system. The company says serving that growth requires investment in power generation and upgrades to the electric grid.

Recent work has included new and replaced distribution poles, additional wiring, and wider use of self-healing grid technology. Regulators review those investments when deciding which costs can be recovered through customer rates and how those costs should be allocated.

Depositphotos

Data centers get a separate rate class

Data centers with electricity demand exceeding 50 megawatts will fall under a separate rate schedule. These facilities often require substantial generating capacity and infrastructure investments to support their operations.

The new rate structure is intended to protect existing electricity customers from the additional costs and financial risks associated with serving large data centers.

snehitdesign/Depositphotos

Reserved power now carries a minimum cost

Covered data centers must pay demand charges based on at least 75% of their contracted electricity demand. That rule still applies when actual power use falls below the amount of capacity reserved for the facility.

Data centers above 100 megawatts also face minimum 15-year contracts. Together, these requirements give the utility more predictable payments when it commits resources and capacity to unusually large customers.

Depositphotos

New facilities require financial backing

The approved framework also addresses the infrastructure built specifically for large data-center projects. Covered customers must make upfront payments for dedicated facilities needed to connect and serve their operations.

Data centers must also provide financial guarantees for transmission upgrades and may face charges if they end their contracts early. These requirements are designed to reduce the risk of existing customers paying for infrastructure that is no longer needed.

postmodernstudio/Depositphotos

Shareholders fund added assistance

The approved outcome includes $20 million in new funding from Duke Energy shareholders to support customers in need. That assistance is separate from money collected through the new residential electricity rates.

The funding will support electricity bill assistance through the Share the Light Fund and eligible home health and safety repairs through the Helping Home Fund. These programs provide additional support to households facing financial difficulties.

Curious how another utility is planning for growing power demand? See what's behind South Dakota's proposed $300 million natural gas project.

Depositphotos

Your bill may differ from examples

Individual electricity bills may increase by different amounts depending on household consumption and applicable rates. The approved orders also provide for customer refunds with interest if Duke Energy fails to complete scheduled infrastructure improvements on time.

Actual bills depend heavily on electricity consumption, which can change with weather, home size, insulation, appliances, and heating or cooling needs. Customers can get a better estimate by comparing their own recent monthly usage with the new rates once they take effect.

text:
LANSING — Gov. Gretchen Whitmer has ordered her state agencies to stop processing requested resource and wastewater permits for Enbridge's oil pipeline tunnel project under the Straits of Mackinac, freezing state resources for the project "until legal questions are resolved."

The order comes after the Michigan Supreme Court in July upended a key permit from the Michigan Public Service Commission, finding that the agency had failed to consider how the continued consumption of hydrocarbons would impact the environment and what potential alternatives could address that consumption.

Following that decision, Whitmer in September ordered other permits issued through the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy to be reconsidered in light of the high court's decision, and urged Enbridge to remove its underwater pipelines from the bottom of the lakebed in the waterway connecting Lakes Michigan and Huron.

With the new directive issued Tuesday, Whitmer is halting consideration of the EGLE permit altogether for Enbridge's Great Lakes Tunnel Project.

"Given what is at stake, and the Michigan Supreme Court's recent decision, I have directed EGLE to suspend further action on its Line 5 Tunnel Project permits at this time," Whitmer said. "Michigan will continue to put the protection of our water, environment, public health, and communities first."

Enbridge, in a statement, noted it has been pursuing permits for the tunnel to relocate Line 5 since 2018, but the high court's July decision introduced "new uncertainty."

"The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy issued permits in July 2026 and previously in 2021," said Ryan Duffy, a spokesman for the Canadian pipeline giant. "Both permitting rounds included detailed technical reviews, public meetings, hearings, and consideration of thousands of public comments. They also involved extensive interaction between Michigan's tribal leaders and state agencies."

The Michigan League of Conservation Voters applauded Whitmer's decision to freeze the permits, calling it a "significant win."

"The ultimate goal must be getting Line 5 out of the Great Lakes altogether and pursuing proven alternatives to meet our region's energy needs, and we encourage Gov. Whitmer to work with Governor-elect Benson to get oil out of our Great Lakes once and for all," said Bentley Johnson, federal government affairs director for the league.

The decision, Whitmer said in a statement, acknowledges the time it will take for Enbridge to seek a new permit from the MPSC that incorporates the issues the Michigan Supreme Court said must be addressed.

It's not clear what legal questions the governor would like resolved before EGLE can resume its consideration of the permits. The governor's statement on the matter did not say which of the several legal processes Whitmer was waiting on and her office declined comment when asked to clarify.

While the governor delays reconsideration, the state and Enbridge remain essentially at a stalemate while the twin spans of Line 5 continue to pump thousands of barrels of light crude oil a day along the lake bottom. Line 5's twin underwater pipelines, now 73 years old, are located at the bottom of Lake Michigan just west of the Mackinac Bridge.

The state is now more than eight years out from an initial agreement Republican former Gov. Rick Snyder had reached with Enbridge for the construction of a tunnel beneath the straits to house a new segment of Line 5.

Initial plans for the tunnel anticipated a 2024 completion.

But the project has been beset by litigation and permitting delays ever since Snyder left office, with both Whitmer and Attorney General Dana Nessel bringing legal challenges that seek to shut down the Straits of Mackinac pipeline segment completely.

So far, those legal efforts have largely been unsuccessful. A federal judge in December said Michigan lacked the authority to shut down the line. His order is being appealed to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals, which will hear oral arguments on the matter Dec. 15.

In October 2021, Canada invoked a never-before-used treaty to stop the state from attempting to shutter the pipeline.

text:
Today, U.S. Representative Salud Carbajal (D-CA-24) released the statement below announcing he cannot support the Senate-passed energy permitting bill, known as BAAJA. As the bill moves forward in the House, Carbajal will push to address the concerns raised by environmental groups and Tribal leaders.

“The Central Coast has always been a leader in environmental protection. From spearheading the recovery after the devastating 2015 Refugio oil spill to establishing the Chumash Heritage National Marine Sanctuary and fighting back against Sable Offshore’s push to restart their aging pipeline, our community knows firsthand how hard it is to secure environmental protections, and how dangerous it can be to give them up.

“That is why I cannot support the Senate’s energy permitting bill, BAAJA, as it is currently written.

“Make no mistake: I want our country to invest in clean energy, modernize our outdated electric grid, and lower utility bills for working families. BAAJA includes several worthwhile provisions such as upgrading the transmission lines we need to ramp up the clean energy build-out and placing tough restrictions on Big Tech’s data centers. Those are commonsense reforms that I support and want to see become law.

“However, I am concerned about the potential impact of other parts of the bill. Federal approvals for fossil fuel projects — including offshore oil and gas leases — would be locked in and shielded from future oversight. At the same time, the bill weakens scientific standards for endangered species, limits California’s ability to safeguard its own water, and undermines historic preservation rules that Chumash leaders and Tribal nations rely on to protect sacred sites.

“While I appreciate the good-faith efforts from some of our Senate colleagues who worked to bring forward a compromise, the House now has the opportunity — and in my view, the responsibility — to fix the serious flaws in this bill. I will be pushing to strengthen protections for our coastline, water, environmental oversight, and Tribal nations so our country can benefit from the clean energy transition without leaving communities and our environment behind.”

text:
British auto startup Ineos Automotive is getting an American accent.

The maker of the rugged, luxury Grenadier SUV and Quartermaster pickup announced Tuesday, Nov. 24 that it will move manufacturing to the United States from France. Ineos opened one of its first U.S. dealerships with the Feldman Automotive Group in Waterford Township in late 2024. It said it will make an assembly site announcement in the next few months with production beginning in 2028.

“This is arguably the biggest moment in the history of Ineos Automotive,” said London-based CEO Lynn Calder. “Americans have already taken the Grenadier to their hearts, and U.S. policies have created an incredibly attractive, pro-growth business environment. Setting up production there makes so much sense. It will empower us to invest, expand, and reach even more customers around the world.”

If plans are consummated, Ineos would be the latest in a wave of new assembly in the U.S. Ineos follows announcements by Audi (new plant in Alabama), Honda (new Ohio plant, reshored Civic production from Mexico to Indiana), Jeep (reshored to Illinois from Canada), Toyota (Texas expansion to reshore Tacoma from Mexico), General Motors (Equinox SUV to move from Mexico to Kansas and Buick Envision from China to Kansas), and more.

Automakers cite stepped-up Trump administration tariffs, auto market deregulation, and proximity to U.S. customers for the moves. With 70% of its sales in the U.S., Ineos has experienced double-digit sales growth this year riding Americans' lust for off-road vehicles.

The Trump administration has increased tariffs on European Union imports in the last two years from 2.5% to 15% on passenger vehicles like the $73,745 Grenadier. In addition to that, the $86,390 Quartermaster faced a daunting 25% tariff on non-North American-produced pickup trucks. The so-called 25% “chicken tax” has protected domestic truck production since the 1960s. Production of nearly all of Quartermaster’s competitors, including Toyota, Honda, Nissan, and Detroit Three midsize pickups, is done in the United States.

“This is a pattern we are seeing,” said Karl Brauer, senior auto analyst for iSeeCars.com. “Ineos is the latest example of an automaker moving production to the U.S. due to U.S. tariff policy.”

Ineos follows startups Slate (Indiana) and Rivian Automotive Inc. (Illinois) with domestic production, but it has deified the ealy-20th-c electric startup trend. Powered by inline-6 cylinder internal-combustion-engines, Ineos is targeting the premium adventure market — specifically Land Rover customers after the fellow British maker stopped assembling ladder-frame vehicles.

Consumer reaction has been favorable, with 4,700 units sold in the U.S. through the third quarter of 2026 (second year in market) up 42% from 2025’s third quarter and 20% year-to-date. The Grenadier also has been embraced by auto media, winning the coveted best Off-Road SUV award from the Texas Auto Writers Association as well as 2026 Adventure Car of the Year at the News UK Motor Awards. Grenadier also has pursued production for military vehicle fleets as well as African safaris. Ineos founder and chairman Sir Jim Radcliffe hatched the Ineos idea after Land Rover abandoned its safari-friendly, ladder-frame Defender construction.

The brand’s gas-powered strategy, however, runs headlong into the European Union’s ban on ICE vehicles by 2035.

By contrast, Washington has coupled its tariff policies with a deregulation of the U.S. market from EU-like federal and California emissions policies aimed at banning the sale of ICE models. Congressional legislation last year, for example, nixed the Golden State’s ability to regulate greenhouse gases.

California has previously mandated that 35% of sales be electric vehicles by the 2026 model year — a regulation that would have severely punished small ICE automakers like Ineos.

“Larger, gas-powered vehicles like Ineos makes were really feeling the government regulations,” said Brauer. “Locating in the U.S. is now the best possible existence for Ineos. They avoid tariffs, produce vehicles Americans want, and operate in a regulatory environment that is favorable to their products.”

In an interview with The Detroit News at Ineos’ U.S. launch in March 2025, CEO Calder addressed the looming complications of the new Trump administration’s tariffs.

“(Tariffs are) a huge worry particularly the levels (Trump) is talking about. We could absorb (a small) tariff giving the size of this market,” she said of the 25% tariff-on-EU-imports in play at the time. That number was reduced to 15% and, in the case of Audi — which recently announced its own $4 billion Alabama investment — to a reported 10% on its remaining imports.

In addition to the entrenched 25% pickup tax, the U.S. imposed similar protectionist measure on foreign automakers in the 1980s under the Reagan administration and a Democratic Congress led on the issue by Michigan’s Rep. John Dingell. The result was a wave of foreign transplant factories from the late 20th century onward by Honda, Toyota, Nissan, Mazda, Hyundai, BMW, Mercedes, Volvo and Volkswagen that now make up about 50% of U.S. auto production.

Calder was more concerned about the EU’s regulatory direction.

“It’s insane. It’s important for the industry to be regulated, (but) there is something about this particular industry that has gone a bit mad,” the CEO said of the EU ICE ban, with Ineos’ home country of Great Britain banning non-hybrid ICE sales like Ineos models by 2030.

“The policy is all wrong,” she continued. “In Europe and the UK right now they want it to be one-size-fits-all, and it’s breaking the industry.”

Ineos said it is in negotiations with Chinese automaker BYD to sell its Hambach, France assembly facility. Ineos bought Hambach from Mercedes where it once built Smart brand cars.

Henry Payne is auto critic for The Detroit News. Find him at hpayne@detroitnews.com or @HenryEPayne.

text:
Economic growth and the push towards the decarbonisation of energy are often seen as competing agendas in some quarters.

But as technology advances and the price of solar energy, in particular, becomes more economical, does that particular argument still hold much weight?

Agnes Dasewicz, who becomes the new chief executive of the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet in January 2027, said economic development and energy decarbonisation should not be mutually exclusive, in an interview.

Dasewicz added that by linking the two of them, clean energy can become a catalyst for jobs, sustainable livelihoods and economic growth.

For example, she said reliable clean energy coupled with productive use such as refrigeration and agricultural processing drives community income and economic activities while reducing carbon emissions.

"We have 3.5 billion people in the world still lacking reliable, affordable electricity," she told me.

"There are also 1.2 billion young people in developing economies who are going to reach working age over the next decade, but only 400 million new jobs are expected to be created."

"Solar is the most affordable and fastest kind of energy right now to be delivered to many communities. It is becoming much more affordable and faster to deploy solar, and we have communities where economic growth can really be accelerated by using these energy systems."

Dasewicz added that large scale alliances with cooperation among governments, utilities, investors and businesses are needed to overcome barriers, scale solutions, and ultimately transform energy systems.

In particular, she said there needs to be more cooperation between electricity and allied sectors such as water, health and education, which often operate independently.

She pointed to the example of Rajasthan in India, where Global Energy Alliance is supporting the state government to provide solar power to farmers and their communities, delivering reliable energy and increasing productivity.

A combination of digital innovation and on-the-ground outreach to farmers successfully accelerated the scaling of the government's existing agri-solarization initiative, installing more than 530,000 new solar-powered irrigation pumps and reaching more than a million farmers with clean energy.

"Energy systems are changing, and they are changing rapidly," said Dasewicz. "Both the demand and the supply of those systems will be very different from what we currently have in 10 years' time, with more distributed energy and mini grids.

"We have to make sure countries are aware of what is happening and are not planning their energy systems using the old assumptions but are really thinking about how energy will be delivered and distributed in the future."

A report published last year by Oxford University's Smith School of Enterprise and Environment claimed a rapid switch to renewables could boost the GDP of low-to-middle income economies by around 10%.

It added renewable energy productivity gains are much higher in the Global South, and claimed clean energy could finally start to close the income gap between rich and poor countries.

The analysis also showed spending on renewables between 2017-2022 boosted the GDP of the 100 largest developing countries by a combined US $1.2 trillion.

The school's interim director, Professor Sam Fankhauser said the perception that renewables are expensive is a legacy from a decade ago, when they cost more than fossil fuels, in an interview.

Professor Fankhauser added renewables are now much cheaper than fossil fuels on a generational basis, although old contracts can still keep prices high in some cases.

He said investment in renewables can provide a "Keynesian" fiscal boost to countries, particularly in the Global South, triggering new jobs and increased spending.

Although Professor Fankhauser said there are still some roadblocks to the further rollout of renewables and electrification, most notably the absence of cheap capital in the Global South.

"Most new electricity investment does go into renewables," he told me.

"We are still paying for the expensive renewables of between 10 and 15 years ago, but we should think of those high costs as the cost of learning. Everything from now on will be cheaper.

"In renewables, the tipping point is here and by 2035, every new car will be an electric vehicle, just because it makes economic sense," he added.

"These market trends will hasten the transition away from fossil fuels much more decisively than any COP declaration."

Aurélien Saussay, an assistant professor at the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, said growth and decarbonisation do not need to be traded off against each other.

Saussay added for European countries which depend on imported oil and gas, switching to clean energy improves the trade balance by keeping that spending in the domestic economy, thereby raising GDP.

"I would be more cautious on job creation," he added. "Building solar panels will not employ 1.2 billion young people by itself, so it's right to focus on how the electricity gets used. Training workers is hard to do at the pace required.

"We also found that a 2% wage premium for green tasks in Europe (5% when comparing green and non-green roles within the same firm and occupation), which is too small on its own to persuade people to retrain."

This article was originally published on Forbes.com
