title: Trump should challenge the EU's carbon border tax without importing its climate policy
description:
To remedy the EU’s discriminatory and extraterritorial regulation, PMI advises the USTR to seek “an exemption for goods of U.S. origin,” not impose “reciprocal” fees (aka carbon border taxes or tariffs).
The US government cannot adopt carbon border taxes without sooner or later adopting domestic carbon taxes.
Some self-styled trade hawks may suppose carbon border taxes need not facilitate the enactment of domestic carbon taxes.
First, by promising protection from less regulated foreign competition, a carbon border tax saps industry’s will to fight costly and infeasible domestic climate policies.
Conclusion In the 119th Congress, President Trump and the outgoing GOP majority achieved numerous energy policy victories.
text:
The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) could make hundreds of US products less competitive in EU markets. Should the US government respond, and if so, how? The US Trade Representative (USTR) recently invited public comment on that question and three others regarding the CBAM’s current and potential adverse effects on US businesses.

In comments of exemplary thoroughness and precision, our colleagues at the Prime Mover Institute (PMI) urge the USTR to investigate, pursuant to Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, whether the CBAM violates US rights “under any trade agreement,” unjustifiably “burdens or restricts” US commerce, or regulates how goods are made in the US and other nations outside the EU’s jurisdiction. To remedy the EU’s discriminatory and extraterritorial regulation, PMI advises the USTR to seek “an exemption for goods of U.S. origin,” not impose “reciprocal” fees (aka carbon border taxes or tariffs).

Why not? Because adopting a US carbon border mechanism “would establish the EU as the default environmental regulator by conceding its preferred form of regulation, and also require federal carbon accounting, at odds with the policy of American energy dominance.” My comments to the USTR emphasize that point, as does this post.

Background

The EU CBAM requires importers of certain commodities and products to report the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with producing those goods. Importers must also pay a charge on those emissions by buying and surrendering CBAM certificates priced in line with emissions allowances under the EU’s multi-sector cap-and-trade program, known as the Emissions Trading System (ETS).

Importers can pass on some of their CBAM costs by raising the price of imported goods. The system’s overall effect on US producers is thus to make their goods more expensive and less competitive in EU markets. As US Ambassador to the EU Adam Puzder put it, the CBAM is a protective tariff “by another name.”

Although CBAM certificates do not go on sale until February 1, 2027, and importers do not have to surrender CBAM certificates until September 30, 2027, covered imports began incurring CBAM obligations on January 1, 2026. Some importers may already be marking up prices to cover their 2026 CBAM obligations. For example, Swedish importer and wholesaler Bossard applies a CBAM surcharge to goods imported as of January 1, 2026.

Currently, the CBAM covers products in six sector categories: aluminum, cement, electricity, fertilizer, hydrogen, and iron and steel. However, that is just the first phase. In December 2025, the European Commission proposed to expand CBAM coverage to more than 180 steel and aluminum downstream products (see Annex I), requiring an additional 7,000-7,100 importers to cover the new product categories.

Nor does it end there. As reported by the USTR, in June 2026, the Council of the EU proposed to expand the CBAM product list by approximately 300 downstream products. Then, in September 2026, the European Parliament adopted an amendment that would expand CBAM coverage to approximately 400 downstream products. The Commission, Council, and Parliament are currently in “trilogue” negotiations to determine the final product list.

Extra-territorial regulation

Because CBAM requirements apply to EU importers, the EU claims it is simply exercising its sovereignty over European markets and not engaging in extraterritorial regulation of US firms (see slides 5 and 20 of this presentation). Not so.

In the first place, under the CBAM, US firms incur de facto obligations, neither enacted by Congress nor adopted by any federal agency, to collect, verify, and report company-specific emissions data. Non-EU firms have the option to rely on estimates of sector-wide emission intensity averages but there are significant cost penalties for failing to provide company-level data. The CBAM markup penalties for cement, aluminum, iron and steel, and hydrogen are 10 percent in 2026, 20 percent in 2027, and 30 percent from 2028 onward (see Annex I).

More fundamentally, “creating incentives for the reduction of emissions by operators in third countries” is a core function of the CBAM (Article 1.1). In other words, the CBAM puts pressure on firms outside the EU’s jurisdiction to change their production processes. As discussed below, a major objective of the CBAM is to “level the playing field” between EU firms subject to carbon pricing penalties and non-EU firms that are not. The EU has shot itself in the foot by raising its firms’ energy-related production costs. So, through the CBAM, the EU seeks to impose such costs on competitors in the US and other countries that prioritize energy affordability and economic growth.

The US government should fight back against this attack on our competitiveness, prosperity, and sovereignty. As explained below, though, US policymakers should not try to fight fire with fire by establishing a US CBAM. Although that may sound “patriotic” or “reciprocal,” it would cede victory to the EU by assimilating our energy policy choices to theirs. The CBAM by design pressures other governments to emulate EU carbon pricing and the associated commitments to Net Zero emission reduction targets. In brief, the EU wants us to shoot ourselves in the foot, too.

Mythology of embedded emissions

The CBAM repeatedly describes its fees as applying to the emissions “embedded” in imported goods or input materials. But production process emissions do not embed in products. The carbon intensity of a can of Diet Coke is entirely in the cola, not in the fuel sources used to make the can.

Process emissions are irrelevant to the health, safety, or environmental characteristics of the product. If US products posed actual health, safety, or environmental hazards to people who handle or purchase them, the EU would be within its sovereign rights to regulate their importation. CBAM charges have nothing to do with such hazards.

Embedded emissions are a fiction used to obfuscate the difference between regulating product quality and regulating foreign businesses and the domestic energy infrastructures on which they rely.

Overview of my comments

My comments to the USTR hit four main themes.

The US government cannot adopt carbon border taxes without sooner or later adopting domestic carbon taxes.

In today’s era of Green New Deal Net Zero climate ambition, a carbon tax “involves the power to destroy” the fossil fuels on which Americans depend for 82 percent of US energy.

The potential costs of carbon taxes far outweigh the potential benefits; hence, an administration that champions new taxes on energy invites fierce popular blowback.

Any policy that makes carbon intensity a touchstone of trade policy would also make it a decision factor in prices, contracts, investment decisions, corporate governance, and business lobbying, vitiating climate policy rollbacks achieved by President Trump and the 119th Congress.

The remainder of this post expands on the first bullet above, which is the linchpin of the argument.

Why border taxes lead to domestic carbon taxes

A key rationale for a CBAM is to “level the playing field” for manufacturers in countries that “put a price on carbon,” whether via carbon taxes or emissions trading schemes. The tax aims to mitigate losses domestic producers incur when competing with producers from countries with less stringent (or simply different) climate policies.

Some self-styled trade hawks may suppose carbon border taxes need not facilitate the enactment of domestic carbon taxes. Accordingly, they may think it smart to give the EU a dose of its own medicine. That is incorrect.

First, by promising protection from less regulated foreign competition, a carbon border tax saps industry’s will to fight costly and infeasible domestic climate policies. That is not mere theory. European industry’s unwillingness to organize opposition to the EU’s onerous Green Deal is partly due to border taxes being a core component of the program.

Second, enacting a policy that imposes carbon taxes solely on foreign-made goods would immediately trigger pressure campaigns for domestic carbon pricing by EU officials, green groups, renewable energy lobbyists, and blue-state politicians. They would likely invoke WTO Article III.2: “The products of the territory of any contracting party imported into the territory of any other contracting party shall not be subject, directly or indirectly, to internal taxes or other internal charges of any kind in excess of those applied, directly or indirectly, to like domestic products.”

Third, the qualifying US carbon price for offsetting CBAM tariff liability is not limited to product-specific emissions intensity charges. Qualifying prices also include emission taxes and tradable emission allowances (see Articles 3.29 and 9.1).

Fourth, imposing border charges on EU products does not offset the CBAM certificate prices that raise the cost of US imports. The only way to do that is to enact domestic US carbon prices (Article 9.1).

Fifth, although products with lower carbon intensities pay lower CBAM charges, having lower carbon intensities than equivalent EU products does not shield US exports from EU border charges. CBAM liability is determined by the imported good’s production process emissions multiplied by the EU ETS carbon price—not by the good’s carbon intensity compared to a competing EU good.

Sixth, since most US policymakers would rather have US firms pay taxes to the US Treasury than to EU member states (Article 20), establishing a US border tax system would likely revive lobbying for carbon taxes as a “green” solution to America’s fiscal woes.

Seventh, mere creation of an official manufacturing emissions intensity database could enable narrow partisan majorities to enact carbon taxes in future reconciliation proceedings. For example, in the Inflation Reduction Act, Democrats took an existing methane emissions reporting program and used the data to impose first-ever climate taxes on the oil and gas industry (IRA § 60113). They accomplished that feat through a Senate vote of 51-50, with Vice President Kamala Harris casting the tie breaker.

Conclusion

In the 119th Congress, President Trump and the outgoing GOP majority achieved numerous energy policy victories. Among the most important are:

Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and initiation of withdrawal from the UN Framework Convention;

Trump and Congress’s repeal of the Biden EPA waivers authorizing California’s zero-emission vehicle mandates;

The EPA’s rescission of the 2009 Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and repeal of all greenhouse gas emission standards for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty on-road vehicles;

Trump and Congress’s repeal of the Biden EPA rule implementing the IRA methane tax;

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s (OBBBA) postponement of the methane tax’s effective date from calendar year 2024 to calendar year 2034;

The OBBBA’s repeal and reduction of numerous IRA green subsidies;

The Interior Department’s acceleration of oil and gas lease sales;

The Securities and Exchange Commission’s abandonment and proposed rescission of its 2024 climate risk disclosure rule;

The Department of Energy’s termination of 321 awards supporting 223 wasteful projects, totaling approximately $7.56 billion;

The OBBBA’s reduction of the statutory Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) program penalties to $0.00 and the Department of Transportation’s reset of the CAFE program to ensure fuel economy standards do not compel vehicle electrification;

The EPA’s partial repeal of the Biden administration’s “carbon pollution standards” for coal and natural gas power plants and proposed rescission of Clean Air Act § 111 authority to regulate GHG emissions from US power plants; and

Trump’s disbanding of the Interagency Working Group on the Social Cost of Greenhouse Gases and the Office of Management and Budget’s subsequent determination that it is “no longer Federal government policy to maintain a uniform estimate of the monetized impacts of greenhouse gas emissions.”

Although litigation might cancel or weaken some of those victories, President Trump’s veto should secure them from repeal by the incoming 120th Congress. Safeguarding that policy legacy is an additional reason to eschew using Section 301 or other trade law authority to adopt carbon border charges. A US CBAM would destroy the clarity and coherence of the President’s energy freedom agenda, import EU carbon metrics into US trade policy, and re-energize the Net Zero policy coalition, with inevitable ramifications for US capital and credit markets, corporate governance, and business lobbying.

Fortunately, I do not think the Trump administration will fall for it. Especially if they consider the issues discussed in this post.

text:
Governor Gretchen Whitmer has ordered the state Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy to pause its work on permits for a proposed tunnel to carry an oil and natural gas liquids pipeline under the Straits of Mackinac.

The Line 5 tunnel project has gotten the go-ahead from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and had also gotten approval from the state departments of Natural Resources and Environment, Great Lakes and Energy.

But a Michigan Supreme Court ruling found the state failed to adequately consider the environmental impacts of the proposal, and sent the project back to regulators for further review.

Now, Whitmer said in a statement on Tuesday, the state is suspending its work on the remaining permits for the project, because Enbridge — the company that owns Line 5 — will need to resubmit its permit application to the Michigan Public Service Commission.

"The Michigan Supreme Court’s decision introduces significant delay and uncertainty," Whitmer said.

The governor, who in 2020 urged Enbridge to shut down Line 5 under the Straits entirely, said her Tuesday announcement is in line with her past actions.

"I have always said my ultimate goal is to get Line 5 out of the water. Just one spill threatens irreparable damage to our water, our economy, and our way of life," Whitmer said.

The U.S. Senate passed H.R. 2347, as amended, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) by a vote of 62-33 November 19. Introduced by Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee; Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), ranking member of the EPW Committee; Mike Lee (R-UT), chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; and Martin Heinrich (D-NM), ranking member of the ENR Committee, BAAJA narrows the scope of environmental reviews, expands exclusions for routine projects, and shortens timelines for environmental decisions. View APTA Press Release Endorsing the Bipartisan Senate Permitting Reform Bill (11.02.2026).

title: New Jersey Joins Growing VPP Movement in PJM Region to Aid Power Grid Capacity
description:

The PJM board previously filed several actions with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) over the summer to mitigate surging power demand from hyperscalers and AI data centers.

text:
State-regulated utilities are stepping in to establish virtual power plant (VPP) programs amid rapid load growth and the need to balance reliability for large energy users alongside existing businesses and residents.

While hyperscalers have turned to behind-the-meter (BTM) and bring-your-own-capacity (BYOC) strategies to bypass long interconnection queues with grid operators, state regulators are taking a parallel track to protect ratepayers. In New Jersey, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (NJBPU) took its first step toward creating a framework that drives energy affordability by paying residents and businesses to support the PJM Interconnection grid.

PowerUp NJ, a new opt-in program announced this month, will turn customer-owned distributed energy resources (DERs), such as smart thermostats, home batteries, EV chargers and smart water heaters, into tools that reduce strain on the grid.

Once launched, the program aims to offer financial incentives to participants and lower customer costs for New Jerseyans during peak demand hours, according to an NJBPU release.

PowerUp NJ is set to initially start with four investor-owned electric utilities in October 2027. Those utilities are Atlantic City Electric (ACE), Jersey Central Power & Light (JCP&L), Public Service Electric & Gas (PSE&G) and Rockland Electric (RECO).

These interim programs will reportedly run for two years to build on technologies and demand response programs the utilities already operate. The goal of these four utilities will be to deliver measurable and verifiable peak demand reductions through gathered data, improving reliability and customer affordability toward a long-term VPP framework for the N.J. program.

The NJBPU Board Staff’s preliminary analysis estimates that a 3% cut in peak demand could avoid roughly $60 million a year in system capacity costs, directly resulting in energy bill savings for all ratepayers. In addition, the agency noted that the program can slowly decrease the state’s reliance on fossil-fuel generation, reducing greenhouse gas emissions and other air pollutants.

“PowerUp NJ turns the smart devices customers already own into powerful tools to reduce grid costs, drive down energy bills and empower customers,” NJBPU President Ben Hertz-Shargel said in a statement. “We will develop this program carefully, learn from real-world results and expand it over time, growing the earnings opportunities for residential and business customers.”

The program’s creation followed Executive Orders No. 1 and No. 2 by New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Jan. 20. The measures declared an energy affordability emergency and directed the NJBPU to develop a VPP program as part of the solution.

Hyperscalers vs. regulated utilities: Growing VPP battleground in the PJM wholesale market

According to global research firm Wood Mackenzie (WoodMac), regional transmission organization (RTO) PJM and independent system operator Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) continue to have the largest utility commitments to data center capacity and the greatest disclosed VPP offtake capacity.

VPP capacity in North America increased roughly 26% year-over-year to reach just over 47 GW of BTM flexible capacity, WoodMac detailed in its 2026 North America Virtual Power Plant Market Report.

Meanwhile, PJM, the largest grid operator in the U.S., has faced mounting strain to secure enough generation for households, businesses and incoming data centers.

The PJM board previously filed several actions with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) over the summer to mitigate surging power demand from hyperscalers and AI data centers. But FERC largely rejected that data center curtailment framework in October, leaving states and utilities to shoulder more of the load-management burden.

FERC’s subsequent rejection came the same month as a federal power grid emergency order from the U.S. Department of Energy directing PJM to manage tight electricity supply conditions across 13 states and Washington, D.C.

As private hyperscaler VPPs and regulated utility VPPs compete to sign up the same pool of residential DERs and commercial loads across PJM, the next major regulatory battleground comes ahead of FERC Order 2222.

The FERC order enables DERs to participate alongside traditional resources in the regional wholesale energy markets through aggregations, opening the broader U.S. wholesale electricity market to competition from smaller, aggregated distributed grid resources. To implement the rule, regional grid operators must revise their tariffs to establish DER aggregations as a “distinct category of market participant.”

This growth reportedly presents opportunities for more resilient energy systems, but it also introduces new complexities for utility planning departments. Those complications include deciding whether a homeowner's battery belongs to their local utility's affordability program, a tech giant's private BYOC contract, or an independent FERC Order 2222 aggregator in the PJM wholesale market.

Parallel utility VPP rollouts across the largest RTO market

Utility provider ComEd received approval from the Illinois Commerce Commission in October for its proposal to launch a new scheduled dispatch virtual power plant (SDVPP) program. The SDVPP, anticipated to begin in March 2027, aims to increase battery storage capacity across northern Illinois that can be deployed during times of high electricity demand.

Along with Illinois, Maryland also has a regulator-mandated utility VPP program rolling out across PJM in 2027. Under the Maryland Public Service Commission’s utility VPP and vehicle-to-grid pilot programs, part of the state’s DRIVE Act proceeding, BGE, Pepco, Delmarva Power and Potomac Edison are targeting roughly 186 MW of peak load reduction ahead of the 2027 summer season.

The Maryland PSC in May advanced VPP and grid modernization efforts to give licensed FERC Order 2222 aggregators access to utility-held DER data by 2028 to support broader VPP deployment, PJM wholesale market participation and grid reliability.

title: Data center climate emissions are worse than previously thought, Harvard study finds
description:

According to the independent market tracking company Clearview, last year there were 1,163 data centers in operation.
That number is expected to skyrocket this year, with 578 new data centers under construction and more proposed.
Some developers have managed to power data centers without connecting to the grid, she said.
text:
The nation’s largest data centers used at least as much energy in one year as the entire state of Michigan, and were responsible for more carbon emissions than some entire countries, according to a new study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

The researchers focused on 403 large facilities and found that the climate pollution driven by these “hyperscale” data centers is three times greater than previously estimated.

Energy use across the country’s thousand-plus data centers is likely much higher than the study captures, said lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctorate researcher at Harvard.

“This paper is just providing a floor estimate,” he said.

Data centers contain the servers and computer chips that enable artificial intelligence, online commerce and cloud storage. They require a constant supply of energy to run and cool internal hardware. Communities near data centers have raised concerns about air pollution, and electricity and water use — issues that some political observers believe moved the needle toward Democrats in this month’s midterm elections.

Scientists had previously taken a stab at projecting the amount of energy used by data centers, but the Harvard research team said few focused on the large facilities that power AI. Their servers process enormous amounts of data and need enormous amounts of electricity to operate. The average data center in the study consumed as much power as 30,000 homes.

The precise amount of electricity used by data centers is difficult to determine because their operators rarely release this information. In this case, the researchers relied on satellite imagery and data from a private company about the facilities’ square footage and their maximum permitted energy use between 2024 and 2025.

Then, the researchers used maps to determine which power plants the data centers likely draw electricity from. Based on the types of fuels those facilities burn, the researchers estimated the climate-warming emissions linked to the data centers.

“We just wanted to find independent numbers,” said Guidi, “and not just companies’ sustainability claims.”

The Harvard team found that the data centers in their sample consumed about 2% of all of the electricity used in the country during the period they studied. And more than half of that energy came from burning fossil fuels.

Can Hankendi, a data center researcher at Boston University who was not involved with the study, called the research “very well built.” He said the lack of transparency around data centers’ energy use is a common challenge for researchers in the field.

In an email to WBUR, Hankendi said the researchers had to make some assumptions, which he called “reasonable.”

“Even though there will be some accuracy issues, they still give us some ballpark numbers to start from,” he wrote. “These estimations are important not only for researchers, but also for policymakers and the public.”

The study also suggests that certain parts of the country are more burdened than others by climate pollution driven by data centers. Fossil fuel-burning power plants were more common in Virginia — the state with the most data centers — and Ohio, whereas other states like Oregon have greener electric grids, so data centers there were potentially responsible for less climate-warming gases.

The data center industry is evolving so quickly that the numbers in the study “are already outdated in a way,” said Guidi.

According to the independent market tracking company Clearview, last year there were 1,163 data centers in operation. That number is expected to skyrocket this year, with 578 new data centers under construction and more proposed.

As companies look to build quickly, they are increasingly turning to on-site power generators, said study co-author Francesca Dominici, professor of biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

Some developers have managed to power data centers without connecting to the grid, she said. But the generators they use often rely on fossil fuels like natural gas or diesel, and they may be less efficient and more polluting than traditional power plants.

In the coming years, Dominici said she hopes that will change. Some energy experts have suggested the power needs of data centers could spur clean energy development.

“In some of the industry the big cloud providers are indeed trying to move into a renewable source of energy,” she said, “but we are not seeing that yet.”

“Data center development could become actually a positive thing for the community if it’s done responsibly,” she said.

(AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) President Trump has made his anti-environmental agenda incredibly clear.
To support Trump’s reckless anti-environmental stance, he nominated former New York congressman and failed governor-elect Lee Zeldin to lead the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

text:
President Donald Trump holds up an executive order he just signed during an event on coal power in the East Room at the White House, Wednesday, Feb. 11, 2026, in Washington. Looking on at right is EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, House Speaker Mike Johnson, center, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum at left. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

President Trump has made his anti-environmental agenda incredibly clear. Since the start of his second term, he has proposed more than 580 initiatives to roll back or threaten the environment and, consequently, the American people’s health.

To support Trump’s reckless anti-environmental stance, he nominated former New York congressman and failed governor-elect Lee Zeldin to lead the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Zeldin is a Trump loyalist who voted against certifying former President Biden as the winner of the 2020 election. His environmental credentials include having previously cast doubt on the severity of climate change and receiving a score of 14 percent from the League of Conservation Voters for his congressional voting record on environmental issues.

Since he was appointed administrator of the EPA, Zeldin has radically altered the agency’s purpose: to protect the environment and public health. His policies and actions have heavily favored fossil fuels over clean energy. At the same time, his massive deregulation plan follows Trump’s rhetoric that dismantling and weakening the EPA will allow the economy to thrive.

Zeldin made his economic agenda clear in February, when the EPA published the “Powering the Great American Comeback” five-pillar plan, which the Associated Press noted had four of the five pillars as economic objectives. These goals are indeed at odds with the EPA’s purpose. Pillar 2 plans to make the United States energy-dominant (essentially investing more in fossil fuels), Pillar 4 declares that the United States will become the AI capital of the world, and Pillar 5 aims to empower the automobile industry.

Zeldin told reporters that he wants to protect Americans facing an expensive economy, and he will do so by dismantling policies aimed at protecting the environment. Zeldin is adamant that the benefits of climate mitigation do not outweigh the steep costs and time it will take to see results.

Zeldin’s outlook on the environment has two catastrophic consequences: it supports actions that worsen climate change and human health, and it promotes the misconception that accounting for and protecting the environment is economically infeasible.

Scientists and climate researchers have heavily criticized policies and actions by the Trump administration and the EPA under Zeldin, which they warn are contributing to higher pollution levels and increasing risks to human health. By weakening or removing protections for areas such as clean air and water, the Associated Press predicts a high risk that billions of dollars will be wasted and tens of thousands of lives will be lost annually.

Trump and Zeldin’s agenda heavily favors protecting businesses, rather than the American people. For example, Zeldin’s EPA published a fact sheet criticizing an EPA rule issued during former President Biden’s presidency that required fossil fuel plants to reduce their carbon emissions. Zeldin complained that the rule was too expensive and subsequently removed the regulation on fossil-fuel power plant companies. Zeldin focused on the fact that the rule cost $15 billion over 20 years and conveniently ignored that the regulation had been saving $20 billion a year, comprising climate, health, and compliance costs.

Given the staggering numbers and long-term benefits of investing in the environment, why do Trump and Zeldin look the other way? The reason is one word: privilege. Both Trump and Zeldin have been lucky enough not to directly experience the damaging effects of the climate crisis. They might never truly experience the pain or fear that come from climate disasters and unhealthy environments, but their children and grandchildren will, and so will many people around the world.

In many places, the effects of climate change and pollutants are ever-present. Yet, the EPA under Zeldin has cut its offices focused on environmental justice. These offices seek to work with minority and low-income communities that are at higher risk for environmental health issues, including disproportionate levels of pollution. Zeldin has been incredibly proud of this devastating move, praising the reversal of what he calls “discrimination programs,” aligning with Trump’s agenda to end diversity, equity, and inclusion. These measures are extremely out of touch and act as a reminder that Trump’s Republican Party does not care about everyday Americans.

Protecting the environment isn’t just about the planet; it’s about the people as well. They are interconnected, and thus it’s essential to consider the environment in politics and business.

title: BAAJA Permitting Reform: Key Changes for Energy, Infrastructure and Data Center Projects
authors: freeman-paul, Forrest, Jeffrey, Garner, S. Keith, hill-landon
description:
According to the bill’s sponsors, BAAJA will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.
How BAAJA Could Accelerate Energy Infrastructure Development For energy infrastructure, BAAJA would facilitate grid expansion and modernization.
The bill would expand the permitting authority of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) over qualifying interstate transmission facilities and strengthen coordinated transmission and generation-interconnection planning.
What to Watch as BAAJA Moves to the House Despite levels of bipartisan support, approval of BAAJA by the House is not guaranteed.
FOOTNOTES [1] Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA): Resource Hub, Bipartisan Pol’y Ctr.
text:
Last week, the U.S. Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (“BAAJA”), setting the stage for a consequential vote in the U.S. House of Representatives after the Thanksgiving recess. Heralded as “the most comprehensive permitting bill to date,”[1] BAAJA would reform key provisions of several federal laws that are critical for infrastructure development, namely, the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”), Clean Water Act (“CWA”), Endangered Species Act (“ESA”), Federal Power Act (“FPA”) and National Historic Preservation Act (“NHPA”). BAAJA is poised to make meaningful changes to the legislative framework related to project development and, in so doing, reshape how federal agencies evaluate and approve projects.

Introduced by a bipartisan coalition of four senators on September 30, 2026, BAAJA marks the culmination of a decades-long effort to reform the federal environmental review and permitting processes. According to the bill’s sponsors, BAAJA will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.[2] On the environmental review and permitting front, the bill’s NEPA amendments would set one- or two-year deadlines for environmental reviews and deadlines for the permitting decisions that follow. The amendments would also limit the alternatives agencies must consider to those that meet both the project’s purpose and need and the non-Federal sponsor’s goals, while retaining the option of taking no action. The bill would also extend maximum CWA permit terms from five to 10 years, shorten the ordinary ESA consultation period from 90 to 60 days, and narrow the activities and effects subject to historic-preservation review. These changes are expected to make development schedules far more predictable.

How BAAJA Could Accelerate Energy Infrastructure Development

For energy infrastructure, BAAJA would facilitate grid expansion and modernization. The bill would expand the permitting authority of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) over qualifying interstate transmission facilities and strengthen coordinated transmission and generation-interconnection planning. Additionally, certain grid upgrades and natural gas pipeline improvements within existing corridors would be exempt from NEPA and NHPA review.

Data Centers: New Rules for Power Costs, Grid Interconnection and Financial Assurance

For data centers, BAAJA would place greater emphasis on infrastructure-cost responsibility. The bill would direct FERC to revise transmission-pricing policies to reflect embedded costs and a reasonable assessment of incremental costs, while prohibiting utilities from shifting retail incremental costs to other customers. For newly interconnecting data centers, utilities would require financial assurances or contributions before building necessary infrastructure, and service arrangements would provide for continued cost recovery even if the customer exits. The bill also recognizes the authority of states to condition service on procuring new generation or accepting limits on grid withdrawals, while generally preserving previously approved arrangements. For developers and investors, these provisions would make power procurement, financial security, and infrastructure-cost allocation central diligence considerations.

Permitting Litigation: Shorter Deadlines and New Limits on Project Challenges

To bring more certainty as to whether an approval is final and non-appealable, which is critical to financing projects, BAAJA would also generally impose 150-day filing windows for specified challenges under NEPA, NHPA, CWA and ESA, with differing triggers and exceptions. This is a dramatic improvement from the existing six-year Administrative Procedure Act statute of limitations. For NEPA and NHPA violations, the ordinary remedy would be remand without vacating approvals or enjoining projects, while preserving preliminary relief for qualifying violations of other laws. Separately, the bill would give qualifying developers additional remedies for federal interference and intentional patterns of disparate treatment, alongside judicial enforcement of certain permitting deadlines. This would provide more stability for both renewable and non-renewable energy projects when administrations change.

What to Watch as BAAJA Moves to the House

Despite levels of bipartisan support, approval of BAAJA by the House is not guaranteed. While the future of BAAJA remains uncertain, the legislative efforts being undertaken show that Congress is taking active steps to improve the legal framework to allow for a more efficient delivery of much-needed infrastructure improvements.

Sheppard is closely monitoring BAAJA’s fate in the House. Stay tuned for updates examining the potential implications for renewable energy, fossil fuels, digital infrastructure and related industries if the bill passes.

text:
On September 30, 2026, the chairs and ranking members of the Senate Environment and Public Works and Energy and Natural Resources Committees, a bipartisan group of senators, introduced S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (the “Bill”), a broad energy and permitting package. On November 19, 2026, the Senate passed the Bill as an amendment to H.R. 2347, a House-passed tax bill. This alert reflects the Senate-passed text, and section references below are to that version.

The provision that is likely most significant to the electric power sector is Section 2101, which rewrites Section 216 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), the federal “backstop” authority for siting interstate electric transmission facilities. First enacted in the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (“EPAct 2005”) and widely regarded as ineffective after the Fourth Circuit’s decision in Piedmont Environmental Council v. FERC, 558 F.3d 304 (4th Cir. 2009), the existing backstop siting framework has never been used to permit any transmission line.

Section 2101 aims to change the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”) backstop authority. It converts FERC’s backstop authority to permit interstate transmission lines from a narrow residual power, available only in corridors designated by the Department of Energy (“DOE”), into a mandatory permitting pathway for high-voltage transmission facilities in the national interest. Under the Bill, FERC would be required, rather than merely authorized, to issue a permit once it makes the required findings.

This alert summarizes the key changes and outlines the practical implications for transmission developers, incumbent utilities, public power and cooperative entities, and large-load customers. It also covers Section 2104, which would let state commissions refer a public utility to FERC for investigation of its local transmission planning, with remedies that include return-on-equity reductions and civil penalties of up to $5 million per facility, credited to the transmission customers that bore the facility’s costs. It also notes related provisions affecting interstate natural gas pipelines regulated by FERC under the Natural Gas Act. Section 2101 does not give FERC eminent domain authority of its own. As under current law, however, FPA Section 216(e) allows the holder of a FERC permit that cannot acquire a needed right-of-way by agreement to acquire it by eminent domain through a condemnation action in federal district court or the appropriate state court. Section 2101 leaves that authority in place but makes two changes: (1) it strikes the existing exclusion for property owned by a state, so that state-owned property (though not federal property) could be condemned, and (2) it provides that condemnation actions in federal court would follow Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 71.1 rather than state practice.

For analysis of the Bill’s parallel reforms to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (“NEPA”), the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act (“NHPA”), see our companion V&E insight, “To the Finish Line: Ten Ways the New Senate Permitting Bill is a Boon for Energy Infrastructure.”

Eliminating the Corridor Prerequisite

Under current law, FERC’s backstop authority to permit new transmission lines is available only within geographic areas that DOE has designated as National Interest Electric Transmission Corridors (“NIETCs”), a cumbersome process that has produced only two designations in more than two decades. Section 2101 eliminates the NIETC prerequisite entirely. The revised FPA Section 216(b) authorizes FERC to issue permits for the construction or modification of electric transmission facilities “necessary in the national interest” without any prior DOE corridor designation. The DOE corridor concept is replaced by a new study process requiring DOE to identify constrained and congested geographic areas every three years (with the first study due within one year of enactment), but the study is informational only and is not a prerequisite to FERC action on a permit application.

Fixing the “Fatal Flaw”: Mandatory Authority and State Denials

The most significant structural change in the Bill is the shift from discretionary to mandatory permitting language. The revised FPA Section 216(b) provides that FERC “shall” issue a permit for the construction or modification of electric transmission facilities when it makes the required findings, replacing the permissive “may” that previously governed. In practice, if the Bill were enacted, FERC would have to issue a permit once two things are shown: (1) one of the state-action triggers in FPA Section 216(b)(1) is met (for example, the state has not acted within one year, has denied the application, or lacks authority to approve it), and (2) the project satisfies the five additional findings in FPA Section 216(b)(2)–(6), described below. FERC would still act only after notice, a hearing, and a public comment period of at least 45 days. The Bill also revises the trigger for FERC jurisdiction under FPA Section 216(b)(1)(C)(i): The one-year state-action clock (the period during which a state has to act on a siting application before FERC may step in) now runs from “the date on which the application was filed with the State commission or other entity,” eliminating the ambiguous “later of” formulation in current law, which measured the year from the later of the date the application was filed or the date DOE designated the relevant corridor. This change addresses state delay by fixing when the one-year period begins, but it does not on its face address the Piedmont problem, in which the Fourth Circuit held that an outright state denial was not a “withholding” of approval and therefore did not trigger FERC backstop jurisdiction. Congress addressed that problem in 2021, when the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act added a separate trigger for a state’s denial of an application. Section 2101 leaves that denial trigger in place and, by eliminating the corridor prerequisite, would make it available outside DOE-designated corridors.

New Findings FERC Must Make

In addition to the existing state-action triggers, the Bill adds five new findings that FERC must make before issuing a backstop permit to construct or modify electric transmission facilities:

Interstate or foreign commerce. The facility must be used in interstate commerce (including transmission from the Outer Continental Shelf (“OCS”) to a state) or in foreign commerce.

Public interest. The permit must be consistent with the public interest.

Consumer protection, improved reliability, and just and reasonable rates. The facility must protect or benefit consumers, provide “improved reliability” as defined in new FPA Section 225(a), and facilitate just and reasonable rates.

Voltage threshold. The facility must be capable of operating at 230 kV or above, or be necessary to safely and reliably interconnect one or more such facilities covered by the permit. An exception applies to facilities using advanced transmission conductors (including superconductors), as defined by FERC, for which FERC may set, on a project-specific basis, the voltage it determines appropriate for facilities of comparable throughput.

Modification standard. Where the permit authorizes modification of existing transmission facilities (including reconductoring, meaning replacement of existing conductors with higher-capacity ones), the project must maximize, to the extent reasonable and economical, the capabilities of existing towers, structures, and rights-of-way.

The 230 kV threshold and the advanced-conductor exception are particularly relevant for developers evaluating reconductoring and grid-enhancing technology projects, which may be able to add capacity within existing rights-of-way. Section 2102 of the Bill further supports this pathway through new FPA Section 216A, which provides that activities to maintain or increase grid transmission capacity within an existing right-of-way (or the minimum adjacent area, up to one-quarter mile from the right-of-way, needed to meet electrical standards or complete the work), including reconductoring, voltage increases, circuit additions, advanced transmission technologies, storage, and parallel circuits, are neither a “major Federal action” under NEPA nor an “undertaking” under NHPA Section 106. Section 2102(b) does the same for interstate natural gas pipelines, as discussed below.

Pre-Filing Timing; Simultaneous Processing Provision Dropped

The introduced version of the Bill included a simultaneous processing provision allowing applicants for transmission facilities rated at 345 kV and above to file a FERC backstop application at the same time as, or any time after, the state siting application. The Senate-passed text does not include that provision. Instead, the Senate-passed Bill addresses only FERC’s pre-filing process, which the Bill does not define. Under the Bill, any FERC pre-filing process may begin before, but must begin no later than, the date the application is submitted to the state commission or other siting authority. Because the one-year state-action clock also runs from the state filing date, early pre-filing would allow developers to build the federal record while the state proceeding is underway. However, FERC still must make findings on the five factors described above before issuing a permit. The Bill does not specify how the start of pre-filing is to be measured or documented and leaves it to FERC to define in its implementing rules.

Preservation of State Authority and Landowner Protections

To address federalism concerns, the Bill includes several provisions designed to preserve state involvement:

State record consideration. States may file with FERC the parts of the record of their state siting proceeding that they consider relevant, and FERC must consider them in deciding whether to issue a permit. The Bill does not specify what weight FERC must give that record; it requires only that FERC consider it.

Consultation requirements. FERC must give affected states, federal agencies, Indian tribes, private property owners, and other interested persons a reasonable opportunity to present their views and recommendations on the need for and impact of the project. The Bill does not prescribe a more detailed process or require FERC to adopt those recommendations.

Landowner input. FERC must take into account “landowner input” from “affected landowners” (defined to include farmers and ranchers), obtained through FERC notification and consultation processes. The Bill defines “affected property” broadly to capture land crossed by or used for the facility, abutting rights-of-way within 500 feet, and residences within 500 feet of the right-of-way. The Bill requires only that FERC take landowner input into account when authorizing the project; it does not prescribe the notice and consultation procedures FERC must use or the weight the input must receive.

No permit without triggering findings. FERC cannot issue a permit except upon making findings on the five factors outlined above.

Expanded Jurisdiction: Public Power, Co-ops, and the ERCOT Carve-Out

New FPA Section 216(k) expands FERC’s backstop siting jurisdiction to cover all transmitting utilities, including government-owned utilities and rural electric cooperatives, with two exceptions: (1) Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”) utilities are excluded, and FPA Section 216 does not apply within ERCOT at all; and (2) exempt transmitting utilities (states and their political subdivisions, and electric cooperatives that receive Rural Electrification Act financing or sell less than 4 million megawatt-hours of electricity per year) that do not voluntarily submit are not covered. The Bill also provides that subjecting a government-owned or cooperatively owned electric utility to backstop siting authority does not make it a “public utility” for other FPA purposes — a firewall that confines the jurisdictional expansion to siting purposes only. In other words, FERC’s authority over these entities is limited to the purposes of FPA Section 216, which include the cost-allocation and transmission-service requirements described below, and does not make them “public utilities” subject to FERC’s general rate regulation under FPA Sections 205 and 206.

Cost Allocation and Ratepayer Protection

New FPA Section 216(f) establishes a cost-allocation framework for the costs of building and operating new or modified transmission facilities permitted. Key features include:

Cost-causation principle. Costs are allocated to customers that benefit, consistent with the principle that costs should be at least roughly commensurate with the benefits they receive. Recognized benefits include improved reliability, reduced congestion, reduced power losses, greater carrying capacity, reduced operating reserves, and improved access to lower-cost generation.

Ratepayer protection. Costs may not be involuntarily allocated to customers that receive no benefit or only trivial benefits, although voluntary agreements remain permissible.

Tariff filings. Transmitting utilities must file tariffs under FPA Section 205; exempt transmitting utilities must provide service under FPA Section 211A, notwithstanding the existing FPA Section 211A(c) limitations.

OCS facilities. Transmission facilities located on the OCS remain eligible for cost allocation if FERC makes the relevant findings.

Separately, a new FPA Section 219(b)(4)(C) authorizes incentive rate recovery for all prudently incurred costs of payments to jurisdictions impacted by facilities developed under FPA Section 216 or the new Section 225 regional/interregional planning provisions. This adds a category of recoverable costs to the existing FPA Section 219 transmission rate incentives, which allows transmission owners to recover certain costs through their FERC-approved rates. The Bill does not define “payments to jurisdictions.”

The Senate-passed text also adds cost-responsibility rules for data centers and other computational loads. At the wholesale level, Section 2107 would require FERC, within 90 days of enactment, to revise its 1994 transmission pricing policy statement so that utilities charge eligible computational load customers the embedded cost of transmission service plus a reasonable assessment of its incremental cost. Incremental costs paid would be credited to the utility’s annual transmission revenue requirement to prevent double recovery from other customers, and customers that elect non-firm service would pay less. FERC would also have to propose a rule implementing the revised policy within the same 90 days and finalize it within one year after proposing it. For facilities allocated under new FPA Section 216(f), Section 225, or Section 228, the incremental cost would be the costs assigned under those provisions. At the retail level, new FPA Section 229 would bar any portion of the retail incremental cost of serving a computational load site from being allocated to other customers, and would confirm that states may charge these customers more than that cost and credit the excess to other ratepayers.

FERC Oversight of Local Transmission Planning

Section 2104 of the Bill adds a new FPA Section 226 giving FERC oversight of local transmission planning and development. The provision applies to “local transmission facilities,” defined as facilities located solely within the retail distribution service territory or footprint of a public utility transmission provider and not selected in a regional transmission plan for cost allocation. The Section 2104 process is triggered only by a state commission referral, although the section preserves FERC’s authority under other provisions of law, and works as follows:

State referral. Within one year of enactment, FERC must establish by rule procedures allowing one or more state commissions to refer a public utility for investigation of the utility’s processes for planning, developing, and replacing local transmission facilities. The referral must identify the processes of concern, the potential harm to wholesale or retail customers, and the state commission’s prior efforts to resolve those concerns.

FERC response and investigation. Upon receiving a referral, FERC must either dismiss it as unsupported and publicly explain why, or notice the investigation for public comment and establish an investigative team made up of one or more non-decisional staff from an office designated by the FERC Chairman and up to three representatives appointed by the referring state commission. The team has all investigative authority available to FERC or its staff in proceedings under or relating to FPA Section 307.

Findings. The investigative team must issue a preliminary findings report within 120 days after FERC notices the investigation. If the team concludes that the processes used by a public utility for planning, developing, and replacing local transmission facilities are not resulting in the selection of the more efficient or cost-effective local transmission facilities, or that those processes are interfering with the processes of the relevant transmission planning region for planning, developing, and replacing regional transmission facilities, the team must issue a final report and recommendation to FERC explaining that conclusion and recommending a remedy.

Potential remedies and penalties. Within 14 business days after receiving the investigative team’s final report and recommendation, FERC must issue a notice requesting comment on the report, and FERC must issue an order within 120 days after issuing that notice. The order may require changes to the utility’s planning processes, reduce its return on equity for local transmission facilities, eliminate the presumption of prudence for those facilities, or impose another appropriate remedy. FERC may also impose a civil penalty of up to $5 million per local transmission facility, credited to the transmission customers that bore the facility’s costs, if the facility was developed or energized during the period beginning 60 days before the referral and ending on the date of the order and FERC determines that doing so was imprudent and financially harmed wholesale or retail customers in the referring state. FERC’s orders are generally subject to rehearing and judicial review.

Section 2104 does not give FERC jurisdiction over retail electricity sales. Harm to retail customers can support a referral and certain remedies, but nothing in the transmission title grants FERC authority over sales of electric energy at retail or the local distribution of electricity.

Key Takeaways and Looking Ahead

For transmission developers: Section 2101 of the Bill is the most significant expansion of federal transmission siting authority since EPAct 2005. The elimination of the corridor prerequisite, the mandatory “shall” standard, and the planning-to-permitting fast track together create a credible federal backstop for the first time, although the Senate-passed text drops the express right to file simultaneously at FERC for lines of 345 kV and above. The advanced-conductor exception and the NEPA and NHPA exemption for reconductoring and other work in existing rights-of-way (Section 2102) further lower barriers for grid-enhancing technology deployments. Developers should also note that Section 2101 leaves in place FPA Section 216(e), under which the holder of a FERC permit that cannot acquire a needed right-of-way by agreement may seek to condemn it by court order, in federal district court or the appropriate state court (provided FERC has determined that it made good-faith efforts to engage landowners early in the process), and extends that authority to state-owned property. A backstop permit would therefore carry eminent domain authority, although condemnation itself requires a court proceeding that is separate from the FERC permit proceeding, and early landowner engagement will be important.

For incumbent utilities and public power/co-ops: The expansion of jurisdiction to public power and electric cooperatives is a major change. While the “firewall” provision limits FERC’s jurisdictional expansion to siting, affected entities should evaluate their transmission planning and siting processes in light of the new federal overlay. The cost-allocation provisions, including the prohibition on involuntary allocation to non-benefiting customers, will likely be contested in the FERC proceedings that implement them. Section 2105 would also prohibit a federal right of first refusal for transmission facilities selected in a regional or interregional plan for cost allocation, except as provided in FERC rules or orders in effect on enactment. Public utilities should also expect closer scrutiny of local transmission projects. Under Section 2104, a state commission could refer a utility to FERC for investigation of how it plans, develops, and replaces local facilities, and the remedies include planning-process changes, ROE reductions, elimination of the presumption of prudence, and civil penalties of up to $5 million per facility, credited to affected transmission customers, in specified circumstances. Utilities should document why their local projects were selected over more efficient or cost-effective alternatives and how they fit with regional planning, and should address state regulators’ concerns early, since a referral must describe the state commission’s prior efforts to resolve them.

For data center and large-load customers: The Bill’s improved reliability and consumer-benefit requirements, combined with the benefits-based cost-allocation framework, cut both ways: They support the transmission large loads need, but they also direct costs to the customers that benefit from it. Large loads dependent on new transmission interconnection or delivery capacity have a strong interest in supporting backstop permit applications. As noted above, the Senate-passed text goes further on cost responsibility in two ways. First, at the wholesale level, Section 2107 would require FERC to revise its 1994 transmission pricing policy statement and to propose a rule implementing it. The revised policy would require utilities to charge eligible computational load customers the embedded cost of transmission service plus a reasonable assessment of its incremental cost. Second, at the retail level, new FPA Section 229 would bar utilities from shifting the retail incremental cost of serving a data center to other customers. It would also confirm that states may charge data centers more than that cost, require financial assurances, and allocate service through open seasons or competitive solicitations. Large loads served through local transmission facilities should also watch Section 2104, because a state referral could change how those facilities are planned and how their costs are recovered.

For all stakeholders: The Senate passed the Bill on November 19, 2026, as an amendment to H.R. 2347, but it has not yet been enacted. The House must now act on the Senate amendment, whether by agreeing to it, amending it further, or going to conference, before the measure can be sent to the President. Whatever the ultimate outcome, Section 2101 as passed by the Senate is likely to serve as a template for any transmission siting reform that advances. Stakeholders should engage now, both in the remaining legislative process and in preparing for any potential changes that would follow enactment.

Please reach out to your Vinson & Elkins team to discuss how these proposed changes to FERC’s backstop transmission siting authority may affect your projects, planning, and regulatory strategy.

text:
DTE Energy is adding up to 150 megawatts of new solar energy in Michigan.

The company is seeking competitive proposals for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan-based solar generation. Projects must achieve commercial operation by June 30, 2030, be located in Michigan and connect to either the MISO transmission system or DTE’s distribution system.

“These projects are an investment in Michigan and the communities we’re proud to serve. The new projects will help reduce the company’s exposure to changing fuel prices over their operating lives. The projects will also support DTE’s goal to provide customers with energy that is reliable, increasingly clean and affordable.

Interested bidders can register and obtain additional information through PowerAdvocate. Proposals are due Jan. 19, 2027, and DTE expects to execute contracts in the second or third quarter of 2027.

text:
Every grid battery has a piece of equipment between it and the power lines that few people notice. The power conversion system, the inverter equipment that turns grid power into something a battery can store and sends it back out when needed, connects to outside networks, and its settings can be changed remotely. At an energy forum in Seoul, Chungbuk National University electrical engineering professor Kim Jae-eon argued that this is where storage buyers should be looking harder.

If someone tampered with the inverter's core software, Kim said, they could disrupt how the battery charges and discharges and threaten the power supply it is meant to support. He also noted that some Chinese-made units are sold in Korea under Korean brands, so the name on the equipment may not match the factory that built it.

His fix is to make security count when storage contracts are awarded. Korea's storage tender this year does not explicitly score resistance to hacking or tampering, and Kim proposed certification standards, so security is weighed alongside price. Korean companies could hold their own against cheaper Chinese rivals in markets that care about safety and security, he said, if they design their own conversion equipment and can prove it stands up to outside interference.

China Builds Most of the Systems

The question reaches well beyond Korea because China assembles most of the world's storage systems. Chinese-headquartered integrators held 76% of the global market in 2025, and eight of the 10 largest were based in China, research firm Wood Mackenzie reported in June. Tesla and Sungrow held the top two spots worldwide, and Tesla led in North America.

Korean-based Samsung SDI recently announced that it will supply Jupiter Power, a BlackRock-owned developer, with 16 gigawatt-hours of lithium iron phosphate batteries from its Indiana plant over three years starting in 2029. In October, the company said it would ship 1 gigawatt-hour of complete storage systems from Kokomo to Alpha Omega Power by year-end. Neither announcement names an inverter supplier.

U.S. Rules Already Reach the Inverter

U.S. regulators have already moved on the equipment Kim described. On July 28, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) added foreign-produced power inverters to its Covered List, which bars new models from receiving U.S. equipment authorizations. After an August revision, the listing covers inverters that can be reached remotely over a wired or wireless connection. Inverters that qualify for the federal manufacturing tax credit under Section 45X no longer count as foreign-produced, and models cleared by the Department of War or the Department of Homeland Security are exempt.

Tax credits raise a related question about who stands behind the equipment. Under IRS Notice 2026-15, developers claiming the Section 48E credit for storage projects that began construction after 2025 have to determine whether a prohibited foreign entity provided material assistance. The rule has pushed buyers to look past a supplier's factory address to who owns and controls it.

Keeping Equipment Running

The FCC did leave room for equipment already in the field. A waiver issued with the July listing lets manufacturers keep sending software and firmware updates that reduce potential harm to U.S. consumers. Over a system's life, whoever services the equipment also shapes who pays when something breaks, a question that has come up in leased storage deals.

Kim wants Korea to go further, with joint testing alongside European certification bodies so Korean equipment can prove its security to buyers abroad. Simply avoiding Chinese products is not enough, he said, and verifiable security should become a Korean standard.
