text:
Introduction

There is bipartisan support among both policymakers and the general public for expanding safe and reliable nuclear power to meet growing demand for electricity. On May 23, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14302, which set a bold goal: commence construction on 10 new large nuclear reactors in the United States by 2030. The most likely candidate for fulfilling this goal is the Westinghouse AP1000, the only fully licensed design that has been recently constructed in the United States. Two AP1000 reactors, Vogtle Units 3 and 4 in Georgia, entered service in 2023 and 2024, respectively, and are now generating large amounts of firm “always on” electricity. The Vogtle project — the first set of new nuclear reactors fully built in the United States in over a generation — was completed significantly behind schedule and over budget. Consequently, financiers and the electric utility industry have been reluctant to embark on the next set of AP1000 projects, and nuclear projects more broadly. New financial modeling from Employ America is set to reveal a credible path to allaying investors’ fears — new nuclear projects can “pencil” for equity investors if the Trump administration unleashes the full power of the financing supports each party backed when it controlled Congress. This credible path to investment viability for new nuclear hinges on administrative policy actions that unlock the full value of what Congress has enacted, specifically with respect to the §48E Investment Tax Credit.

The Fission Possible series from Employ America will detail how new nuclear construction projects can pencil — projects are financially viable and attractive under an attainable set of financial and policy assumptions. Key to establishing these conditions is a set of administrative actions that can maximize the potential of the §48E Investment Tax Credit, which plays a critical role in shaping financial returns for nuclear projects. The next piece in the series will break down the assumptions, calculations, and insights stemming from our financial modeling of a hypothetical AP1000 project. This will be followed by pieces that identify how administrative implementation of §48E can be improved, including Domestic Content Requirements, Direct Pay monetization, and the Energy Communities bonus.

Our Analysis Shows Vogtle Costs Are No Longer Fatal

Employ America’s financial modeling demonstrates that the next two AP1000 reactors can “pencil” for investors across several scenarios. By “pencil,” we mean that new AP1000 projects can achieve the requisite internal rates of return (IRRs) and returns on equity (ROEs) under relatively conservative construction cost assumptions. Project equity can earn mid-teens returns, comparable to other large renewable infrastructure projects, even in a scenario where the next pair of AP1000 reactors are built at the same high construction costs as the Vogtle project. This is a conservative assumption because the Vogtle project broke ground with an incomplete reactor design, had to stand up a workforce and supply chain from scratch, and overcame the bankruptcy of its lead construction contractor in the middle of the build phase. The project also faced additional construction delays stemming from the once-in-a-generation global pandemic. These unique factors resulted in significant cost escalation that the next reactor builds should be able to avoid. In fact, significantly greater upside exists for investors who facilitate stronger project execution than the Vogtle project experienced.

Employ America has dedicated significant resources to building a robust financial model of a two-reactor AP1000 project, the only project type with both a completed design and a recent construction track record in the United States. We conducted an extensive literature review of other AP1000 financial modeling efforts, and also pulled specific line item costs from the Vogtle project’s public filings to strengthen our estimates. We built our financial model in collaboration with Pooja Reddy, an investment banker with significant experience in capital-intensive and regulated industries, and with previous transaction experience in infrastructure project finance.

The financial viability of the next AP1000 projects, when using conservative assumptions of total capital expenditures, depends on the Trump administration both unlocking the full potential of the §48E Investment Tax Credit (ITC) and deploying the lending power of the Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (DOE EDF). This memo goes through the range of implementation barriers that are currently stymieing the full potential of the ITC, and is the first in Employ America’s series exploring how a revitalized ITC, paired with DOE EDF lending, can catalyze the promised nuclear launch.

The Current ITC Implementation Falls Short of Its Promise

The ITC is one of the two principal tax credits authorized by Congress to incentivize new emissions-free electricity generation; the other is the §45Y Production Tax Credit (PTC). The ITC is calculated as a percentage of total eligible project costs and is traditionally claimed in the tax year when the project is placed in service, commonly called the Commercial Operations Date (COD). The PTC, on the other hand, is calculated based on the amount of electricity, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), that a project generates once operational during the 10-year credit window. Both credits are claimed by the project owner during tax season. The ITC should, at least in theory, be far more valuable than the PTC for new nuclear projects due to their high upfront capital costs, as shown in analysis within DOE’s Pathways to Commercial Liftoff: Advanced Nuclear report. Given this, our analysis focuses solely on strategies to unlock the ITC.

The One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB), passed by a Republican Congress in 2025, maintained the full ITC for new nuclear projects that commence construction by 2033, even as OBBB made many other changes to energy policy relative to what was legislated under a Democratic Congress in the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022.

The base and bonus structure of the ITC is consistent across the IRA and OBBB, and breaks down as follows:

6% Base ITC when no bonus conditions are met: If a nuclear project meets none of the bonus conditions, the “base” credit only covers 6% of eligible project costs.

30% ITC with Wage & Apprenticeship: The ITC is quintupled to 30% of eligible project costs if Prevailing Wage & Apprenticeship (PW&A) requirements are satisfied. The additional bonuses described in the following bullets, Domestic Content Requirements and Energy Communities, are quintupled as well.

40% ITC with Wage & Apprenticeship + Domestic Content: If the project satisfies Domestic Content Requirements (DCR) by being constructed with specified amounts of domestic materials and manufactured inputs, the project receives a 2% bonus credit, but when coupled with the PW&A quintupling, it becomes a 10% bonus credit. Therefore, when the PW&A requirement is met and DCR is satisfied, the ITC will cover 40% of eligible project costs.

50% ITC with Wage & Apprenticeship + Domestic Content + Energy Communities: Finally, if project construction occurs in an “Energy Community” as defined in the ITC statute, an additional bonus credit is unlocked. As before, if PW&A requirements are not met, the Energy Communities bonus credit is 2%, but quintuples to 10% if PW&A requirements are met. If all three conditions are met — PW&A, DCR, and Energy Communities — then the federal government will pick up half of all eligible project costs.

The Current ITC Struggles to Catalyze New Nuclear Builds

At first glance, the current ITC seems incredibly valuable for new nuclear. Leaders at the Department of Energy have occasionally touted the ITC provisions as “buy one reactor, get one free” — a compelling proposition for utilities and project developers. Unfortunately, the guidance issued during the Biden administration established a much more challenging environment to fully monetize the ITC for new nuclear construction projects. There are at least five major roadblocks keeping the maximum ITC out of reach for developers of new nuclear:

Developers typically monetize the value of their tax credits by selling them to taxpayers with sufficient tax liability, but this type of transaction has never occurred at the scale required to build large nuclear reactors. There is a narrow set of taxpayers that would have both sufficient tax liability and interest in purchasing the tax credit. They would likely demand a steep haircut for making such a purchase.

The net present value of the ITC is significantly diluted when it is paid at project completion, which weighs on technologies and assets that require longer construction timelines.

Congressional and IRS “normalization” requirements — discussed further below — prevent regulated utilities from immediately passing ITC savings to ratepayers (consumers).

The IRS has yet to issue Domestic Content Safe Harbor Tables for new nuclear, which creates multiple limitations, including making it harder to capture the 10% DCR bonus.

IRS guidance on the Energy Communities bonus issued during the Biden administration did not account for key implementation and interpretation realities, including nuclear-specific considerations related to longer development timelines and higher pre-construction reliance interests.

Markets Have Never Monetized a Credit at This Scale

Assuming that a new nuclear project earns a 50% ITC, it is unclear whether the tax equity market is deep and liquid enough to monetize what would amount to a $10 to $17 billion tax credit for a single two-reactor build. The tax equity market refers to the group of buyers and sellers trading energy tax credits issued by the federal government. The IRA, passed by a Democratic Congress in 2022, enabled energy tax credits to be transferred and sold at scale for the first time, as described in 26 U.S.C. §6418. This provision of the law aimed to address the issue of energy project developers not having the requisite tax liability to monetize tax credits on their own books. The new transferability regime enabled project developers to legally sell and transfer the tax credits to any willing buyer with a large enough tax liability to monetize the credit. New markets formed: tax credits were traded privately between different parties, with banks acting as intermediaries, and traded on new online tax equity marketplaces like Crux. The OBBB accelerated the phaseout of tax credits for traditional renewables and prohibited tax credit transfers to specific foreign entities of concern, but otherwise left the transferability regime established by the IRA in place. The federal government collected a total of $452 billion of corporate income taxes in FY25. Setting aside the misalignment of corporate tax reporting years with federal budget years, the closest publicly reported proxy of a company’s federal tax liability is the ‘current federal income tax expense’ that companies report in their annual 10-K filings to the SEC. Individual companies also calculate this figure differently, but the general scale of the figures is what matters. The top five public companies with the largest federal income tax expense in their most recently reported fiscal year were:

NVIDIA — $19.0 billion

Reporting period January 2025 to January 2026.

Alphabet (Google) — $13.4 billion

Reporting period January 2025 to December 2025.

Berkshire Hathaway — $13.0 billion

Reporting period January 2025 to December 2025.

Apple — $11.3 billion

Reporting period September 2025 to September 2026.

Wells Fargo — $5.1 billion

Reporting period January 2025 to December 2025.

Corporate income taxes are noisy, full of one-time payments, deferrals, and a litany of additional intricacies that muddy these simplified figures. Even when read with error bars, these numbers do provide a ballpark for estimating the maximum possible ITC that could be monetized by an individual corporation in one tax year. DOE estimated in 2024 that the last two AP1000s were built at an overnight capital cost of ~$11,000/kW, which the report inflation adjusts to ~$15,000/kW in 2024 dollars. Most public cost modeling, including a separate estimate from the DOE, assumes that the next two AP1000s would come in below $15,000/kW. Employ America will publish the results of our own cost modeling in future pieces. Even so, the $15,000/kW figure provides a reasonable ceiling estimate on the total cost for the next two reactors, and therefore acts as a helpful high-water mark on the potential quantum of a 50% ITC. If the next two AP1000s were built at $15,000/kW, the total project cost would be $33.5 billion and the 50% ITC would be close to $17 billion, larger than all but one annual corporate tax bill.

There is some potential for a consortium of corporations to jointly monetize portions of such a gargantuan ITC. Offshore wind is the closest comparable: Vineyard Wind 1 closed on what was described as “the largest single asset tax equity financing” deal in United States history with JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo in 2023. But even the size of that tax equity package, $1.2 billion, is an order of magnitude smaller than what is required for two new AP1000s. The purpose of the transferability regime was to enable energy tax credits to be sold and transferred to entities that have the requisite tax liability to monetize the credits, but there is a very short list of entities capable of absorbing even a portion of the tax credits that a new large nuclear project would generate. The purchasers of these tax credits, upon realizing their significant market leverage, would be able to demand a steep haircut per dollar of credit, diluting the value of the tax credits for the nuclear developer. It is challenging to estimate what size haircut an ITC would take for a new nuclear build, given that a transaction of this scale has never occurred. The energy tax equity marketplace Crux reported in its 2026 Mid-Year Market Intelligence Report that ITCs transacted at an average of $0.91 on the dollar in the first half of 2026, representing a 9% haircut for project developers. However, the idea that a nearly $17 billion ITC could be successfully monetized at this same 9% haircut warrants significant skepticism given that Crux also estimates that the total size of the entire tax credit transferability market in 2025 was $42 billion. Based on this assessment of the market’s depth, a transaction for a pair of AP1000s could easily exhaust potential purchasers of the tax credits.

Utilities and state governments are only in the initial phases of grappling with how the ITC would be practically monetized. New York Governor Kathy Hochul called for a 5 gigawatt new nuclear backbone to be constructed in New York State. NYSERDA and NY DPS released an Advanced Nuclear Policy Options paper laying out in extensive detail a strategy for the state to procure additional nuclear power. The paper models a 40% ITC for new large light water reactor projects, but “does not include a quantification of the transaction costs” on the tax credits themselves. The scale of the transaction costs is indeed a black box, but simple supply-demand reasoning suggests that the haircuts on transacted tax credits would be unprecedentedly steep under current policy. Solutions must be brought to this tax equity monetization challenge because the ITC represents the linchpin tax incentive for building modern nuclear reactors, which would represent some of the most ambitious commercial power projects ever pursued.

The Net Present Value of the ITC Is Diluted When Paid at Project Completion

Even assuming that the ITC can be monetized without a steep haircut, the timeline for monetization is generally suboptimal for developers and ratepayers. Treasury regulations for the ITC state that tax credits are typically earned the year that the power plant is “placed in service,” what developers commonly refer to as the Commercial Operations Date (COD). Construction timelines between the pouring of first nuclear concrete and the project COD can span the better part of a decade. The “backloaded” nature of the ITC significantly dilutes its net present value for the nuclear developer. At a 7–10% cost of capital, a dollar of credit arriving eight years later is worth roughly half as much as it would be at Final Investment Decision (FID), when the developer first commits capital to construction. Banks could offer bridge financing to help developers capture the value of an ITC monetized in the future, but that path involves additional value dilution via transaction costs, bank fees, and interest rates.

Normalization Requirements Prevent Utilities from Passing ITC Savings to Ratepayers

Regulated investor-owned utilities (IOUs) are typically subject to ‘normalization’ requirements when claiming Investment Tax Credits for any new assets they develop and own. Normalization is an arcane feature of public utility accounting and tax law that requires any tax credits earned by IOUs to be “normalized” across the lifetime of the asset, as stated in §50(d)(2). Put simply, this requirement prevents an IOU that builds new nuclear from passing their ITC windfall along to ratepayers immediately — instead they can only pass the savings on to ratepayers extremely gradually, over the multi-decade lifespan of the new nuclear power plant. The perverse result: the public utility commission that oversees the IOU is less likely to approve the construction of new nuclear because the savings from the ITC cannot be passed on to ratepayers promptly, making the project look artificially expensive on ratepayer bills in the short run.

The 10% Domestic Content Bonus Requires Safe Harbor Tables

The high price tag of new nuclear will be easier to stomach for developers, public utility commissions, and ratepayers if there is a clear path to the projects earning the full 50% ITC. That path does not exist today for either of the 10% bonus credits. The first, the Domestic Content bonus, requires that new nuclear projects meet a two-part requirement:

The ‘Steel and Iron’ requirement: 100% of structural steel and iron products must be produced in the United States.

The ‘Manufactured Products’ requirement: 55% of the total value of all Manufactured Products must be made in the United States.

The test starts with a nuclear power plant being broken down into distinct systems, referred to as “Applicable Project Components” (APCs). These macro-level APCs are classified as either structural ‘Steel and Iron’ products or ‘Manufactured Products.’

The federal government has yet to release information on what the APCs of a nuclear power plant are, or how the APCs are categorized into either the ‘Steel and Iron’ category or the ‘Manufactured Products’ category. The Treasury Department issued Notice 2023-38, which states that the ‘Steel and Iron’ requirements only apply to “construction materials that are made primarily of steel or iron and are structural in function” — this is somewhat helpful, but more specifics are needed in order for nuclear developers to accurately classify all of the components of a nuclear power plant into the correct category. It would be especially helpful if the Treasury released Safe Harbor Tables that define APCs for nuclear projects and provide standardized cost percentages. Treasury has already issued tables for other energy technologies including hydro, solar, wind, and battery energy storage systems. Treasury should take a careful approach for nuclear that both incentivizes domestic manufacturing and recognizes the complexity of nuclear power plants and the supply chains for their subcomponents. Many of these subcomponents are unlikely to be manufactured domestically on a reasonable timeline. If classification is conducted with prudence, a pathway for new nuclear to earn the Domestic Content bonus can be preserved within the constraints of the global supply chain.

The Energy Communities Bonus Does Not Apply to the Most Promising Sites for New Nuclear

The second 10% bonus — the Energy Communities bonus — is earned when a new nuclear project is constructed in specific parts of the country, but the implementation was poorly calibrated to the sites best suited for the next wave of nuclear construction, namely at existing nuclear sites. The pathway for most existing nuclear sites to capture the Energy Communities bonus runs through a definition the Treasury Department suboptimally implemented, making it excessively unstable for investment planning.

To satisfy the Energy Communities bonus, the new nuclear project must meet at least one of the following definitions:

Be located in a brownfield site as defined in the US Code;

Be located in a Metropolitan or Non-Metropolitan Statistical Area that meets specific labor market criteria, including a meaningful share of direct employment related to hydrocarbon industries and an unemployment rate at or above the national average; or

Be located in a Census tract with either a coal mine closure after 1999 or a coal-fired power plant retirement after 2009, or an adjacent Census tract.

These definitions are complex enough that the Treasury Department had to clarify which sites do and do not qualify. Treasury published a 44-page document laying out their methodology to determine the full list across the second and third definitions. It updates this list every year because the qualifying locations change over time.

The first and third definitions are relatively stable and aligned with what is generally required to target investment, in contrast to the second definition. They tend to only expand their geographic scope over time, and do not remove any geographic location that has previously qualified. On the other hand, the second definition, as currently interpreted by the Treasury, is highly unstable because of how local area unemployment rates are estimated and compared to the national average. Sites that satisfy this Energy Communities definition in one year can easily fail to do so in a subsequent year, thereby making it difficult to plan investments into these sites.

The unfortunate fact for nuclear and other ITC-supported technologies is that the first and third definitions, despite their stability, are poorly suited to the other geographic factors relevant for siting development. The next wave of new nuclear projects is likely to be built at the sites of the existing nuclear fleet. Existing nuclear sites have benefits including established interconnection infrastructure and strong support from local communities who recognize the benefits of hosting nuclear power. The first definition disfavors sites that previously required permits related to the Clean Water Act, which disfavors existing nuclear sites. The third definition is useful for existing or previous coal sites, but offers little relevance to new nuclear projects planned at existing nuclear sites. Employ America will discuss these issues in greater detail in a forthcoming piece on the limitations of Energy Communities definitions.

If existing nuclear sites are to capture the Energy Communities bonus for the ITC, the second definition will need an implementation overhaul. There is no way for a nuclear developer to site a project — a decision made years in advance of when construction actually commences — to ensure that the second Energy Communities definition is satisfied based on the current IRS guidance. Employ America will be publishing a detailed whitepaper outlining our potential solutions for making the bonus substantially more effective through revised IRS guidance.

There was a flawed attempt in the OBBB to create a fourth Energy Communities definition to grandfather in existing reactor sites. This definition only applied to the PTC and was explicitly made inapplicable to the ITC. This attempt at grandfathering also comes with its own deficiencies, and has thus complicated the IRS’s ability to provide the requisite guidance to make this definition fully usable for nuclear developers interested in pursuing the nuclear PTC.

Taken together, this litany of challenges highlights the gulf between the “buy one, get one” claim and the tough policy reality on the ground. The good news is that these challenges can be addressed. In fact, a bold administration can address these issues credibly without additional congressional action.

Potential Congressional Fixes Face an Uphill Climb

The discussed problems could be solved by passing bills through Congress. Multiple pieces of legislation have been introduced that are targeted at some of these challenges, including bills introduced by Representatives Pat Harrigan and Dan Newhouse as well as Senator Tim Scott.

The Department of Energy has signaled that they are interested in pursuing legislative solutions to these ITC challenges. DOE EDF Director Greg Beard and Acting Chief Investment Officer Julie Kozeracki joined Thomas Hochman on the Right of Way Podcast to push Congress to pass legislation that would deliver a range of fixes to the ITC for new nuclear development. Employ America is supportive of these efforts, but legislation is always a challenging exercise. What may prove more promising: an alternative pathway to those same policy outcomes, but based solely on administrative actions and authority.

Unlocking Direct Pay and QPEs for Projects through Administrative Action

Congress has already legislated a solution that allows a certain class of project owners to bypass many of these ITC challenges: Direct Pay. This provision of the tax code, which is also referred to as Elective Pay, bypasses the need to sell the ITC through “transferability” and allows a project developer to monetize the value of the tax credit as a direct cash payment from the IRS. The steep haircut that a developer would face by selling the tax credit would be fully avoided. Direct Pay under current law also allows the project owner to monetize the ITC through Qualified Progress Expenditures (QPEs). QPEs allow a portion of the ITC to be paid out every year based on construction spending during that year, rather than in one lump sum at project COD. Current law bans the transfer (sale) of QPE tax credits into the tax equity market, but Direct Pay bypasses the need for transferability altogether. It is hard to overstate how transformative these payments during construction would be for improving project economics and lowering perceived project risk.

The success of Direct Pay and QPEs as an ITC monetization mechanism can be seen in a different industry with similar levels of capital intensity: semiconductors. The bipartisan CHIPS Act of 2022 provided direct funding and tax credits to encourage domestic semiconductor fabrication in the United States. $38.2 billion of direct funding was appropriated by Congress for FY2022 through FY2026 for manufacturing incentives, with awardees selected by the Commerce Department. Additionally, the law created the §48D ITC (unrelated to the §48E ITC that applies to nuclear). The §48D ITC provided a 25% tax credit for qualifying semiconductor advanced manufacturing facility investments that break ground by the end of 2026. Notably, the law allowed for-profit chip manufacturers to claim their tax credits using Direct Pay and QPEs. The CHIPS Act achieved its desired goal: billions of new investment dollars flowed into semiconductor production on domestic soil. In fact, estimates on uptake of the §48D ITC have been larger than what was initially anticipated by the Congressional Budget Office. At least some of this outsized uptake can be attributed to the frictionless mechanics of Direct Pay and QPEs.

There are two challenges to making Direct Pay and QPEs viable for the nuclear ITC. The first is that claiming Direct Pay requires that a nuclear project also satisfy virtually the same Domestic Content Requirements as those specified for the 10% Domestic Content bonus. This requirement magnifies the importance of the federal government issuing Domestic Content guidance that enables a path for new nuclear to earn the Domestic Content bonus within existing supply chains. The second challenge appears more daunting. The current statute states that Direct Pay can only be claimed by the following entities:

Tax-exempt organizations (non-profits, universities, religious organizations, etc.)

States or political subdivisions of states (e.g., the New York Power Authority)

The Tennessee Valley Authority

Any Indian tribal government or Alaska Native Corporation

Rural electric cooperatives

It is essential to appreciate that access to Direct Pay depends on how the IRS defines and determines the owner of a particular project. The IRS’s inquiry is highly qualitative, doctrinal, and substantive. In some important ways, this inquiry diverges from conventional understandings of ownership. Employ America has identified a potentially viable pathway for IOUs and Independent Power Producers (IPPs), by contracting with and for a tax-exempt entity, to access the benefits of Direct Pay and QPEs for §48E ITC projects. This pathway would also allow IOUs to potentially avoid normalization requirements. Employ America will offer more details about this potential pathway in a separate piece.

In an ideal world, the IRS would adopt additional guidance that provides a safe harbor framework for defining the ownership structures that are eligible for Direct Pay under the §48E ITC. This outcome is economically desirable, legally feasible, and politically aligned with the administration’s broader energy policy objectives. If guidance proves too time-consuming to promulgate, private developers and tax-exempt entities can pay for a Private Letter Ruling from the IRS to assess eligibility for Direct Pay in their specific circumstances.

How to Make a 50% ITC a Reality for New Nuclear

Direct Pay and QPEs are most valuable for new nuclear if they are paired with a full 50% ITC. The path to earning a 50% ITC is not clear today for new nuclear — but it can be. The clarification required to unlock the 50% ITC pathway can even be achieved without congressional action, and the simplicity and speed of this solution is worth pursuing.

First, the Treasury Department and the IRS can promulgate a Domestic Content Safe Harbor Table that is strategically structured to account for the complexity of new nuclear, its existing supply chains, and the reality that final manufacturing processes are occurring in the United States. This is critical to enable both the 10% Domestic Content bonus and the only Direct Pay pathway for the ITC that does not require new legislation.

Second, the validity of the existing Direct Pay pathway could be formalized through additional IRS guidance, or, more narrowly validated through individual Private Letter Rulings. Tax-exempt organizations can serve as project owners for the purposes of the IRS and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission by taking on certain requisite burdens, while still giving developers and utilities the upside and project risk profile that they seek. The incomplete V.C. Summer project in South Carolina is one example of an AP1000 project that could benefit from identifying a structure that maintains sufficient ownership burden on the tax-exempt entity, even as there are contractual arrangements involving a for-profit developer. Santee Cooper, a state-owned utility eligible for Direct Pay, remains the official owner at V.C. Summer, even as it has sought out Brookfield, a private for-profit entity, to lead the development efforts. If the ownership structure and contractual arrangements can satisfy all relevant tax laws and doctrines, the ITC for V.C. Summer’s development could be monetized through Direct Pay & QPEs. Employ America has identified the potential for such an ownership structure that could still satisfy the relevant tax and nuclear regulatory considerations for ownership.

Third, the Treasury Department can revise the Energy Communities guidance to align it with the realities of project development timelines for technologies that currently qualify for the ITC. The original Energy Communities guidance was implemented suboptimally and remains poorly aligned with any technology that involves substantial pre-FID reliance interests. Revised guidance could yield a more functional and stable definition compared to the one Treasury originally adopted, which ignored some basic realities of how the Bureau of Labor Statistics develops its estimates. Employ America has identified an alternative interpretation of the statute that is superior on legal, statistical, and economic grounds. As noted earlier, Employ America will lay out the full set of issues associated with the current Energy Communities guidance, which inadvertently puts a thumb on the scale against technologies that involve higher upfront costs prior to construction.

The US Treasury Department can demonstrate its commitment to following through on the 10 reactor goal articulated in President Trump’s 2025 Executive Order by using its administrative authority to unlock the full force of the ITC for new nuclear. Absent Treasury action, these fixes would require a rare bipartisan window to pass complex energy tax law revisions — an admirable but substantially more speculative proposition.

Conclusion

The United States invented and commercialized civilian nuclear reactors: a safe, clean, and reliable way to generate large amounts of electricity. The financial support Congress has passed, with Democratic and Republican endorsement, can open up a real chance to scale the relevant learning curves and bring down costs. The promise of delivering new large nuclear projects on time and on budget is simply too valuable — whether for economic security, technological leadership, or broader prosperity — to pass up.

Employ America’s forthcoming public financial model indicates that the future of nuclear deployment is quite bright, but it hinges on maximizing the tools that Congress has already passed on a bipartisan basis. The next AP1000 projects will struggle to pencil with DOE EDF debt alone, and will require that debt be paired with a revitalized ITC. ITC fixes can occur through new legislation, but there is a more straightforward path that relies solely on administrative action. Employ America will publish a series of pieces that show how this pathway can be realized across the dimensions of Domestic Content, Direct Pay with QPEs, and Energy Communities.

title: NEPA is an environmental protection law - Legal Planet
description:
That is as true in environmental law as in any other area of law.
That makes it particularly frustrating to see this post today – which asserts that “NEPA is not an environmental protection law” simply because it has no substantive mandates.
That alone makes NEPA an environmental protection law.
There’s more, indirect, ways in which NEPA achieves environmental protection – as I’ve written before as well.
Of course, all that does not mean that NEPA is a perfect environmental protection law, or that it can’t be made better, or that incentivizing federal agencies to avoid environmental impacts is an unmitigated good.
text:
Claims to the contrary are just wrong

As I’ve written before, substance and procedure are not easily separated when you are talking about law. As practicing politicians, lawyers, and political scientists all have noted, procedure shapes substantive outcomes. That is as true in environmental law as in any other area of law.

That makes it particularly frustrating to see this post today – which asserts that “NEPA is not an environmental protection law” simply because it has no substantive mandates. That is wrong.

NEPA imposes potentially onerous obligations on federal projects that have significant environmental impacts. If nothing else, that creates an incentive for federal agencies to avoid projects with significant environmental impacts! Which in turn reduces (some) environmental harms. That alone makes NEPA an environmental protection law. Indeed, the common practice of federal agencies imposing mandatory mitigation measures on projects to avoid a finding of significant impacts is a nice example of how NEPA works in this way.

There’s more, indirect, ways in which NEPA achieves environmental protection – as I’ve written before as well. Public disclosure of those impacts can create pressure to reduce or avoid them. Requiring agencies to do environmental analyses may have changed who staffs those agencies, and agency culture, to more seriously consider environmental impacts. NEPA’s requirement that agencies consider environmental impacts removed the default argument agencies had before the law that environmental considerations were outside the scope of the issues they were to consider in making decisions.

Of course, all that does not mean that NEPA is a perfect environmental protection law, or that it can’t be made better, or that incentivizing federal agencies to avoid environmental impacts is an unmitigated good. Federal projects may both benefit and harm the environment, and we may think the benefits (far) outweigh the costs. For instance, federal agency permitting of wind or solar projects has climate change benefits, but can also have small-scale habitat impacts. We may think the climate change benefits far outweigh the habitat impacts. In that case, NEPA’s incentives to avoid environmental harms may be counterproductive. More broadly, we may be concerned that NEPA’s incentives to avoid harm are too strong, at the expense of other important social goals besides environmental protection. For instance, NEPA can exacerbate status quo bias in agency decisionmaking – and if we think change is important, that is costly.

And there are other ways in which NEPA might be problematic. As I’ve noted, the uncertainty of how environmental review is applied can be costly, because it exacerbates risk aversion and status quo bias. But of course, one could have NEPA that is more certain, but that is still procedural only, and would still to some extent deter agencies from taking environmentally harmful actions. Uncertainty, in other words, is a somewhat different question from whether a procedural only statute protects the environment.

text:
Further context: Additions made to the permitting bill specifically address the licensing and transparency of nuclear projects, as well as the compensation of employees at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. If this sounds familiar, that’s because the House passed six nuclear permitting bills this fall following extensive discussions during committee and markup hearings in the summer.

The Senate counterparts of four of these bills can be found in the amended version of BAAJA:

A provision that would make uncontested hearings the NRC conducts in its licensing reviews optional instead of mandatory.

A provision to allow the construction of a uranium enrichment facility to begin prior to license issuance by aligning the licensing requirements of these facilities with other fuel cycle facilities.

A provision to better compensate NRC staff, giving the regulatory agency a better chance to compete against private nuclear industry employers.

A provision that would require greater transparency from the Department of Energy in its authorization of reactors. This would require the secretary of energy to submit an annual report to the House Energy and Commerce and Senate Energy and Natural Resources committees detailing the DOE’s activities to authorize nuclear facilities during the previous calendar year.

Quotables: The bipartisan bloc behind the permitting bill praised its passage in the Senate.

“Tonight, the passage of permitting reform in the Senate finally became reality and we took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people,” said sponsor Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R., W.Va.). “I have spent years trying to achieve bipartisan compromise on legislation that gets our nation back to building, and the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the culmination of those efforts.”

Among his social media posts on the bill, sponsor Sen. Shelden Whitehouse (D., R.I.) said, “Our permitting reform bill kicks off Democrats bringing down energy costs, lowering emissions, creating well-paying jobs, and ending the free ride for data centers. Passing BAAJA in the Senate was a major step forward, and I’m grateful to my colleagues and our friends in the labor movement and the clean energy industry for their hard work to make this happen.”

The Nuclear Innovation Alliance supports the bill and its inclusion of the nuclear permitting–specific amendments. President and CEO Judi Greenwald said, “These provisions would help create the conditions needed for a successful and robust nuclear energy sector. Together, they would improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s licensing processes, support the deployment of domestic nuclear fuel infrastructure, and strengthen the NRC’s ability to attract and retain a highly qualified workforce. They would also increase transparency around DOE’s nuclear safety standards and authorization processes, helping build public confidence that reforms under way maintain rigorous safety oversight while creating an effective and durable framework for nuclear energy deployment.”

Ahead of the Senate vote, Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy issued a white paper analyzing BAAJA, calling it the “most comprehensive effort in years to reform federal energy infrastructure permitting.” According to its findings, projects could get approved faster and permits could face fewer legal hurdles. Electric transmission projects could benefit the most, lower energy bills are a possibility, and the reforms likely would produce a net reduction in emissions— although the extent by which emissions may drop is unknown. Some provisions, however, could be strengthened to prevent unintended consequences, the findings added.

Next steps: BAAJA’s fate in the House is up in the air, despite bipartisan backing. Multiple news reports have said some environmental groups and Native American tribes oppose the legislation because it would alter requirements in the National Environment Policy Act, Clean Water Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act.

There is division within the Democratic Party on whether to wait it out until the new year, when the Democrats take control of both the Senate and House. For instance, Sen. Raphael Warnock (D., Ga.) voted ‘no’ on BAAJA, despite arguing for the need to reform permitting.

“I had hoped that a robust amendment process could’ve addressed these shortcomings in the bill that Georgians have rightly raised, but in its absence, I am voting no. I believe we can get a better bill when a new Congress is sworn in this January,” he said in a statement.

Furthermore, after Thanksgiving, lawmakers will have to turn their attention to passing a government funding bill ahead of a December 11 deadline to avoid a government shutdown.

authors: Teresa Tomassoni, Anita Hofschneider, Richard Schiffman, Alex Nguyen, Anna Merlan, Mariana Duran, Audrey Gray, Inae Oh

text:
This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

In a historic first, the Department of Interior has leased more than 31 million acres of Pacific waters to a deep-sea mining company seeking to exploit mineral-rich deposits from the ocean floor off American Samoa.

“This is the first time that a lease has been issued for deep-sea mining in US waters,” said Arlo Hemphill, US project lead against deep-sea mining for Greenpeace USA.

Deep-sea mining is a highly contested, emerging industry that aims to extract rock-like deposits on the seabed called polymetallic nodules, formed over millions of years. They contain cobalt, copper, manganese and nickel—so-called “critical minerals” used in batteries, electronics and other devices that have historically been mined on land. To date, no commercial deep-sea mining operations have begun anywhere in the world.

Scientists, environmentalists and Indigenous peoples with strong cultural connections to the ocean aim to stop the industry from moving forward at all. “Once mining strips away habitat that took millions of years to form, no amount of money can bring it back,” said Hemphill in a statement. “Congress should press the administration to suspend these leases before work begins.”

The lease sale took place Thursday, during a live auction held at the Ventura County Fire Department in Thousand Oaks, California, as Hemphill and dozens of other activists from American Samoa and across the Pacific rallied, prayed and sang outside in protest.

“This is not just seabed on a map. This is our home, our livelihoods, our identity, and our responsibility to protect,” said Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, American Samoa’s youth and environment nonprofit, who traveled from American Samoa to protest the auction. “Ocean rights are human rights, and our home is not for sale,” she said in a statement.

Representatives from just two companies attended the auction, including Adepth Minerals Inc., from Norway, and Wetstone US Ventures, a New York-based offshore critical minerals exploration and deep-sea mining company.

Ultimately, Wetstone bid $6 million on two areas marked for mineral exploration that lie adjacent to the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a marine protected area established by President George W. Bush in 2009 to protect more than 10,000 square miles of ocean from commercial fishing and other forms of extraction.

The bid made Wetstone the provisional winner of the auction, according to a spokesperson from the Marine Minerals Administration. The new office was established earlier this year within the Department of Interior to help promote the Trump administration’s agenda to secure critical minerals.

“A dependable critical minerals supply chain is essential to American manufacturing and the technologies that power our economy and national defense,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, in a statement about Thursday’s auction. “Today’s sale opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”

The areas offered for leasing will be open for exploration activities, which include mapping and surveying the seabed to locate mineral rich deposits. Actual mining would require further federal approvals. But Hemphill and others warn that exploration in itself is a dangerous step towards paving the way for an industry that could threaten ocean ecosystems and the people that depend on them.

“The industry will push to move from surveys to exploration to extraction, putting profits ahead of marine life and trampling the culture, livelihood and objections of communities that have said no again and again,” Hemphill said.

Ever since the proposed lease sale was announced earlier this year, many American Samoan leaders and communities have voiced their concerns. Several lawsuits were filed against the Trump Administration to stop it from happening.

Just a few days before the lease sale, a federal judge in Hawaiʻi ruled the Marine Minerals Administration had violated the Endangered Species Act by approving the lease sale without taking into account the potential impacts of exploration and mining on endangered species.

The areas leased are home to several dozen endangered species including the blue whale, fin whale, sei whale and sperm whale, as well as the leatherback sea turtle, oceanic whitetip shark, and giant manta ray.

Many of these species are already threatened by climate change, which is altering their sources of prey and migration patterns. More than 1,000 marine science and policy experts from 75 countries say deep-sea mining could further add to the stress these marine animals are facing.

“In deciding to move forward with today’s scheduled sale, the Trump administration has performed a renegade, unlawful act,” said Chris Eaton, attorney at Earthjustice, an environmental nonprofit that represented American Samoan and Hawaiian plaintiffs in the lawsuit. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” he said in a statement Thursday.

text:
Why It Matters

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has partially approved three San Joaquin Valley Unified Air Pollution Control District air permitting rules, effective Dec. 21. ​

The decision incorporates updated permitting requirements into California's federally enforceable air pollution control plan while identifying deficiencies that the district must address to avoid federal sanctions. For lobbyists representing manufacturers, industrial facilities, developers, and transportation interests, the focus shifts to corrective regulatory changes, emissions offset requirements, and potential highway funding restrictions.

What Changes for Businesses Seeking Air Permits?

The final rule updates federal air permitting regulations for California and incorporates three revised district rules. EPA identified three outstanding deficiencies:

The district's definition of volatile organic compounds omits a chemical exemption recognized under federal regulations.

References to standardized emissions testing methods fail to specify which versions of those methods apply.

Permitting requirements for new and modified industrial facilities lack a federally approved definition of emission reduction credits.

The third deficiency is especially relevant to businesses that rely on emission reduction credits to obtain permits for new facilities or expansions. The district can continue enforcing its existing rules locally while addressing these deficiencies.

When Could Federal Sanctions Take Effect?

Unless EPA approves corrective revisions, two sanctions deadlines will follow the Dec. 21 effective date:

June 21, 2028: Emissions offset sanctions could increase permitting requirements for new or expanding industrial facilities.

Dec. 21, 2028: Federal highway funding sanctions could take effect.

EPA must also establish a federal air pollution control plan within 24 months unless it approves corrective revisions before then.

During the public comment period, five environmental and community organizations argued that the district had not adequately corrected deficiencies identified in a previous EPA action. EPA disagreed, finding that the earlier deficiencies had been addressed.

Who Is Lobbying on Air Permitting?

Federal disclosures identify companies engaged in air permitting policy, although the cited activity does not specifically reference the San Joaquin Valley rule-making.

Caterpillar Inc. reported $50,000 in first-quarter lobbying and $20,000 in second-quarter lobbying, identifying air permitting issues in its disclosures.

Which other organizations are lobbying on air permitting, emissions standards, and Clean Air Act requirements? Explore additional disclosures on Legis1.

Next Steps

Organizations seeking to challenge the final rule in federal court must file by Jan. 19, 2027. Asking EPA to reconsider its decision does not extend that deadline or postpone the rule's effectiveness. EPA intends to work with the district to correct the deficiencies.

Industry representatives should assess clients' pending and planned permits, determine how potential sanctions could affect expansion projects, and engage with local regulators as they develop corrective measures.

name: Clean Energy
title: Opinion - Voters Don't Want What the Senate is Considering - KVNF
description:
Americans are equally clear about their love of public lands and the freedom to enjoy them.
The voters didn’t demand industrial oil and gas development over every acre of America’s Arctic, one of our wildest places.
The biggest threats are provisions that risk locking in development on our public lands.
The bill imposes tight, new timelines and requires taxpayers to reimburse corporate permitting costs if deadlines are missed.
We can build a clean energy future while protecting public lands, the clean air and water they provide, and the opportunities we owe future generations.
text:
The country just held an election centered on the high costs of living. The electorate spoke loudly and clearly.

Americans are equally clear about their love of public lands and the freedom to enjoy them. Poll after poll shows it. The voters didn’t demand industrial oil and gas development over every acre of America’s Arctic, one of our wildest places. They didn’t ask that we give a foreign company the permanent option to build a sulfide-ore copper mine upstream from Minnesota’s pristine Boundary Waters. They didn’t clamor for unchecked data centers and oil rigs across the West.

They certainly didn’t vote to surrender their say in what happens to lands that belong to all of us.

Unfortunately, that and more would result from the permitting reform bill before Congress, euphemistically called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

The bill includes important provisions to improve the electrical power grid and permit renewable energy projects the president unfairly sidelined. But the cost of those reforms is far too high. The biggest threats are provisions that risk locking in development on our public lands. Once a project gets a green light, future administrations would be severely limited in the ability to alter or rescind it, even if the project is unlawful, or even if new science shows it would be destructive.

Courts couldn’t halt or invalidate permits over flawed reviews. A judge could only demand paperwork revisions while development continues.

Imagine what this administration, or any future administration, could do with this corporate get-out-of-jail-free card? Picture industrial development across what used to be Bears Ears National Monument, your favorite family campsite or smack in the middle of elk winter range. Future generations may have no way to undo the damage.

And that’s just one tradeoff. The bill further guts the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act and the National Environmental Policy Act — our safeguards that protect clean air and water, wildlife and community involvement.

Tribal nations and organizations have also sounded the alarm over how it usurps tribal sovereignty, undermining how and when the federal government must consult with tribes under the National Historic Preservation Act over development that might affect their treaty rights and tribal homelands.

As some have noted, the result of the bill would be a fundamental shift in how government works. Government would protect corporate interests from the public rather than protecting the public from corporate interests.

There’s also a practical problem. The bill imposes tight, new timelines and requires taxpayers to reimburse corporate permitting costs if deadlines are missed.

When I ran the Bureau of Land Management, it had close to 10,000 employees. Even then, we needed more capacity. Still, working closely with the Fish and Wildlife Service, we issued thousands of permits, including three major transmission lines and two critical mineral mines. We set records for permitting both renewable energy and oil and gas.

Today, however, the BLM has roughly half that staff — 5,500 employees — after being DOGEd and attacked by this administration. The Fish and Wildlife Service has been similarly gutted. Same with the Forest Service. Permitting requires people to get on the ground, assess problems and solve them. It requires ensuring communities have a voice in protecting clean air, clean water and wildlife. Dismantled agencies won’t be able to meet these deadlines.

You don’t make a horse run faster by starving it half to death and hope if you whip it harder, it will magically run faster. If Congress wants to speed up permits, it should focus on hiring agency staff as a critical first step. If it wants to solve the problem of not enough power lines, it should pass that portion of the bill.

Above all, Congress must not give this administration the ability to permanently hand our shared public lands over to corporate interests. The oil and gas industry has made $130 billion in windfall profits just since the president began the Iran war. It doesn’t need more favors from Congress.

Americans went to the polls demanding that Washington address their immediate needs, not those of powerful corporations. Congress should listen. We can build a clean energy future while protecting public lands, the clean air and water they provide, and the opportunities we owe future generations. That’s the kind of permitting reform Americans deserve.

name: Congress
title: Climate scientists come out against BAAJA — and Sheldon Whitehouse
description:
And in his 300th climate speech last year, Whitehouse expressed gratitude toward early climate researchers.
“They got it right.” But now, some of the scientists Whitehouse has urged others to listen to say he is failing to heed his own advice.
In the letter, the scientists say BAAJA would slow the transition to net zero emissions by prolonging the fossil fuel era, locking in future emissions and catastrophic climate change.
Whitehouse and other tech-adjacent climate advocates argue that BAAJA will help the climate by speeding the transition to renewable energy.
“I have great respect for these climate scientists, and I am sorry to disagree with them here,” he said.
text:
Since 2012, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse has delivered more than 300 speeches on the Senate floor about climate change. And in those speeches, time and again, the Democrat from Rhode Island has urged his fellow lawmakers to listen to scientists.

“We are not elected to be scientists; we are elected to listen to them,” Whitehouse said in his 100th climate floor speech in 2015. “How is it that we don’t listen to the scientists on this, particularly right here in this room, in this Chamber?” he asked in his 177th speech in 2017. “Listen to the scientists. We could do more of that,” he said in his 272nd speech in 2020. And in his 300th climate speech last year, Whitehouse expressed gratitude toward early climate researchers. “God bless the scientists,” he said. “They got it right.”

But now, some of the scientists Whitehouse has urged others to listen to say he is failing to heed his own advice.

In an open letter released Monday afternoon, more than 100 climate scientists and scholars urged the House of Representatives to vote no on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA)—the sweeping permitting bill Whitehouse helped write and push through the Senate last week.

In the letter, the scientists say BAAJA would slow the transition to net zero emissions by prolonging the fossil fuel era, locking in future emissions and catastrophic climate change.

”We understand the need for trade-offs and compromise when passing bipartisan legislation,” the letter reads. “But as scientists we feel strongly that the costs of this bill to the climate are too high.”

The bill, in a nutshell, would loosen some longstanding environmental and tribal laws in order to speed up development of large projects in the U.S., from wind turbines to gas pipelines to data centers. It passed the Senate last week with no committee hearings, markups or legislative reports—and as HEATED reported, very little media coverage.

Whitehouse and other tech-adjacent climate advocates argue that BAAJA will help the climate by speeding the transition to renewable energy. They say that easing restrictions will make wind, solar, and the power lines needed to deliver their electricity easier to build—and new provisions will protect those projects from hostile administrations. They say gains in renewables will outweigh the harm of making fossil fuel projects easier to build. They often point to a Rhodium Group analysis projecting that the bill could prevent up to 1.5 billion metric tons of U.S. climate pollution through 2040 compared with current policy.

But climate scientists rejected much of that case in their open letter. While they shared the goal of building renewable energy faster, they argued that BAAJA would also make fossil fuel projects easier to build, harder to regulate, and harder to phase out. They said the legal protections intended to shield wind and solar projects from hostile administrations could help fossil fuel companies in the same way. And they said the Rhodium Group analysis was flawed, because it left out how the bill’s changes to environmental laws could increase pollution and make future emissions cuts harder.

They instead pointed to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, a mechanical engineering professor at Purdue University, whose modeling found that BAAJA would likely increase U.S. greenhouse gas emissions and deaths from fossil fuel air pollution.

Even if the projected emissions savings materialized, the scientists argued, they would fall short of what’s needed to stop catastrophic warming, because fossil fuels would remain the dominant energy source. “Even reduced emissions continue to make global warming worse so long as they are ongoing,” the letter reads.

The signatories of Monday’s letter include many climate scientists whose work Whitehouse has cited in his “Time to Wake Up” floor speeches: Michael Mann, a climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania; Michael Oppenheimer, a climate scientist at Princeton; and Robert Brulle, an environmental sociologist at Brown whose research has helped expose the fossil fuel industry’s efforts to obstruct climate action.

Signatories also include many other respected climate researchers, like atmospheric physicist Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Arctic climate scientist Jennifer Francis, clean energy researcher Daniel Kammen, and biogeochemist Robert Howarth, who studies methane pollution from oil and gas.

In a statement to HEATED, Whitehouse acknowledged the disagreements, but stuck to his guns.

“I have great respect for these climate scientists, and I am sorry to disagree with them here,” he said. “The important takeaways about this bill are the gigaton-scale emissions reductions, the freed-up clean power, the $10 billion in annual consumer electricity savings, and the $35 billion whack at data centers.” (The $35 billion figure refers to an estimate by consultancy Grid Strategies of how much more large data centers would pay for electric transmission over 10 years under BAAJA).

Senator Martin Heinrich, the other Democratic co-sponsor, did not respond to HEATED’s request for comment.

Mann and Brulle helped organize the letter alongside J. Timmons Roberts, an environmental sociologist at Brown, and Genevieve Guenther, founding director of End Climate Silence. In interviews with HEATED, Mann and Brulle said they felt confused and betrayed by Whitehouse, whom they’ve long considered an ally in the fight for science-backed climate policy.

“He’s long been one of my heroes, and nothing pains me more than to find him not only in support of the bill but in fact one of its principal backers,” said Mann. “It’s the very sort of thing he’s spent his whole career fighting, and it just doesn’t compute.”

“Claude’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is easier to understand than his support of this bill,” he added.

Brulle echoed Mann’s sentiments.

”Senator Whitehouse has been an extraordinary champion and an inspiration to me for over a decade,” he said. “To say that I'm disappointed is only half of it. … it really makes me question his leadership and commitment to dealing with climate change.”

Support original climate reporting

Some more insights from the letter organizers

I asked Brulle and Mann to explain why they decided to take the step of organizing an open letter, and to detail some of their biggest concerns with the bill. Here’s what they said.

On why they decided to write an open letter:

Mann: “The speed with which this thing seems headed toward passage without the due diligence and scrutiny any such far-reaching bill demands, pushed through in the proverbial dark of night of the Thanksgiving holiday lull of a lame duck congressional session, and backed by a veritable who’s who of bad fossil fuel and dark money actors.”

Brulle: “We are advocates for following the science and climate policy. … We feel it’s our job to remind the politicians of the requirements of science to be able to deal with climate change. And so, therefore, we are addressing this to the House of Representatives, that still has a decision to make over this bill.”

On why it’s so important not to forget that oil industry loves this bill:

Brulle: For me, this is an example of a very, very carefully and excellently executed public relations campaign … I don’t know how they divided the work up between the API, National Association of Manufacturers, and Koch Enterprises. But Americans for Prosperity is all over this thing. … And as a social scientist who has studied many, many climate obstruction strategies, my considered professional opinion is that the way they started pushing it through a lame duck congress without any hearings was by designed to try to conceal from the public what’s really in this bill.

On why building out renewables isn’t enough:

Brulle: “To solve climate, you have to stop using fossil fuels. The natural environment doesn’t care that you have a whole bunch of renewable energy. Doesn’t care. That’s not going to affect climate change. What will affect climate change is when you shut down the coal power plant or the natural gas plant

”This bill basically makes it easier to add to fossil-fuel infrastructure. And so therefore it runs counter to the science of climate change that’s adopted by the IPCC.”

Mann: “The claim [that BAAJA will accelerate the energy transition] is based on the rosiest of scenarios that neglects all of the loopholes and mechanisms bad actors, including the Trump administration, have at their disposal to make sure the bad stuff (massive, indiscriminant greenlighting of new fossil fuel infrastructure and a dismantling of basic environmental protections) gets implemented while none of the good stuff (e.g. new clean energy projects) does, and none of the safeguards survive.

On what you would say a member of Congress who is sitting on the fence

Mann: I would say: think about your children, think about your grandchildren, think about their future. This does nothing but mortgage it.

Further reading

Sheldon Whitehouse is still the only Senator at international climate negotiations this year. This is probably an extra relevant thing to note, given the criticisms in today’s letter. Whitehouse did an extensive interview with Ocean State Media on the fight for climate progress abroad.

Those international talks fell apart over fossil fuels.CNBC reports: “On Sunday, after negotiations overran by almost two days, the latest cover proposal made no mention of fossil fuels, prompting outcry from governments and campaigners. Speaking on behalf of the EU, Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’Brien said the conference was “hijacked by some oil states,” when asked by Reuters about Saudi Arabia’s role in the negotiations.”

Why BAAJA is so polarizing for environmentalists. This New York Times piece is a good primer on understanding the divide between Whitehouse and others in the environmental movement.

text:
A district judge recently dealt ExxonMobil (XOM) a $339.56 million blow over oil sludge that's "continuously seeped" into soil, surface water, and an aquifer in northwest Louisiana for half a century. Legal experts say the first-of-its-kind judgment paves the way for future citizen lawsuits against oil giants in the state, which has long rated among the most polluted in the U.S.

"Exxon got walloped," said Robert Verchick, a professor of environmental law at Loyola University New Orleans. "I definitely think we will see more lawsuits like this," he said, due to the size of the verdict and the $12.7 million in fees awarded to the attorneys.

NOW PLAYING How This Uranium Enrichment Technology Aims To Solve The Nuclear Fuel Bottleneck For Big Tech

The 42nd Judicial Court in DeSoto Parish, Louisiana, found that an Exxon predecessor — Standard Oil Company of Louisiana — had, since 1954, abandoned 43 unlined pits of sludge across 243 acres of land. The court identified five violations against the state's Environmental Quality Act — for the pollution itself, for not cleaning it up and for failing to report it. But the daily fines levied against Exxon only stretch back to 1980, when the state enacted the environmental law.

The plaintiffs sought $848.9 million, all of which would've gone to the state, according to Verchick. The plaintiffs and legal experts expect the company to appeal. A spokesperson for Exxon said the company doesn't comment on pending litigation. Exxon said it only learned of the pollution through the lawsuit, according to the Oct. 30 judgment.

'Large Enough'

"The court considers the (nearly $340 million) penalty to be large enough that Exxon will not consider it to be merely the cost of doing business and believes it will deter this action in the future," the judgment said.

For context, Exxon told investors it had $12.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents on hand at the end of the third quarter (ending Sept. 30). In the quarterly filing, the company called the likelihood that lawsuits brought against it will harm its financial condition "remote." Analysts project that Exxon's coffers will nearly double to $23.2 billion in Q4 and rise to $94.2 billion by the end of the decade, according to a FactSet consensus.

"This is the biggest penalty I've ever seen in a citizen suit under state or federal law," said Patrick Parenteau, an emeritus professor and senior climate policy fellow at Vermont Law and Graduate School. In an email, he called the nearly $13 million in additional attorney fees, to be paid by Exxon, a "huge incentive for more cases." Parenteau cited Shell (SHEL), BP (BP), Sunoco (SUN) and Suncor (SU) among other potential near-term targets for environmental suits in the state.

In Louisiana, citizens can sue for violations of the state's environmental laws, but they have to give the state a chance to prosecute first. If the state government declines to do so, they effectively get the go-ahead, explained Verchick. Environmental laws have such provisions "because, the idea is, you can't always rely on government enforcers because there's not enough resources," he said. "Because the fines don't go to the citizen," Verchick added, "you are looking at a plaintiff who's just really interested in fairness and in getting this thing cleaned up," rather than seeking a lot of money in a "tort" lawsuit to settle a civil wrong.

'A Veritable Hotbed'

Parenteau sees cases rising across the U.S. against oil firms for the "legacy pollution they are leaving behind." He called Louisiana "a veritable hotbed for this litigation."

In the first quarter, Exxon warned investors that local Louisiana governments have filed "unprecedented legal proceedings" against it, "requesting compensation for the restoration of coastal marsh erosion in the state." Exxon called the basis of the cases "meritless."

Along with retaking Congress, Democrats' sweeping midterm election victories included securing key court seats in states across the U.S., including Texas and Indiana. While the Louisiana verdict centers on pollution, Verchick thinks the blue wave will limit oil companies' ability to successfully lobby for protections against climate lawsuits. Verchick believes such cases to be oil companies' primary concern.

Victor Flatt, who teaches environmental law at Case Western Reserve University, doesn't see the midterms changing the course of environmental suits at the federal level, citing President Donald Trump's veto powers. But, he said, "certainly the midterms signaled a 'vibe' shift and perhaps more willingness to pursue legacy pollution in general." Flatt expects that the Louisiana lawsuit in particular "will be changed on appeal and/or settled by the state."

Making A Fortune

This year, Exxon, Chevron (CVX), and other supermajor oil names have made a fortune on high gasoline and diesel prices related to the U.S./Israeli war on Iran and the Russia-Ukraine war.

Analysts expect Exxon's full-year earnings to surge 95% to $13.62 a share in 2026, per FactSet. They see it declining 9% in 2027, falling a further 17% in 2028 and dipping 2% in 2029. In a recent report, Valens analysts said Exxon's earnings must grow by 10% each year for the next three years to justify current valuations.

Exxon stock rose 1.1% to 158.58 in Tuesday afternoon trade, rebounding slightly off the 200-day line. Shares have tumbled from a record 188.50 on Oct. 30 as oil, diesel and especially gasoline prices have tumbled.
