text:
Less than a week after the fall – and subsequent rise – of Nvidia’s founding CEO Jensen Huang, the House Select Committee on the CCP heard from four witnesses about how to compete with China in the age of advanced technologies. Every one of them wanted more export controls, more restrictions, and more protections for industry. No one left room for leniency.

“We need more aggressive action on tariffs and preventing continued market share erosion in these (Section 232 tariffed) areas,” said witness Pat Gelsinger, General Partner of Playground Global, a $1.7 billion venture capital firm. “I think there will be more pressure on memory chips from China. The worldwide shortage is causing acute pressure on manufacturers and people saying, ‘well, let’s take some of those chips from China to alleviate the shortages,’ but we have to watch out for that,” he said in the Q&A session of a Nov. 20 hearing titled Outproducing the CCP and Restoring American Manufacturing. “You have to do this if you want to protect the semiconductor industry, which is the most important industry for everything else we do in the world. With Nvidia, I hope our IP was protected. AI is the industrial race of today and we want to protect it at all levels – the hardware, the chips, and protect the models. To do that, we need more aggressive levels of trade protection and export rules.”

Tim O’Leary, CEO of JetZero, said, “Any policy that makes it easy for the Chinese to purchase anything advanced technology right now is puzzling to me until they stop practices like IP theft, which is our primary concern as a technology company.” JetZero makes new types of aircraft, known as “blended wing.” Rather than looking like a traditional commercial aircraft, blended wing planes are more triangular and look like some fighter jets. Aerospace is one the advanced technology sectors where the U.S. maintains a consistent trade surplus, but O’Leary thinks that will eventually erode as China is throwing capital at the sector, led by Airbus and Boeing’s new Asian rival Comac.

Executives at the hearing were also wary about letting Chinese companies invest in the U.S.. This was especially true in the solar space, where Chinese multinationals, already a dominant force in solar, were benefiting from tax breaks in the Inflation Reduction Act. This effectively gave Chinese multinational solar companies a double subsidy: tax breaks in the U.S. and a whole host of incentives back home in China.

“My concern is Chinese companies use domestic investment as an avenue to get access to our market and then later use it as a backend to dump other products here,” said First Solar CEO Mark Widmar. “Let them stay in China. We don’t need them. We have great American companies that can do this here. Let’s invest in American companies first,” he said, a thinly veiled nod at the Trump administration’s year-one Executive Order titled the America First Investment Policy.

On the question of protective trade policies, Widmar mentioned the Section 232 polysilicon tariff regime, which goes into effect on Dec. 6:

“As this Committee has seen, solar built on China supply chains can be switched off by Beijing the moment it decides to use its leverage. The best remedies are specific, based on national security risk, economic abuse, and where we have the domestic capacity to build up local supply,” he said. “The Section 232s for polysilicon will do that. If you can properly enforce imports on polysilicon under the tariff policy, then you will create American jobs.”

Not only that, of course, the U.S. will command more of the solar power supply chain from top to bottom, something the country still lacks and remains reliant upon China for.

The overall takeaway from the hearing was that House CCP select committee members believe China copies and innovates on top of what they copy, and then replaces what they’ve copied. This runs across industries – from basic consumer goods sold on Amazon, to high tech products (like reusable rockets) and media services (such as TikTok). Witnesses called for extensions of tax credits that are expiring this year, and for more, long lasting industrial policies like the Inflation Reduction Act and the CHIPS Act. Rhetorically, the Committee is fully in favor of reshoring key industries. Of those mentioned were biotech/pharma; aerospace; renewable energy technologies and computer hardware, like Nvidia GPUs, for example. No one dared utter the words “friend shoring” in the hearing.

Witnesses said they needed policy uniformity from both parties regarding long term trade in order for them to feel more confident in investing domestically. Still, two companies – First Solar and JetZero – were both heavily invested in the U.S. Both want to make sure those investments are protected from an arch rival across the Pacific that has a completely different playbook from the West.

“The CCP has spent decades executing a global campaign to target economic sectors that matter most and China has now surpassed us in many of those areas, not because of market forces, but by strategic design,” said Committee Chairman John Moolenaar (R-MI-2) in his opening remarks. “The results have been disastrous. American workers and innovators have paid the price and our industrial base has been hollowed out.”

Committee Ranking Member Ro Khanna (D-CA-17) was the only Democrat to attend the hearing last week, however, Khanna said there was strong bipartisan support for China policy on trade and export restrictions.

He blamed corporations for “putting profits over countries” and added that it “led to the loss of the social and moral fabric of this country. We depend on China for everything to build the technologies of the future and a country that does that will not win the future.”

Rep. Khanna was the only member to talk about his interactions with constituents, including solar manufacturers and textile producers. He said he asked one company if the high tariffs on China yarns was helping them. “They said it doesn’t matter because the Chinese companies just eat the tariff,” Khanna said. “The textiles business there runs like a jobs program.”

Rep. Khanna also mentioned Nvidia, which at the time seemed to have punished its CEO for his moral ambiguity and misadventures in Singapore.

“China has proven that they can easily circumvent our export control laws,” Khanna said, wondering out loud if that meant that one day China will be able to reverse engineer the most advanced technology the U.S. has to offer.

“China already dominates in the machine tool industry now; that is becoming almost fully Chinese run. Last spring, I visited First Solar and I saw that with the right policies, we can restore domestic manufacturing and lower prices. If we invest in our workers and in manufacturing, we can outproduce the CCP,” Khanna said.

Rep. Jefferson Shreve (R-IN-6), who is not a member of the Committee, asked about pharmaceutical sourcing. “Are there transparency requirements that we ought to be working on in our jurisdictions to make it clear the vulnerabilities that our (pharma supply chain) faces,” he asked.

CPA’s Economics Team has invested heavily in research work in this space over the past couple of years.

Owen Herrnstadt, former member of the Board of Directors at the Export Import Bank (EXIM), appointed by former President Joe Biden, said he thought it would be hard to get to full transparency for the pharmaceuticals supply chain.

“Maybe companies will know at the tier 1 or tier 2 level, but further down the supply chain will be difficult and have less visibility,” he told Rep. Shreve. “We need to work with the private sector to figure out how we can get that visibility responsibly and accurately.”

Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC-10), also not a Committee member, said American and European companies were enmeshed in China’s critical supply chains. His comment speaks to the call for derisking from China, juxtaposed against the yeoman’s task of decoupling from China.

Last week, during the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, Xi Jinping called on the U.S. to reconsider decoupling, a suggestion that will definitely not fall on deaf ears in Washington due, in large part, to this entanglement of U.S. and Chinese supply chains.

“Boeing relies on thousands of Chinese components. They sell into our industries, or buy their way in,” Harrigan said, noting Chinese aviation giant AVIC, an entity list company, owns airframe maker Cirrus Design Corporation, a U.S. company listed in Hong Kong.

O’Leary (of JetZero) said AVIC is not alone. “There have been many aerospace manufacturers that have been purchased by Chinese companies and you wonder how this was approved in the first place. Twenty years ago, no one would have believed in Detroit automotive circles that China would become the world’s No. 1 car manufacturer, and yet today people doubt it will be a large or rather the largest aerospace manufacturer. We have to put our foot on the throttle on the anecdotes,” he said.

The Committee members asked about some solutions, beyond tariffs. Herrnstadt called the Made in America initiative at the Export Import Bank “crucial” because it is tied to U.S. manufacturing jobs.

“The future is about building a trade policy that is worker centered,” Herrnstadt said, taking a cue from another Biden appointee, former USTR Katherine Tai, who held to a similar line of thinking on trade and the labor force.

“The government needs to prioritize strong domestic sourcing requirements. We need to double down on that and make sure that domestic content requirements means the material is coming from the US, the manufacturing is being done in the U.S., and that it is not some imaginary label,” he said as one immediate solution. “Government procurement should go to U.S. workers and to U.S. companies.”

The Committee recently released a report titled “Rigging the Game.” The report focused on four sectors, including biotech and new machine tooling.

Across sectors, Beijing has used state tools to reduce the country’s dependence on foreign suppliers – including companies like Nvidia, which stands as a challenger to Huawei in Asia. China has also been able to benefit from its cost structure, helped by its manufacturing scalability, to expand the world’s dependence on Chinese production.

The House CCP select committee report’s final takeaway is that China has not yet achieved technological leadership in every sector, but its ability to mobilize capital, scale up quickly, and sustain investment over long time horizons “presents a significant challenge to U.S. manufacturing and national security.”

text:
KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.

She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.

She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.

Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.

Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.

"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."

The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.

The mine, known as COMMUS, is owned by Chinese multinational Zijin and lies in Kolwezi, a city of more than 500,000 people in the heart of Congo's copper belt, a southern region with vast mineral reserves.

Congo is the world's second-largest producer of copper, and also the source of over 70% of the world's cobalt, a metal that is critical to the electric-vehicle revolution because of its use in rechargeable batteries.

Last year, the U.S. signed a sweeping economic partnership with Congo aimed at attracting American investment and challenging the dominance of Chinese companies in the country's mining industry

Despite the global importance of Congo's copper and cobalt mines, however, environmental pollution from the industry has received comparatively little scrutiny.

In Kolwezi, pollution is severe. Neighborhoods near mines are often filled with an acrid smell that residents attribute to the sulfuric acid used to process minerals. A study published in June by environmental research organization Source International — carried out with the advocacy groups RAID and Afrewatch, and scientists from Congo's University of Lubumbashi — also highlighted the scale of the contamination.

Researchers found that levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, in Kolwezi were three to six times the World Health Organization's air quality guideline. The highest concentrations were recorded near the COMMUS mine.

These tiny particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure poses health risks generally, but is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and young children.

The researchers also tested dust samples and found residue of copper, cobalt and manganese, which they said pointed to mining waste as the main source. When the study was released, Source International's executive director, Flaviano Bianchini, said that "these are among the most concerning air quality results we have documented in years of monitoring pollution at industrial mining sites around the world."

The study did not examine health impacts directly, and the authors recommended formal epidemiological research. Residents and health workers in Kolwezi nonetheless point to a string of ailments that they blame on a polluted environment.

In a dilapidated health clinic in the shadow of a mountain of waste from the COMMUS mine, nurse Héritier Bukassa said that people routinely break out in itchy hives. "Some sick people scratch themselves with knives to relieve itching," he explained.

Bukassa added that women in the area also suffer from high rates of miscarriage, and that he had referred four babies born with congenital malformations — mostly cleft palates — to hospitals this year alone.

Respiratory illnesses are common too, Bukassa said, especially in otherwise healthy babies who develop breathing problems a few weeks after birth. "No one from the [mining] company has ever come to talk to us about this," the nurse said.

Zijin, the owner of COMMUS, did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Neither did Congo's mining and environment ministries.

The Cobalt Institute, an industry lobby, said that understanding environmental pollution requires "an evidence-based approach that considers all potential sources and contributors." It added that companies perform environmental monitoring and carry out mitigation measures.

RAID, which is supporting the plaintiffs alongside Afrewatch, described the case this month as one of "the most ambitious legal challenges yet brought by Congolese residents over industrial mining pollution."

The suit is an important test case that could lead to communities challenging other mines in the future, it added.

The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.

The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."

title: Fracking, but for clean energy? UC scientists are working on it | University of California
description:
The old limits on geothermal power Geothermal power is not actually a new idea.
Geothermal power is poised to grow more than 50-fold in the next 25 years, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Making geothermal energy safer for U.S. communities Can geothermal energy developers borrow tech from the fracking industry without also borrowing its consequences?
Qomi’s team now includes scientists from UC Berkeley, UC Irvine, UC Riverside, UC San Diego, UC Santa Cruz, plus Los Alamos, Lawrence Livermore and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratories, and three industry partners.
And if they can figure that out, America could soon be on its way to powering up to 70 million homes with renewable, reliable, 24-7 geothermal energy.
text:
Heat is energy. That’s why we burn stuff, like oil and gas, to run our cars and generate electricity. But fossil fuels aren’t the only sources of energy buried beneath our feet. Just ask anyone who’s worked a shift in 130-degree temperatures at the bottom of a mine: Deep underground, the rock itself is plenty hot. Could we put that heat to use?

“There is more than enough potential geothermal energy underground to power the entire United States, but unlocking it safely and economically is still a major challenge,” says UC Irvine engineer Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi. Now, with funding from the U.S. Department of Energy, Qomi leads a team of UC scientists that’s taking on this challenge

The goal: to tap into an inexhaustible source of energy that could help meet the nation’s growing need for electricity safely and economically, without contributing more climate-warming carbon to the atmosphere.

The old limits on geothermal power

Geothermal power is not actually a new idea. People have been tapping into the Earth’s buried heat for millennia, building homes over hot spots to keep warm all winter, for instance, or bathing in natural hot springs. These days we have power plants that pull steam or hot water from natural reservoirs in the earth’s crust and pipe it through turbines to generate electricity.

Today these benefits are mostly confined to the few places on Earth where water percolates through hot, porous rock, somewhere close enough to the surface that people can drill down and reach it. Iceland fits the bill: geothermal power supplies 30% of the country’s electricity. So does the Geyers, a geothermal field in Northern California, where 18 power plants generate about 2% of California’s electricity.

Most everywhere else, the rock is too dry, or too dense, or the heat is too far underground. But now that’s starting to change. Geothermal power is poised to grow more than 50-fold in the next 25 years, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. And the coming boom in reliable, renewable, zero-carbon energy has a surprising source: the fracking industry.

Fracking technology could unlock more geothermal energy

In the past 20 years, petroleum engineers have gotten better at drilling deep, and at drilling horizontally underground. Then they pipe in water, sand and chemicals to fracture the rock and release oil and gas trapped within. These methods, known as fracking, tapped deposits that other methods couldn't, and made the U.S. the world’s top exporter of liquified natural gas.

If fracking works for fossil fuels, could it also work for heat? That’s the idea behind so-called enhanced geothermal energy systems, says Qomi.

“If you drill down deep enough — three, four, even six kilometers — you reach the point where the crust is uniformly hot,” Qomi says. “Then you can drill horizontally, create fractures, and pipe in water.” The rock heats the water, turning it to steam that can run turbines that generate electricity.

“Instead of offering geothermal energy for only a few who are located in very special places,” geothermal plants could become a lot more common, Qomi says.

Making geothermal energy safer for U.S. communities

Can geothermal energy developers borrow tech from the fracking industry without also borrowing its consequences? In addition to the general hazards of burning fossil fuels — including air pollution and a changing climate — fracking in particular has caused some serious problems for local communities.

For instance: Injecting fluid in the Earth’s crust can cause what’s known in the business as induced seismicity. Between 2008 and 2019, Oklahoma saw a 900-fold increase in earthquakes as fracking expanded across the state.

Those quake swarms are a product of overlapping forces deep underground, where pressure, heat, fluids and chemistry interact in ways that scientists are only beginning to understand. It’s the kind of problem that artificial intelligence, which can detect never-before-seen patterns in complex systems, is primed to help solve.

With funding from the UC Office of the President, Qomi began assembling a team of UC experts to take on this challenge two years ago. Now, the U.S. Department of Energy is backing Qomi’s team as part of its Genesis Mission, a nationwide effort that puts AI to work for breakthroughs in energy, discovery, and national security. UC scientists lead 40 of the first 278 projects funded by the Genesis Mission, announced in July.

Qomi’s team now includes scientists from UC Berkeley, UC Irvine, UC Riverside, UC San Diego, UC Santa Cruz, plus Los Alamos, Lawrence Livermore and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratories, and three industry partners. They’re blending large language models, physics-based models, and real-world data from existing geothermal sites into an artificial intelligence platform that illuminates invisible dynamics deep underground. The tool will help energy developers determine where and how to drill state-of-the-art geothermal wells safely and economically — avoiding hazards like earthquakes, groundwater contamination or broken drills.

And if they can figure that out, America could soon be on its way to powering up to 70 million homes with renewable, reliable, 24-7 geothermal energy. “This is not some sort of a science fiction kind of thing,” Qomi says. “It has its challenges, but it can be realized.”

text:
One of Budget 2026’s most consequential long-term investments, $1.6 billion over 10 years to improve energy reliability in northern communities, has so far received little attention despite its far-reaching potential for positive impact for communities across the country’s North.

The announcement responds to a challenge that northern energy leaders – including communities, research bodies, and advocacy groups – have highlighted for decades. Namely, the need for modern and reliable energy solutions that can support economic opportunity, strengthen energy security, and give communities more control over their own energy systems.

It also acknowledges that for the federal government to meet its ambitious economic and security agenda it will need to invest in reliable northern energy systems.

For years, Northern energy infrastructure has been increasingly strained by growing demand and decades of underinvestment. More recently, this strain has become undeniable in the face of community-wide evacuations from systems failure, threats of rolling blackouts in capital cities, and the increasing cost of fuel.

At the intersection of these shortfalls are more than 200 remote communities across Canada, including every community in the territories, who remain disconnected from the North American electricity grid and rely primarily on diesel fuel to generate electricity and heat homes. This dependence creates vulnerabilities that are difficult to appreciate south of 60.

Every litre of diesel fuel must be shipped vast distances by road, barge or air, whether that’s from refineries in Canada, Asia, or elsewhere on the planet. Costs are high and increasingly volatile. Supply chains are vulnerable to disruptions. Aging infrastructure requires growing maintenance as demand for energy rises. And the pressures on these systems are only intensifying.

Northern populations are growing. Climate change is altering landscapes, transportation routes and infrastructure conditions throughout the Arctic. At the same time, both the federal government and private sector are increasing their focus on Northern development, from housing and transportation investments to critical mineral projects and defence infrastructure.

Canada is rightly devoting greater attention to Arctic sovereignty and security under uncertain geopolitical and economic conditions. But it is only now becoming clearer that strategic ambitions alone will not strengthen the North; for the government’s ambitious agenda to succeed, it will also need to invest in reliable, modern community infrastructure.

The encouraging news is that we have evidence of what works – diversified, modernized, and locally-built energy infrastructure.

Over the past decade, Indigenous and local leaders have advocated for and built these exact solutions with the support of innovative federal programs and partners. This collaborative effort has helped communities build hundreds of clean energy projects across the country, reducing more than 142 million litres of diesel since 2016, creating good jobs, local expertise, and strengthened energy security in the process. Altogether, recent research from the Pembina Institute shows that these efforts have spurred the most significant energy transition in remote and Northern communities since the 1950s when the diesel generators were originally installed in the North.

The most successful of these projects have emerged from partnerships between communities, Indigenous leaders, northern utilities and governments working toward shared goals of energy independence, affordability, and emissions reduction. Their success demonstrates what can happen when local leadership is matched with long-term support and investment.

That is why the new funding announced in Budget 2026 presents such an important opportunity. When done in partnership, real progress can be made on difficult and seemingly entrenched infrastructure and policy issues.

But, while past programs have achieved significant success, they were also designed for a different moment, and the needs of communities and industry in remote and Northern areas of the country are changing. More than a decade after the early programs were implemented, today's energy landscape is shaped by new realities including rising costs, growing electricity demand, heightened interest in critical mineral development and increased defence investments.

Meeting these challenges will require both recapitalization of existing programs and deeply focused and collaborative work to advance the next generation or projects. Necessarily, this will require a concerted effort to address the embedded regulatory and policy fissures that continue to hold back the type of progress needed to meet this moment at pace and scale. Ultimately, this means that the next generation of federal support must be durable, flexible and shaped alongside the communities it is intended to serve.

For a budget measure that attracted relatively little attention, the stakes could hardly be higher. This is because reliable energy is not only about keeping the lights on, but also about ensuring all communities have the tools they need to build economic opportunity, resilience and prosperity. Budget 2026's investment recognizes this reality. Now comes the harder and more important task of turning that commitment into lasting results.

text:
Updated November 24, 2026 at 12:09 PM EST

KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.

She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.

She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.

Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.

Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.

"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."

The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.

The mine, known as COMMUS, is owned by Chinese multinational Zijin and lies in Kolwezi, a city of more than 500,000 people in the heart of Congo's copper belt, a southern region with vast mineral reserves.

Congo is the world's second-largest producer of copper, and also the source of over 70% of the world's cobalt, a metal that is critical to the electric-vehicle revolution because of its use in rechargeable batteries.

Last year, the U.S. signed a sweeping economic partnership with Congo aimed at attracting American investment and challenging the dominance of Chinese companies in the country's mining industry

Despite the global importance of Congo's copper and cobalt mines, however, environmental pollution from the industry has received comparatively little scrutiny.

In Kolwezi, pollution is severe. Neighborhoods near mines are often filled with an acrid smell that residents attribute to the sulfuric acid used to process minerals. A study published in June by environmental research organization Source International — carried out with the advocacy groups RAID and Afrewatch, and scientists from Congo's University of Lubumbashi — also highlighted the scale of the contamination.

Researchers found that levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, in Kolwezi were three to six times the World Health Organization's air quality guideline. The highest concentrations were recorded near the COMMUS mine.

These tiny particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure poses health risks generally, but is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and young children.

The researchers also tested dust samples and found residue of copper, cobalt and manganese, which they said pointed to mining waste as the main source. When the study was released, Source International's executive director, Flaviano Bianchini, said that "these are among the most concerning air quality results we have documented in years of monitoring pollution at industrial mining sites around the world."

The study did not examine health impacts directly, and the authors recommended formal epidemiological research. Residents and health workers in Kolwezi nonetheless point to a string of ailments that they blame on a polluted environment.

In a dilapidated health clinic in the shadow of a mountain of waste from the COMMUS mine, nurse Héritier Bukassa said that people routinely break out in itchy hives. "Some sick people scratch themselves with knives to relieve itching," he explained.

Bukassa added that women in the area also suffer from high rates of miscarriage, and that he had referred four babies born with congenital malformations — mostly cleft palates — to hospitals this year alone.

Respiratory illnesses are common too, Bukassa said, especially in otherwise healthy babies who develop breathing problems a few weeks after birth. "No one from the [mining] company has ever come to talk to us about this," the nurse said.

Zijin, the owner of COMMUS, did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Neither did Congo's mining and environment ministries.

The Cobalt Institute, an industry lobby, said that understanding environmental pollution requires "an evidence-based approach that considers all potential sources and contributors." It added that companies perform environmental monitoring and carry out mitigation measures.

RAID, which is supporting the plaintiffs alongside Afrewatch, described the case this month as one of "the most ambitious legal challenges yet brought by Congolese residents over industrial mining pollution."

The suit is an important test case that could lead to communities challenging other mines in the future, it added.

The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.

The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."

description:

text:
In copies of a letter that arrived at the offices of every member of the US House of Representatives late Monday, more than 160 climate scientists said they were aware of the need for “trade-offs and compromise when passing bipartisan legislation” like the permitting reform bill being pushed by Democrats including Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich.

“But as scientists we feel strongly that the costs of this bill to the climate are too high,” said the experts, urging lawmakers to vote against the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA).

Whitehouse, Heinrich, and other supporters of the bill have argued the legislation, which passed in the Senate last week with 15 members of the Democratic caucus joining 47 Republicans in approving it, would speed the construction of renewable energy infrastructure.

The bill would limit federal courts’ authority to block a variety of energy projects due to environmental protections, and could stop future administrations from rolling back approvals of projects that have previously been permitted. BAAJA could potentially speed up the modernization of electric grids and transmission lines for solar and wind energy projects.

But with international climate experts warning in recent months that continued fossil fuel emissions have all but eliminated the possibility of avoiding a global temperature rise surpassing 1.5°C over preindustrial levels—and more of the catastrophic, deadly extreme weather that such warming causes—the climate scientists emphasized on Monday that the benefits to renewable energy industries won’t outweigh the dangers embedded in the bill, which would also speed up approvals for oil and gas projects and pollution-causing data centers.

The bill would “prevent the rapid and nearly total phaseout of coal, oil, and fossil gas from the US and global energy systems,” reads the letter. “Without this phaseout, and the subsequent reduction of emissions to (net) zero, the world will be unable to halt global heating. BAAJA represents a step away from the transition to a (net) zero economy.”

The scientists noted that under the “Disparate Treatment” standard in the bill, which creates a right for developers to challenge project delays and denials, “even if Congress passes climate legislation in the future, fossil-energy companies can sue federal agencies and win the full cost of their projects, plus attorney fees and economic damages,” to be paid with public funds.

“This means that agencies may be required, by law, to continue permitting fossil fuel projects, lest they be sued and the government be subject to massive penalties,” wrote the scientists, including Michal Mann of the University of Pennsylvania, Michal Oppenheimer of Princeton University, and J. Timmons Roberts of Brown University. “This Disparate Treatment standard will be, moreover, measured against the collective decisions of six years of the Trump administrations and four of the Biden administration, when clean energy met new demand but did not yet replace fossil energy.”

The legislation, therefore, would create “a regulatory regime that makes the current balance of energy sources permanent” and “runs counter to what science shows we need to do to resolve climate change.”

Along with climate scientists, energy experts have acknowledged in recent years that the world must transition away from fossil fuels to avoid the worst impacts of planetary heating, which has already been linked to deadly heatwaves, flooding, and wildfires.

The scientists questioned an analysis frequently cited by proponents of BAAJA, in which the Rhodium Group projected that the legislation could prevent up to 1.5 billion metric tons of US emissions through 2040.

“But that represents roughly 1/36th of current annual emissions, a tiny fraction of the reductions we need to achieve (net) zero emissions,” they wrote. “In Rhodium’s high-emissions scenario US emissions rise between 2033-2040.”

“Moreover, the Rhodium Group estimate is based primarily on the transmission provisions of BAAJA, and does not take into account what the bill does to the [National Environmental Policy Act] and other environmental laws,” the scientists added, referring to the bill’s exemptions for projects including pipeline expansions from environmental reviews.

The experts urged members of Congress to instead consider modeling from Purdue University engineering professor Kevin Kirchner, who found “that BAAJA likely increases domestic greenhouse gas emissions outright and also increases domestic mortality attributable to air pollution,” and a report from Columbia University’s Center for Global Energy Policy, which warned that “the emissions effects of the bill are ‘highly uncertain.’”

“It is our opinion as climate and Earth scientists that, even if BAAJA reduced emissions to the degree modeled above, those reductions would not offset the bill’s codifying of coal, oil, and natural gas in the US energy mix,” the experts said. “Even reduced emissions continue to make global warming worse so long as they are ongoing.”

In recent weeks, journalist and lawyer Aaron Regunberg said, the public has heard “lots of back-and-forth about whether BAAJA, backed by both the clean energy industry and Big Oil, is good or bad for climate.”

“Climate scientists just weighed in with a very loud ‘BAD,’” he said.

On Tuesday, US Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) explained on social media why she is “a strong NO on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act when it comes to the House,” noting that the bill disregards tribal sovereignty and creates “forever permits” for broadly unpopular artificial intelligence data centers.

“Democrats are ready to accelerate the clean energy transition—BAAJA is not how we reach that, though,” said Jayapal. “I am proud to be one of 164 members who support the Energy Bills Relief Act, legislation that we should quickly pass next Congress. Waiting until the next Congress to pass permitting reform would provide a real opportunity to negotiate that never occurred with the current bill. I urge my colleagues to vote NO on this bill and listen to the resounding call of voters across the country to fight for our agenda, not fold.”

title: Tesla (TSLA Stock) Wins Key FSD Approval in Italy as EV Maker Expands Across Europe
description:
Tesla has won an important regulatory approval in Italy for its Full Self-Driving (FSD) technology, giving the electric vehicle (EV) maker a new opening in one of Europe’s largest car markets.
The approval is an important step for Tesla because Europe has some of the world’s strictest vehicle safety and regulatory rules.
Winning access to Italy could also help the company build support for wider approval across the region.
FSD Still Requires Drivers to Stay in Control Despite its name, Tesla’s FSD system does not make a car fully autonomous.
European Approval Could Support Tesla’s Software Business The Italian decision could give Tesla another source of growth beyond vehicle sales.
text:
Tesla has won an important regulatory approval in Italy for its Full Self-Driving (FSD) technology, giving the electric vehicle (EV) maker a new opening in one of Europe’s largest car markets. Italy’s Transport Ministry approved Tesla’s Assisted Driving system on November 20, 2026. The decision makes the country the first major European Union (EU) market to accept the technology ahead of a wider EU approval process.

The move could help Tesla expand its software business in Europe. It also comes as the company works to grow its EV and energy businesses while cutting emissions across its supply chain.

However, the approval does not mean Tesla cars can drive without human control. FSD remains a supervised driver-assistance system. Drivers must stay alert, watch the road, and remain ready to take control.

Italy Gives Tesla a Major Regulatory Win

Italy’s Transport Ministry approved Tesla’s Assisted Driving system, which the company calls Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in other markets. The decision came after the Netherlands granted the system its first European type approval in April 2026.

Italy has now become the 12th EU country to accept the technology, according to the Italian Transport Ministry. It is also the first among the EU’s four most populous countries to allow the system. Germany, France, and Spain have not yet followed.

Tesla said the rollout in Italy would begin soon, but it has not announced a firm launch date. Eligible vehicles will need a software update before owners can use the feature.

The approval is an important step for Tesla because Europe has some of the world’s strictest vehicle safety and regulatory rules. Winning access to Italy could also help the company build support for wider approval across the region.

Still, this is not yet full EU-wide approval. The Dutch regulator, RDW, has submitted an application for wider recognition. EU member states must review and vote on that request before the system can be used across the bloc under a common approval.

FSD Still Requires Drivers to Stay in Control

Despite its name, Tesla’s FSD system does not make a car fully autonomous. The technology can steer, accelerate, brake, and handle many driving tasks. But it still requires active driver supervision. Drivers must pay attention at all times and remain responsible for the vehicle.

The Dutch vehicle regulator has made this point clear. It said FSD is a driver-controlled assistance system, not a self-driving system.

The regulator also said its approval followed more than 18 months of testing on test tracks and public roads. The review included more than 3,000 hours of testing, over 1,000 test runs, and data from 1.8 million kilometers driven in Europe.

Safety remains a major issue in the debate over the technology. The European Transport Safety Council (ETSC), a road safety group, has raised concerns about how the system handles speed limits. It urged EU countries to reject approval unless these concerns were addressed.

These concerns show why Tesla’s European expansion depends on more than software performance. The company must also meet local safety rules and gain the trust of regulators and drivers.

RELEVANT: Tesla vs. Waymo: Who Will Win the Robotaxi Race?

European Approval Could Support Tesla’s Software Business

The Italian decision could give Tesla another source of growth beyond vehicle sales. FSD is part of the company’s wider push to earn more from software, subscriptions, and connected services. Customers can pay to use advanced driving features, giving Tesla a chance to generate income after selling a vehicle.

Tesla reported growing demand for FSD in its third-quarter 2026 update. The company said it recorded a new high in net subscriptions during the quarter. More than 75% of new vehicle deliveries in North America included FSD subscriptions.

In Europe, Tesla said the system was available in nine countries at the end of the third quarter. More than 100,000 customers had used it, with total driving distance above 160 million kilometers since its initial approval.

Italy’s approval could help increase that customer base. However, the system’s growth will depend on further regulatory decisions and how quickly Tesla can make it available to eligible drivers.

Tesla’s latest financial filing also showed that higher FSD subscription revenue helped support automotive sales revenue in the third quarter. This matters as the company seeks to build a business that earns more from services and software, not just the sale of cars.

Tesla Stock Rebounds in Premarket Trading

The strategy is part of a wider shift in Tesla’s business model. Its plans include driver-assistance software, robotaxis, energy storage, and other services that could create new sources of revenue.

Tesla (TSLA) stock was trading at around $360.90 in premarket trading on November 23, up 4.36% from Friday’s close of $345.82. The rebound follows a sharp 7.64% drop on November 20, when Tesla shares fell alongside a broader sell-off in technology and AI stocks. US stock futures also pointed to a market recovery on Monday.

Tesla’s EVs Can Cut Transport Emissions

Beyond the software business, Tesla’s main environmental contribution comes from its electric vehicles and clean energy products. Battery-electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions while driving. Their total climate impact is not zero, however. Making vehicles and batteries creates emissions, and the power used to charge EVs can still come from fossil fuels.

A 2025 study by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) found that battery-electric cars sold in the EU produce about 73% less lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions than comparable gasoline cars.

The study estimated average lifecycle emissions of 63 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilometer for battery-electric cars. Comparable gasoline cars produced about 235 grams per kilometer.

The analysis included emissions from vehicle and battery production, electricity and fuel use, maintenance, and recycling. It also found that EV production creates higher emissions at the start, mainly because of battery manufacturing.

But EVs make up for this difference through lower emissions while driving. The study estimated that battery-electric cars reach this point after about 17,000 kilometers of use.

This gives Tesla a clear role in the shift toward lower-emission transport. However, the full climate benefit depends on cleaner electricity, more efficient production, and better battery supply chains.

Battery Production Remains a Key ESG Challenge

Tesla’s environmental impact also depends on how it sources materials and makes its vehicles. Battery production requires materials such as lithium, nickel, graphite, and other minerals. Mining and processing these materials can use large amounts of energy and water. They can also affect local ecosystems and communities.

In its 2025 Impact Report, Tesla said its battery supply chain accounted for 26% of its total supply chain greenhouse gas emissions. It reported cutting these battery-related emissions by 9% in 2025.

The company also said it used 3.5 terawatt-hours (TWh) of renewable energy in its battery supply chain during the year. It is working with suppliers to improve energy efficiency and increase the use of renewable power.

Tesla also reported that its Supercharger network had been matched with 100% renewable electricity for five consecutive years. This can lower emissions from charging its vehicles. However, the climate benefit also depends on the electricity used at other charging points.

The company has set a goal of reaching net-zero greenhouse gas emissions across its full value chain by 2040. This target covers more than its factories and offices. It also includes emissions linked to suppliers, products, and customers.

Tesla Reports Major Emissions Savings But Faces More Work

The EV giant said its global products helped customers avoid nearly 37 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions in 2025. That figure covers its combined portfolio of electric vehicles, solar products, and energy storage systems. It should not be treated as emissions savings from EVs alone.

The company also reported progress in its energy business. It deployed 36 gigawatt-hours of energy storage products through the first three quarters of 2026, according to its latest financial filing.

These products can support the wider shift to renewable energy. Large battery systems store electricity when supply is high and release it when demand rises, or renewable generation falls.

Still, Tesla faces pressure to reduce emissions from mining, battery production, and vehicle manufacturing. It must also show that its advanced driving technology meets safety rules as it enters more markets.

Italy’s decision is a major step for Tesla’s European software plans. It could help the company reach more customers and build its subscription business. However, the wider story remains tied to Tesla’s ability to grow its EV and energy businesses while improving safety and reducing its environmental footprint.

text:
Updated November 24, 2026 at 11:09 AM CST

KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.

She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.

She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.

Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.

Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.

"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."

The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.

The mine, known as COMMUS, is owned by Chinese multinational Zijin and lies in Kolwezi, a city of more than 500,000 people in the heart of Congo's copper belt, a southern region with vast mineral reserves.

Congo is the world's second-largest producer of copper, and also the source of over 70% of the world's cobalt, a metal that is critical to the electric-vehicle revolution because of its use in rechargeable batteries.

Last year, the U.S. signed a sweeping economic partnership with Congo aimed at attracting American investment and challenging the dominance of Chinese companies in the country's mining industry

Despite the global importance of Congo's copper and cobalt mines, however, environmental pollution from the industry has received comparatively little scrutiny.

In Kolwezi, pollution is severe. Neighborhoods near mines are often filled with an acrid smell that residents attribute to the sulfuric acid used to process minerals. A study published in June by environmental research organization Source International — carried out with the advocacy groups RAID and Afrewatch, and scientists from Congo's University of Lubumbashi — also highlighted the scale of the contamination.

Researchers found that levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, in Kolwezi were three to six times the World Health Organization's air quality guideline. The highest concentrations were recorded near the COMMUS mine.

These tiny particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure poses health risks generally, but is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and young children.

The researchers also tested dust samples and found residue of copper, cobalt and manganese, which they said pointed to mining waste as the main source. When the study was released, Source International's executive director, Flaviano Bianchini, said that "these are among the most concerning air quality results we have documented in years of monitoring pollution at industrial mining sites around the world."

The study did not examine health impacts directly, and the authors recommended formal epidemiological research. Residents and health workers in Kolwezi nonetheless point to a string of ailments that they blame on a polluted environment.

In a dilapidated health clinic in the shadow of a mountain of waste from the COMMUS mine, nurse Héritier Bukassa said that people routinely break out in itchy hives. "Some sick people scratch themselves with knives to relieve itching," he explained.

Bukassa added that women in the area also suffer from high rates of miscarriage, and that he had referred four babies born with congenital malformations — mostly cleft palates — to hospitals this year alone.

Respiratory illnesses are common too, Bukassa said, especially in otherwise healthy babies who develop breathing problems a few weeks after birth. "No one from the [mining] company has ever come to talk to us about this," the nurse said.

Zijin, the owner of COMMUS, did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Neither did Congo's mining and environment ministries.

The Cobalt Institute, an industry lobby, said that understanding environmental pollution requires "an evidence-based approach that considers all potential sources and contributors." It added that companies perform environmental monitoring and carry out mitigation measures.

RAID, which is supporting the plaintiffs alongside Afrewatch, described the case this month as one of "the most ambitious legal challenges yet brought by Congolese residents over industrial mining pollution."

The suit is an important test case that could lead to communities challenging other mines in the future, it added.

The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.

The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."
