title: Landmark NRC Construction Permit Ushers in Next Phase for Dow's Xe-100 HTGR Nuclear Project
description:
The construction permit (CPAR-3), issued to Long Mott Energy LLC, a wholly owned Dow subsidiary, authorizes construction of the proposed Long Mott Generating Station in Calhoun County, Texas.
The chemical manufacturer has stressed, however, that securing a construction permit does not constitute a commitment to build Long Mott.
The arrangement, notably, allows Long Mott Energy to incur project expenditures before receiving federal cost-sharing reimbursements under the ARDP.
According to the FSER, Long Mott Energy has also selected a subsidiary of NextEra Energy Resources to operate the facility.
Five days before the NRC issued Long Mott’s construction permit, X-energy announced its first procurement of steam generator tubing for the Xe-100.
text:
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) on Nov. 9 issued its first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) in nearly six decades, authorizing construction of four X-energy Xe-100 reactors that could supply electricity and high-temperature process steam to Dow’s chemical manufacturing operations on the Texas Gulf Coast. While the authorization follows nearly eight years of technical and regulatory engagement between X-energy and the NRC, development of the first commercial Xe-100 facility will require extensive engineering, fuel and materials qualification, component procurement and manufacturing, and a series of capital investment decisions by Dow.

The construction permit (CPAR-3), issued to Long Mott Energy LLC, a wholly owned Dow subsidiary, authorizes construction of the proposed Long Mott Generating Station in Calhoun County, Texas. The facility is expected to comprise four helium-cooled, graphite-moderated pebble-bed reactors, each rated at 200 MW of thermal capacity (MWth) and 80 MW of electrical capacity (MWe), to replace aging energy and steam generation assets at Dow’s adjacent Seadrift Operations complex.

The NRC’s 852-page final safety evaluation report (FSER), issued Oct. 30, and an independent assessment by its Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS) detail the technical basis for construction authorization, the safety questions that remain to be resolved, and the extent of design and analytical work required before the facility can be licensed to operate. The regulatory record also sheds new light on Dow’s financial arrangements and its selection of a NextEra Energy Resources subsidiary to operate the plant.

The Long Mott authorization is the NRC’s third advanced reactor construction permit this year, following permits issued for TerraPower’s sodium-cooled Kemmerer Unit 1 in Wyoming on March 9 and the Tennessee Valley Authority’s (TVA’s) BWRX-300 light-water reactor at Clinch River in Tennessee on Sept. 28. As the NRC noted, the Long Mott permit marks several regulatory firsts for the agency: authorization of a multimodule advanced reactor facility, a pebble-bed reactor core, and a reactor design that refuels during operation, as well as the first HTGR review under the risk-informed Licensing Modernization Project framework.

Supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP), Long Mott is advancing through Dow’s phased capital investment process. According to X-energy, Dow is expected to consider a preliminary investment decision in 2027, ahead of a separate final investment decision that would authorize full-scale nuclear construction. For now, the companies are targeting initial energy delivery in the early 2030s.

Eight Years of Regulatory Groundwork

The historic construction permit is the first for an HTGR since September 1968, when U.S. nuclear regulators authorized Public Service Co. of Colorado to build Fort St. Vrain, an 842-MWth plant that used prismatic graphite fuel blocks and subsequently supplied electricity to the Colorado grid. While Long Mott would have nearly the same thermal capacity—800 MWth—it would distribute heat production across four continuously refueled pebble-bed reactors designed to supply both electricity and industrial process steam.

X-energy began pre-application engagement with the NRC in 2018, two years before the DOE selected the Xe-100 for one of its two principal ARDP demonstration awards. At the time, the company envisioned deploying its first four-reactor facility with Energy Northwest in Washington state by 2028. The demonstration, however, took a markedly different direction in March 2023, when X-energy signed a joint development agreement with Dow and shifted the project to the Texas Gulf Coast. The DOE added Dow as a sub-awardee under the ARDP cooperative agreement, and the companies committed to an engineering program valued at up to $50 million, including preparation of a construction permit application. The change introduced an industrial application for the first commercial demonstration of the Xe-100, though the DOE retained Energy Northwest as a sub-awardee to preserve the potential for a subsequent Washington deployment.

Dow and X-energy selected Seadrift in May 2023. By the time Long Mott Energy submitted its construction permit application on March 31, 2025, several of the analytical methodologies needed to establish the Xe-100’s safety basis had already undergone individual NRC reviews. X-energy says it has now secured approval of 14 topical reports that apply generically to the Xe-100, covering some of the most technically demanding aspects of licensing a gas-cooled pebble-bed reactor: fuel and graphite qualification, reactor core behavior, thermal-hydraulic transients, radioactive material releases and atmospheric dispersion, emergency planning, and control room staffing. Developers of subsequent Xe-100 projects can incorporate those methodologies by reference, subject to their prescribed limitations and conditions, though each facility will require an individual licensing review.

Integral to Long Mott’s application was the Licensing Modernization Project (LMP) methodology, an industry-developed approach to licensing non-light-water reactors that the NRC endorsed in 2020 through Regulatory Guide 1.233. The methodology, notably, uses the frequency and radiological consequences of postulated events to inform which safety functions a reactor must perform, which equipment it relies on to perform them, and whether the design incorporates adequate defense-in-depth.

For the Xe-100, the five fundamental safety functions are retaining radionuclides, controlling reactivity, controlling heat removal, controlling water and steam ingress, and maintaining geometry. The resulting classification of structures, systems, and components as safety-related, non-safety-related with special treatment, or non-safety-related without special treatment has implications well beyond the safety analysis itself. It informs how equipment will be specified, procured, qualified, and maintained throughout the plant’s operating life.

The NRC accepted Long Mott Energy’s application for docketing on May 12, 2025, and established an 18-month review schedule the following month. In May 2026, as POWER reported, the NRC issued its final environmental assessment and a finding of no significant impact, determining that the project did not warrant preparation of an environmental impact statement (EIS).

By September, Long Mott Energy had incorporated eight supplements into a consolidated revision of its application, six addressing the preliminary safety analysis report and two concerning general and financial information and regulatory exemptions. The NRC held its mandatory hearing on Sept. 22. The ACRS reported to the Commission on Oct. 16 that its review “supports issuance of the construction permit,” and NRC staff completed the FSER later that month, one month ahead of its scheduled November milestone.

“We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction,” NRC Chairman Ho Nieh said in the agency’s Nov. 9 announcement.

For X-energy, the licensing process has unfolded alongside a substantial overhaul of U.S. nuclear regulation. Congress, through the Nuclear Energy Innovation and Modernization Act (NEIMA) of 2019 and the bipartisan Accelerating Deployment of Versatile, Advanced Nuclear for Clean Energy (ADVANCE) Act of 2024, directed the NRC to modernize its advanced reactor licensing framework, improve the predictability of reviews, and establish expedited licensing procedures. The reform effort intensified on May 23, 2025—just 11 days after the NRC accepted Long Mott’s application for docketing—when President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14300, directing the agency to establish fixed licensing deadlines and undertake a comprehensive revision of its regulations and guidance. The NRC, notably, identified Long Mott’s 18-month review schedule among its initiatives to accelerate licensing.

“Getting the construction permit earlier than expected is reflective of the thorough and efficient work of the NRC, the reforms that have been put in place by the Congress over the last six years, and the phenomenal work of the X-energy and Dow teams,” X-energy CEO Clay Sell said in the companies’ joint announcement.

Engineering a Four-Reactor Industrial Nuclear Facility

Dow’s plans for the Xe-100 at Seadrift, where the company manufactures polyethylene, glycols, and oxide derivatives, hinge on the reactor’s ability to supply both electricity and high-temperature process steam. According to X-energy, the reactor can produce steam at temperatures of up to 565C (1,049F), considerably higher than those typically achieved by conventional light-water reactors, which could broaden the range of industrial applications for nuclear heat.

While Long Mott’s aggregate reactor capacity of 800 MWth corresponds to a nominal electrical generating capacity of 320 MWe, the plant’s proposed conventional island would incorporate turbine-generators, extraction steam systems, and dedicated process steam supply equipment to accommodate Seadrift’s electrical and thermal energy requirements. According to the FSER, any excess power would be exported to the electrical grid.

The Xe-100’s pebble-bed fuel configuration allows the reactor to be refueled during operation, an important consideration for industrial facilities that require a continuous supply of process steam. According to the FSER, each reactor core contains approximately 220,000 spherical fuel elements embedded with uranium oxycarbide tristructural isotropic (TRISO) coated fuel particles. Essentially, helium circulates through the pebble bed, transferring heat generated by fission to secondary-side water in the steam generator to produce superheated steam.

The fuel pebbles, meanwhile, circulate through a dedicated fuel handling system, which loads them at the top of the reactor vessel and conveys them using gravitational and pneumatic forces. The system measures the accumulated burnup of pebbles discharged from the bottom of the core and determines whether they should be returned to the reactor or transferred to storage. Operators can thus replenish the core continuously during operation, eliminating the need for the periodic batch refueling outages characteristic of conventional light-water reactors.

Although Long Mott would comprise four reactors, each rated at 200 MWth and equipped with its own steam generator, the NRC evaluated the facility as a single multimodule nuclear power plant. The four reactor and steam generator pairs would occupy a common nuclear island and share a reactor building foundation, a shield structure, and several auxiliary systems. The regulatory review, notably, assessed the safety implications of equipment sharing under the design’s Principal Design Criterion 5, which governs shared structures, systems, and components.

The proposed facility would occupy approximately 1,537 acres of Dow-owned land in the coastal prairie of the Guadalupe River delta, about 22 miles southeast of Victoria. Its proximity to an established petrochemical manufacturing complex required the NRC to evaluate potential hazards associated with industrial accidents, fires, toxic chemical releases, and the transportation of hazardous materials, in addition to the hurricanes and flooding characteristic of the Texas Gulf Coast.

Fuel Performance, Safety Analysis, and Design Qualification

Unlike conventional light-water reactors, the Xe-100 does not rely on a leak-tight, pressure-retaining containment structure. Instead, it incorporates what the NRC calls “functional containment”—a series of barriers to radioactive material transport, principally the successive coating layers surrounding individual TRISO fuel kernels. A central question in the NRC’s safety analysis was how well those coatings would retain fission products under prolonged neutron irradiation and at the elevated temperatures predicted under postulated accident conditions.

Fuel Performance and Accident Analysis. For a depressurized loss-of-forced-cooling event, Long Mott Energy calculated a nominal peak fuel temperature of 1,803C (3,277F), compared with 1,788C (3,250F) in the NRC’s independent confirmatory calculations using its MELCOR accident analysis code. The applicant’s calculated peak, however, rose to 1,885C (3,425F) when it incorporated analytical uncertainties.

The preliminary peak temperatures for the limiting design-basis accident, the NRC noted in its FSER, “are beyond the limits typically associated with TRISO fuel particles, including the results from the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Advanced Gas Reactor (AGR) program.” While the preliminary radiological analyses account for increased fission product releases at elevated temperatures and indicate a maximum 30-day dose of 14.4 rem at the exclusion area boundary—below the applicable 25-rem regulatory criterion—Long Mott Energy must further substantiate its fuel performance assumptions.

The ACRS, which supported issuance of the construction permit in its Oct. 16 letter to the Commission, similarly cautioned that “both fuel and structural materials are challenged by the peak temperatures predicted under limiting accident conditions.” The committee identified fuel performance, functional containment, mechanistic source term analysis—the assessment of radioactive material release and transport during an accident—and graphite and metallic component performance as areas that “require significant additional development.”

Notably, the committee questioned the use of correlations derived from uranium dioxide fuel in the applicant’s source term analysis, given that the Xe-100 uses uranium oxycarbide. It noted, however, that data from the AGR program show substantially lower cesium release from uranium oxycarbide and that the calculated doses are therefore likely conservative.

Long Mott Energy, meanwhile, has proposed a plume exposure pathway emergency planning zone extending 400 meters (about a quarter mile), compared with the roughly 10-mile zone generally associated with conventional U.S. light-water power reactors. The proposal draws on an X-energy methodology the NRC approved in February 2026, subject to seven limitations and conditions, though the agency will evaluate final emergency planning arrangements during its operating license review.

Qualification of the Final Design. Under the two-step licensing process established in Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, the NRC can authorize construction before an applicant resolves all outstanding safety questions, provided the applicant establishes a research and development (R&D) program reasonably designed to resolve them before completing construction. Long Mott Energy, notably, did not request Commission approval of any design feature under 10 CFR 50.35(b), and it must substantiate its final design through a separate operating license application.

The NRC found that Long Mott Energy’s R&D program, which covers TRISO fuel, the graphite core assembly, and safety-related metallic components, is reasonably designed to resolve the outstanding safety questions. The NRC’s approval of X-energy’s graphite core assembly qualification and design methodologies alone carries 25 conditions that Long Mott Energy plans to address through testing, development of analytical methodologies, or both before completing its operating license application.

Engineering for Gulf Coast Flooding. At Seadrift, hurricane-driven storm surge presents a separate engineering challenge. While Long Mott Energy proposes a finished site grade of 31 feet for the nuclear island area relative to the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 (NAVD 88), its calculations indicate a stillwater storm surge elevation of 36.38 feet, rising to 46.49 feet when wave runup is included.

Because the applicant had not submitted detailed designs for site grading and passive flood protection features, the NRC stipulated in Paragraph 3.D of the construction permit that Long Mott Energy must notify the agency when those designs are available for examination. The permit anticipates that notification will occur before the placement of safety-significant concrete for structure foundations. The designs should demonstrate that safety-related structures, systems, and components, along with non-safety-related components that must remain functional, are protected during and after the design-basis flood.

Fuel qualification, flooding, and financial qualifications also featured in a contested licensing proceeding brought by the San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper. On Nov. 6, three days before the NRC issued the construction permit, the Commission denied the organization’s petition for review of six licensing board decisions and orders, leaving in place the board’s termination of the contested proceeding.

Dow’s Investment Decision and Federal Cost-Sharing

While Dow and X-energy initially envisioned a 2026 construction start and project completion by the end of the decade, Dow now projects construction could begin later this decade, with startup in the early 2030s. The chemical manufacturer has stressed, however, that securing a construction permit does not constitute a commitment to build Long Mott.

“As we move forward, we will continue to evaluate the project through the lens of competitiveness, execution readiness, and capital affordability before any decision regarding construction is made,” Edward Stones, Dow’s business vice president for energy and climate, said in the company’s Nov. 9 announcement.

During X-energy’s Nov. 12 earnings call, CEO Clay Sell elaborated on Dow’s formal investment decision process, through which the chemical manufacturer assesses whether engineering has sufficiently advanced, whether cost targets are being met, and whether operations and maintenance (O&M) assumptions have been validated before investment decisions reach its board. X-energy is still developing manufacturing drawings and detailed construction plans, Sell noted, and while the company does not expect to complete the final reactor design before Dow’s anticipated 2027 preliminary investment decision, it intends to do so before construction begins.

Sell underscored the importance of completing detailed engineering before construction, given the industry’s history of cost overruns and schedule delays. “Now we also have to avoid other mistakes that have been made in our industry in the past, like starting construction before you have it completely designed,” he told analysts. Sell did not, however, specify the level of engineering completion or the class of cost estimate Dow would require to sanction the investment.

Construction Financing and Federal Reimbursements. Although the companies have not publicly disclosed an overall construction cost estimate for Long Mott, Dow has committed to providing financial support exceeding half of the projected construction cost, according to the FSER. Under a Feb. 23, 2026, financial support agreement, The Dow Chemical Company agreed to fund construction costs up to a specified amount unless it secures substitute financial assurance through a loan facility, a letter of credit, or both, with the NRC’s written consent. The arrangement, notably, allows Long Mott Energy to incur project expenditures before receiving federal cost-sharing reimbursements under the ARDP.

On that basis, the NRC determined that Long Mott Energy appears financially qualified to undertake construction. The agency granted an exemption from the construction permit financial qualification requirements in 10 CFR 50.33(f) and Appendix C to Part 50, applying instead the standard under 10 CFR 70.23(a)(5), under which an applicant must appear financially qualified to engage in the proposed activities.

X-energy, meanwhile, said on Nov. 9 that it had been informed of an intended increase in the total value of its ARDP award to $2.15 billion, encompassing both the Long Mott demonstration and its TRISO-X fuel fabrication facility in Tennessee. The DOE had previously indicated it could invest up to $1.23 billion over seven years in the reactor and fuel facility, though the agency did not address the increased award amount in its Nov. 13 announcement on the construction permit.

X-energy reported $66.3 million in revenue and grant income for the third quarter of 2026, including $51.5 million in services revenue, primarily from Xe-100 design work under the ARDP, and $14.8 million in grant income tied to the Dow demonstration. The company incurred $71.8 million in capital expenditures for construction projects, including its TX-1 fuel fabrication facility, and received $27.8 million in associated cash reimbursements from the DOE during the quarter.

X-energy Chief Financial Officer Daniel Gross told analysts that cumulative ARDP reimbursements had reached $618 million through September 2026. While the program reimburses roughly half of eligible expenditures, Gross noted that X-energy must first incur the costs and invoice the DOE, and its financial statements also include capital and operating expenditures from other projects that do not qualify for federal cost-sharing.

Operating License and Construction Schedule. Long Mott’s construction permit specifies July 1, 2033, as the earliest date for completion of construction and Dec. 31, 2033, as the latest. The permit expires on the latter date unless the NRC extends it. X-energy has already begun developing the operating license application, which Sell anticipates filing approximately two years before commissioning, allowing for an expected 18-month NRC review ahead of initial fuel loading and startup.

For subsequent Xe-100 deployments, X-energy expects to reuse much of the engineering and safety analysis undertaken for Long Mott, particularly for the standardized nuclear island, which comprises the reactor and nuclear steam supply system. Sell said the company anticipates substantially shorter construction permit reviews for subsequent applications, citing unofficial indications from the NRC that the agency is targeting review periods of six to 12 months.

Project Delivery and the Xe-100 Supply Chain

Still, while Dow is evaluating the investment, X-energy has committed its own capital to reserve manufacturing capacity and procure long-lead materials, including graphite, steel forgings, and steam generator tubing. “We’ve chosen to make some early investments to secure capacity and to buy early material with the full expectation that when our customers reach their investment decisions, they will take over those obligations on a go-forward basis,” Sell told analysts.

Project Engineering and Nuclear Operations. Dow, notably, has enlisted NextEra Energy Resources to provide technical support in nuclear procurement, licensing, personnel training, and the development of operating disciplines. According to the FSER, Long Mott Energy has also selected a subsidiary of NextEra Energy Resources to operate the facility. In assessing Long Mott Energy’s technical qualifications, the NRC considered the complementary expertise of the three companies: Dow’s experience in industrial energy production and large capital projects, X-energy’s reactor engineering capabilities, and the operating experience of NextEra Energy’s nuclear fleet, which comprises seven light-water reactors across four sites.

Fluor, a U.S. engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) firm, has also secured engineering contracts for X-energy’s two most advanced U.S. reactor projects. On Nov. 5, X-energy selected Fluor to provide engineering, design development, supply chain, estimating, and project controls services for the nuclear island of Energy Northwest’s proposed Cascade Advanced Energy Facility near Richland, Washington, following an earlier 2026 award for similar services at Seadrift. At Cascade, Cascade Nuclear Partners, a joint venture of Kiewit, Black & Veatch, and Aecon, holds the progressive design-build contract. Sell noted that Fluor is supporting the design of systems within Cascade’s nuclear island, while Cascade Nuclear Partners is advancing the conventional island design and coordinating requirements across the broader plant.

The Cascade project, which would initially employ four Xe-100 reactors with provisions for expansion to 12 modules totaling 960 MW, would be sited near Energy Northwest’s Columbia Generating Station, where X-energy originally planned its ARDP demonstration. It is the first project under X-energy’s collaboration with Amazon, which aims to support deployment of more than 5 GW of new U.S. nuclear capacity by 2039.

Component Testing and Manufacturing Readiness. X-energy is expanding component fabrication, machining, and testing capabilities at its 90,000-square-foot X-energy Technology Advancement Center (XTAC) in Frederick, Maryland. The company has begun testing graphite components and expects over the next couple of years to commission a helium test loop to validate the mechanical systems that operate in the helium environment. Those systems, Sell noted, fall broadly into three groups: the fuel handling system, the helium circulator system, and the control rods and their drive mechanisms.

Sell said the testing program is intended to refine manufacturing and installation procedures and validate long-term O&M assumptions before commercial deployment, though he noted that work at XTAC is not a significant input to Dow’s preliminary investment decision. “In the simplest terms, we want to have done it at the XTAC before we do it in the field,” he said.

Component Procurement. Five days before the NRC issued Long Mott’s construction permit, X-energy announced its first procurement of steam generator tubing for the Xe-100. Swedish specialty materials manufacturer Alleima will supply specialized stainless steel tubing to South Korean nuclear component manufacturer Doosan Enerbility, which will bend it into helical coils for Long Mott’s steam generators. The companies, however, did not disclose the quantity, contract value, or delivery schedule.

The procurement follows a December 2025 agreement under which X-energy, as POWER reported, reserved manufacturing capacity at Doosan for 16 sets of reactor pressure vessels, steam generator pressure vessels, and additional steel components of the main power system. According to Doosan, the reservation covers the four proposed Long Mott reactors and the potential 12-reactor Cascade development in Washington. Doosan has also committed to building a dedicated small modular reactor fabrication facility in Changwon, South Korea, which X-energy says could support production of components for approximately 20 Xe-100 reactors annually at full capacity.

Beyond steel forgings and steam generator tubing, X-energy has secured graphite manufacturing capacity and materials through Toyo Tanso and SGL Carbon.

“Regulatory approval is not on the critical path for any of our projects. It really relates more to the supply chain, which is why we are making early investments in the supply chain because that’s the best opportunity to reduce schedule on our future projects,” Sell told analysts.

Commercial-Scale Fuel Fabrication. In Oak Ridge, Tennessee, X-energy’s wholly owned fuel subsidiary TRISO-X completed vertical construction of the shell of its TX-1 fuel fabrication facility on schedule in the third quarter of 2026, according to X-energy’s third-quarter financial results. The next phase encompasses interior buildout, installation of fuel fabrication equipment, and construction of supporting facilities, including a graphite matrix powder facility that will prepare and blend graphite materials for fuel pebble fabrication.

In February, the NRC granted TRISO-X a 40-year special nuclear material license—the first Category II fuel fabrication license for processing high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU). The DOE characterizes TX-1 as the first commercial-scale HALEU fuel fabrication facility in the U.S. to receive NRC approval.

TX-1 has a designed production capacity of approximately 700,000 fuel pebbles annually, equivalent to 5 metric tons of uranium and sufficient to support operation of up to 11 Xe-100 reactors. TRISO-X, which will also require a reliable supply of enriched uranium feedstock, received an initial HALEU allocation from the DOE in April 2025 that X-energy says will be used to manufacture fuel for Long Mott’s first core loads.

X-energy is also advancing design work for TX-2, its second planned commercial fuel fabrication facility, and TX-L, a dedicated R&D center. Costs associated with TX-2’s design and site preparation are currently being expensed rather than capitalized, Gross noted, owing to the project’s stage of development.

The company’s ambitions for TRISO-X, notably, extend beyond supplying its own reactor fleet. Sell said the Part 70 license authorizes commercial fuel manufacturing using uranium enriched up to 20% at its first two commercial facilities, and the company intends to pursue third-party customers developing reactors and microreactors that use coated particle fuel.

X-energy, meanwhile, continues to pursue qualification of its own TRISO fuel through an irradiation campaign at the Advanced Test Reactor in Idaho. Asked about the campaign on Nov. 12, Sell said interim results had met the company’s expectations, though X-energy has yet to complete the campaign and publish its assessment.

Building a Commercial Reactor Portfolio. X-energy, which reported $1.8 billion in cash and investments and no debt as of Sept. 30, has a prospective commercial portfolio encompassing 144 reactors representing approximately 11.5 GW of generating capacity, assuming each customer exercises its contingent rights in full. Of those, Sell said, up to 40 reactors are associated with identified project plans and development partnerships involving Dow, Energy Northwest, American Electric Power (AEP), and Centrica.

Beyond Long Mott and Cascade, the prospective deployments include a 960-MW project involving Amazon and AEP in Sullivan County, Indiana, where AEP is evaluating redevelopment of a former coal-fired generation site with an existing PJM Interconnection grid connection. The parties are committing resources to site characterization, feasibility studies, community engagement, preparation for a construction permit application, and development of the prospective commercial arrangement between Amazon and AEP.

In the UK, where X-energy’s Xe-100 entered the Generic Design Assessment process in September, the company is pursuing a collaboration with Centrica targeting up to 6 GW. Sell said expanded cooperation between U.S. and UK nuclear regulators enables X-energy to draw on NRC-approved technical documentation and safety analyses during the British assessment.

For X-energy, whose commercial strategy includes sales of reactor technology, associated services, and fuel over the operating lives of its customers’ plants, executing the first commercial deployment at Seadrift will be critical to establishing the cost and schedule assumptions for subsequent projects.

“This is the process. This is where we develop the mastery through repetition, to move from the first, more expensive plants all the way down to lower cost lower risk, shorter scheduled plants that can be financed and deployed at scale,” Sell said.

text:
The energy transition runs on batteries

The global battery market is at a pivotal inflection point. Demand for lithium-ion batteries is forecast to grow at a CAGR of around 20% through 2032, driven by the accelerating transition to electric vehicles, rapidly expanding stationary energy storage for grids and data centers, and the electrification of commercial vehicles. The stationary energy storage systems (BESS) segment alone is projected to more than triple in size between 2024 and 2030.

Yet the opportunity comes with compounding complexity. Battery architectures are evolving fast – solid-state cells, sodium-ion chemistries, and next-generation anode materials are all challenging the dominance of conventional lithium-ion. Battery prices have fallen dramatically over the past decade, but cost pressure, raw material volatility, and high scrap rates in cell manufacturing continue to squeeze margins across the value chain. Investors and equity markets are recalibrating their expectations as the early hypergrowth phase matures, which is reflected in the recent pressure on battery-related stocks.

For engineering leaders, product managers, and executives, the stakes have never been higher. Decisions made today on cell chemistry, pack architecture, safety validation, and supply chain structure will define competitive position for the next decade.

Where battery projects succeed or fail

The battery market is no longer simply "booming" – it has entered a more complex phase characterized by short-term turbulence against powerful long-term demand tailwinds. Companies that get this right will combine a clear market view with the engineering and commercial depth to act on it.

At Roland Berger, we believe the companies that will lead this next phase are those that close the gap between strategic intent and engineering execution. That means making rigorous, evidence-based decisions on battery architecture and cell selection, designing for manufacturability and safety from day one, managing supplier and regulatory risk proactively, and building commercialization roadmaps that are grounded in real cost and performance data.

Breakthroughs in battery technology are real but uneven in their commercial readiness. Solid-state batteries promise step-change improvements in energy density and safety, but timelines to mass production remain uncertain. Meanwhile, incremental improvements to lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and NMC chemistries continue to deliver meaningful gains today. In practice, the most commercially successful battery programs tend to be built on well-understood chemistry, optimized for the specific application, rather than the technology attracting the most headlines.

title: Will Batteries Kill Off Gas Turbines at Data Centers | OilPrice.com
description:
Abundant daytime solar energy displaces higher-cost forms of power generation during daylight hours.
Said differently, in wholesale power markets, batteries are underpricing gas-fired generation.
Obviously, this is disruptive, meaning simply that the owner of a particular type of power generation suddenly finds its assets impaired, or as we call it, stranded.
In the near to intermediate term, it will coexist happily with renewable technologies because of continuing growth in power demand.
However, high levels of electricity demand in the US and elsewhere will obscure this trend—until they don’t.
text:
Perhaps you have heard about the daily “duck curve” in electricity markets. Abundant daytime solar energy displaces higher-cost forms of power generation during daylight hours. It creates a price chart for power that resembles the belly and neck of a duck. In the old days,, as the sun went down, gas-fired turbines (CTs) were called upon to provide power for shoulder periods of daily electricity demand when power needs were still elevated. albeit trending down. What’s changed? A few electricity markets with extensive solar and battery penetration, like California, are using their gas-fired CTs a lot less, because they are being displaced by cheaper electricity from batteries. Said differently, in wholesale power markets, batteries are underpricing gas-fired generation.

Obviously, this is disruptive, meaning simply that the owner of a particular type of power generation suddenly finds its assets impaired, or as we call it, stranded. Many recent articles have focused on the unrelenting downward cost of solar, onshore wind, and batteries. This is all true. But will it be disruptive? One way to tell is by looking at changes in capital investment. No utility executive wants to lose money on a new big power plant or transmission line. According to the EIA, the US will add 86 GW of capacity in 2026, 89% of which will be solar and battery, and only 7% gas-fired. (The 2025 additions were similar in terms of fuel mix.)

We are seeing a big upswing in demand for electricity. AI just turbocharged it. Looking at those projections, one might conclude that gas is being displaced by renewables, but we sure can’t see it. Gas-fueled electricity production has held steady. It simply doesn't appear to matter that renewables provide cheaper energy, at least for now. Our best analogy is telegraph (a legacy technology) vs telephone (disruptive technology) in the early twentieth century. Everyone knows how the story ends. But few remember that these two competing technologies co-existed happily for several decades because there was adequate demand and revenue for both. And then the former simply went away. (The same happened with gas lighting, which co-existed with electric lighting for decades before expiring.) And that’s our best guess for fossil-fired generation. In the near to intermediate term, it will coexist happily with renewable technologies because of continuing growth in power demand. Related: What Is Trump Up To Bombing Iran’s Qeshm Island?

But this is not to say there will be no revenue disruption at all for utilities, just that people are looking for it in the wrong place, in the big power generating assets. Potential disruption could come from three sources.

First, the rapid increase in gas generation build-out adds many large businesses like data centers to the domestic market. This increased demand will inevitably add upward pressure on gas prices. Also, if the US continues to export increasing quantities of LNG such that it becomes priced on a world market like oil, that too would add another level of unattractive price volatility. Both trends bear watching.

Second, there is potential for disruption in the utility asset class that is considered the lowest risk: transmission and distribution. Distributed power generation, making and storing power closer to its demand source, could change everything. Essentially, this means shrinking the number of “poles and wires”. Power is produced at the customer’s home or office with renewables (solar and batteries) and propane backup.

Western Power, serving southwest Australia including the city of Perth, has in its rural areas one of the lowest customer densities in the country, about 13 customers per kilometer. This customer profile resembles those of many rural co-ops in the US. Abandoning poles and wires and providing electric service to customers in the above-mentioned fashion. In remote rural areas, the economic benefits are obvious. A few relatively small revenue-generating customers per mile of distribution system is a money loser for utilities anywhere in the world. If this trend accelerates, and we believe it will, this suggests that rural electric co-ops and the like could be the first to be impacted by increased renewables penetration.

But Western Power noted on its website that over three years, its distributed microgrids had avoided 189 hours of customer outages; that’s almost 8 days' worth. Comparable data on this is not readily available, but it seems like a lot. The company stated that since most outages were related to malfunctions of poles and wires, eliminating those customer connections and replacing them with fully distributed systems greatly increased reliability and resilience. All this while, the utility itself saved money by reducing expenditures for line maintenance. If the value consumers place on electrical reliability increases, this trend could and likely will accelerate. From a business perspective, rural utilities have far more exposure here than urban utilities. As we’ve written before, everyone wants electricity. And almost no one cares how they get it. So, who cares if it comes from the grid or not?

The third risk is the one that has received the least attention, which is battery-on-battery competition. If battery technologies continue to improve, which we think is likely, then new, lower-cost batteries will begin to displace older, more expensive or less efficient ones. Competition among new battery technologies looks to us like the videos of fighting robots doing karate and spin kicks. Except in this example, the superior “fighter” will be made of less expensive materials, sodium instead of lithium, for example.

But our point here is broader and potentially more dramatic for utility economics. The impact of batteries is that they are beginning to flatten the daily price curves for electricity. They raise prices during the day as they charge with cheap solar energy. And they lower prices in the evening as they discharge. As electricity price curves flatten, profitability for all power suppliers declines. This, to borrow a phrase, is the future that’s already here. Eventually, if this trend continues, only the lowest cost producers survive.

Our severest critics will ask (fairly) why we should care about this. If robust electricity demand is more than likely for the foreseeable future, then almost all energy producers will make some money, even old, coal-fired plants. Our response is simple. Utility assets typically have an operating life between thirty and forty years on average. Right now, energy users, like Anthropic, are still paying for coal-fired power plants to remain open in addition to their huge demand for gas-fired energy. However, despite this huge increase in demand, no coal plant owner that we know of is willing to engage in major capital refurbishments. This is like refusing to maintain a very old car that still runs, saying, “Well, I’ll just drive it till it breaks down and then junk it.” Eventually this could happen to all fossil-fired power-generating assets. People won't stop using them if they can produce electricity. But they will stop reinvesting new capital. For us that’s a key milestone. Renewables plus batteries will continue to undercut fossil-fired alternatives on a price basis. However, high levels of electricity demand in the US and elsewhere will obscure this trend—until they don’t.

title: Residents rally for clean energy as officials debate project approvals - Hudson Valley One
description:
The town board and planning board have heard from both supporters and opponents over the past several months.
The planning board held a public hearing on the proposal Tuesday night, but a decision on a special-use permit is still pending.
Both petition drives were organized by New Yorkers for Clean Power, a Kingston-based statewide advocacy group whose mission is to help New York rapidly shift to an equitable clean energy economy.
The group engages the public, local governments and businesses on solar, wind, storage, energy efficiency, heat pumps and electric vehicles to support the environment, meet the state’s clean energy goals and create jobs in related fields.
“Battery storage is the backbone of a modern clean energy grid,” Iachetta said.
text:
A petition drive supporting battery energy storage system (BESS) proposals in Saugerties and New Paltz generated over 1,000 signatures last week, giving municipal boards added pressure as they weigh the proposals’ fate.

A petition was delivered to Saugerties Town Hall on Tuesday, November 17, where a BESS proposal by Key Capture Energy is under review. The town board and planning board have heard from both supporters and opponents over the past several months. The planning board held a public hearing on the proposal Tuesday night, but a decision on a special-use permit is still pending.

Both petition drives were organized by New Yorkers for Clean Power, a Kingston-based statewide advocacy group whose mission is to help New York rapidly shift to an equitable clean energy economy. The group engages the public, local governments and businesses on solar, wind, storage, energy efficiency, heat pumps and electric vehicles to support the environment, meet the state’s clean energy goals and create jobs in related fields.

At the Saugerties petition drop, Kate McCann, an organizer for New Yorkers for Clean Power, said residents supported the proposal “because they recognize that battery energy storage is a common-sense solution.”

“By storing clean, inexpensive power when demand is low and feeding it back to the grid when needed most, this project can protect local families’ wallets and power Ulster County,” McCann said. “As battery storage projects are proposed in Ulster County, we’ve also seen fear and misinformation arise. We’ve taken an active role in reaching out to residents, hosting educational events, and, above all, meeting people where they are.”

Detractors of battery energy storage systems cite the risk of dangerous fires, which have occurred at some facilities in other parts of the country. BESS advocates argue such incidents are rare and less likely with current systems.

“Having seen the documents assembled and studied by the lead agency, I’m deeply impressed and reassured by their thoroughness,” said Saugerties resident Stephen Shafer at last week’s petition drop. “They know enough to make a declaration. I don’t know what it will be, but I personally believe there is no significant adverse environmental effect from this project.”

Skip Arthur, another Saugerties resident, agreed.

“Widespread use of BESS systems in Texas and California, where there has been significant buildout, has shown these are more than promises — they’ve helped stabilize operations and pricing,” Arthur said. “We can be part of this broader effort.”

New Paltz battery storage dispute

A similar petition, with over 1,000 signatures and endorsements from 33 local businesses, was delivered last week to the New Paltz Town Board, which is also reviewing a Key Capture proposal set for Paradies Lane.

“More than 1,000 New Paltz residents and 33 local businesses came together to deliver a clear message: our community is ready for safe, reliable battery energy storage,” said Madeline Barber, an organizer with New Yorkers for Clean Power. “By storing clean power when it’s abundant and inexpensive, and delivering it back to the grid during peak demand, these projects protect local families from utility rate spikes.”

Melissa Iachetta highlighted New Paltz’s reputation as a climate action leader.

“Battery storage is the backbone of a modern clean energy grid,” Iachetta said. “It lets us maximize renewable power, strengthen resilience against severe storms and keep energy affordable in Ulster County.”

Tim Lacy is a SUNY New Paltz student and clean energy advocate.

“Students at SUNY New Paltz care deeply about building a livable, clean-energy future right here in our community,” Lacy said. “The town board has a clear opportunity to listen to over a thousand residents and move New Paltz toward cleaner air, lower bills and a more reliable grid.”

The New Paltz Planning Board is currently debating with Ulster County Planning Director Dennis Doyle over who should be lead agency for the proposed BESS. At a planning board meeting on Monday, November 9, Doyle said the county characterized the project as an unlisted action under the State Environmental Quality Review (SEQR) and has required Key Capture to complete numerous studies.

Some planning board members believe the county’s criteria don’t go far enough, with Matthew DiDonna and Doyle debating semantics.

“The closest residential property to the proposed site is about 700 feet away,” DiDonna said. “You’re asking to be lead agency in a town where we believe those residents need to be represented by this board. Even though the project benefits the planet, those eight or nine houses within 700 feet will be directly impacted by a battery energy storage system.”

Doyle suggested that if the county addressed concerns about nearby neighbors, “the county is more than willing to represent those interests” as lead agency. “And we’re more than willing to give the planning board a voice in how those interests are represented.”

By the end of the meeting, neither side was willing to relinquish its claim to serve as lead agency.

Town of Ulster faces battery boom

While the towns of Saugerties and New Paltz are reviewing single BESS proposals, the Town of Ulster has three separate proposals under consideration. These include the 250 MW Alcazar Energy Storage project proposed by Terra-Gen, which is located partly at the former John A. Coleman Catholic High School property due to its close proximity to the Hurley Avenue substation.

Other proposals in the Town of Ulster include a 120 MW facility proposed by Mission Clean Energy.

title: Inside Ford's BlueOval Battery Park: How Fathom's LFP Cells Are Made | GreenCars
description:
Ford announced the plant in February 2023 to manufacture lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells for its electric vehicles.
And CATL cells are already all over the road.
The company provides the LFP batteries in most China-built Tesla Model 3s and Model Ys.
From CATL, Ford gained insight into building LFP prismatic cells at high volume.
The Fathom will have Ford’s first structural battery pack.
text:
Fast Facts | Ford's BlueOval Battery Park

Location

Marshall, Michigan

Chemistry

Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic cells, built with technology licensed from CATL

Output

Two cell lines at 40 cells per minute each, or 4,800 cells per hour combined

Pack

Ford's first structural pack, with 84 or 108 cells and no modules

Timing

Full-volume production and customer deliveries projected for the fourth quarter of 2027

Ford Is Officially in the Battery Business

Last week, Ford invited a group of journalists back to its BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall, Michigan, for an update on progress there. Ford announced the plant in February 2023 to manufacture lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells for its electric vehicles. The project faced plenty of pushback from the local community and some politicians, but as of November 2026, it's up and running. The Marshall plant is building LFP cells and shipping batteries to its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky, where they're installed into validation prototypes of the upcoming Ford Fathom.

LFP trades some energy density for lower cost, strong cycle life, and the elimination of nickel and cobalt from the cathode, so compare LFP with the other battery chemistries used in modern EVs ➜

Ford Got Some Help From the World's Biggest Battery Maker

Ford originally built its other two battery plants in Tennessee and Kentucky as a joint venture with Korea’s SK On, which has since been dissolved, with Ford getting the Kentucky plant and SK On getting the Tennessee facility. The Marshall plant was different, as Ford always planned to own it outright. That doesn’t mean Ford did everything on its own, though. Virtually every large-scale manufacturing facility leans heavily on its equipment suppliers. In this case, Ford decided to license some of its cell technology from China’s CATL, the world’s largest supplier of lithium-ion batteries.

In 2025, CATL sold an estimated 661 gigawatt-hours of lithium batteries of various chemistry types, including LFP and nickel-rich cells. Its involvement caused much of the controversy around the Marshall plant, but CATL holds no equity stake in the plant or its equipment. And CATL cells are already all over the road. The company provides the LFP batteries in most China-built Tesla Model 3s and Model Ys. It also supplied the LFP batteries used in the standard-range Ford Mustang Mach-E for the past few years, and it supplies the current Chevrolet Bolt.

From CATL, Ford gained insight into building LFP prismatic cells at high volume. It also got CATL's cell design and its list of equipment suppliers. Ford bought many of the more than 1,000 pieces of equipment in the Marshall plant from those same suppliers. Right now, the plant is in the commissioning phase, which means crews are running much of that equipment for the first time and testing and calibrating it. Several dozen CATL employees work on-site in three-month stints to help with commissioning and train local staff. By the end of 2026, the plant will employ about 800 people. Ford expects that number to climb to about 1,700 at full production.

Inside a Mile-Long Battery Factory

The plant itself is massive. It stretches about a mile and is actually two buildings joined together. The main part of the factory is the cell manufacturing plant, which contains two production lines. The process is pretty similar to what you’ll find in other facilities: coating, calendering, assembly, and formation.

Coating is where the cell's active materials go onto huge rolls of aluminum and copper foil, each about 3,000 meters long. A machine that works like a sophisticated inkjet printer coats both sides of the aluminum cathode roll with five strips of a mixture of lithium, iron, and phosphate. The copper anode roll gets five layers of graphite. After coating, the rolls go through a heater that dries the slurry, and then they're rolled back up.

Next comes calendering. A series of rollers squeezes the jumbo rolls under 40 tonnes of pressure. That compresses the cathode and anode coatings to a precise thickness and arranges the particles for optimum performance. Each 1,800-pound jumbo roll is then cut into five single-strip "whopper" rolls. Each strip is split again to make two "pancake" rolls. Automated guided vehicles shuttle all these rolls between machines. Ford maintains about four hours of inventory at various stages, so production can keep running if a machine goes down or needs repair.

From Pancake Rolls to Jelly Rolls

The pancake rolls then head to assembly. First, the uncoated foils are cut to form the tabs. Then a machine sandwiches the anode, cathode, and separator together and winds them onto a spool, creating the so-called "jelly" roll. Each jelly roll holds a little over 10 meters. Finally, the jelly roll is pressed flat.

Machine vision systems monitor every step for quality control. A tab that's improperly spaced or folded can lead to safety or performance issues later. When that happens, the bad section gets scrapped and sent to the plant's recycling area. Ford recycles all cuttings and scrap, recovers virtually all of the material, and sends it back through the process.

Battery manufacturing creates valuable scrap long before a vehicle ever reaches the road, so see how the growing battery-recycling industry is working to recover those materials for reuse ➜

Next, two jelly rolls are friction-welded together with a connector, folded over, and inserted into a rectangular aluminum can. After the bottom of the can is laser-welded shut, the fill hole has two jobs. Before it takes in electrolyte, Ford uses it to inject helium to test for leaks. If the weld leaks, the cell goes to an offline repair station, where the bottom plate is removed and rewelded.

Once a cell passes a leak test, it's filled with electrolyte, sealed, and given an initial charge. Then it sits for 24 hours as part of the formation process. Over five and a half days, the cell is partially discharged and recharged several times to activate the whole cell. Finished cells then go through a doorway into the pack assembly building.

Ford's First Structural Battery Pack

I didn’t get to tour the pack assembly area since it's still being commissioned, but Ford's engineers gave us a presentation and showed us a cutaway pack. The Fathom will have Ford’s first structural battery pack. The case absorbs about 60 percent of the structural load, and the cells absorb about 40 percent. Ford will ship finished packs to Louisville, where the seats, carpet, and much of the interior mount directly on the pack. After that come the front and rear unicastings, then the suspension, brakes, steering, and other systems.

Those Michigan-made cells are central to Ford’s new affordable truck, so see what Ford has already confirmed about the Fathom’s price, platform, technology, and 2027 launch ➜

The pack will come in two sizes, and neither includes any modules. The larger pack will have 108 cells and a likely capacity of about 75 to 80 kilowatt-hours, providing at least 300 miles of range. The smaller pack will probably have 84 cells. The cells have their terminals on top. During assembly, Ford lays a single sheet called a bus-bar module across the top. This sheet contains all the copper bus bars to connect the cells to one another and to the motors and the e-box power electronics module. Once the sheet is laid on top of the cells, every terminal is laser-welded to the module.

Currently, one cell line is running. The second is still being commissioned, and Ford expects it to be ready for production in the coming weeks. Once both lines are fully ramped up, each will produce 40 cells per minute, or 4,800 cells per hour. Ford still projects full-volume production and customer deliveries for the fourth quarter of 2027.

title: What if excess renewable energy could power new industrial processes? | MIT News

text:
As the U.S. expands its reliance on renewable energy, a considerable amount of excess electricity will be generated by solar and wind power plants. A new study explores how this energy could potentially be harnessed by certain technologies or production processes, reducing costs and increasing energy efficiency.

Researchers from MIT and Georgia Tech studied future situations in which the build-out of solar and wind farms has scaled up enough that 80 percent of the electricity supplied to customers in the U.S. is generated from renewable sources. They modeled systems with different mixtures of wind and solar power capacities.

They found that solar and wind farms could produce as much as 10 percent more power than the grid could immediately use or store in electricity systems that cost-effectively meet demand with 80 percent renewable energy. If not utilized, this excess electricity would go to waste.

This finding holds true even when the cost of energy-storage devices like batteries is low, and it remains largely consistent across the U.S. in many future scenarios.

The researchers’ model reveals when excess electricity will likely be available. It shows that periods of excess will generally occur in the spring and fall and usually persist for several hours at a time.

This predictability presents an opportunity for some industrial processes that, with the right scheduling and capacity scaling strategy, could use this otherwise excess energy. Examples include raw materials grinding and even electrified steel production. The excess could also be tapped to help meet the growing electricity demands of data centers.

While it can be more challenging to run industrial processes intermittently than continuously, the predictability of potential excesses helps, the authors say. Additionally, strategies like designing less-capital-intensive machinery, or even sharing equipment across manufacturing sites, could also be useful.

“In this era where there is a need for additional electricity, where demands are growing to support data centers and other end users, we wanted to understand what this excess electricity will potentially look like so we can design processes to benefit from these excesses. Our work can help technology developers and other stakeholders plan for future infrastructure needs and start innovating toward these technologies now,” says Jessika Trancik, a professor in the MIT Institute of Data Systems and Society (IDSS) and a senior author of this study.

She is joined on the paper by lead author Micah S. Ziegler, a former IDSS postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Aliza Khurram, a former IDSS postdoc now at the Toyota Research Institute; and Shannon Y.S. Hwang a PhD student in IDSS. The research appears today in Joule.

Examining excess

Wind and solar energy are variable resources because they are dependent on weather. During periods when supply exceeds demand, operators often take measures to either store the excess or reduce energy production altogether.

But “another way to think about that curtailed energy is as an opportunity to use this excess electricity for some other processes,” Trancik says.

“Excesses could instead be used productively in a range of processes including making materials and training AI models,” Ziegler adds.

To help engineers design processes to utilize this resource, the MIT researchers modeled the dynamics, durations, and frequencies of excess energy events.

They used an energy systems model to study systems that combine wind, solar, and energy storage to meet different percentages of electricity demand in many future scenarios. The model can also simulate how these systems might operate hourly over decades.

They fed this model 40 years of data that captured weather extremes and fluctuations in wind and solar resources across the United States. They also incorporated technology-related factors, such as the cost of building different types of batteries or other kinds of energy storage, as well as electricity demand profiles for specific regions.

“All these costs are changing, so we wanted to study many different combinations of technologies to help people plan amid all this uncertainty about what the future power system is going to look like,” Trancik says.

They designed the model to handle this enormous amount of data, while balancing the level of detail so the problem was computationally tractable.

In the end, the researchers found that significant amounts of excess energy would be generated in electricity systems that meet a significant portion of demand with renewable energy. Even when systems are designed to minimize the costs of delivering renewable energy, the amount of potentially excess power available would regularly double the amount used to meet demand.

“We found that considerable excess energy could be available even in systems with very low-cost storage, including at costs an order of magnitude lower than what battery storage costs today,” Ziegler explains.

“There is a huge amount of renewable energy that might be wasted in these cost-optimal systems, and there is not as much sensitivity to location as one might have thought. This energy is broadly available across the U.S.” Trancik says.

The model shows that the greatest potential periods of excess energy would occur in the spring, with smaller amounts of excess available in the mid- to late fall. These excess periods typically continue for seven to 12 hours, usually occur midday through the afternoon, and sometimes last for multiple days.

Leveraging surplus energy

Because these excess energy patterns are somewhat predictable, scientists and engineers could design processes to capitalize on this resource, Trancik says.

“In many of the scenarios, excess energy was often available for seven to 12 hours continuously, which suggests this duration could be a good target for technology developers and system planners when they design and schedule processes,” Ziegler explains. “When the same characteristic is found consistently across a wide range of possible energy systems, it can be considered more robust to our uncertainty about the future.”

For example, some industrial machinery, like electric arc furnaces in steel production or mills for grinding raw materials, could be switched on and operated during these times.

This electricity could also power equipment to manufacture products used seasonally, like fertilizer or concrete, which tend to be used more during spring, summer, and fall, and less during the winter. This coincides with several periods where more excess electricity is available. The energy could also power flexible computing, such as AI training processes that can be scheduled for times of day, or even months, when excesses are more likely available.

The researchers hope these results inform the development of technologies designed to utilize excess renewable energy, like periodic manufacturing processes that efficiently operate for a few hours at a time.

In the future, they plan to study the costs of developing infrastructure, equipment, and technologies that can benefit from these excesses.

“In many places today, we enjoy inexpensive electricity, but there could be more constraints on the system going forward. This excess renewable energy could be a resource that we might utilize to meet increasing demands,” says Trancik.

“If we can develop cost-effective ways to use this excess energy, we could potentially reduce some costs of transitioning to low-carbon energy resources,” Ziegler adds.

This research was funded by the MIT Climate Grand Challenges as part of the Weather and Climate Extremes project, and by the MIT Portugal Partnership Research Seed Fund Program, the MIT Technology and Policy Program, Georgia Tech, the MIT Energy Initiative, and the National Science Foundation (NSF).

text:
Electric and hybrid vehicle sales across Europe dominated total car sales last month, representing around 75% of all new vehicle registrations, while gasoline and diesel car sales dropped, highlighting demand sensitivity to soaring energy commodity prices.

The data comes from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, which reported that battery electric vehicle sales specifically represented 29.8% of the total and plug-in hybrids accounted for 10.9% of the total in the European Union alone. The share of battery electric cars in October was a substantial increase on an annual basis, with battery EV sales in October 2025 at just 18.9% of the total.

In comparison, gasoline car sales represented 16.9% of the total for October, and diesel car sales stood at a modest 5.4% of the total. Hybrid electric car sales represented a solid 33.7% share of total European car sales last month.

Electric and hybrid car sales have been moving with strong momentum this year in Europe thanks not only to government subsidies but also to the war-related surge in fuel prices across the continent, which made many previous sceptics warm up to electric transportation. Ironically, the war-related energy cost surge has not excluded electricity.

That said, record-high gasoline and diesel prices definitely played a leading part in the continued surge in electric and hybrid vehicle sales in Europe. The strong increase in hybrid vehicle sales suggests that a lot of drivers are hedging their bets with a dual-technology car, able to take advantage of both lower fuel prices when they materialize and electricity when fuel prices are unacceptably high.

Besides the cost aspect, the expansion of models on offer also helped drive EV and hybrid sales higher, ACEA said in its report. “Electrified powertrains continued to drive market growth notably in major European markets, supported by demand-support measures and a broader model offering,” ACEA said. The broader offering, however, came from China, not European carmakers, which actually lost market share in October to their Chinese rivals.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) released the following statement on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which passed in the U.S. Senate on November 19th and is anticipated to come up for a vote in the U.S. House of Representatives.

“I am a strong NO on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act when it comes to the House.

“Tribes, environmental organizations, and community groups appealed to the sponsors of the BAAJA, asking them to remove or modify provisions that would undermine Tribal sovereignty and roll back key environmental laws. The Senate-passed bill functionally addressed none of those concerns. This bill rolls back environmental protections, catastrophically undermining the Clean Water Act, and allowing new offshore drilling. This bill would also create ‘forever permits’ for data centers. Voters made their opposition to data centers clear and now is not the moment to let Donald Trump hand a blank check to developers who want to continue building these sites in communities across the country.

“This bill completely disregards Tribal sovereignty. Especially in a moment of democratic backsliding, Tribal consultation and collaboration must remain a meaningful and enforceable component of federal decision-making. Protections for sacred sites are not bargaining chips to be traded. Democrats are ready to accelerate the clean energy transition — BAAJA is not how we reach that, though. I am proud to be one of 164 members who support the Energy Bills Relief Act, legislation that we should quickly pass next Congress.

“Waiting until the next Congress to pass permitting reform would provide a real opportunity to negotiate that never occurred with the current bill. I urge my colleagues to vote NO on this bill and listen to the resounding call of voters across the country to fight for our agenda, not fold.”

description:

In Mexico, pairing solar PV with energy storage and advanced power conversion allows developers to curb curtailment and transform renewable plants into flexible assets that actively support the grid.
Q: How do battery energy storage systems (BESS) and advanced inverters help stabilize high-renewable grids?
In addition, direct DC integration captures solar energy that would otherwise be lost to inverter clipping, storing it for later dispatch through energy-shifting strategies.
text:
Q: What are the primary grid stability challenges facing Latin American electricity markets like Mexico as renewable penetration grows?

A: The main challenge is integrating rising solar and wind capacity into grids capable of managing variable generation without sacrificing system stability or power quality. Higher renewable shares increase demand for frequency and voltage control, rapid disturbance response, and reliable operation across more dynamic networks.

For developers and investors, grid stability is central to the energy transition because it directly affects project bankability, availability, and long-term asset value. Evaluate grid conditions, interconnection rules, and voltage or frequency support requirements from the earliest design stages to reduce connection risks and avoid costly retrofits. In Mexico, pairing solar PV with energy storage and advanced power conversion allows developers to curb curtailment and transform renewable plants into flexible assets that actively support the grid.

Q: How do battery energy storage systems (BESS) and advanced inverters help stabilize high-renewable grids?

A: Storage systems allow operators to shift energy dispatch, reduce curtailment, manage demand peaks, and backstop grid services. By doing so, BESS turns variable renewable generation into a predictable, dispatchable resource that strengthens both grid reliability and project revenue models.

Advanced inverters complement storage by delivering the fast, precise regulation needed to manage grid interaction, including active frequency and voltage support. Combining BESS, advanced power conversion, and intelligent plant-level controls shifts a project from being a passive power generator to an integrated grid-stability asset.

Q: What role does grid-forming technology play in this context, particularly in weak or isolated networks?

A: Grid-forming capabilities allow inverter-based systems to actively establish and stabilize the grid’s electrical references rather than merely following them. This becomes critical as conventional synchronous generation declines across power systems.

Grid-forming functions provide voltage and frequency support, synthetic inertia, and fast response during grid disturbances. These capabilities are especially valuable in weak grids, isolated systems, or areas with high renewable penetration where stability constraints would otherwise block new capacity additions.

Q: How is utility-scale solar-plus-storage design evolving, and what advantages does a DC-coupled architecture offer over conventional configurations?

A: The industry is moving away from standalone PV and BESS installations toward unified hybrid power plants designed as a single energy system. Developers need to capture more generation, manage clipping and curtailment, optimize CAPEX, and unlock new revenue streams without adding unnecessary operational complexity.

The SMA Stability Enhanced DC Coupled Hybrid Solution addresses this shift by integrating PV generation, battery storage, power conversion, and plant control within a single coordinated architecture. Connecting solar PV and batteries on the direct-current (DC) side eliminates intermediate conversion stages, reducing conversion losses and simplifying equipment and balance-of-plant infrastructure. Compared with conventional AC-coupled designs, this streamlined layout lowers initial CAPEX without compromising technical performance.

Q: Beyond CAPEX optimization, how does this integrated architecture improve energy yield and overall project performance?

A: Combining a DC-coupled architecture with Silicon Carbide (SiC) MOSFET semiconductor technology achieves conversion efficiencies of up to 99.5% on the DC side and 99.45% on the AC side. In addition, direct DC integration captures solar energy that would otherwise be lost to inverter clipping, storing it for later dispatch through energy-shifting strategies.

For utility-scale developers in Mexico and across Latin America, this architecture maximizes usable energy yield while equipping plants with grid-forming and coordinated control capabilities to meet increasingly strict operational requirements.

Q: What technical and regulatory changes are needed across Latin America to accelerate the adoption of hybrid and grid-forming technologies?

A: Grid codes and regulatory frameworks must evolve to establish clear, verifiable, and consistent technical standards for solar PV, BESS, and grid-forming functions. Regulatory clarity reduces development uncertainty and enables engineers to design compliant plants from the outset.

At the same time, electricity markets need formal mechanisms to recognize and remunerate ancillary services such as frequency regulation, voltage support, spinning reserves, and synthetic inertia. Monetizing these services creates new revenue streams for storage, improves project bankability, and accelerates private investment in grid reliability.

Q: Which technological trends and operational factors will define grid reliability in the region over the coming years?

A: Three technological trends will shape Latin America’s power sector: deeper integration between solar PV and storage, wider deployment of grid-forming inverters, and increasingly intelligent plant-level control systems. Together, these technologies maximize energy output, manage grid constraints, and deliver essential stability services.

Achieving that potential also requires early collaboration among developers, grid operators, and regulators so project designs align with evolving system needs.

text:
Across Wake County operations, public buildings are becoming more energy efficient as the County expands solar power, modernizes building systems and incorporates cleaner technologies into new construction and renovations. Together, these investments support reliable public services while lowering energy use and advancing the County’s long-term clean energy goals.

The new Wake County Public Health Center, the County’s latest flagship facility, uses 65% less energy than the building it replaced. Its energy-efficient design is complemented by a 625-kilowatt solar installation, which will generate about 20% of the building’s electricity and further reduce its reliance on traditional power sources.

This facility is one of the latest projects supporting Wake County’s Clean Energy Resolution and its goal of achieving 100% clean energy by 2050.

Clean energy projects across Wake County

Several County facilities demonstrate how these strategies work together. At Beech Bluff County Park, an energy-efficient building combines geothermal heating and cooling with a 58.5-kilowatt solar installation. The facility was able to offset 80% of its energy from clean sources last year.

At West Regional Library, improvements to lighting, heating and cooling equipment and building controls have cut energy use per square foot by more than 50%. The Sandy Plains Public Safety Station takes another approach, with an all-electric design that uses heat pumps for heating, cooling and water heating, along with a 90-kilowatt solar installation.

In addition, facilities that are in the design and construction phase also demonstrate multiple strategies including Cary Main and Five Points EMS stations, Crowder Park and Lake Crabtree, and the Wendell North Public Safety that are being designed or built with heat pump heating and cooling systems and solar installations where feasible.

Expanding solar power and planning for the future

Solar power is another growing part of the effort. Wake County has solar installations at 23 buildings and facilities, with the capacity to generate more than 1.4 megawatts of electricity and more projects are underway.

GSA and FD&C are also looking to find ways to make the upcoming projects more efficient. With two large projects at the Detention Center and the future campus at the Wake County Office Park, there is significant potential for demonstrating the County’s efforts toward the Clean Energy goal.

“Every project gives us another opportunity to improve how our buildings use energy,” Davidson said. “We’re looking at what we can do in existing facilities and making energy efficiency and clean energy part of the conversation as we plan for the future.”

Tracking progress toward clean energy goals

The County’s Energy Advisory Commission also helps guide the effort by providing input on projects and monitoring progress. Wake County, Wake County Public School System, and Wake Tech each have clean energy guidelines designed for their specific facilities and operations and provide annual progress updates.

title: Federal legislation pits energy development against conservation and historic preservation
authors: Greta Solsaa, Tierney Flavin, Charlotte Oliver, Shaun Robinson, Emma White
description:
