text:
This story was produced and originally published by Wisconsin Watch, a nonprofit, nonpartisan newsroom. It was made possible by donors like you.

Wisconsin’s electricity needs are on track to skyrocket. Utilities plan to spend billions of dollars to keep up, and ratepayers — residents, businesses and data center operators — will pick up the bill.

The three-member Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities, is responsible for guarding ratepayers’ wallets from unreasonable spending, but Wisconsin law gives it relatively little sway over how utilities plan for the future.

The commission can review proposed power plants on a case-by-case basis, but not as part of a broader blueprint for keeping the lights on as affordably as possible.

That hasn’t always been the case. Bureaucratic gridlock and a near-blackout prompted Wisconsin lawmakers to scrap a more hands-on approach to energy planning three decades ago.

Utilities don’t mourn its loss. Ratepayer advocates, however, argue the hands-off approach that followed caused Wisconsin’s electricity prices to climb faster than necessary.

A flurry of new power plant projects spurred in part by the data center boom is pushing that once-arcane disagreement into the public eye, and regulators themselves are now taking a side.

Wisconsin once gave regulators broad planning power

Investor-owned utilities generally operate as regulated monopolies: State and federal commissions grant them exclusive rights to sell electricity to consumers within a defined territory in exchange for government oversight of their rates and infrastructure projects.

That basic model dates back more than a century in Wisconsin, which formed its Public Service Commission — among the nation’s first utility regulators — in 1907.

The mass adoption of air conditioning and the rise of nuclear power complicated the picture in the mid-20th century.

Wisconsin lawmakers responded in the 1970s by empowering the Public Service Commission to take the lead on energy planning, hoping to steer utilities toward the most cost-effective path to meeting skyrocketing electricity demand.

Those powers took shape as the “Advanced Plan”: 20-year road maps for utilities to meet electricity needs. Working in two-year cycles alongside consumer advocates and other players, the commission could revise the road map to fit its priorities, and especially to save ratepayers money.

“This approach requires that the utilities focus on the most cost effective means of meeting customers’ energy service needs,” the commissioners explained in a 1987 biannual report.

Utilities have a strong incentive to build new power plants. Ratepayers pay for newly built plants, along with a commission-approved “rate of return” on every dollar spent on the projects, passed along to the utility’s shareholders. The commission could use the Advanced Plan to reconfigure utilities’ construction plans in search of savings. Later iterations embraced demand-side fixes, trimming future energy needs by incentivizing customers to switch to energy-efficient appliances or run factories at off-peak hours.

The PSC used its planning power to chip away at utility monopolies in 1989 by beginning to open utility-owned transmission lines to other power producers. Wisconsin was an early adopter of an open transmission system, hoping to keep prices in check by encouraging competition in the electricity market. State lawmakers later directed utilities to pass control of their transmission infrastructure to a new, independent company to protect other power producers’ access to the grid. That company, now called the American Transmission Company, was the country’s first multi-state, transmission-only utility.

The PSC went further in 1993, inviting third-party developers to bid for power plant projects outlined in utilities’ long-term plans. Commissioners awarded a natural gas plant in Whitewater to a New York-based developer later that year, saving We Energies’ customers an estimated $66 million.

Other states deregulated their electricity markets entirely. Chaos ensued, most notably in California, where flawed execution, price gouging and a drought caused regional blackouts, a major utility bankruptcy filing and billions of dollars in economic losses.

Lawmakers let utilities take the lead

Wisconsin didn’t copy California’s experiment. It did, however, scrap the Advanced Plan.

Utilities argued comprehensive planning was cumbersome and prone to gridlock, blaming it for a slowdown in power plant and transmission construction in the mid-1990s. Some commission staff also recognized the Advanced Plan’s deficiencies.

“It became an anti-utility regulatory mechanism that put electric reliability at risk,” recalled Randel Pilo, the PSC’s chief energy economist through much of the 1990s.

A close call in the summer of 1997 pushed Wisconsin’s political and business leaders, and even some ratepayer advocacy groups, to rethink the state’s approach. With nuclear power plants in Wisconsin and Illinois unexpectedly offline for repairs, utilities warned that summertime air conditioning use might stretch the state’s supply past its limits and trigger widespread blackouts.

State lawmakers abolished the Advanced Plan the following year. They replaced it with what Pilo called a “regulation-lite” approach, leaving planning for Wisconsin’s energy future mostly in utilities’ hands.

The PSC still considers the cost of and market justification for new power plants, but not as part of a broader strategy for balancing affordability and reliability.

Utilities made the most of the new landscape. We Energies embarked on a $7 billion “Power the Future” construction spree only a few years later — the largest energy buildout in Wisconsin history. The present power plant construction boom may surpass that record if projections of data centers’ energy needs prove accurate.

Shift to ‘regulation-lite’ approach

Ratepayer advocacy groups and some independent energy developers argue the “regulation-lite” approach to energy planning is taking a toll on Wisconsinites’ budgets.

“Without a robust planning process, we don’t have balance and we’re left with higher bills,” said Tom Content, executive director of the Wisconsin Citizens Utility Board. Under the current system, he argues, “utilities present their spending plans to investors eager for the higher profits that come from their build-build-build agenda.”

Had regulators retained greater energy planning authority, Content believes they might have more closely scrutinized We Energies’ investments in coal-fired generators just before the fracking boom made natural gas cheap and abundant in the late 2000s. Wisconsin’s average electricity rates — the second-lowest in the Midwest in 1998 — soared during the Power the Future buildout. They are the region’s second-highest as of August.

Former Republican Sen. Robert Cowles, a longtime ally of ratepayer advocacy groups who chaired the Senate’s energy committee at several points in his 38-year Senate tenure, voted alone against the 1998 bill. He told Wisconsin Watch that preserving advanced planning could have curbed some of those rate hikes by reducing demand through energy efficiency programs.

“To the extent that we can avoid building additional capacity, it saves us money,” he said.

Skeptics of the current system don’t uniformly oppose construction. A 2026 study by Advanced Energy United — a clean energy trade group that supports comprehensive planning — estimated that We Energies’ customers could have saved roughly $150 per year between 2021 and 2024 had the utility replaced its Elm Road plant with renewables and battery storage, in part by avoiding the cost of fueling and maintaining older coal and natural gas plants.

Utilities maintain that the PSC already has sufficient authority to protect ratepayer interests.

“State regulatory staff, intervenors and the public thoroughly evaluate our projects, including their costs compared to alternatives, environmental impacts, and the actual need for these new generation resources,” We Energies spokesperson Brendan Conway wrote in an email. “This robust review process ensures customers are protected every step of the way.”

How Wisconsin compares to neighboring states

Wisconsin’s current approach to energy planning sets it apart from most neighboring states — and most of the country.

Minnesota’s Public Utilities Commission has required utilities to develop comprehensive plans since the early 1990s. Illinois adopted the practice earlier this year, and Michigan lawmakers re-introduced comprehensive planning a decade ago during a transitional period in the energy sector.

“We knew that there were a number of plants that were scheduled for retirement,” said Michigan Public Service Commission chair Dan Scripps, and “a better planning process was needed” to replace them.

Michigan’s residential electricity prices nevertheless remain the highest in the Midwest, but supporters of the state’s planning approach argue other factors obscure the policy’s positive results.

“Michigan’s energy bills are driven much more by distribution system upgrades than by generation costs,” said Michigan Energy Innovation Council President Laura Sherman, citing years of deferred power line maintenance for power lines. “Without the long-term planning and competition,” she added, “I think we’d see higher generation costs as well.”

“It is effectively impossible to know what rates would be” had Michigan not adopted comprehensive energy planning, said Jonathan Kim, a Chicago-based researcher with the watchdog Energy and Policy Institute. Any number of variables — even weather — can skew comparisons between states that take a hands-on approach to planning and those that do not.

Iowans, for instance, pay the lowest retail electricity prices in the Midwest even without a comprehensive energy planning process. Kim attributes those low prices to Iowa’s early and speedy adoption of renewables, which spare the state’s ratepayers from “fossil fuel price instability.” Renewables, and especially wind turbines, account for roughly 60 percent of Iowa’s in-state electricity generation, compared to about 12 percent in Michigan and Wisconsin.

Kim also underscored that utilities can take advantage of the long-term energy planning process at ratepayers’ expense.

“We’ve seen utilities routinely overproject demand growth or need for new projects so that the amount they have to build seems greater,” he said. If regulators approve a utility’s construction to-do list in one go, Kim added, “the incentive for utilities to cheat the system, as well as the need for heightened scrutiny and rigorous ratepayer advocacy, grow even stronger.”

Data center boom revives planning debate

With a massive energy buildout on the near horizon, even Wisconsin’s regulators are joining the push to rethink the state’s energy planning paradigm.

The Public Service Commission’s most recent draft strategic energy assessment — a biennial forecast introduced as a nonbinding Advanced Plan substitute — projects Wisconsin’s energy use will climb by roughly 40 percent over the next five years, driven mostly by new data centers.

We Energies’ parent company alone expects to spend nearly $47.5 billion on new infrastructure over that time frame.

Those plans await commission approval on a project-by-project basis. Among them: a pair of natural gas plants in southeastern Wisconsin.

We Energies isn’t building the plants itself. That responsibility falls to Invenergy, the nation’s largest independent energy infrastructure developer.

The same 1998 law that axed the Advanced Plan also streamlined permitting for independent “merchant plants” built to sell electricity on the wholesale market — a move lawmakers believed would spur competition. Invenergy’s proposed plants in Kenosha and Walworth counties qualify for that streamlined review, preventing commissioners from scrutinizing their price tags.

Invenergy brought the plants to the commission for approval last year. We Energies promptly applied to buy the facilities to power its data center customers for a combined $2.3 billion; that price tag has since climbed to roughly $2.8 billion.

While We Energies must still prove the natural gas plants would provide more reasonable prices than generators powered by a different fuel, it need not demonstrate that Invenergy offered a better deal than competing developers. Microsoft, which plans to “subscribe” to the Kenosha County plant’s power and pay for its purchase, declined to comment.

Wisconsin utilities have used the same maneuver at least a half-dozen times since 2018, mostly to develop solar and wind farms.

“When developers like Invenergy develop a project, they take on all the risk and responsibility of making that project viable, that protects our customers,” Conway wrote.

Commission Chair Summer Strand isn’t convinced. Speaking at the commission’s Oct. 15 hearing on Invenergy’s applications, Strand argued Wisconsin’s “piecemeal, often whack-a-mole approach” to energy planning enables the end-around.

Strand and her fellow commissioners emphasized that current law leaves them unable to consider the We Energies-Invenergy deal as a package, even if doing so could help identify a more cost-effective alternative. The commission approved Invenergy’s permits last month; it has yet to weigh in on We Energies’ purchase plans.

“The deficiencies in the current framework are ripe for legislative action,” Strand said.

Outgoing Gov. Tony Evers proposed granting the PSC comprehensive planning powers in his most recent draft budget, but the Republican-controlled Legislature rejected the provision. The question now falls to Gov.-elect David Crowley and a new Democratic-majority Legislature.

Pilo likewise believes Wisconsin’s energy planning model needs “modest reform,” even as he recalls the Advanced Plan’s flaws. In his view, a “major transformation” in Wisconsin’s energy sector calls for a planning model more focused on affordability, competition and “public stewardship.”

Ratepayer groups enthusiastically agree.

“It’s long overdue that we give the state the tools it lacks,” Content wrote in an October press release. “Until we do, the PSC is trying to guide the state down the ‘energy future highway’ without a GPS, or even a map.”

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to correct a figure related to planned infrastructure spending. WEC Energy Group, the parent company of We Energies, plans to spend $47.5 billion across its portfolio. A previous version incorrectly attributed that figure to We Energies alone.

text:
There are gaps in Australia's battery capability, a CSIRO engineer says. Photo: Dan Himbrechts/AAP PHOTOS

Australia has the natural resources and know-how to create a thriving battery manufacturing industry but is missing opportunities by exporting critical minerals rather than turning them into high-value products.

Scientists from the CSIRO issued the warning at an event on Tuesday, also recommending more international partnerships and a greater focus on manufacturing individual components rather than trying to make entire batteries.

The call comes as Australians embrace battery technology, with more than 600,000 home batteries installed under a federal scheme since July 2025 and rapid electric vehicle sales since March.

Advertisement

Ad

Around 600,000 home batteries have been installed across Australia since 2025. (Simon Dallinger/AAP PHOTOS)

Speaking at an event called Australia's Battery Opportunity, CSIRO mineral resources principal research scientist Joanne Loh said the nation had enviable access to valuable raw materials.

"We have all the minerals needed for batteries, specifically lithium-ion batteries - we're the number one producer in terms of lithium… we have nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper, graphite, you name it," she said.

"However, we export all of these as raw materials overseas so even though we might have it, we're actually sending it overseas for processing, then importing them back as batteries."

Advertisement

Ad

The nation also shredded batteries at the end of their lives and exported the materials, Dr Loh said, rather than using them.

Australia had also stopped manufacturing elements that could be used in batteries, such as aluminium foil, CSIRO senior research engineer Geoff de Looze said.

Australia is on a path to a bright future with energy security, a scientist says. (Simon Dallinger/AAP PHOTOS)

The nation could re-establish that facility, he said, and target the local production of key components like aluminium casings and copper foil.

"We do have some gaps in Australia's capability so when we look at them we need to rank them and work out which ones we can take on and which ones we want to leave alone," Mr de Looze said.

text:
The “Yalta 2.0” narrative is not just wrong, though it is that, too, but premised in a gross historical misreading that must be confronted lest it further pollute Western policy discourse. There has been a growing tendency since the Soviet collapse to liken Yalta and the Potsdam conference that succeeded it to a kind of modern-day Treaty of Tordesillas-- an exercise between two great powers of yore, Spain and Portugal, in divvying up distant lands.

The reality is different. As it became clear toward 1945 that the second world war was moving toward complete allied victory, the leaders of the three great allied powers —Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin — naturally devoted more of their attention to the delineation and security architecture of postwar Europe. Understandings reached on the postwar status of European countries occupied respectively by the Western allies and the Soviet Union served mostly to ratify existing facts on the ground.

It was a concession to reality, not to Stalin, to acknowledge that the Soviet army, by defeating the German army in the East, had already gained control over most of Eastern Europe whether Western leaders recognized this control or not — and, alas, whether the populations of eastern Europe liked it or not.

Short of a new war with the USSR — that U.S. and British populations and soldiers would have categorically rejected and that they would probably have lost — FDR and Churchill had no ability to challenge, let alone attempt to reverse, Moscow’s assertion of a sphere of influence in Eastern Europe. Recognition of that assessment should therefore be seen not as a betrayal but as both inevitable and an act of prudence. Yalta was a first step towards establishing the geopolitical guardrails that later helped prevent the Cold War in Europe from spiraling into open and cataclysmic conflict and laid the foundations for U.S. containment strategy that prevented further Soviet expansion without recourse to war.

The Yalta comparison is also a false, and even ridiculous description of what is being discussed today. Russia would be completely incapable of occupying eastern Europe, even if it had any desire to do so, which it does not. The Russian army has proved incapable of conquering most of Ukraine. The only Russian demand for additional territorial control is the 2,000 square miles of the Donbas still occupied by Ukraine. That really does not compare to Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and the other states subjected to Soviet communism after World War II.

Nor is China in any position to imitate the U.S. in 1945 and occupy Japan, South Korea and the Philippines. The cliche "if you're not at the table, you're on the menu” that so often accompanies the contemporary “Yalta 2.0” discourse is therefore obviously untrue.

Even during the Cold War, Yugoslavia, India, as well as swathes of Africa and the Middle East were able to practice non-alignment — effectively opting out of having to choose a side in the bipolar competition — without being carved up by Washington or Moscow. That is very much the desire, and the ability, of most states in the world today, including for example former Soviet states in Central Asia, which have no desire at all to choose between Russian, Chinese or U.S. hegemony. Their declared strategy is a “multi-vector” one.

Let us grant, for the sake of argument, the fantastical notion that the White House is keen on somehow “handing over” former Soviet and Warsaw Pact countries to Russia or East Asian states to China. Who in these two regions would possibly go along with such a scheme, and how can they be compelled to do so in the absence of military conquest?

The Russian demand for the withdrawal of NATO forces to the lines they occupied in the 1990s does not require the new NATO members of eastern Europe to leave NATO, or to disarm their own forces, let alone that they submit to regime change and Russian political control ( in any case a ridiculous idea, for anyone who knows the Poles and the Balts).

It should rather be seen as the first move in a new disarmament process; and NATO, instead of rejecting it out of hand, should come back with proposals of its own whereby limits in NATO forces on Russia’s borders should be matched by strict reciprocal limits on Russian forces in Belarus and Kaliningrad.

The model and inspiration should be seen not as “Yalta” but the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaties of the 1990s. The common NATO line is now that “Russia has no say in European security.” No sane person would have said that during the Cold War, and today, alas, hundreds of thousands of dead in Ukraine also demonstrate the opposite.

In any case, the Trilateral summit in Shenzhen did not talk about any of these issues. The official statement that followed the talks contained just two elements, both of which should be seen as valuable for humanity. The summit’s call for new nuclear limitation agreements, however vaguely formulated, should be seen as a tentative first step to a restoration of the treaties agreed by the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. in the later years of the Cold War — not to end that war, but to try to ensure that it did not escalate into universal catastrophe.

More generally, the summit symbolized a truth of vast significance: that if basic peace and order in the world is to be secured, then this will depend above all on reasonably peaceful relations between the world’s most powerful states, secured by agreements regulating those relations.

So if there is a legacy of the Cold War to which we should look, it is that of great powers assuming a degree of shared responsibility for maintaining a stable, working international system to be passed down to future generations. The Shenzhen summit represents a significant first step in that direction.

Finally, on the score of spheres of influence, it is perhaps worth noting that one is tacitly accepted by virtually the entire world, including China. Nobody is challenging the U.S. insistence on absolute military hegemony in Central America and the Caribbean, because they know that any attempt to do so would bring ferocious U.S. retaliation. Nor have the Europeans, for all their supposed commitment to a “rules-based order” pushed back in any way against the extreme hardening of the Monroe Doctrine under Donald Trump, as witnessed with regard to Venezuela, Cuba, and alleged drug traffickers.

Fortunately, there is no chance whatsoever of Russia or China being able to follow this particular U.S. rule.

Schumer went on to criticize the President for not securing any concessions from his counterparts, including on curbing Chinese espionage or preventing Beijing and Moscow from helping Iran target American troops.

The emphasis of Schumer’s remarks was striking given that dissatisfaction with Trump’s foreign policy and its economic ramifications helped propel Democrats back into the Senate majority earlier this month.

As Democrats debate whether their electoral victory presents an opportunity to rethink the party's foreign policy, Schumer's remarks suggest that some of its longtime leaders remain wedded to an older approach.

That tension is also emerging as a central dividing line in the contest to lead the new Democratic majority. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who announced last week that he would challenge Schumer, has made their disagreements over foreign policy, and in particular over how to approach the issues in the Middle East, as central to his pitch.

The two senators represent competing visions of the Democratic Party’s future. Faiz Shakir, a senior advisor to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who has supported Van Hollen’s challenge, recently described him to NPR as a“pragmatic progressive” who is “going to know what the people of this country are asking us to do at this moment” and “can bring a lot of factions of the party together.”

Much of the debate is over how Democrats should approach using their power of the purse to cut off funding for the war in Iran before the new Congress is seated in January. Van Hollen and a number of his Democratic colleagues have called on the party to insist on a government funding bill that excludes money for the Iran war, which they say will force Trump and the Republicans to decide whether to risk a shutdown to continue the war. Other Democrats argue that a shutdown would be politically risky for the party, and that Democrats should wait until they are in the majority to force the issue.

Schumer, for his part, has not clarified his stance, as he continues to say that the war must end and a shutdown must be avoided.

Schumer's reluctance to say that he will prioritize ending the war has renewed scrutiny on his longstanding hawkishness toward Iran. Many foreign policy analysts and congressional critics have highlighted his place as one of a few Democratic opponents to the Obama-era Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), commonly known as the Iran nuclear deal, as one clear example.

Van Hollen has made this contrast central to his leadership campaign. “I don't see how after an election like this where ending the war and bringing down prices was a priority, we can cast a vote to fund the war,” he said recently. “And of course, Senator Schumer was one of the folks who originally opposed President Obama and the JCPOA, but I think the caucus wants to bring this war to an end,”

Progressives have also condemned Schumer’s approach in the lead-up to the war, during which he attacked Trump’s diplomacy with Tehran and, critics say, did not act quickly enough to slow the president’s march to war in February.

On Thursday, during his floor speech, Schumer questioned what “commitments” Trump made and what he “gave away” over dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, echoing his controversial June 2025 accusations that Trump was negotiating “side deals” and “folding on Iran.”

The disagreements extend beyond Iran. Van Hollen has taken a leading role in the effort to remove provisions of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) that would deepen military and intelligence cooperation between the United States and Israel.

“The agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology,” Van Hollen and 11 Senate colleagues wrote in a recent letter to congressional leadership. “If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement.”

The letter further argues that the provisions would shift U.S. military assistance to Israel to more “opaque, less discernible avenues,” which the Senators call particularly troubling given Israel's conduct in Gaza, the West Bank, and elsewhere in the region.

Schumer has not publicly commented on these provisions, but is seen as one of Israel’s strongest supporters in Congress. In 2025, he told the New York Times that his “job...is to keep the left pro-Israel.” He has repeatedly called himself a “guardian of Israel” throughout his congressional career, which spans 45 years.

Their perspectives on the U.S-Israel relationship appears to be a key dividing line between the two senators. Van Hollen was first elected as an establishment-supported, Israel-friendly candidate, but his views have shifted. “Times have changed in a lot of ways, where the Democratic base has changed in a lot of ways, and he has changed along with it,” Yousef Munayyer of the Arab Center recently told The Intercept. “I don’t know that the same can be said for a lot of other folks, like Chuck Schumer.”

Independent trackers show that the sitting minority leader currently has more support, though the tallies remain close. The vote for majority leader is expected to take place in a secret ballot on Dec. 1.

But what a difference a year can make with Trump. On October 21, U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel publicly described the relationship as experiencing “turbulence.” Lee’s government, for its part, has tried to downplay recent tensions, arguing that overheated domestic politics in both countries need not undermine the strong foundation of the alliance. As South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told Parliament in late October, “When you’re in turbulence, fasten your seat belt and it won’t be a problem.”

In truth, some of the turbulence is of Seoul’s own making. In March, for example, South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young publicly identified a North Korean uranium enrichment facility, potentially compromising sensitive sources and methods. The Lee government insists that the information was already public, but Washington disagrees and has retaliated by restricting certain satellite-derived intelligence about North Korea and excluded Seoul from a trilateral meeting on North Korean cyber threats.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has complained about intelligence sharing broadly with Seoul, and South Korean Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha acknowledged as recently as last month that his government had not fully addressed Washington’s concerns.

South Korea has also been slow in deciding how to invest its pledged $350 billion, angering Trump in the process. For instance, Trump wants Seoul to invest roughly $54 billion in the Alaska LNG pipeline project, but Lee’s government has questioned its commercial viability. Although he has expressed confidence that South Korea will eventually follow through, Trump has made vague threats to resume tariffs if the deals remain stalled.

Separately, South Korean regulators imposed a fine of $423 million on Coupang, a U.S.-listed e-commerce company, following a massive consumer data breach. The Trump administration and congressional Republicans were outraged by the move, calling it discrimination against American companies, while the Lee administration justified the measure to protect consumer privacy data.

But the Trump administration shares much of the blame for the increasingly contentious bilateral relationship. For one thing, even though Washington and Seoul already agreed in June 2025 to reduce tariffs from 25% to 15% in 2025, Trump periodically threatens to raise tariff rates again to 25% when he gets angry about something. This has surprised and frustrated South Korean officials, who may no longer see Washington as a reliable strategic ally. And perhaps neither do the South Korean people. According to a Pew Research survey from August, 55% of them hold an unfavorable view of the United States — the highest such mark in more than 20 years.

North Korea poses a bilateral challenge as well. To be sure, both Trump and Lee want to prioritize renewed engagement with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un rather than deterrence. But the Trump administration’s preferred approach differs from Seoul’s. Trump surprised South Korea by shortening the annual bilateral military drills, known as Ulchi Freedom Guardian, just hours before they began. He argued that they were unnecessarily provocative toward Kim, whom Trump hopes will join him in a summit.

Although he publicly accepted Trump’s decision to cut back combined military exercises, Lee would rather derive diplomatic leverage from enhanced military preparedness against North Korea, and the deterrence that comes with it, prior to negotiations. Trump further blamed South Korea for not contributing to the U.S. naval operation to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, in turn questioning why Washington continues to defend South Korea on the peninsula.

Deepening disagreements over China represent yet another irritant. The Trump administration clearly seeks greater “flexibility” in how it uses the approximately 28,500 U.S. troops deployed to South Korea. Rather than focusing exclusively on North Korea, Washington has publicly intimated that China could be the target of their future military operations, and that Seoul would be expected to support that mission.

Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge “Bridge” Colby, for example, visited Seoul in January and gave a speech at the Sejong Institute that curiously did not mention North Korea at all, and instead, replaced it with multiple references to countering China. To the shock of South Korean officials, Trump’s National Security Strategy, released last November, neglected to mention North Korea either and focused instead on the need for South Korea to help the U.S. and Japan secure the First Island Chain — a clear reference to containing China. Although Trump’s National Defense Strategy from January did reference North Korea, it avoided stating that denuclearization was still a U.S. priority and put the responsibility to deal with the regime more squarely on Seoul, with limited American support.

Trump’s submarine and shipbuilding deals are also in limbo. On the submarines, Trump wants them built at the South Korean defense firm Hanwha’s shipyard in Philadelphia, but the Lee government argues that South Korea offers more appropriate shipyards because they are already outfitted with advanced submarine-building capabilities. There is also the question surrounding the enriched nuclear fuel and associated sensitive technologies, which Seoul wants Washington to provide. But rules governing the bilateral relationship currently do not permit such transfers without specific exemptions or additional authorizations.

When the submarine deal was first announced in October 2025, none of these issues had been properly considered by the Trump administration, provoking the current disputes. And on broader shipbuilding, South Korea’s $150 billion financial commitment has largely stalled. Indeed, the president’s Make American Shipbuilding Great Again (MASGA) initiative has yielded zero concrete projects, embarrassing Trump, who wants to reenergize the U.S. defense industrial base and add manufacturing jobs. Progress on MASGA has also been hampered by a mix of legal, political, and financial obstacles.

Finally, the fallout from the September 2025 ICE raids on South Korean workers at the Hyundai-LG battery plant in the United States continues. Although Seoul wrapped up its internal investigation without retaliating against the U.S. government, attorneys representing more than 300 of the workers, who were allegedly shackled and abused during the ordeal, are now pursuing administrative damages, possibly a precursor to civil lawsuits, against the Department of Justice, the Department of Homeland Security, the FBI, and others. The political rhetoric surrounding the case became heated on both sides as the legal process continues to unfold.

Despite the growing tensions between them, South Korea and the U.S. remain staunch allies, and in fact, the Trump administration has referred to Seoul as a “model ally,” especially because of its increased defense spending. Lee and Trump reportedly spoke about future diplomatic engagements on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China this week. But difficulties remain, and the next two years under Trump and Lee could prove even more turbulent when it comes to trade, investment, military cooperation, and foreign policy.

Additionally, while many have interpreted the midterm elections as a rebuke of Trump’s foreign policy, they are unlikely to affect U.S.-Korea relations in substantive ways. The president typically has the lead on foreign policy, and lame-duck presidents tend to intensify their focus on it to secure their legacy. For South Korea, this likely means more, not less, of Trump, adding to Seoul’s urgency to somehow figure him out and stop making unforced errors.

text:
From: Mercom India

Enel, through its wholly owned subsidiaries Enel Green Power North America and EGPNA Project Holdco 7, has signed an agreement with energyRe to acquire a 317 MW solar portfolio in South Carolina.

The portfolio is expected to generate more than 540 GWh of electricity annually after entering service.

Enel said the acquisition is expected to increase the Enel Group’s net financial debt by approximately $255 million after accounting for the effects associated with the projects entering service.

The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to customary conditions, including approvals from the U.S. antitrust authority and the U.S. government for foreign direct investments.

After the transaction closes, Enel expects the portfolio to contribute approximately $30 million annually to the group’s EBITDA.

Following the transaction, Enel Group expects its installed renewable energy capacity in North America to reach approximately 13.5 GW across wind, solar, and energy storage facilities.

Enel said the acquisition forms part of its plan to increase renewable generation capacity, including through acquisitions of operating or developed assets in Tier 1 countries. The company presented the strategy during its Capital Markets Day in February of this year.

In September, Enel completed the acquisition of a 625 MW solar portfolio in the United States from Excelsior Energy Capital for approximately $760 million through its wholly owned subsidiaries Enel Green Power North America and EGPNA Project Holdco 2.

According to Mercom’s 9M and Q3 2026 Solar Funding and M&A report, approximately 34.4 GW of solar projects were acquired in the first nine months of 2026, compared to 29 GW in the same period during 2025.

title: Beyond the Negotiating Halls: What COP31 Means for Electrification and Climate Action
description:
Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) played an important role at COP31, helping to advance and strengthen the global electrification agenda and coordinate the electrification delivery package.
Bringing the COP31 Action Agenda to Life In a first for a UN Climate Summit, real on-the-ground action was at the heart of the conference through the Global Climate Action Agenda.
SEforALL was instrumental in developing the COP31 Global Climate Action Agenda Electrification Delivery Package involving over 150 countries, the EU, 37 cities and more than 260 businesses across 6 continents.
Making 35-by-35 Work for Everyone Electrification had already moved ahead on a voluntary track, through the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge and commitments from governments, cities, civil society, and businesses.
We launched the report on 10 November at the Global Electrification Ministerial and Forum, hosted by the COP31 Presidency.
text:
COP31’s impasse does not diminish the opportunities of the Action Agenda, where country commitments and broad-based coalitions can translate ambition into tangible progress for those most vulnerable to climate change.

COP31 ended in Antalya on 22 November, two days late and without agreement on its headline decisions. The inconclusive talks followed days of deadlock, with negotiators unable to bridge differences amid calls for stronger commitment to move away from fossil fuels. Parties also acknowledged shortcomings in areas including climate finance, loss and damage and the just transition.

Multiple compromise drafts circulated by COP31 co-presidents Australia and Türkiye sought to win consensus, but the effort ultimately failed, with negotiators arguing the text weakened previous commitments and fell far short of the action required to address the climate crisis.

Despite the lack of consensus on the final text, significant progress was made during the conference, including through individual country pledges, the Leaders’ Summit, and initiatives under the COP31 Action Agenda aimed at accelerating electrification, resilience and investment.

Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) played an important role at COP31, helping to advance and strengthen the global electrification agenda and coordinate the electrification delivery package. Through strategic engagement, technical contributions and collaboration with governments and partners, SEforALL helped elevate electrification as a critical priority for accelerating universal energy access, driving sustainable development, harnessing climate finance and delivering a just and inclusive energy transition.

We also spotlighted practical solutions, showing how people-centred transitions can be translated into action, while highlighting the resources, partnerships and support needed to accelerate progress, particularly in developing countries and in support of vulnerable communities.

Bringing the COP31 Action Agenda to Life

In a first for a UN Climate Summit, real on-the-ground action was at the heart of the conference through the Global Climate Action Agenda.

SEforALL was instrumental in developing the COP31 Global Climate Action Agenda Electrification Delivery Package involving over 150 countries, the EU, 37 cities and more than 260 businesses across 6 continents. SEforALL is part of the Coordination Group of Axis 1 (Transitioning Energy, Industry and Transport) of the Global Climate Action Agenda together with the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD), the International Energy Agency (IEA), the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) and the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), facilitated by the Climate Champions Team under the leadership of the Climate High-Level Champions.

Governments, utilities and businesses used the package to set out commitments on grids, finance and clean energy. It also highlighted progress from our work on energy access, including the Universal Energy Facility (UEF), the results-based financing facility we manage, and the Health Facility Electrification Compact, which we convene with partners to electrify health facilities.

The Action Agenda was an important platform for SEforALL to continue the work started at COP30 where we chair three Plans to Accelerate Solutions (PAS) to 2030 and these include: the Platform for Clean Cooking in Schools, Mission Efficiency (Energy Efficiency), and Universal Access to Electricity.

Making 35-by-35 Work for Everyone

Electrification had already moved ahead on a voluntary track, through the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge and commitments from governments, cities, civil society, and businesses.

SEforALL used COP31 to put emerging and developing economies at the centre of this conversation. In Antalya, our work centred on three priorities: expanding energy access, increasing grid capacity to meet growing demand and helping countries develop investment-ready national energy plans.

Those priorities were reflected in The Electrification Opportunity: Delivering Energy Security, Development and Climate Action in Emerging Markets and Developing Economies, the report we developed in partnership with the Australian Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. We launched the report on 10 November at the Global Electrification Ministerial and Forum, hosted by the COP31 Presidency.

COP31 President Murat Kurum invited governments, businesses and investors to "make electrification work for all". The report sets out three pathways: expanding electricity access, meeting new demand and electrifying cooking, transport and industry.

The report shows that the global electrification opportunity is achievable but we must account for differentiated national pathways that reflect national circumstances, economic structure and starting points. Therefore, a one-size-fits-all approach will not work, and countries need to plan for electrification deliberately, align it with their growth and access priorities and work towards mobilizing the finance and institutions to deliver it.

Spotlighting Tanzania’s Energy Transition

Our work in Tanzania transitioning institutional cooking was spotlighted at COP31. With support from the World Food Programme (WFP) and SEforALL, the government is introducing electric cooking in four regions, with an initial target of 50 schools and 5,000 more identified for expansion.

At our joint COP31 session, President Samia Suluhu Hassan, who headlined the event, said: "No country should have to choose between economic development and environmental protection." Tanzania's energy transition and investment plan, developed with our support and due to launch on 26 January 2027, includes clean cooking alongside electricity infrastructure and green industrialization.

The COP31 event also explored how carbon markets, including cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, can mobilize additional results-based financing for institutional clean cooking.

Ensuring Grids Keep Pace With Demand

With demand rising from homes, businesses and industry, grids have become one of the biggest bottlenecks in the energy transition. "If renewables are the heart of the energy transition, grids are its arteries," UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on 12 November at an event on the Global Grids Accelerator, that he convened for Heads of State and Government and leaders from development banks, international organizations, financial institutions and the private sector.

The Accelerator, which is co-convened by SEforALL, UNDP and UNOPS will work around nationally and regionally owned priorities to accelerate grid investment and implementation by connecting political leadership, technical expertise and financing, and strengthening and coordinating existing international support, with initial focus on Africa and the ASEAN region.

COP31 provided an opportunity to move the Accelerator into its next phase (after its initial launch at the United Nations General Assembly), bringing forward country and regional priorities and mobilizing partners and resources around their delivery.

Government representatives, private sector and funders at the event committed to supporting the Accelerator and ensuring greater progress in emerging economies and developing countries.

Strengthening Developing Countries’ Participation in Carbon Markets

To strengthen international cooperation on climate finance, the Government of Italy, with support from SEforALL, launched the Carbon Leadership for Emissions Accounting and Regulation (CLEAR) Fund at COP31.

Financed by Italy’s Ministry of Environment and Energy Security and implemented by SEforALL with support from the Italian Institute for Environmental Protection and Research (ISPRA), the CLEAR Fund will provide countries with support to build the technical capacity, regulatory frameworks and investment-ready project pipelines needed to engage effectively in international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

The Fund will initially focus on Tanzania, Ethiopia and Cuba, working with these governments to identify credible emissions-reduction opportunities, strengthen national institutions and develop projects capable of attracting international investment.

Accelerating Green Industrialization

We spotlighted the importance of accelerating Africa’s green industrialization through clean energy investment, technology cooperation and stronger industrial supply chains.

At a high-level policymakers roundtable at COP31, that we organized alongside the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), the Africa-Europe Foundation and Enabel (the Belgian International Cooperation Agency), and championed by United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) and Africa Green Industrialization Initiative (AGII), we underscored the importance of aligning Africa’s energy access and security priorities with industrialization and job creation to advance socioeconomic development and a just energy transition.

The roundtable identified four priority areas for continued cooperation: scaling clean energy finance for productive use and industrial development; strengthening Africa’s clean technology manufacturing base; advancing strategic industrial value chains along regional economic corridors; and keeping green industrialization high on the agenda ahead of COP32 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

The roundtable reinforced a shared ambition between Europe and Africa to ensure the energy transition creates the foundations for competitive industries, jobs, domestic value addition and sustainable economic growth.

What Addis Ababa Inherits

Focus now shifts to COP32 in Addis Ababa, where governments will face many of the questions left unanswered in Antalya.

As the Secretary-General has said, ‘there is no ambiguity in the science. Climate change is a reality experienced by communities across our planet, and no country or region will be spared its dire consequences.’

COP32 will be the true test of climate action, as it comes immediately after an unprecedented COP, and SEforALL will continue advocating for accelerated energy transitions and greater ambition to tackle climate change. We will work with the COP32 Presidency to ensure the solutions needed for the Global South are top of the agenda.

We look forward to working with new and existing partners to drive more international political and financial commitments toward a just and equitable energy transition that will significantly increase deployed capital, scale existing technical solutions, and increase the capacity of governments and workforces to address electrification and grids, and accelerate countries’ journeys toward net-zero.

More From SEforALL at COP31

Investor roundtable on Senegal and Liberia (10 November): Together with Octopus Energy and the UK's Association for Renewable Energy and Clean Technology, we convened investors to discuss financing clean energy projects in Senegal and Liberia.

Africa Rising (10 November): At the OPEC Fund pavilion, Sierra Leone presented its progress on electricity access, which has risen from under 5% to 36%, with more than 100 mini-grids built through its off-grid programme.

Technical Session on Electrification (13 November): We presented the findings of The Electrification Opportunity at the Australia Pavilion, sharing its evidence on how countries can turn the 35-by-35 goal into national action.

Energy for Peace Film Screening (13 November): With Energy Peace Partners and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security, we co-hosted a screening of Renewable Peace, a documentary series on how clean energy is helping to build peace in conflict-affected communities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Nigeria and South Sudan.

Energy Labour Market in Emerging Economies (16 November): Together with partners, we spotlighted research on the energy labour market, highlighted skills gaps in BRICS, and explored ways to bridge them.

Nature for Cooling Challenge Showcase (17 November): We spotlighted the Nature for Cooling Challenge project that we are implementing with UNEP in Africa, Asia and Latin America.

Energy Access for the Global South (17 November): Together with IRENA, we convened a high-level event highlighting credible pathways, investable propositions, and practical partnerships that can close energy access gaps globally.

Sustainable cooling (17 November): A day after the Third Annual Cooling Ministerial, our Deputy CEO Stefano Marguccio joined a high-level panel on implementing the Global Cooling Pledge and its Heat Resilience Roadmap ahead of COP32. In a short video from Antalya, he explained how rising temperatures are changing electricity demand. We also spoke at the UNEP Cool Coalition's session on the Nature for Cooling Challenge, which we help implement in Brazil, Cambodia and Côte d'Ivoire to show how nature-based solutions can cool cities.

text:
Our overview of the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) examines its spending and performance. It brings together insights from our reports and other publicly available sources including DESNZ’s annual report and accounts.

Jump to downloads

Key takeaways

The Department for Energy Security & Net Zero

Purpose: The Department for Energy Security & Net Zero (DESNZ) is responsible for the government’s mission for the UK to become a “clean energy superpower”. The mission has two pillars: Clean Power by 2030 and Accelerate to Net Zero, supported by four strategic outcomes.

Financial management

Total net spending: DESNZ’s spending doubled to £13.4 billion in 2025-26 – an increase of £6.7 billion from 2024-25. This is spending that DESNZ controls directly and through its arm’s-length bodies (ALBs).

Managing major projects: DESNZ’s major projects and programmes include: Sizewell C (£4.7 billion) – a new nuclear power station in Suffolk; nuclear decommissioning (£3 billion); and interventions intended to support affordable energy and action on climate change (£2.7 billion).

Spending Review settlement: DESNZ received a 16% a year real-terms increase in its capital budget between 2023-24 and 2029-30, excluding Sizewell C. However, since then DESNZ has had a net reduction of around £3.1 billion from its budget for 2026 to 2030, which reduces the amount it can spend on equity and loans, and increases the proportion of its capital grants that are fully allocated.

Managing financial liabilities: DESNZ and its ALBs manage a range of complex and long-term financial liabilities needed to build and run energy infrastructure and manage the ongoing costs left by nuclear and fossil fuel infrastructure after it has closed. At 31 March 2026, DESNZ had net liabilities of £228.9 billion. Its scheme to support low-carbon electricity generation, Contracts for Difference, had the largest increase.

Resilience and risk

Managing organisational and project risks: DESNZ is managing long-term strategic risks, such as maintaining affordable and secure energy supplies, securing the private investment needed for the energy transition to clean power, protecting critical energy infrastructure from disruption, and ensuring it has the funding, skills and organisational capacity required to deliver its objectives. DESNZ also has 12 of the government’s portfolio of 81 major projects, each with significant delivery risks.

Developing a new finance model for Sizewell C: DESNZ reached a final investment decision on Sizewell C in 2025-26, using a novel delivery and financing model that combines public and private investment with a Regulated Asset Base mechanism. The project is intended to strengthen long-term energy security, but achieving the expected benefits will depend on successful delivery of this complex major project.

Overseeing an upgrade to the grid: Delivering Clean Power 2030 depends on upgrading an ageing electricity transmission network, with £70 billion of planned investment by 2031 – around four times the current rate. But delivering these upgrades on time will be very challenging.

Reforming home retrofit: Weaknesses in the design, oversight, quality assurance and consumer protection arrangements for DESNZ’s Energy Company Obligation (ECO) scheme contributed to widespread installation problems in up to 23,000 homes with external wall insulation, and suspected fraud. DESNZ ended the scheme and is consulting on reforms to consumer protection under the Warm Homes Plan.

Productivity

Nuclear decommissioning: Cleaning up the UK’s legacy nuclear sites will take until 2150 and cost £115 billion. The estimated cost of decommissioning has increased because some work is now expected to start later or take longer, extending the cost of keeping ageing sites safe and operational.

Efficiency savings: DESNZ has committed to efficiency savings of £157 million a year by 2028-29 through workforce, digital and operational reform.

text:
Advocacy News – Nov. 20, 2026

What’s happening: Last night, the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) (H.R. 2347) by a 62–33 vote to overhaul federal environmental and energy infrastructure permitting rules. The bill passed with broad bipartisan backing, including 47 Republicans and 15 Democrats. Thirty-one Democrats and two Republicans voted against it, citing concerns over environmental laws, tribal sovereignty, and federal transmission authority.

Failed Last-Minute Amendments: A final-hour effort to pass a bipartisan manager’s amendment and vote on roughly 19 additional proposals stalled. Oregon Democrats, led by Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden, blocked the necessary time agreement after Republican leadership rejected a vote to ban data centers on public lands, forcing the Senate to skip floor amendments and vote directly on the main bill.

Earlier Compromises That Secured the Deal

The broad coalition behind the bill relied on a foundational manager’s amendment released on November 7, 2026, which bridged key gaps between clean energy advocates, fossil fuel supporters, and wary lawmakers:

Data Center & Utility Rules: Added requirements for large data centers to cover full grid-upgrade costs, created a DOE assistance program, and restricted behind-the-meter gas plant power sales to under 5 megawatts.

Permitting & Judgment Fund Guardrails: Modified Section 1402 by extending the historical baseline to 10 years and restricting Judgment Fund payouts strictly to court orders or court-approved settlements to prevent collusive litigation.

Transmission & Siting: Maintained FERC interregional planning rules, introduced a one-year state review window prior to federal backstop siting authority, and exempted Southeast monopoly utilities from joint planning mandates.

Project Revocation & Tribal Reviews: Clarified that agencies can revoke permits under court order and made adjustments to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act regarding cultural and sacred sites, though tribal concerns kept some Democrats opposed.

Next Steps: The legislation now moves to the House of Representatives, where leadership aims to pass the Senate text during the lame-duck session before the new Congress convenes in January 2027.

What we are saying: This legislation is key to making critical investments in building out and modernizing our grid. The Chamber will continue to encourage Michigan’s Congressional delegation to support this effort as it comes before them for a vote.

text:
Australians are subsidising kerbside chargers whether they like it or not, but only one of these subsidies creates an incentive to buy an electric vehicle, says a senior executive at Australia’s biggest distributed network company.

Nick Black, the head of fleet and charger logistics at Ausgrid, says the New South Wales (NSW) government has kicked in up to 80 per cent of the cost of installing all 530 kerbside chargers in the company’s Sydney network.

A second scheme will see the federal government is about to cover up to another 30 per cent of installation costs via a new public charger fund.

But while taxpayer funding can boost charger numbers, only electricity distributors can also lower the cost of charging itself, Black says.

“Either [consumers are] investing through tax, or it’s paid for in the electricity bill, but at a lower rate because it’s scaled,” he told Renew Economy.

“It’s really about opening up that access and appreciating that … they’re being funded today so what’s the fairest way to fund a kerbside charger to create truly public infrastructure that lowers the cost to the consumer?”

Black is stepping into a debate about whether electricity distributors should be allowed to compete with the private sector to install electric vehicle (EV) chargers, and add a potentially lucrative new asset to the pool they earn revenue from.

It’s one that is reaching white-hot temperatures following a federal intervention that gives $33.3 million to electricity distributors to fill gaps in street charging infrastructure left by private companies, and forcing a change in energy market rules to allow them to do so.

Private charger companies, electricity consumer groups and some industry experts and lobbyists say it’s a land grab that will crowd out private companies, and that electricity distributors are the reason why private companies have struggled to gain a foothold.

With the federal win under their belt, electricity distributors are now trying to justify the significant departure from rules – and why they couldn’t enable the new industry within them.

The vision Ausgrid and other distributors are pitching is that they are best placed to bring down charging costs for all EV owners, even if all electricity consumers have to share the bill (estimated at just $1 per household per year by the market rule maker).

They argue that as more people will see EV chargers, they will be more confident to buy EVs, and that the increased use of the network will eventually mean lower power bills for consumers.

Black says an extra 400,000 electric vehicles on the Ausgrid network could lower power bills by as much as $12 a year.

He denies that Ausgrid has deliberately made it difficult for private companies to lease or access the city power poles it owns, and says they have worked within ring-fencing rules but so far it simply hasn’t delivered enough chargers for Sydney’s packed streets.

“We’ve been working a lot on creating critical peak tariffs that work for the market as well as specifically for EV charging operators,” Black says.

“In addition to that, we’ve been streamlining all our processes to ensure that charge point operators can apply for access to place their charging equipment on our power poles.

“That’s been quite successful with us already seeing over 530 kerbside chargers rolling out, but… it’s still not enough.

“We’ve tried with the tariffs, we’ve opened up the access, and then we still believe there’s more that needs to be done.”

Genuinely helpful?

But the idea that Ausgrid in particular and distributors in general have been genuinely trying to enable private sector charging infrastructure is met with skepticism by the industry.

Multiple sources have told Renew Economy that DNSPs in New South Wales (NSW) and Victoria in particular have made it very difficult to get permission to use poles for kerbside chargers, and expensive.

Even the energy rule maker is skeptical of distributor claims that they’ve been helpful.

A draft rule change, needed to make the federal charging plan possible, pointedly acknowledged barriers to entry including months-long connection timeframes and power pole access charges ranging between zero and $300,000 a pole.

Inside the rule change it suggested “a targeted and time-limited program” to encourage distributors to cooperate.

The federal ‘Accelerating EVCharging Program’ also sets a fixed $700 connection fee and caps pole leases at $250 a year for kerbside chargers.

Black would not reveal Ausgrid’s usual rates nor whether they are higher than the federal fees, saying each of the five charge point operators currently running the 530 chargers in its grid “negotiated an outcome… that works for their business model.”

Software neutral, hardware competition

Where electricity distributors could offer a real edge for EV owners is their open platform model, which is open to any charging retailer and covers the cost of being on the platform and the cost of power.

It will still compete with private companies wanting to install their own chargers on poles.

But Black says the software platform at least will be a “neutral host” and this is one way they will be able to offer cheaper charging for consumers. Companies such as Chargefox have already shifted away from owning hardware to being software-only, providing the app, billing and other services inside the charger.

“The proposed DNSP model is that we create competition at the socket… we open up access to any electricity retailer or e-mobility service provider to compete for the customer at each socket on the street,” he says.

“What the model is proposed to do is to extend home charging to the curb and create this open access model.”

Black says they could deliver similar rates to what Citipower is offering in its 100-charger trial in Melbourne of 20-24c/kilowatt-hour (kWh).

That’s a much better deal than the 50c/kWh peak rates currently offered by EVX, for example, in Sydney and Melbourne.

“So there’s competition at a charger level as opposed to an infrastructure level,” Black says.

“There’s not really any competition for customers who want to charge on the street because they’re locked into whoever that single provider is at that 55c/kWh.”

Black would not say how much of the ongoing infrastructure cost, currently included in the price paid at privately-owned chargers, will be passed on to Ausgrid bill payers.

The Australian Energy Market Commission (AEMC) suggested in its draft rule change the capital cost of installation might be in the realm of $1 per year extra on bills, but didn’t offer any insight into ongoing running costs.

But with battery electric cars out-selling petrol for the third month in a row in October and forecast to just keep going, more chargers are needed and consumers may need to swallow that cost.

The private sector says they shouldn’t swallow this forever as incremental charges on electricity bills.

But Black argues that if governments and consumers want kerbside chargers to appear faster, they have to accept network involvement.

text:
For big corporations in North Carolina with ambitious climate goals, the clean transition tariff is becoming something of a white whale.

Tech firms and other large electricity consumers have long sought this special rate structure because, across most of the state, they can buy electricity only from Duke Energy, a vertically integrated monopoly utility. A clean tariff would let them contract for their own renewable electrons using Duke as a go-between, without violating the law.

In spring 2024, Duke announced its intention to pursue such a plan but never followed through. Earlier this year, the company said it would evaluate the clean tariff ​“in good faith,” but made no commitments.

Last month, the whale got closer than ever, when Duke said it would definitely begin negotiations on a clean tariff in early 2027. Proponents of the policy urged state officials to back up that pledge with an order and an enforceable deadline. They hoped that such a directive would be tucked somewhere in the hundreds of pages of regulatory decisions issued last week.

It was not.

Instead, the state Utilities Commission, a five-member panel controlled by Republicans, offered encouragement.

“The Commission declines at this time to direct Duke to file or propose a clean customer tariff,” its Nov. 16 order said. ​“The Commission nevertheless recognizes Duke’s representation that it remains willing to collaborate with interested parties. … [It] encourages Duke to work with the interested parties to work on a proposal for a Clean Transition Tariff.”

Steve Levitas, a longtime clean energy lawyer — and, briefly, a commissioner himself — welcomed the verbiage but called it insufficient.

“This issue is just too important to leave to Duke’s discretion,” said Levitas, now the interim executive director of New Energy Economics, a nonprofit that provides expert testimony in state regulatory proceedings.

Levitas testified this year on behalf of the Corporate Energy Buyers Association, whose 300-plus business members run the gamut from hospitality to manufacturing to tech companies.

“All CEBA and many other interveners asked the commission to do was to require Duke to file a new, voluntary customer program,” Levitas said. ​“That wasn’t really a huge ask.”

The snub from regulators came on the same day that they approved Duke’s request to raise household rates by about 9.5% in the next two years and to establish special terms of service for data centers. The new rules provide some protections for average customers, consumer and clean energy advocates believe, but a clean transition tariff would offer more.

“One thing that is clear from the election is that one of the biggest concerns of the public — and of many elected officials — is ensuring that data centers do not impose any energy costs on the ratepayers,” Levitas said. ​“The only way to really do that is to make the data centers pay directly for the generation that they require.”

Duke does have a suite of programs called Green Source Advantage Choice for large business customers that want to contract for their own clean energy in the state, but these programs have largely flopped. Not one large customer has applied for the utility’s ​“resource acceleration option,” which ostensibly speeds up the addition of solar fields to the Duke grid.

Corporations with aggressive clean energy goals say that’s because those carbon-free electrons could have connected to the grid without them. (To verify their sustainability claims, they need to show they aren’t simply paying for renewables Duke is already developing.)

“There isn’t really a viable pathway that works for a majority of these large loads that are coming to this state, for them to be able to credibly say, ​‘We’re coming to your community. We are bringing this clean energy,’” Katie Southworth, a deputy director at CEBA, explained in a recent webinar.

While no party has outright objected to a clean transition tariff, the state-sanctioned customer advocate, Public Staff, has expressed doubts. Those include the difficulty of designing such a program and ensuring that average customers don’t end up footing the bill for expensive solar projects. In last week’s order, the commission reiterated those critiques at length.

But similar challenges have been overcome in other vertically integrated markets. Google helped enact a clean transition tariff in Nevada and is pursuing ones in Indiana and Minnesota. Georgia Power has a ​“customer identified resource” program that allows large customers to work with developers to propose and pay for new solar projects.

Commissioner Floyd McKissick, a Democrat who’s served on the panel since 2019, told Canary Media, ​“I’m optimistic that Duke and the stakeholders will be able to craft a proposal that will receive serious consideration by the commission.” He added: ​“Obviously, Green Source Advantage has not worked.”

The midterm elections have also led to renewed optimism that state lawmakers could simply require a clean tariff outright.

After more than a decade in the minority, Democrats will control the state House of Representatives next year and be one seat shy of a majority in the state Senate. Meanwhile, Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, has created a bipartisan energy-policy task force that is expected to issue a set of proposals in February.

“There’s a high likelihood that it will make recommendations regarding a voluntary customer program or clean transition tariff or bring your own generation,” said Levitas, who serves on the task force with advocates, legislators, and other experts. ​“So, I wouldn’t be at all surprised if we see legislation introduced on this subject in the session next year.”

text:
EIB backs construction in Romania of plant for manufacturing high-performance composite materials through €20 million in financing for Swiss cleantech Bcomp.

Support by EIB also covers Bcomp research and development in Switzerland.

Backed by InvestEU programme, financing in form of venture debt to help spur alternatives to conventional carbon fibre, glass fibre and plastics for range of industrial uses.

The European Investment Bank (EIB) is providing €20 million in financing to Swiss cleantech company Bcomp to increase production of high-performance composite materials. The financing will support construction of a high-volume manufacturing plant in the Romanian city of Timișoara and continued research and development in Fribourg, Switzerland.

Bcomp develops composite materials based primarily on flax fibres instead of conventional carbon fibre, glass fibre and plastics. The company’s materials, which offer a significant lower environmental footprint, are designed for use in a range of industries including automotive, motorsport, and recreational equipment.

The EIB backing for Bcomp takes the form of €20 million in venture debt, supporting the company’s €47.6 million investment programme to expand manufacturing capacity in Romania and further develop its R&D activities in Switzerland.

“Europe needs to turn technological innovation into industrial production if we are to strengthen our competitiveness and accelerate the green transition,” said EIB Vice-President Ioannis Tsakiris. “By supporting Bcomp in Romania and Switzerland, we are helping European innovation reach industrial scale and unlock new opportunities for sustainable growth.”

Bcomp, whose main manufacturing and development facilities are located in Fribourg, plans to carry out its investment project between 2027 and 2030.

As a result, the company expects to significantly expand its workforce through 2030, with the Timișoara plant in Romania’s western region of Vest representing a key driver of future employment growth. Around 61% of Bcomp’s planned investment will take place in Vest, supporting regional development and economic cohesion in the European Union.

"Scaling up our natural fibre composites production is an important step towards making these materials available to more manufacturers and applications, while supporting the EU’s transition towards a circular economy," said Christian Fischer, Bcomp Chief Executive Officer. "The EIB's support will allow us to expand production and continue investing in R&D, strengthening our ability to serve industrial customers and accelerating the adoption of our high-performance natural fibre materials.”

Innovative companies often face hurdles securing the risk capital needed to scale up, particularly when investing in new technologies and production capacity. Backed by the EU’s InvestEU programme, the EIB financing for Bcomp addresses this funding gap while providing a strong signal to the market that could help the company attract further financing as it grows.

The operation contributes to the EIB Group’s TechEU programme and advances EU policy goals in the areas of innovation, climate action and the bioeconomy.

Background information

EIB Group

The European Investment Bank (ElB) Group is the financing arm of the European Union, owned by the 27 Member States, and one of the largest multilateral development banks in the world. In 2025, the EIB Group signed €100 billion of new financing and advisory services for over 870 high-impact projects in eight core priorities that support EU policy objectives: climate action and the environment, digitalisation and technological innovation, security and defence, territorial cohesion, agriculture and the bioeconomy, social infrastructure, strong global partnerships and the savings and investment union. Beyond long-term loans for large infrastructure, the EIB Group crowds in private investment for high-risk innovative projects and businesses, with a growing role in Europe’s markets for venture debt, venture capital, guarantees and securitisations.

The European Investment Fund (EIF) is the subsidiary of the EIB Group specialised in providing guarantees, securitisation and equity to improve access to finance for small and medium-sized businesses and startups across Europe. Acting as an anchor investor, through its extensive network of partnering banks and investment funds, the EIF mobilises private investment and nurtures the ecosystem of venture capital funds to support innovative European entrepreneurs.

With the support of all 27 EU governments, the EIF has joined forces with institutional investors in a pan-European alliance to mobilise up to €80 billion for investment into innovative companies scaling up to become global leaders. The joint effort will expand the size and scope of the highly successful European Tech Champions Initiative, which has helped create 15 European mega-funds and scale 45 companies, including 16 unicorns, since being established three years ago.

High-quality, up-to-date photos of the EIB Group’s headquarters for media use are available here.

The InvestEU programme provides the European Union with crucial long-term funding by leveraging substantial private and public funds in support of a sustainable economy. It helps generate additional investment in line with EU policy priorities, including technological transformation, strategic investment, innovation, resilience, long-term competitiveness, and support for small and medium-sized enterprises InvestEU brings all EU financial instruments together under one roof, making funding for investment projects in Europe simpler, more efficient, and more flexible. The programme consists of three components: the InvestEU Fund, the InvestEU Advisory Hub, and the InvestEU Portal. The InvestEU Fund is implemented through financial partners who invest in projects using the EU budget guarantee of €26.2 billion. This guarantee increases their risk-bearing capacity, thus mobilising at least €372 billion in additional investment. With top-ups from the Member State compartment and several EU initiatives, it has already mobilised €400 billion in public and private capital across the key priority sectors.

About Bcomp

Bcomp is a Swiss cleantech company and global leader in high-performance bio-based materials. Its proprietary natural fibre-based reinforcement materials — ampliTex™ and powerRibs™ — help decarbonise manufacturing and reduce environmental impacts while enabling lightweight performance, extensive design freedom and plug-and-play integration into existing processes in a wide range of high-performance applications. From concept through to industrial manufacturing, Bcomp’s team offers global hands-on engineering and design support out of its headquarters in Fribourg, Switzerland and through its presence across Europe, Asia and North America
