text:
A working group of business leaders, state-agency heads and environmental organizations offered recommendations Monday for how Colorado can speed permitting for emissions-reducing projects and ensure buildout of transmission lines needed to power the grid.

The report from the Environment and Sustainability Working Group, formed after Gov. Jared Polis directed agency heads in April to work with each other and key stakeholders to reduce barriers to emissions reductions and electrification, is the result of seven months of work. It proffers 15 potential solutions for existing logjams in those two areas, calling in each case for state and local governments and businesses to work together to create more efficiency and consistency in permitting while simultaneously cleaning Colorado’s air.

While Polis formally received the recommendations, the report is largely aimed at Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, who ran on promises to improve the state’s environment and to reform cumbersome regulations. The suggestions in the report aim to hit both of those marks, offering businesses the regulatory certainty they feel has been lacking after years of new environmental laws while also aiming the proposed reform at bringing cleaner energy and industrial projects online.

“Colorado businesses need and want to be part of the solution when it comes to protecting our environment and building a more sustainable future,” said Loren Furman, president/CEO of the Colorado Chamber of Commerce, which worked closely with Polis’ office on the formation of the group following the convening of business task force on the subject and then gathered the business leaders who participated in the group. “This report demonstrates that we can advance our climate goals while also making Colorado a highly competitive place to do business.”

Report focuses on two kinds of permitting

The report — compiled by the Keystone Policy Center, which served as a facilitator for the working group — notes the current challenges to the dual goals of reducing emissions while giving businesses a predictable atmosphere in which they can flourish. State permitting processes can be lengthy, unpredictable and confusing, while the process for laying transmission lines that are needed to electrify hard-to-decarbonize sectors is siloed and leaves Colorado at risk of having inadequate transmission capacity.

Working group members dug into both subjects and divided the report into two sections, offering numerous pathways forward to reform permitting. The recommendations did not receive votes like some other governor-appointed commissions have taken but represent a general consensus of big-picture ideas coming from the discussions.

Regarding permitting, for example, the group recommended boosting transparency of a system in which major air-quality projects now take an average of roughly two years to get permits, according to state figures. This could be done first by creating a publicly accessible permit-tracking system in which applicants, community groups and state leaders can see where permits are in the consideration process and can learn where the pinch points are and how to address them, the group suggested.

Recommendations for special portal, permitting simplification

The group also recommended building off an August executive order by Polis that created a pilot project in which semiconductor-industry projects are coordinated through a special portal to coordinate among agencies and move the permitting process more quickly. That same structure could be copied for air-quality-permit applicants who specifically are seeking permission to install equipment that will reduce emissions from industrial and other facilities statewide, the group said.

Many of the permitting recommendations revolved around boosting communications between applicants and permit reviewers. The state could establish dedicated times for applicants to speak with reviewers to clear up questions that could be holding up a project. The state could require the use of standardized permit templates developed with permit applicants. And Colorado could publish expected timelines for permitting processes that currently do not have established timelines.

And in some cases, the state should consider new approaches to make permitting more efficient, the group recommended. For example, when a business seeks to add or modify equipment in a way that could lead to emissions reductions, regulators should verify emissions from that equipment — but not from other equipment in a facility that will not be modified and already has gone through state review. This could speed permitting.

Wide range of interests participated

“I think the most valuable thing about this group was that it happened at all. Everyone recognized that there were real challenges in the permitting space — not just for oil and gas but for the transmission space as well,” said Ryan Steadley, vice president of regulatory affairs at the Colorado Oil & Gas Association, who served as working-group member. “The fact that there was a recognition from the Polis administration that this needed to be addressed, I think is very encouraging. I hope the Weiser administration will take a look at this as well.”

In addition to oil and gas, sectors represented by business leaders included utilities, manufacturing, waste management, commercial buildings and general business groups. Participating state agencies included the Department of Public Health and Environment, Colorado Energy Office, Department of Natural Resources, Public Utilities Commission, Office of Economic Development and International Trade and Department of Local Affairs. Representatives from The Nature Conservancy, Rocky Mountain Institute and Clean Air Task Force represented environmental viewpoints. And Colorado Counties Inc. and the group Counties & Commissioners Acting Together offered local-government viewpoints on transmission issues.

On transmission issues, many of the proposed solutions looked at establishing clearer guidance between governments and the companies looking to build transmission lines. One recommendation, for example, was for the Colorado Department of Transportation, State Land Board and Colorado Parks & Wildlife to offer guidance upfront on what applicants must do to establish rights-of-way on state land, so that applications can address that on submittal.

Transmission permitting became a discussion

Several recommendations seek to improve intergovernmental cooperation. One suggests the state work with local governments to develop guidance and resources that can be offered to counties on best practices for local siting and permitting processes. Another asks the state to look at dedicating a project manager to coordinate between state, local and federal governments on transmission-buildout applications.

Some of the recommendations involve looking at new ways to undertake projects or resolve progress-halting disputes. One encourages the state to look for alternative development structures when new partners want to work with incumbent utilities to build transmission lines. Another suggests that the state, working with the land-trust community, should look at how conservation-easement holders could consider modifications regarding transmission development across easements without going to court.

Finally, some of the recommendations involve the state taking a more proactive role in ensuring buildout of transmission lines. One, for example, asks the governor to encourage the PUC, which has the final say on proposed transmission projects, to streamline often lengthy approval processes and to consider the long-term needs for increased transmission as much as members consider the short-term costs that added transmission could bring to utility customers.

Steadley noted that while transmission-permitting reform often doesn’t get as much attention as air-quality permitting reform, which the state has been working on for several years now, it is an equally vital part of industrial companies reducing emissions. One of his members inquired with a local utility about running a transmission line out to an active facility in a rural area and was told it likely would take about 20 years to do so and cost the customer about $40 million.

More talks requested

“The ability to more efficiently permit the critical infrastructure is part of the equation,” Steadley said. “There’s a lot of threads to pull on in this Gordian knot.”

Lastly, the working group recommended the next governor, working with more business and environmental stakeholders, continue the working group in 2027 to maintain a forum that brings diverse perspectives together for productive discussion on these issues.

Polis, in a statement, thanked the Colorado Chamber and all the participants in the group for collaborating on recommendations that can both grow the economy and protect the environment.

“Colorado is a national leader in clean energy, and we are building on that success by finding new ways to reduce emissions, protect our environment and create good-paying jobs,” the governor said. “By cutting red tape and speeding up permitting for efforts that reduce emissions, we are unlocking new investments that strengthen our economy.”

Waga Energy has agreed to build a renewable natural gas (RNG) production unit at Randolph Farms Landfill in Modoc, Indiana. The project is a partnership with Randolph Farms and Best Way Disposal, both part of family-owned The Balkema Companies.

It is the second project between Waga Energy and The Balkema Companies. The first, the Decatur Hills RNG Facility in Greensburg, Indiana, was commissioned in August 2026.

Waga Energy will finance, build, own and operate the facility for at least 20 years, and will share the revenue from RNG sales with Randolph Farms. Randolph Farms will manage the landfill gas collection system and support the civil works.

The unit will use Waga Energy's patented WAGABOX technology. At full capacity it will process up to 3,200 m³/h of raw biogas and produce up to 120GWh of RNG a year. Commissioning is scheduled for early 2028.

The WAGABOX will replace the existing landfill gas upgrading system at Randolph Farms, which currently produces RNG for Best Way Disposal's onsite fuelling station. Output from the new unit will instead be injected into a nearby interstate pipeline and supplied to natural gas markets, including transport fuel.

By displacing fossil natural gas, the facility is expected to avoid around 31,700 tons of CO₂ equivalent a year, roughly equal to the emissions from burning 2.8 million gallons of diesel. Randolph Farms has many years of disposal capacity remaining, giving the project a long-term supply of landfill gas.

The WAGABOX uses cryogenic separation to upgrade landfill gas into high-quality RNG that can be injected straight into gas grids, whatever the composition of the biogas.

"Landfill gas is a natural byproduct of our operations, and this project allows us to turn that resource into something valuable rather than letting it go to waste," said Jessica Routley, CEO of The Balkema Companies. "We've had a successful partnership with Waga Energy at Decatur Hills, and we're pleased to build on that relationship at Randolph Farms."

Guénaël Prince, CEO of Waga Energy Inc., said: "This second facility strengthens our footprint in Indiana, where we are creating a true renewable energy hub."

description:
Abundant daytime solar energy displaces higher-cost forms of power generation during daylight hours.
Obviously, this is disruptive, meaning simply that the owner of a particular type of power generation suddenly finds its assets impaired, or as we call it, stranded.
In the near to intermediate term, it will coexist happily with renewable technologies because of continuing growth in power demand.
First, the rapid increase in gas generation build-out adds many large businesses like data centers to the domestic market.
However, high levels of electricity demand in the US and elsewhere will obscure this trend—until they don't.
text:
Perhaps you have heard about the daily "duck curve" in electricity markets. Abundant daytime solar energy displaces higher-cost forms of power generation during daylight hours. It creates a price chart for power that resembles the belly and neck of a duck. In the old days,, as the sun went down, gas-fired turbines (CTs) were called upon to provide power for shoulder periods of daily electricity demand when power needs were still elevated. albeit trending down. What's changed? A few electricity markets with extensive solar and battery penetration, like California, are using their gas-fired CTs a lot less, because they are being displaced by cheaper electricity from batteries. Said differently, in wholesale power markets, batteries are underpricing gas-fired generation.

Obviously, this is disruptive, meaning simply that the owner of a particular type of power generation suddenly finds its assets impaired, or as we call it, stranded. Many recent articles have focused on the unrelenting downward cost of solar, onshore wind, and batteries. This is all true. But will it be disruptive? One way to tell is by looking at changes in capital investment. No utility executive wants to lose money on a new big power plant or transmission line. According to the EIA, the US will add 86 GW of capacity in 2026, 89% of which will be solar and battery, and only 7% gas-fired. (The 2025 additions were similar in terms of fuel mix.)

We are seeing a big upswing in demand for electricity. AI just turbocharged it. Looking at those projections, one might conclude that gas is being displaced by renewables, but we sure can't see it. Gas-fueled electricity production has held steady. It simply doesn't appear to matter that renewables provide cheaper energy, at least for now. Our best analogy is telegraph (a legacy technology) vs telephone (disruptive technology) in the early twentieth century. Everyone knows how the story ends. But few remember that these two competing technologies co-existed happily for several decades because there was adequate demand and revenue for both. And then the former simply went away. (The same happened with gas lighting, which co-existed with electric lighting for decades before expiring.) And that's our best guess for fossil-fired generation. In the near to intermediate term, it will coexist happily with renewable technologies because of continuing growth in power demand.

Related: What Is Trump Up To Bombing Iran's Qeshm Island?

But this is not to say there will be no revenue disruption at all for utilities, just that people are looking for it in the wrong place, in the big power generating assets. Potential disruption could come from three sources.

First, the rapid increase in gas generation build-out adds many large businesses like data centers to the domestic market. This increased demand will inevitably add upward pressure on gas prices. Also, if the US continues to export increasing quantities of LNG such that it becomes priced on a world market like oil, that too would add another level of unattractive price volatility. Both trends bear watching.

Second, there is potential for disruption in the utility asset class that is considered the lowest risk: transmission and distribution. Distributed power generation, making and storing power closer to its demand source, could change everything. Essentially, this means shrinking the number of "poles and wires". Power is produced at the customer's home or office with renewables (solar and batteries) and propane backup.

Western Power, serving southwest Australia including the city of Perth, has in its rural areas one of the lowest customer densities in the country, about 13 customers per kilometer. This customer profile resembles those of many rural co-ops in the US. Abandoning poles and wires and providing electric service to customers in the above-mentioned fashion. In remote rural areas, the economic benefits are obvious. A few relatively small revenue-generating customers per mile of distribution system is a money loser for utilities anywhere in the world. If this trend accelerates, and we believe it will, this suggests that rural electric co-ops and the like could be the first to be impacted by increased renewables penetration.

But Western Power noted on its website that over three years, its distributed microgrids had avoided 189 hours of customer outages; that's almost 8 days' worth. Comparable data on this is not readily available, but it seems like a lot. The company stated that since most outages were related to malfunctions of poles and wires, eliminating those customer connections and replacing them with fully distributed systems greatly increased reliability and resilience. All this while, the utility itself saved money by reducing expenditures for line maintenance. If the value consumers place on electrical reliability increases, this trend could and likely will accelerate. From a business perspective, rural utilities have far more exposure here than urban utilities. As we've written before, everyone wants electricity. And almost no one cares how they get it. So, who cares if it comes from the grid or not?

The third risk is the one that has received the least attention, which is battery-on-battery competition. If battery technologies continue to improve, which we think is likely, then new, lower-cost batteries will begin to displace older, more expensive or less efficient ones. Competition among new battery technologies looks to us like the videos of fighting robots doing karate and spin kicks. Except in this example, the superior "fighter" will be made of less expensive materials, sodium instead of lithium, for example.

But our point here is broader and potentially more dramatic for utility economics. The impact of batteries is that they are beginning to flatten the daily price curves for electricity. They raise prices during the day as they charge with cheap solar energy. And they lower prices in the evening as they discharge. As electricity price curves flatten, profitability for all power suppliers declines. This, to borrow a phrase, is the future that's already here. Eventually, if this trend continues, only the lowest cost producers survive.

Our severest critics will ask (fairly) why we should care about this. If robust electricity demand is more than likely for the foreseeable future, then almost all energy producers will make some money, even old, coal-fired plants. Our response is simple. Utility assets typically have an operating life between thirty and forty years on average. Right now, energy users, like Anthropic, are still paying for coal-fired power plants to remain open in addition to their huge demand for gas-fired energy. However, despite this huge increase in demand, no coal plant owner that we know of is willing to engage in major capital refurbishments. This is like refusing to maintain a very old car that still runs, saying, "Well, I'll just drive it till it breaks down and then junk it." Eventually this could happen to all fossil-fired power-generating assets. People won't stop using them if they can produce electricity. But they will stop reinvesting new capital. For us that's a key milestone. Renewables plus batteries will continue to undercut fossil-fired alternatives on a price basis. However, high levels of electricity demand in the US and elsewhere will obscure this trend—until they don't.

A $5.5 billion lithium-ion battery operation, scheduled to start operations in a few months, could power Queen Creek’s rise in the advanced-manufacturing sector, say town officials.

South Korea-based LG Energy Solution (LGES) has been hiring as it ramps up for a mid-to-late first-quarter 2027 opening, according to company officials.

It has hired more than 300 workers for what will become a 1,500-employee workforce at full capacity.

The LGES complex is located along the State Route 24 corridor in Queen Creek’s northern tier, east of Ironwood Road between Germann and Pecos roads on former State Trust land.

“Landing a project of that magnitude – an international company with a multibillion-dollar investment – shows other employers that Queen Creek is a viable location with available land and an outstanding workforce,” said Doreen Cott, Queen Creek economic development director.

“It has solidified our place in the industrial, advanced-manufacturing world.”

Queen Creek is talking with LGES suppliers about locating in town.

“We’ve been actively working with several other companies, putting projects in the pipeline for us,” Cott said, adding she hopes to make announcements soon about some of those support businesses coming to town.

The freeway access provided by State Route 24 has been key to recruitment efforts, Cott said.

title: The next energy chapter is being written here
description:
There was a time when the Middle East’s role in the global energy system was relatively easy to define.
The Gulf, in particular, remains a pillar of global energy security.
For the Gulf, where energy infrastructure supports both domestic economies and global energy flows, protecting those assets and keeping the wider system functioning is an essential part of the investment equation.
Today, it is building an energy system for a different era, one that needs more electricity, a more diverse energy mix and the resilience to withstand a world that can change quickly.
The next energy chapter being written here is largely driven by pragmatism, speed and execution, and we are proud to help shape it.
text:
There was a time when the Middle East’s role in the global energy system was relatively easy to define. The region had resources the world needed, and its importance was measured largely by how reliably it could supply them.

That is no longer the full story.

When the energy world meets in Abu Dhabi for ADIPEC this year, it does so at a crucial moment for the region. The Gulf, in particular, remains a pillar of global energy security. At the same time, it is building something worth watching: more complex power systems, new industries and new sources of economic growth.

What makes this transformation globally relevant is not simply its scale, but the fact that the region must solve several energy challenges at once: meeting rapidly rising demand, diversifying the generation mix, and building systems capable of operating through disruption. The latter proved of utmost relevance this year.

Electricity demand is moving firmly in one direction. Current estimates point to global electricity consumption growing by 3.6% in 2026 and a further 3.8% in 2027. Artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, desalination, expanding cities and economic diversification are all adding momentum.

The UAE captures many of these forces in one place. It has raised its target for clean energy, including nuclear and renewables, to 35% by 2030–2031. New generation, grids, and storage are being developed simultaneously to support an economy with much greater electricity needs.

At the same time, events this year have been a reminder of how important the security of the region’s energy infrastructure remains. Physical and cyber threats can put critical assets under pressure with little warning. For the Gulf, where energy infrastructure supports both domestic economies and global energy flows, protecting those assets and keeping the wider system functioning is an essential part of the investment equation.

That gives resilience a very practical meaning here. It starts with protecting critical assets against physical and cyber threats. But it also means designing a power system with enough flexibility to absorb disruption, and having the people, parts and repair capabilities nearby to restore equipment quickly when something does go wrong.

This becomes even more important as the region’s power system grows more diverse.

Solar can provide abundant low-emission electricity. Nuclear offers stable generation. Storage can shift power across hours. Stronger grids move electricity to where it is needed. Gas-fired generation provides dispatchable power when demand changes, or renewable output fluctuates. The strength of the system comes from how these elements work together and how quickly they can respond when circumstances change.

We can already see that approach taking shape across the region.

Taweelah C in Abu Dhabi will add 2.6 GW of dispatchable capacity, designed to strengthen grid stability and support the integration of more renewable energy. The planned Al Zawra plant in Ajman will add further flexible capacity to support future demand. In Oman, the Misfah and Duqm combined-cycle power plants will together provide nearly 2.6 GW, increasing the country’s electricity capacity by almost 20%. Siemens Energy is supplying turbines and power generation technology for each project, giving us a close view of how quickly these requirements are translating into real investment.

These projects are part of a broader shift. Renewable capacity is expanding rapidly, while investment in dispatchable generation is continuing alongside it. This is not a contradiction. It reflects the reality of building a power system that must manage higher demand in a less predictable operating environment.

The same logic applies to the region’s existing energy infrastructure.

A substantial installed energy base will remain critical for years to come. And a turbine that needs repair cannot support the system while waiting for expertise, tools or parts to arrive from another continent. Local repair facilities, spare parts, field service teams and engineering expertise can shorten response times and reduce exposure to disruptions in global supply chains.

That is why localisation has become so central to the region’s energy ambitions. It creates skills, industrial capability and economic value, but its importance goes further. The more capability that exists close to where energy is produced, the better the ability to maintain, repair, and restore critical infrastructure when it is needed most. Local capability is no longer an industrial advantage; it is part of energy resilience.

For Siemens Energy, that changes what partnership means. Technology matters, but resilience cannot simply be shipped in when it is needed. It has to be built into the system through local service capabilities, skilled people, long-term support for critical assets and technology that can adapt as the energy system evolves.

The Middle East has spent decades helping power the global economy. Today, it is building an energy system for a different era, one that needs more electricity, a more diverse energy mix and the resilience to withstand a world that can change quickly.

The next energy chapter being written here is largely driven by pragmatism, speed and execution, and we are proud to help shape it.

text:
Australia has the natural resources and know-how to create a thriving battery manufacturing industry but is missing opportunities by exporting critical minerals rather than turning them into high-value products.

Scientists from the CSIRO issued the warning at an event on Tuesday, also recommending more international partnerships and a greater focus on manufacturing individual components rather than trying to make entire batteries.

The call comes as Australians embrace battery technology, with more than 600,000 home batteries installed under a federal scheme since July 2025 and rapid electric vehicle sales since March.

Speaking at an event called Australia’s Battery Opportunity, CSIRO mineral resources principal research scientist Joanne Loh said the nation had enviable access to valuable raw materials.

“We have all the minerals needed for batteries, specifically lithium-ion batteries – we’re the number one producer in terms of lithium… we have nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper, graphite, you name it,” she said.

“However, we export all of these as raw materials overseas so even though we might have it, we’re actually sending it overseas for processing, then importing them back as batteries.”

The nation also shredded batteries at the end of their lives and exported the materials, Dr Loh said, rather than using them.

Australia had also stopped manufacturing elements that could be used in batteries, such as aluminium foil, CSIRO senior research engineer Geoff de Looze said.

The nation could re-establish that facility, he said, and target the local production of key components like aluminium casings and copper foil.

“We do have some gaps in Australia’s capability so when we look at them we need to rank them and work out which ones we can take on and which ones we want to leave alone,” Mr de Looze said.

“Any of the manufactured parts going into batteries, Australia can take on.”

A CSIRO report released early in November found Australia could use its expertise in manufacturing aluminium aerosol cans to produce battery casings, for example, or manufacture copper foil from scrap wire.

Identifying gaps in the global battery supply chain could allow Australian companies to partner with larger manufacturing firms from the region, CSIRO senior principal research scientist Adam Best said, rather than competing with an established industry.

“We need to work closely with our partners in Asia, Pacific, North America, Europe, to find where we fit in this middle part such that we can do… that manufacturing, that value-adding, to capture more value from our resources,” he said.

“Then Australia does have a brighter future that can lead to a future with energy security.”

“On the whole, this bill is an important step forward,” said Sen. Ruben Gallego, who was one of 14 Democrats to vote for BAAJA last week, helping the bill pass the Senate.

It could also quicken the construction of new ICE detention centers.

Opponents, including tribal leaders and conservation groups, who have criticized the legislation’s potential environmental impacts, describe the 500-page bill as “rushed” and say it undermines tribal sovereignty. Tohono O’odham Chairman Verlon Jose has called on Congress to hold public hearings on the bill “to better understand its impacts.”

If the bill passes, it would alter the National Environmental Protection Act – a decades-old law that’s been used in recent months to stall the construction of new ICE detention centers.

Earlier this year, for instance, Attorney General Kris Mayes sued the federal government over its planned facility in Surprise, Arizona – a move that forced the Department of Homeland Security to conduct an environmental assessment of the facility before it became operational. (DHS recently completed its draft environmental assessment of the Surprise facility, though the agency is now in the midst of a 30-day public comment period.) Attorneys general in other states, including Maryland and New Jersey, have also wielded NEPA in an attempt to halt the development of new ICE facilities.

Passing BAAJA, critics argue, would destroy that line of defense.

“The consequences are serious. We're talking about a detention system where people are dying in custody, facing medical neglect, and suffering abuse,” Congresswoman Adelita Grijalva said in a statement last week.

The law would place a 150-day statute of limitations for plaintiffs to file a lawsuit against a project that may have violated NEPA. What’s more, it would become significantly more difficult for a federal judge to order a stop to such a project, according to an analysis from the watchdog group Project Salt Box.

“It would severely limit the ability of courts to block unlawful projects, making it much harder for communities to hold ICE accountable,” said Illinois Congresswoman Delia Ramirez in a joint statement with Grijalva.

text:
Australia has the natural resources and know-how to create a thriving battery manufacturing industry but is missing opportunities by exporting critical minerals rather than turning them into high-value products.

Scientists from the CSIRO issued the warning at an event on Tuesday, also recommending more international partnerships and a greater focus on manufacturing individual components rather than trying to make entire batteries.

The call comes as Australians embrace battery technology, with more than 600,000 home batteries installed under a federal scheme since July 2025 and rapid electric vehicle sales since March.

Speaking at an event called Australia’s Battery Opportunity, CSIRO mineral resources principal research scientist Joanne Loh said the nation had enviable access to valuable raw materials.

“We have all the minerals needed for batteries, specifically lithium-ion batteries – we’re the number one producer in terms of lithium… we have nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper, graphite, you name it,” she said.

“However, we export all of these as raw materials overseas so even though we might have it, we’re actually sending it overseas for processing, then importing them back as batteries.”

The nation also shredded batteries at the end of their lives and exported the materials, Dr Loh said, rather than using them.

Australia had also stopped manufacturing elements that could be used in batteries, such as aluminium foil, CSIRO senior research engineer Geoff de Looze said.

The nation could re-establish that facility, he said, and target the local production of key components like aluminium casings and copper foil.

“We do have some gaps in Australia’s capability so when we look at them we need to rank them and work out which ones we can take on and which ones we want to leave alone,” Mr de Looze said.

“Any of the manufactured parts going into batteries, Australia can take on.”

A CSIRO report released early in November found Australia could use its expertise in manufacturing aluminium aerosol cans to produce battery casings, for example, or manufacture copper foil from scrap wire.

Identifying gaps in the global battery supply chain could allow Australian companies to partner with larger manufacturing firms from the region, CSIRO senior principal research scientist Adam Best said, rather than competing with an established industry.

“We need to work closely with our partners in Asia, Pacific, North America, Europe, to find where we fit in this middle part such that we can do… that manufacturing, that value-adding, to capture more value from our resources,” he said.

“Then Australia does have a brighter future that can lead to a future with energy security.”

AAP

description:

Start of the Tender: Charging Infrastructure at Managed Rest Areas With the truck rapid charging network on highways, the government is creating an efficient basic supply along the main routes of freight traffic.

In addition, the discussion covers flexible grid connection contracts for infrastructure development and the question of how networking charging infrastructure in depots can provide the sector with additional charging opportunities alongside publicly accessible charging infrastructure.
text:
The tender for charging infrastructure at managed rest areas has been launched by the Autobahn GmbH des Bundes with a competitive bidding process. This means that this infrastructure project, which is crucial for the transformation of the transportation sector, is entering the next phase. At the 4th BMV Conference on Climate-Friendly Commercial Vehicles in Berlin, the focus is also on the results of this year's Cleanroom Talks and numerous practical insights. Representatives from politics, the commercial vehicle industry, logistics, associations, and research are discussing perspectives, framework conditions, and measures for the ramp-up of climate-friendly commercial vehicles in Germany and Europe at the 4th BMV Conference on Climate-Friendly Commercial Vehicles in Berlin.

Start of the Tender: Charging Infrastructure at Managed Rest Areas

With the truck rapid charging network on highways, the government is creating an efficient basic supply along the main routes of freight traffic. Today, the tender for 227 managed rest areas begins: The Autobahn GmbH, on behalf of the government, is awarding contracts for the planning, construction, and operation of truck rapid charging infrastructure in five lots as part of a competitive bidding process – each lot includes larger and smaller locations at managed rest areas. The layout of the lots ensures a balanced distribution of the e-truck rapid charging infrastructure throughout the country. The contracts for the 124 locations at unmanaged rest areas were already awarded in the summer and are now in the implementation phase.

"The number of climate-friendly commercial vehicles is growing, and the industry is determinedly making the switch. We are shaping the necessary framework conditions: With the extension of the toll exemption and the amendment of the GHG quota trade, we are setting long-term incentives for the switch to climate-friendly commercial vehicles," stated Federal Minister of Transport Steffen Bilger (CDU).

The government will support the development of a comprehensive charging infrastructure for electric trucks at rest areas along the highways, in depots, in commercial areas, at truck stops, and at logistics hubs over the next few years with several billion euros from the Climate and Transformation Fund. This aims to advance the transformation of road freight transport and bring more climate protection onto the road, Bilger further stated. In addition, the promotion for the establishment of hydrogen refueling infrastructure on the main routes is further accelerating the ramp-up of another future-proof technology on the way to climate-friendly road freight transport, Bilger added.

Michael Güntner, Chairman of the Management Board of Autobahn GmbH, sees managed rest areas as important points of contact for heavy freight traffic on our highways. In his view, the development of the truck fast-charging infrastructure depends not only on the installation of the charging facilities but also on reliable operation in everyday life. The different structural and operational requirements of the rest areas must be considered. By tendering, the foundation is laid to drive the development forward in a targeted manner and to create reliable charging opportunities for freight transport.

“Climate-friendly heavy commercial vehicles are mature and have proven themselves in everyday use. The question is no longer if, but when they will replace the old diesel engines," explains Dagmar Fehler, CEO and spokesperson for NOW GmbH.

She referred to the so-called Cleanroom reports of the years 2022, 2024, and 2026, which would clearly show the major leaps in development. According to the manufacturers' assessment, battery trucks will be competitive with diesel trucks by 2030 in many applications when considering total costs, and they will replace diesel as the dominant power source by 2035. It is now crucial to swiftly expand the charging infrastructure and establish reliable economic conditions to accelerate market ramp-up. NOW evaluates the exchange on behalf of the Federal Ministry of Transport (BMV) to detect bottlenecks early on and to develop solutions together with the federal government and the industry.

Technology change is coming, battery-electric trucks the most profitable option

The "Cleanroom Report" from the BMV mainly contains planned sales figures from manufacturers in the coming years as well as the underlying strategic orientations. It is being published for the third time. This year's forecasts show: the ramp-up of zero-emission trucks is happening, but slower than manufacturers predicted in the 2024 survey. According to manufacturers, battery-electric trucks will account for around 50 percent of new registrations in Germany by 2035, thus replacing diesel trucks as the dominant drive. Fuel cells, hydrogen internal combustion engines, and biogas will complement battery-electric trucks, and the series launch of hydrogen-based drives is therefore postponed to 2029 or later.

Profitability already under certain conditions

The profitability of electric trucks is already given today under certain conditions and with appropriate mileage. A majority of manufacturers expect that battery-electric trucks can achieve total cost parity with diesel trucks for all applications by 2030. As a key requirement, manufacturers cite the rapid expansion of public charging and fueling infrastructure as well as support for building depot charging infrastructure. At the same time, European manufacturers take competitors from China very seriously and demand equal competitive conditions.

Impulses from Practice

Examples from practice at the conference demonstrate how the switch to electric trucks can be economically viable today. Logistics companies, manufacturers, and energy providers report on how the transition to climate-friendly commercial vehicles can be successful, how energy can become a new business field for logistics companies, and how shippers can create charging infrastructure for their transport service providers. In addition, the discussion covers flexible grid connection contracts for infrastructure development and the question of how networking charging infrastructure in depots can provide the sector with additional charging opportunities alongside publicly accessible charging infrastructure. The test projects Hola and BELLE report on current insights from the practical test. Regarding hydrogen refueling infrastructure for trucks, the BMV and the participants draw conclusions from the funding.

SwitchCHECK: Is the switch to electric trucks worthwhile?

With SwitchCHECK, the National Charging Infrastructure Steering Office provides transport companies with a free digital calculator that allows them to determine, using their own figures or industry-standard benchmarks, when the switch to electric trucks becomes worthwhile and which factors make the difference. For depot charging, the check provides an assessment of power requirements and anticipated investment costs. The SwitchCHECK was developed in collaboration with the logistics industry.

text:
The Senate passed a bill to encourage energy production and job creation, but environmental groups are concerned about how it will do so.

“We support building clean energy and housing faster. We don’t support giving up the public’s voice on public lands to do it," said Stacey Wittek, Executive Director, Conserve Southwest Utah. “This bill gets transmission right, but the fine print would lock in projects on Utah’s public lands before the public has a fair chance to weigh in.”

The bill — Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) — is co-sponsored by Utah Sen. Mike Lee. It passed the Senate 62-33 and has not yet been voted on by the House. It could increase energy production, create jobs, and lower energy costs by accelerating project approval processes.

MORE: Kalshi pauses Utah operations amid legal fight over gambling laws

Jessica Wiarda, a member of the Hopi-Tewa Tribe and an Indigenous educator, said speeding up development could harm tribal communities and their lands. Her tribe has lived on its land for 1,000 years, but she feels lawmakers do not seek tribal input about what should happen there.

“Colonization is still happening today,” Wiarda said. “The soul of the land is at stake, and speeding things up has never gone well for us as tribes. It really breaks my heart because I have to articulate my humanity every day to representatives that have bare minimum knowledge of what we actually go through."

Wiarda said tribes support portions of the bill, including building green energy, but questioned what costs could come with accelerating development.

“Our tribes do need the parts of the bill that are good,” she said. “Yes, we do need to build green energy. That’s not a problem, necessarily. The main issue is, what are the costs that they are literally going to remove to get to progress?”

Steve Bloch, legal director with the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, said laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act and National Historic Preservation Act require federal agencies to share information about proposed projects and conduct environmental or cultural resource analyses before acting.

BAAJA “turns that on its head,” he said.

Among the concerns raised about the bill are that it would shorten and simplify environmental reviews, reduce the time available to file legal challenges, and limit the ability to halt projects before construction begins.

Bloch said he worries agencies could feel less incentive to follow environmental laws if there is little penalty for violating them.

“I feel like the BAAJA bill is going to be bad for Utah and bad for the places Utahns know and love,” Bloch said. "If it is a data center, if it is a transmission line through your neighborhood, if it's an oil and gas project that has real significant impacts on tribal resources, the project may not have to stop in its tracks and wait until we know what those impacts are and the agency takes steps to address it. Instead, the project may move ahead."

"Once issued, permits would be nearly impossible for future administrations to revisit. These rules apply equally to oil and gas, mining and industrial development on the lands where Utahns hike, ride, hunt and graze," added Wittek. "Speeding up permits is a worthy goal. Making them nearly impossible to revisit, even when the review was done improperly, is not.”

Bloch said the bill has important goals, including creating jobs, supporting renewable energy, and making transmission lines more affordable and predictable. However, he believes those goals could be met while still protecting clean air and water and public lands.

“It’s so buried with all the bad that we don’t think it’s worth the cost,” he said. "There's really not going to be the checks and balances that people expect to be there to make sure the projects are being done in a thoughtful way."

Wiarda said accelerating development could sacrifice the attention to community needs. She said past projects have not hired tribal members and have harmed the landscape.

“Utah really lacks that big picture,” she said. “All they focus on is, ‘What’s the immediate GDP? What’s the dollar sign?’ You might be making more dollars, but there’s only so many dollars we can make before it’s unsustainable. I kind of think we've reached this precipice of like, there's only so much growth Utah can do. Utah can only claim the best in the world economy for so long before we actually run out of resources, and I think we've hit that."

2News reached out to Senator Lee's office but did not receive a response. Key questions include: how lawmakers will ensure Utah's lands and cultural resources will still be protected, how will they ensure future jobs go to locals and tribal nations, and what specific projects — energy development, transmission lines, or data centers — would be built if this passes the House.

Advocates for environmental and tribal rights say they're hoping for a different result for the House.

"We urge Utah’s House delegation to insist this bill be fixed before it becomes law, so that we can build what we need without giving up the public’s voice," Wittek said.

text:
MADISON HEIGHTS, Mich. — As electric bikes and other motorized rides become more popular across Metro Detroit, Madison Heights is putting new rules in place on where and how they can be used.

WATCH here:

Madison Heights approves new rules for e-bikes and e-motos

The Madison Heights City Council unanimously approved a new ordinance Monday night covering e-bikes and e-motos.

“They are and can be very dangerous,” Mayor Corey Haines said.

The ordinance adds safeguards and establishes rules for where the vehicles can be ridden throughout the city.

City Councilman Quinn Wright, who rides an electric scooter himself, said the growing popularity of e-bikes means both riders and drivers are still learning how to safely share the road.

“I think these e-bikes are something we’re all getting used to,” Wright said. “Everyone doesn’t know there are different classes and different categories, and so it’s just something we need to be more mindful of and be more considerate when we’re out on the road.”

Wright said owning an electric bike or scooter comes with a responsibility to operate it safely.

“I think that you can have one, but you have to be safe on it,” Wright said. “I have a helmet, and I try to be responsible in riding it.”

What are the new e-bike rules?

The ordinance establishes age, helmet and speed requirements based on the class of e-bike.

Under the new rules, a Class 3 e-bike cannot be operated by anyone under 14 years old. Riders between the ages of 14 and 18 are required to wear a helmet.

City leaders say education will be an important part of implementing the ordinance.

“What we want to do is we want to educate our parents,” Mayor Haines said. “Educate them on what is safe, what isn’t, what rules need to be followed.”

Mayor Haines says this couldn't have come at a better time.

"The timing is really really good for this. As far as...we’re right here before Black Friday with all the shopping sales and discounts there may be on some of these items. Parents really take a hard look and do some research on their own.”

Violating the city's e-bike ordinance could result in a $100 fine. Violations involving e-motos and mopeds will fall under existing state laws.

Riders hope for coexistence

E-bike rider Ron Ramirez said he is glad the city didn't do an outright ban on e-bikes.

“I just want this to be a coexisting effort,” Ramirez said.

Ramirez said he relies on his e-bike for transportation and tries to follow traffic laws and ride responsibly.

“For some, this is the only transportation,” Ramirez said. “What about the law-abiding ones that abide by the traffic rules and stuff?”

title: After more than 50 extra hours of talks, world climate conference ends without final agreement
description:
The first has to do with a reference to fossil fuels.
And an acknowledgment that poorer countries, with less carbon emissions, suffered the most severe effects of climate change with limited resources to adequately respond.
In a statement, Canada’s Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said COP31 was not what Canada had hoped for but reaffirmed the country’s commitment to the Paris Agreement and the UN’s climate change process.
It will be left to delegates at that conference to pick where COP31 could find no consensus.
Until then, activists here in Canada are urging the federal to look at its own actions to address climate change.
text:
Despite more than 50 hours of additional negotiations, attempts to reach a consensus at COP31 failed on Sunday, ending hopes the annual conference could present a unifying document to rally countries around the world in the fight against climate change.

Aly Hyder Ali is the Senior Program Manager for Oil and Gas with Canada’s Environmental Defence. He attended COP31 in Antalya, Turkiye, and he says he is angered and disappointed by the inability of global leaders to come together on the issue.

“You do expect there to be some consensus and some urgency from these 200 countries that have arrived with the intention of fighting climate change, with the intention of finding solutions,” he said. “With the intention of moving beyond to a world where we’re not struggling with climate change day in and day out.”

How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The failure to come to a final agreement, otherwise known as a cover decision at COP conferences, is being blamed on two issues.

The first has to do with a reference to fossil fuels.

Oil producing countries like Russia and Saudi Arabia successfully lobbied to exclude those words from the final communique, sparking a heated response from many countries, including the 27-member nations of the European Union.

Ireland’s Environment Minister Darragh O’Brien said the omission was “unconscionable.”

“We will not endorse a cover decision or an Atalya pact,” he said, “that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is a key driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time.”

Instead of fossil fuels, the final communique had explicit language on carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which some delegates described as an attempt at greenwashing oil and gas.

“Carbon capture is a false climate solution most of the time globally,” said Mike Morrice, the recently elected leader of Canada’s Green Party. “When it’s been implemented, emissions have actually gone up.”

“All this technology captures,” he said, “is public money for foreign owned oil and gas giants.”

The other issue that divided delegates in Turkiye was the lack of financial commitment to help developing countries deal with climate change.

Back in 2021, during COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, it was agreed that wealthier countries would send billions of dollars to poorer countries to help fund climate adaptations.

It was an acknowledgement that much of the historic climate impacts were the result of industrial activities carried out by richer countries. And an acknowledgment that poorer countries, with less carbon emissions, suffered the most severe effects of climate change with limited resources to adequately respond.

At COP31 in Turkiye, Canada committed $13-billion over five years for climate related support.

But the UN’s goal of raising $1.2 billion for its Climate Adaptation Fund came up very short. Just over $50 million was committed, slightly less than 4.2 per cent of what the UN had hoped.

“It’s just a shame that wealthy countries that are the most responsible for the climate crisis … did not pay what they owe, and did not commit to any stronger actions,” said Hyder Ali.

In a statement, Canada’s Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said COP31 was not what Canada had hoped for but reaffirmed the country’s commitment to the Paris Agreement and the UN’s climate change process.

“We have one year until COP32,” she said. “It is incumbent upon all parties to use that time to reflect on this process and make sure we can achieve tangible outcomes that move us forward and advances the global transition to electrification and net-zero.”

The next UN Climate Conference will be held next year in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

It will be left to delegates at that conference to pick where COP31 could find no consensus.

Until then, activists here in Canada are urging the federal to look at its own actions to address climate change.

“Countries like Canada are expanding fossil fuels domestically, expanding or pushing forward a million barrel a day pipelines, the Pacific Link, or advancing LNG projects, or building carbon capture projects, while on a global stage, demanding other countries do better,” said Hyder Ali. “You can’t have both.”

title: Battery Storage Boom Faces Growing Resistance As Moratoriums Spread - Bisnow
description:
America’s battery storage boom is colliding with the same opposition that has slowed data centers.
A growing number of communities are responding with moratoriums and development restrictions on battery facilities, even though many have no relation to artificial intelligence.
There are 177 BESS moratoriums across the country, according to research from Carina Energy, a battery development firm.
The challenge is that unlike data centers, which often seek tracts of rural land, BESS projects work best closest to users.
Many opponents link their negative feelings to data centers.
text:
America’s battery storage boom is colliding with the same opposition that has slowed data centers. A growing number of communities are responding with moratoriums and development restrictions on battery facilities, even though many have no relation to artificial intelligence.

The pushback comes at a critical moment for battery energy storage systems, or BESS, which are expected to expand rapidly through the end of the decade as utilities, institutions and commercial property owners seek more reliable power.

“This conflation of batteries with data centers is totally unhelpful,” said Marguerite Wells, executive director of the Alliance for Clean Energy New York. “From the public's perspective, all they know is that it's a big facility with no windows and no jobs, and there's energy in there, and it's probably dangerous, and it probably shouldn't happen in my town.”

Misinformation, public fear over fires, and the technology’s association with controversial data center projects are fueling local resistance, threatening delays for projects that many states view as essential to grid reliability and future economic growth.

There are 177 BESS moratoriums across the country, according to research from Carina Energy, a battery development firm. The number is on the rise.

Not all moratoriums become bans. Many are purely meant to give municipalities and local leaders time to better understand the issue. But these pauses can still create costly delays for developers.

The BESS sector has rapidly expanded in recent years, pushed ahead by growing energy needs, an emphasis on energy resiliency, and a 30% tax incentive from the Inflation Reduction Act.

The sector is projected to grow 50% over the next five years, according to Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association. Many installations are meant as backup power sources, including those attached to a variety of commercial real estate sites, like hospitals and factories.

The challenge is that unlike data centers, which often seek tracts of rural land, BESS projects work best closest to users. This brings them closer to residential and commercial areas, which can make neighbors uneasy, Carina Managing Director Malaquias Encarnacion said.

“They're closer to civilization, in a way, and that's why you see some more towns and just propagating these [moratoriums], and it's spreading,” he said.

Many opponents link their negative feelings to data centers. BESS systems can be, but aren’t always, paired with larger data center projects.

Others point to past fires and safety incidents with large-scale battery installations, including the 2019 Surprise, Arizona, fire in which an explosion hurt first responders, and the 2025 Moss Landing fire in the San Francisco Bay Area, which displaced more than 1,200 people.

BESS facilities have a continually improving safety record, due to continued education and new manufacturing codes, according to data collected by the Electric Power Research Institute as part of its system failure incident database.

The number of fire incidents has shrunk 98% since 2018, even as deployment of batteries has rapidly accelerated from a few gigawatts in 2018 to more than 600 GW today, said Lakshmi Srinavasan, EPRI principal team lead and senior tech leader. There hasn’t been a reported injury or fatality from a battery system incident since 2019, according to EPRI.

“These incidents aren't as impactful from a community public perspective,” Srinavasan said. “Really, what you're talking about is property damage and lost revenue from the operation of the system, and not injuries, fatalities or other public impacts.”

But that hasn’t stopped moratoriums or fully eased anxiety in the industry. Wells said the concern level is “very high,” in large part due to siting. It is challenging for battery developers to move their project to a friendlier town, because the most helpful, valuable places to put battery storage are densely populated places with tight grids.

“The business case for batteries tends to be where people live,” she said.

New York has seen one of the biggest expansions of the BESS industry, due in part to state clean energy mandates. In September, New York approved eight projects totaling 950 megawatts, a significant step toward the state goal of getting 6 GW online by 2030. But Wells said she expects some of these projects to be delayed or stopped due to the rising public backlash.

To counter the backlash and ease resident anxiety, Wells and others in the industry have made it a habit to bring in fire departments to discuss their experiences with BESS.

“‘Hey, I work for FDNY, and I'm not afraid of batteries’ is about the most powerful message you can get,” Wells said.

There is a spectrum of local action. Moratoriums are often good faith efforts to understand the technology, risks and economic benefits. On the other end of the spectrum are moratoriums that get extended indefinitely — basically a ban by another name.

“Because the development cycle for all these projects is several years anyway, a one-year moratorium isn't a death knell for a project,” Wells said. “But if they extend it into a three- or four-year moratorium, then it certainly could be.”

There is a general sense in the industry that formidable BESS growth is still expected for the foreseeable future, Wells said. The Inflation Reduction Act tax credits don’t expire until 2032. But the rise in community pushback has added some uncertainty.

“Growth is certainly the trajectory for the foreseeable future, and data centers actually drive overall grid expansion, including batteries in the broadest sense of the word,” Wells said. “But you also never know what other shoe might drop tomorrow. So if you want to get projects built, try to get them built yesterday, before things change again.”

title: Detroit residents could gain a direct say in how $1.75 million is spent across their neighborhoods
description:
Detroit residents could soon have that opportunity through a new participatory budgeting pilot that proposes $1.75 million for neighborhood improvements, subject to city budget approval.
Depositphotos Residents help set the rules first Before anyone votes on sidewalk repairs or park improvements, the city needs a clear process.
Those are examples of projects residents could propose when the idea submission period officially opens next year.
Depositphotos Ideas are expected next spring Detroit plans to begin collecting residents' project ideas in May 2027.
Residents would not simply describe their priorities; they would help select eligible neighborhood projects for funding under the proposed program.
text:
actionsports/Depositphotos

A new way to shape Detroit

What if you could help decide how your neighborhood spends public money? Detroit residents could soon have that opportunity through a new participatory budgeting pilot that proposes $1.75 million for neighborhood improvements, subject to city budget approval.

Instead of only speaking at public meetings, residents will help develop ideas and choose projects. The pilot aims to bring neighborhood voices into decisions about a portion of city spending.

Depositphotos

Seven districts get equal shares

Detroit plans to divide the $1.75 million pilot fund evenly among its seven City Council districts. Under the proposal, each district would receive $250,000 for eligible neighborhood improvements selected through resident participation.

That district approach gives communities their own pool of money to consider. A project in one area will be weighed against other priorities nearby, rather than proposals from across Detroit.

Depositphotos

Residents help set the rules first

Before anyone votes on sidewalk repairs or park improvements, the city needs a clear process. The first phase lets selected residents help establish how Detroit's participatory budgeting pilot will work.

Members of a design committee will help shape proposal guidelines, voting rules and other procedures. Their work sets the foundation for the wider public to suggest projects and make choices.

Depositphotos

Applications opened Nov. 16

Detroit opened applications for its design committee on Nov. 16, following the program announcement four days earlier. Residents interested in shaping the process can apply through the city's official website.

Applying does not mean someone automatically joins the committee. The city will select participants, and committee members will work with local organizations, city departments and fellow residents on program rules.

Depositphotos

A small group has a big assignment

The design committee will have 16 resident members, selected through an application review process. Members will help determine how suggestions become proposals and what rules guide the eventual public vote.

Selected committee members are scheduled to attend an orientation on January 9, 2027, followed by weekly meetings during the initial design phase. That preparation is meant to make later decisions clearer for participating neighborhoods.

Depositphotos

The next team will review project ideas

A separate resident delegate committee will take over much of the proposal work after the rules are established. Applications for the delegate committee are expected to open in February 2027, according to the city's announced timeline.

Delegates will examine suggestions submitted by neighbors, consider whether projects are practical and develop proposals for a final ballot. Their job connects community ideas with options the city could deliver.

Depositphotos

Parks could get some attention

Detroit's pilot focuses on physical improvements, including upgrades to parks and recreation centers. Those are examples of projects residents could propose when the idea submission period officially opens next year.

A neighborhood might want to improve shared outdoor spaces or update a recreation facility. No particular project has been selected yet, and eligible proposals must go through the review process.

Depositphotos

Sidewalks and streets are on the table

Street and sidewalk upgrades are also among the improvements city leaders have highlighted. Residents will be able to flag local problems they want addressed when project submissions begin in 2027.

These proposals could focus on places people walk, travel or gather. However, being suggested does not guarantee funding; each idea must fit the program rules and reach the selection stage.

Little-known fact: Detroit's 2027 budget resolution had already called for participatory budgeting, including $250,000 per district, before the city's November pilot announcement.

Depositphotos

Safety and appearance matter too

The city has identified community safety infrastructure and neighborhood beautification as other potential uses for the money. Both categories allow residents to point out possible changes they want near home.

The program is designed for small to medium physical improvements, not every city expense. That distinction will help guide which suggestions can be developed into projects for a resident vote.

Fun fact: Participatory budgeting began in Porto Alegre, Brazil, in 1989, and the idea reached the United States in 2009 when Chicago introduced its first program.

Depositphotos

Ideas are expected next spring

Detroit plans to begin collecting residents' project ideas in May 2027. Residents will then have a chance to submit proposals for their own districts.

Those submissions will move through review and refinement before reaching a ballot. The schedule gives time to examine costs and feasibility rather than placing every initial suggestion directly before voters.

Depositphotos

A neighborhood vote comes later

Detroit plans to let residents eventually vote on a final set of eligible projects in October 2027. The vote will come after committees help turn suggestions into workable spending proposals.

This is the central difference from a typical comment period. Residents would not simply describe their priorities; they would help select eligible neighborhood projects for funding under the proposed program.

Depositphotos

Detroiters can follow the next steps

Residents who want to help shape the pilot can find information and committee applications on Detroit's participatory budgeting webpage. The current opening concerns designing the rules, not voting on projects.

Later opportunities will include sharing neighborhood improvement ideas and choosing among reviewed proposals. For Detroiters who have long wanted a stronger voice in local spending, the process offers a path.

text:
Waga Energy, a France-based landfill gas-to-energy technology provider, has signed an agreement with Randolph Farms Landfill and Best Way Disposal, both part of Indianapolis-based The Balkema Cos., to build a renewable natural gas (RNG) production facility in Modoc, Indiana.

This project is the second collaboration between Waga Energy and The Balkema Cos., following the Decatur Hills RNG Facility that has been operating since July in Greensburg, Indiana.

“We are proud to build on our successful collaboration with The Balkema Companies through this new project at Randolph Farms Landfill, alongside Best Way Disposal. Their commitment and long-term vision made our first collaboration at Decatur Hills a success,” says Waga Energy CEO Guénaël Prince. “It is the trust we built together on that project that makes this new unit possible. This second facility strengthens our footprint in Indiana, where we are creating a true renewable energy hub.”

Waga Energy will finance, build, own and operate the RNG facility for at least 20 years. Randolph Farms will manage the landfill gas collection system and support the civil works for the project. Waga Energy and Randolph Farms say they will share the revenues generated by the sale of the RNG.

The facility will use Waga Energy’s Wagabox technology to process up to 2,000 scfm (3,200 m³/h) of raw biogas and produce up to 407,000 MMBtu (120 GWh) of RNG per year at full capacity. Waga Energy says the Wagabox unit will replace the existing landfill gas upgrading technology at Randolph Farms, where RNG is currently produced for Best Way Disposal's on-site fueling facility. Commissioning is scheduled for early 2028.

“At Randolph Farms and Best Way, we're always looking for practical ways to improve our operations and manage costs,” says Jessica Routley, CEO of The Balkema Cos. “Landfill gas is a natural byproduct of our operations, and this project allows us to turn that resource into something valuable rather than letting it go to waste. We’ve had a successful partnership with Waga Energy at Decatur Hills, and we’re pleased to build on that relationship at Randolph Farms.”

text:
BMW's Spartanburg, South Carolina, plant has begun production of the iX5, making the electric SUV the brand's first EV built on American soil.

The plant is building about 70 of the electric SUVs a day, Automotive News reported on Nov. 17. The same report says suppliers are now planning around 60,000 iX5s for 2027, against an earlier figure of 100,000. For both 2028 and 2029, the number they were given is 175,000 electric BMWs a year, and that one may yet move. BMW has not published any of those numbers.

The iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800 plus a $1,450 destination charge, and BMW's US launch release puts it in showrooms in the first quarter of 2027.

Its two motors make a combined 570 hp and 593 lb-ft of torque. The battery holds 144 kWh of usable energy, and BMW's preliminary estimate is 435 miles of range.

The Batteries Travel 15 Miles

The battery packs come from BMW's new plant in Woodruff, 15 miles from Spartanburg, which opened on Nov. 13. More than 300 employees and about 250 robots assemble the sixth-generation packs there, from cells BMW buys from outside cell makers. Woodruff is the fourth plant to build them, after Debrecen in Hungary, Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Germany and Shenyang in China.

When BMW announced its $1.7 billion investment in October 2022, $1 billion was earmarked to prepare Spartanburg for electric vehicles and $700 million for the Woodruff plant.

In BMW's release on the Woodruff opening, BMW board member Raymond Wittmann, who is responsible for production, set out the plan for Spartanburg.

"Electromobility is our most important growth area. That is why we are systematically electrifying our portfolio, with the US playing a key role: By 2030, we will be assembling at least six fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg," he said.

Spartanburg Built 412,799 X Models in 2025

The same release quoted South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, who was at the Woodruff groundbreaking in 2023.

"BMW continues to deliver on its commitments to South Carolina. Just a few years ago, I stood on this site with BMW leadership to break ground on this facility. Today, we are seeing that investment come to life and marking another milestone in BMW's commitment to South Carolina," McMaster said.

The iX5 is one of five drivetrains BMW offers in the new X5, and Spartanburg is the first plant in the company's network able to build one model with all five on a single assembly line.

The plant assembled 412,799 BMW X models in 2025. More than 7.3 million BMWs have come out of South Carolina since the plant opened its line in 1994.

description:
They warned that the bill would undermine tribal sovereignty and roll back longstanding environmental protections.
U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) said lawmakers have made no meaningful progress in addressing the concerns raised by tribal nations and environmental organizations.
Joey Sanchez, chairman of the All Pueblo Council of Governors, said tribal nations have a responsibility to speak for the lands, waters and places that cannot speak for themselves.
He added that NCAI would continue opposing the legislation unless it is amended to respect the federal government’s obligations to tribal nations.
