text:
Following the U.S. Senate’s passage last Thursday of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), lawmakers, tribal leaders and environmental organizations held a press call Monday urging the House of Representatives to reject the legislation. They warned that the bill would undermine tribal sovereignty and roll back longstanding environmental protections.

During the press call, speakers reiterated their opposition to the permitting legislation, arguing that its provisions would weaken federal laws protecting clean air, water, wildlife and public lands while giving corporations and the executive branch greater authority over decisions affecting Tribal nations and local communities.

The coalition acknowledged the need to improve the federal permitting process but argued that reform should not come at the expense of environmental safeguards, tribal consultation and public participation.

The lawmakers decried the fact the bill was rushed through the Senate without committee hearings or floor markups.

“We all understand the need for permitting reform and cutting red tape. But this is a bad bill, at a bad time, that does bad things,” said U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.).

Stansbury called on House members to oppose the legislation and pursue a more comprehensive permitting reform effort in the next Congress.

She said any future legislation should be negotiated, bipartisan, developed through meaningful tribal consultation and include a transparent public process.

The current legislation, she argued, would serve as a “blank check” for the fossil fuel industry and the Trump administration rather than benefit the broader American public.

U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) also criticized the legislation, warning that weakening environmental laws could jeopardize protections for some of the nation’s most important natural resources.

“America moves forward on important issues like clean energy and clean water because we know their importance to our nation and how to get that achieved; not because we undercut fundamental laws,” Cantwell said.

She pointed to Bristol Bay in Alaska, the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and protections for clean water as examples of resources that could face renewed threats if longstanding environmental safeguards are weakened.

U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) said Democrats in the House are drawing a clear distinction between responsible permitting reform and legislation that sacrifices environmental protections and the rights of affected communities.

“We are not opposed to responsible permitting reform … but we need to do that in a way that doesn’t throw bedrock environmental protections and tribes and impacted communities and states under the bus,” Huffman said.

U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) said lawmakers have made no meaningful progress in addressing the concerns raised by tribal nations and environmental organizations.

She specifically cited provisions affecting the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act and the Clean Water Act, warning that the legislation would weaken protections for public lands and natural resources.

Grijalva also highlighted the potential consequences for Southern Arizona, where the proposed Copper World Mine could generate an estimated 1.9 billion tons of toxic waste on lands associated with the Coronado National Forest.

“There has been zero progress in addressing the litany of concerns we all have with this bill,” Grijalva said. “Still the same blatant disregard and disrespect for tribal sovereignty.”

Tribal sovereignty at the center of opposition

For Tribal leaders, the legislation raises fundamental questions about the federal government’s responsibility to respect tribal sovereignty and protect Indigenous homelands.

Joey Sanchez, chairman of the All Pueblo Council of Governors, said tribal nations have a responsibility to speak for the lands, waters and places that cannot speak for themselves.

“We speak for the areas that we want to protect. We speak for items that are places that can’t speak for themselves. That’s why we’re in this fight. That’s why we’re opposing [BAAJA],” Sanchez said. “We don’t just look at it as for us as Indigenous people. We look at it for everyone.”

Sanchez said the legislation is “just a bad bill.”

“As Indigenous communities, we’re not opposed to infrastructure. We’re not opposed to to advancement of technology. We’re not opposed to to advancement of technology,” Sanchez said. “All we’re saying is we want a seat at the table to have our voices heard for us to protect areas that are important, to protect areas that are significant to our culture, to our history. That’s what we want: is to make sure that those areas are protected.”

Lenny Fineday, general counsel for the National Congress of American Indians (NCAI), called on the House to stop the legislation or, at a minimum, hold hearings examining its potential effects on tribal nations.

Fineday said tribal concerns must be addressed before Congress moves forward.

“We are very strongly asking the House of Representatives to not move forward with this legislation, to stop the legislation, or at least to hold hearings on [how] the … wording of this legislation would impact tribal nations,” Fineday said.

He added that NCAI would continue opposing the legislation unless it is amended to respect the federal government’s obligations to tribal nations.

“We remain committed to opposing this legislation until the end or until it’s amended to uphold the sacred obligations that the United States owes to Tribal nations,” he said.

Environmental groups warn of lasting consequences

Environmental organizations also warned that BAAJA could have consequences extending well beyond the permitting process.

Raul Garcia, vice president of policy and legislation for Earthjustice Action, argued that the legislation would expand presidential authority while making certain federal decisions more difficult to challenge in court or reverse under future administrations.

Garcia said the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections demonstrated that voters wanted Congress to serve as a check on the Trump administration.

“Through the midterm elections, the American public spoke and they gave Congress a mandate,” Garcia said. “The mandate is to check Trump’s power.”

He questioned why Congress would consider legislation that, in his view, would give the president even more authority and limit the ability of courts and future administrations to address potentially harmful decisions.

Tracy Stone-Manning, president of the Wilderness Society, said Congress should focus on addressing legitimate permitting delays by improving agency staffing and rebuilding federal land management capacity rather than weakening environmental protections.

“Congress wants to tackle our transmission problems, and it should,” Stone-Manning said. “It should pass that portion of [BAAJA].”

She argued that increasing staffing and resources for federal agencies would be a more effective way to improve permitting than undermining protections for public lands, air and water or tribal sovereignty.

Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the Natural Resources Defense Council, warned that BAAJA could have long-term consequences for the climate, environment, public health, affordability and American democracy.

She also expressed concern about how the Trump administration could use the authority provided under the legislation.

“We do not have any indication that they will stop blocking clean energy. But we know they intend to do everything in their power to build data centers, pipelines, and mines,” Goldfuss said. “That’s what the president said he wants to do, and we should believe him.”

The coalition’s appeal now turns to the House, where opponents are pressing lawmakers to reject the Senate legislation rather than accept changes they believe would diminish environmental protections and federal responsibilities to Tribal nations.

For tribal leaders, the debate is about more than accelerating federal permits. It is about ensuring that decisions involving Indigenous lands, sacred places, water and natural resources do not move forward without respecting tribal sovereignty and the United States’ longstanding obligations to tribal nations.

text:
As lawmakers discuss offering tax benefits for electric vehicles produced in South Korea, expectations are rising that the scope of support will be expanded ahead of the government’s announcement of measures to strengthen the competitiveness of the electric vehicle industry. Electric vehicles were excluded from the government’s domestic production tax credit, but lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties have since proposed a series of related amendment bills.

On Nov. 23, the Tax Subcommittee of the National Assembly’s Finance and Economy Planning Committee reviewed an amendment to the Restriction of Special Taxation Act that would establish a domestic production tax credit, but failed to reach a conclusion on whether to include electric vehicles. It will continue reviewing tax amendment bills, including related proposals, on Nov. 24.

The domestic production tax credit is a system that provides income or corporate tax credits based on a company’s production and sales of strategic industry products in South Korea. Unlike the existing investment tax credit, which is based on the amount invested in facilities, it supports actual production. In August, the government proposed six eligible sectors: solar power generation, wind power generation, secondary batteries, semiconductors, key materials, and AI robot components.

Although the bills proposed by lawmakers from both parties share the goal of adding electric vehicles, they differ in the details of how support would be provided. A bill proposed by Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Lee Eonju would offer a tax credit of up to 4 million won per vehicle for electric vehicles produced in South Korea and sold domestically or exported, while giving preferential treatment to production outside the Seoul metropolitan area. A bill proposed by People Power Party lawmaker Yun Youngseok would vary the credit according to the production region, with some designated areas outside the Seoul metropolitan area eligible for up to three times the basic level of support available in the capital region.

The cap on the tax credit is also a point of contention. An amendment proposed by Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Yun Hudeok, People Power Party lawmaker Yun Hanhong and others would raise the credit cap to 100% of cumulative investment in production facilities. The government’s proposal sets the cap at 50% of cumulative investment. Thus, in addition to whether to include electric vehicles, the volume of exports, the level of regional preferences, and the overall credit cap remain issues for lawmakers to reconcile during discussions.

The government has yet to decide whether to add electric vehicles. At a press briefing on Nov. 23, Lee Hyeongil, deputy prime minister and minister of finance and economy, said the government would make an overall assessment of efforts to strengthen the competitiveness of electric vehicles themselves and improve the industry ecosystem, including cooperation between automakers and parts companies.

The government is preparing measures to strengthen the competitiveness of the electric vehicle industry, with the goal of announcing them this week. However, the announcement schedule may change. Attention is focused on whether electric vehicles will be included among the products eligible for the domestic production tax credit and how the specific terms of support will be set, as the government develops its measures and the National Assembly reviews the bills.

title: Governor Sherrill's Ponders Data Center "Faustian Bargain' - Insider NJ
description:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) combines some clean energy provisions and the promise of jobs with reduced environmental protections.
Doug O’Malley, director of Environment New Jersey, called it a “Faustian bargain” that the nation should not accept and he praised Sens.
Kathy Hochul, who in July put in place a moratorium on the development of new large scale data centers.
Two polls found New Jerseyans oppose the siting of data centers in their communities and some 110 municipalities in the state have passed ordinances banning them.
Yet Attorney General Jennifer Davenport was not among the 17 attorneys general who sent a letter to Senate leaders earlier this month in opposition to the permitting bill.
text:
BY COLLEEN O'DEA

New Jersey’s U.S. senators both voted last Thursday against a divisive bill that seeks to speed permitting for new energy projects and require data centers to pay for the power they use, while also weakening environmental protections.

Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s position on the bill, which still needs to pass the House, where its future is uncertain, is less clear. Her office declined to comment on it.

Energy policy has been a priority of hers since taking office 11 months ago. New Jersey needs to increase supply in order to blunt electricity increases – last year, power bills jumped by about 20%. But the state also has strong environmental laws and a population that values the clean water and open spaces in the most densely populated state in the nation.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) combines some clean energy provisions and the promise of jobs with reduced environmental protections. It has pitted the Citizens Climate Lobby and AFL-CIO against the Sierra Club and NAACP. It divided the Democratic caucus, with 14 Democrats joining the Republican majority Thursday to pass the bill 62-33 and send it to the House of Representatives. Only two Republicans opposed the bill. If sent to his desk, President Trump likely would sign it. A policy statement from the White House touted a number of provisions of the bill, saying it would “remove major obstacles to building the infrastructure we need in this country.”

The New Jersey State Chamber of Commerce and four regional chambers signed on to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s statement of support for quick action on the bill: “Permitting reform is ultimately about delivering results. When needed investments are delayed, families and businesses face higher costs, longer wait times, and fewer opportunities. Communities wait longer for congestion relief, the broadband connections needed to support work, education, health care, and entrepreneurship, improved access to clean water, and the energy infrastructure needed to meet growing demand. A more efficient permitting process can help deliver these benefits sooner by reducing unnecessary delays and improving certainty while maintaining strong environmental protections and opportunities for community engagement.”

But many environmental organizations disagree and oppose some or all of the bill’s provisions to weaken environmental protections.

Doug O’Malley, director of Environment New Jersey, called it a “Faustian bargain” that the nation should not accept and he praised Sens. Cory Booker and Andy Kim, both Democrats, for voting against the measure.

“This would be a really bad deal for New Jersey and the country,” O’Malley said. “We would be sacrificing the natural environment for the promise of clean energy but there would be a ton of rollbacks of permitting protections for fossil fuel projects.”

The bill would weaken a number of environmental protection laws, including the Clean Water Act, making it harder for groups to stop projects that could harm the environment. One such project is the Northeast Supply Enhancement Project or NESE, a proposed expansion of a pipeline carrying natural gas from Pennsylvania through New Jersey to New York and that would require the installation of six miles of pipeline through the Raritan Bay. The project is back before the state Department of Environmental Protection after a federal appeals court vacated state approvals for it two months ago.

“It’s a false choice,” O’Malley said of the bill. “We think you don’t think you have to sacrifice environmental protections for clean energy.”

While the bill would require data center developers to cover the costs of the electricity they consume, there would still be “huge environmental impacts,” including in water usage that cools the high-capacity computers needed for artificial intelligence processes, O’Malley said.

In voting no, both Booker and Kim said that while they support the bill’s clean energy goals, it does not do enough to stop potential abuses of a new permitting system by Trump, including those involving new immigration detention systems.

"I believe the climate crisis demands urgent action, and smart permitting reform can unleash a generation of new good-paying union jobs and new technology,” Kim said in a statement. “I voted earlier in the process to allow a debate and amendment process that could improve the bill before final passage. Unfortunately, those improvements, which would rein in the worst impulses of the Trump Administration, were not made, and the potential consequences for New Jersey are unacceptable.”

Booker’s statement explaining his “no” vote went further.

"I respect the work done on this bill with the goal of accelerating clean energy and building out our grid, but I do not believe it meets the mandate voters have charged us with to put a check on the corruption, chaos and cruelty of Trump's administration,” he said. “I am particularly concerned that the legislation would eliminate the courts’ authority to block the administration’s illegal projects, including ICE detention centers.”

As the Senate considered the bill, Kim had proposed several amendments, including one that would allow local communities to challenge immigration facilities that skipped environmental review. One of those is in Roxbury, where federal officials recently signed a contract to advance the conversion of a warehouse to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility despite having agreed to halt work at the site until they conduct required environmental reviews in response to a lawsuit filed by the state and the township.

Sherrill, who opposes the ICE plans for Roxbury, has signed legislation and taken a number of other steps meant to increase the state’s energy supply and prevent further electricity increases due to data center development, though she has not gone as far as New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who in July put in place a moratorium on the development of new large scale data centers. Two polls found New Jerseyans oppose the siting of data centers in their communities and some 110 municipalities in the state have passed ordinances banning them. Yet Attorney General Jennifer Davenport was not among the 17 attorneys general who sent a letter to Senate leaders earlier this month in opposition to the permitting bill.

New Jersey’s senators’ opposition to the bill was clear.

“The bill would weaken bedrock environmental laws and strip away important tribal sovereignty protections,” Booker said. “We should fight for a better deal that centers communities and helps us build out a clean energy future and lower costs for working people, without sacrificing environmental safeguards that have protected us from this current lawless Administration."

The fate of BAAJA’s in the House is unclear. O’Malley said opponents would be contacting the state’s House delegation to express their feelings soon.

text:
The Department of Energy’s Office of Nuclear Energy has designated the Idaho National Laboratory Computing Facility (INLCF) as an official user facility, making it the first such facility in the United States for high-performance computing focused on nuclear energy research.

Christian Natoni, the deputy manager for facilities, programs, and partnerships at the DOE Idaho Operations Office, said, “Making these computing resources available as a DOE Office of Nuclear Energy user facility gives researchers across the nuclear energy community access to capabilities they need to tackle complex challenges.”

The user facility designation aligns with INL’s role in the DOE’s Genesis Mission, the federally supported national initiative to accelerate scientific discovery through artificial intelligence. It also provides a boost for INL as it leads the 32-partner collaboration called Prometheus, which recently received a Genesis Mission award to deploy AI across nuclear power plant design, licensing, manufacturing, construction, and operations.

INLCF: INLCF and its Collaborative Computing Center offer advanced modeling and simulation resources that support a range of research activities, including multiscale multiphysics performance analyses of nuclear fuels, reactors, and other nuclear-related materials and equipment. The lab is available to users in industry, universities, national laboratories, and federal agencies. The Nuclear Science User Facilities provides support for INLCF.

INLCF hosts a number of high-performance supercomputing systems, including two recent additions, Teton and Arco. These two newest computer systems provide researchers with complementary central processing unit (CPU) and graphics processing unit (GPU) resources for demanding nuclear energy research workloads.

Teton: Teton, which was commissioned for business this past January, contains 1,024 compute nodes, each equipped with 384 compute cores and 768 GB of memory, and it can deliver 20.8 quadrillion calculations per second. This supercomputer has quadrupled the computing capacity of INL. It is being used to support advanced computational research in a variety of scientific domains, including regarding the modeling and simulation codes that are needed for nuclear reactor design.

Arco: Arco—which arrived at INL this past July and was officially launched to coincide with the DOE-NE user facility designation—is a GPU-accelerated supercomputer featuring Nvidia H200 GPUs and a Hewlett Packard Enterprise XD670 deep learning distributed memory system. Arco is optimized for the complex modeling, simulation, and automation requirements of nuclear energy research, including machine learning and artificial intelligence workloads. It will be used for’ Genesis Mission and Prometheus work.

Libya faces losses of 365,000 barrels per day According to the NOC, the disruption at Sharara could remove approximately 350,000 barrels of oil per day from production.

text:
The Sharara pipeline in Libya remains shut down after an unauthorized group closed one of the valves used to transport crude oil from the field. The National Oil Corporation (NOC) reported that this action could result in a loss of approximately 350,000 barrels per day of production.

The incident is affecting operations at the oil field managed by Akakus Oil Operations in the southwest of the country. The situation is further complicated by the closure of the Hamada pipeline, which has been out of service for more than two weeks.

Libya faces losses of 365,000 barrels per day

According to the NOC, the disruption at Sharara could remove approximately 350,000 barrels of oil per day from production. This is in addition to the 15,000 barrels per day that have already been lost due to the closure of the Hamada pipeline.

The combined loss is estimated at 365,000 barrels per day, a considerable figure for a country that depends on oil revenues and is going through economic difficulties.

The closure of these facilities also limits the transport of crude oil from the fields to the processing centers. Until the flow through both lines is restored, production will continue to be subject to operational restrictions.

The closure of Hamada worsens the situation

Problems with Libya's oil infrastructure began before the Sharara incident. The Hamada pipeline had already been out of service for more than two weeks when the National Oil Corporation (NOC) reported the latest shutdown.

This pipeline transports oil to the Zawiya area, where crude oil processing facilities are located. Its shutdown has resulted in approximately 15,000 barrels per day being taken out of production.

With both disruptions ongoing, oil authorities face greater difficulties in restoring normal production levels. The situation has also brought back to the forefront the need to protect the infrastructure that transports oil between producing fields and terminals.

The NOC requests protection for the pipelines

After learning what had happened, the NOC Board of Directors condemned the closure of the Sharara valve and asked the Petroleum Facilities Guard to intervene to protect the infrastructure.

The corporation also asked government authorities to take measures to prevent further disruptions and allow the two pipelines to be reopened as soon as possible.

In its statement on November 23, the state-owned company warned that these actions directly harm the Libyan economy and affect the resources on which a large part of the population depends.

He also announced that he will take appropriate legal action against those responsible for the closure, in order to demand accountability in accordance with current legislation.

Energy security is once again under pressure.

The incident at the Sharara pipeline adds to other episodes that have affected oil transport in Libya. In September 2026, the closure of a valve on the line carrying crude oil to Zawiya also caused a temporary disruption to operations.

These precedents show the difficulties the sector faces in maintaining continuity of production when facilities are exposed to unauthorized interventions.

The situation is even more significant given the economic context highlighted by the NOC. According to the corporation, the disruptions are occurring while international oil prices are rising, a scenario in which every barrel that is not produced represents revenue that the country could lose.

For now, the NOC is focusing its efforts on reopening Sharara and Hamada. Production recovery will depend on restoring crude oil transport and ensuring the safety of the affected facilities.

News of additional interest

Vår Energi buys ConocoPhillips assets for US$4.425M

Norwegian oil company Vår Energi has agreed to acquire ConocoPhillips' oil and gas assets in Norway, along with some of its infrastructure in the UK. The deal, valued at $4.425 billion, will allow the company to increase its production and gain ground in the North Sea, one of Europe's key oil-producing regions.

The acquisition includes stakes in 13 producing fields, operations in the Greater Ekofisk area, and the Teesside terminal in the UK. The deal could close by the end of March 2027, pending regulatory approvals. With this addition, Vår Energi expects to exceed 500,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day and maintain that level until the middle of the next decade.

Energy crisis will change global consumption in 2026

The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz is affecting energy consumption in various parts of the world. The International Energy Agency (IEA) forecasts that global demand will remain almost the same as in 2025, even though the economy is expected to grow by about 3%. Supply disruptions and rising prices have led many households and businesses to use less energy.

According to the report, energy efficiency will improve by about 3% this year, compared to 2% in 2025. However, some of this improvement is due to industries reducing their activity because of high costs. While a drop in oil and gas consumption is expected, electricity demand will grow by 3.6%, driven by electric vehicles and data centers.

European companies warn of cuts to clean energy

More than 75 European companies and industry associations have expressed concern about the proposed cuts to the European Competitiveness Fund. Among the signatories are the French energy company EDF and the battery manufacturer PowerCo. In a letter to European Union leaders, they warned that reducing these funds would hinder companies' growth and their ability to compete with the United States and China.

The warning comes days before a summit in Brussels, where the European budget for the 2028-2034 period will be discussed. Antonio Costa, president of the meeting, proposed a €40 billion cut compared to the previous proposal. Businesses, for their part, support the European Parliament's initiative to increase the Competitiveness Fund by €26.6 billion.

Wind energy reduces coal and gas use in Germany

The return of strong winds to Germany has transformed the country's electricity production during November. According to the Federal Network Agency, wind power generation jumped from less than 100 to more than 1,100 gigawatt-hours per day in the first three weeks of the month. On November 18, wind turbines accounted for nearly 65% of the country's electricity production.

With more electricity coming from wind, coal and gas-fired power plants reduced their activity. Lignite generation fell from over 316 gigawatt-hours on November 10 to less than 149 on the 18th. Natural gas also saw a sharp decline: its electricity production decreased by around 75% in just five days.

text:
Rivian Automotive is entering a new phase of its evolution, with its R2 SUV at the center of a strategy to lower production costs, simplify manufacturing and build a technology platform that could shape the future of the automaker.

The smaller, more affordable R2, which began reaching customers in June, became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle in the third quarter, helping drive record deliveries of 19,248 vehicles, up 46% from the previous quarter.

Third-quarter revenue rose 38% to $2.2 billion (Nasdaq: RIVN).

But the significance of the R2 extends beyond its early sales performance.

“The cost of an R2, in bill of materials, is half of an R1,” Chief Operating Officer Javier Varela told the Business Journal.

That cost difference is central to Rivian’s longer-term strategy, giving the automaker an opportunity to reach a broader customer base.

Automotive cost of goods sold per vehicle declined by $12,000 from the second quarter, reflecting a higher mix of R2 vehicles and greater fixed-cost leverage, according to Rivian’s earnings presentation.

The company is expanding R2 production with a second shift at its Normal, Illinois, manufacturing facility, which produced 19,751 vehicles in the third quarter, up 84% from a year earlier.

The automaker expects the R2 to account for the majority of its total deliveries in the fourth quarter. It projects full-year deliveries of 67,000 to 70,000 vehicles, raising the low end of its previous outlook.

An Up-and-Down History

Founded in 2009 by RJ Scaringe, who serves as CEO, Rivian has experienced its share of growing pains on the road to becoming a major electric vehicle manufacturer.

The company went public in November 2021, briefly reaching a valuation exceeding $100 billion. Its stock surged to nearly $180 within its first week of trading before losing much of its value in the years that followed.

Shares closed at $10.33 on Nov. 20, more than 90% below their peak, giving Rivian a market capitalization of about $15 billion.

The automaker has also struggled with mounting losses, slowing demand for electric vehicles and repeated layoffs. Rivian has undergone at least five rounds of job cuts since June 2025, including more than 600 positions eliminated last October and additional cuts this June, shortly after R2 deliveries began. The latest reductions affected employees in its title and registration department, according to an Oct. 12 report by an EV industry news outlet.

The expiration of federal tax credits of up to $7,500 for eligible new electric vehicles last year has also slowed demand, adding pressure on EV makers. U.S. electric vehicle sales fell 27% year over year in the first quarter of 2026, with the decline deepening to 39.5% in the third quarter, according to Irvine-based Kelley Blue Book.

Rivian has also faced challenges expanding its manufacturing operations. The company operates a plant in Normal, Illinois, and announced plans for a $5 billion factory east of Atlanta, Georgia, projected to eventually produce up to 400,000 vehicles annually.

The automaker paused construction in 2024 amid cost-cutting efforts before reviving the project earlier this year, with completion targeted for 2028.

Building a Different Kind of Automaker

Varela, who joined Rivian in 2024 after working at Volvo, Toyota and Stellantis, said the company’s approach to vehicle development differs from that of traditional automakers.

Much of that comes from building its vehicles and technology architecture from “a clean sheet” rather than adapting systems developed over decades, as many automakers do. That means Rivian controls its entire technology stack, including computers, sensors, displays, lighting and sound.

“We treat the vehicle as a platform, a software platform that improves over time,” Varela said. “That’s a big advantage here, while the legacy players need to transform from old architectures.”

The company can also deliver new features and improvements through over-the-air software updates, extending the vehicle’s capabilities after it leaves the factory.

“Our vehicles are all connected, and based on that software foundation and that connectivity, we receive information,” Varela said. “We get data immediately, either from the factory or from the cars that are with our customers, and that information is integrated, is analyzed, and we learn from that.”

The Next Frontier: Autonomy

Rivian is developing its own driver-assistance and autonomous driving technology, using data collected from vehicles on the road to improve its systems.

“We are using the equivalent to large language models,” Varela said. “We have created our own ‘Large Driving Model,’ and we are learning from miles and miles of driving our cars and with that, we are defining the software for autonomy.”

The next major development in Rivian’s Autonomy+ platform, which launched in April, will be point-to-point navigation.

Its existing universal, hands-free driving capability covers more than 3.5 million miles of mapped roads in the United States and Canada. The planned point-to-point feature would allow drivers to enter a destination and have the vehicle navigate the route, including city streets and highways, with driver supervision.

“We believe point-to-point capabilities are going to be an important purchase criteria for customers and is becoming a driver of market share,” Scaringe told analysts. “And today, in the market, there’s really only one other product that has that, of course, with Tesla’s FSD (Full Self-Driving).”

Rivian plans to introduce the new capabilities to a limited group of customers later this year, with a broader release scheduled for 2027.

Rivian’s software architecture also has potential applications in its commercial vans and future mobility services, including robotaxi development under its work with Uber.

Its acquisition of Third Dimension AI Inc., a firm specializing in AI-powered 3D spatial generation, is intended to help advance the development of driver-assistance and autonomous driving systems.

While autonomy has not yet become a primary purchase consideration for most U.S. vehicle buyers, Scaringe believes that is changing.

“I do think that we’re at the base of a very significant inflection point, though, where we’re going to start to see a much broader set of customers start to really look for advanced capabilities.”

Agility in a Competitive Industry

Despite its recent sales gains, Rivian still faces a fundamental challenge: turning higher vehicle deliveries into a profitable business. Although it generated positive gross profit in 2025, the automaker remains in the red. It reported a net loss of $3.6 billion last year, compared with $4.75 billion in 2024.

“We expect that R2 will help us achieve a positive automotive gross margin exit rate for the year,” interim Chief Financial Officer Derek Mulvey told analysts.

Reno production growth and 127% increase in third-quarter revenue support continued focus on commercial execution and expansion

XCF Global, Inc. (NASDAQ:SAFX) (“XCF” or the “Company”), a U.S.-based producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, today outlined its continued focus on growing renewable fuel production, strengthening commercial performance and advancing its expansion strategy as it prepares for a planned transition to over-the-counter trading. On November 18, 2026, the Company received a notice from the Listing Qualifications Department of The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC (“Nasdaq”) determining to delist XCF’s Class A common stock from The Nasdaq Capital Market.

“We are building on tangible progress at Reno, where production increased each month during the third quarter and revenue grew 127% year over year,” said Chris Cooper, XCF Global Chief Executive Officer. “With Southern Energy and DevvStream Corp. now part of XCF and a definitive agreement signed for the proposed Paramount acquisition, we have expanded our capabilities and established opportunities for future growth. Our priority is to convert that progress into consistent production, stronger customer relationships and improved cash generation. We remain confident in the opportunity to build a significant domestic renewable fuels business that supports American agriculture and energy security, and we are committed to earning shareholder confidence through execution and results.”

XCF’s operating progress provides a foundation for its next phase of development. Following the July restart at New Rise Renewables Reno, monthly renewable diesel production increased from approximately 0.55 million gallons in July to 1.01 million gallons in August and 1.35 million gallons in September. Commercial shipments increased 15.5% from August to September to 1.46 million gallons, and third-quarter 2026 revenue increased 127% year over year to $21.7 million.

In October, XCF completed its business combination with Southern Energy Renewables Inc. and DevvStream Corp., broadening its renewable fuel technology capabilities and adding expertise in environmental asset management and monetization. The Company also signed a definitive agreement to acquire the Paramount, California renewable fuel refinery. The proposed acquisition remains subject to closing conditions, financing and other requirements.

Building on these developments, XCF is focused on improving production consistency and commercial performance at Reno, advancing planning for Paramount and evaluating additional renewable fuel development opportunities. The Company’s strategy centers on expanding U.S. renewable fuel production, creating additional markets for domestic agricultural feedstocks and building long-term shareholder value.

On November 16, 2026, the Company filed its Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. XCF intends to continue providing shareholders with updates on its financial performance, operating progress and strategic initiatives through SEC filings and public announcements.

The Staff’s determination was triggered by the Company’s Class A common stock having a closing bid price of $0.10 or less for ten consecutive trading days, from November 4, 2026, through November 17, 2026. Under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A)(iii), if a company’s security has a closing bid price of $0.10 or less for ten consecutive trading days during a compliance period for the minimum bid price requirement, the Staff is required to issue a delisting determination, regardless of any time remaining in that compliance period.

At the time of the determination, XCF was in a compliance period under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2), which requires listed securities to maintain a minimum bid price of $1.00 per share (the “Minimum Bid Price Requirement”). As previously disclosed, Nasdaq notified the Company on December 9, 2025, that its Class A common stock had closed below $1.00 per share for 30 consecutive business days. The Company received an initial 180-calendar-day compliance period through June 8, 2026, and, on June 9, 2026, an additional 180-calendar-day period through December 7, 2026. The Company has not regained compliance with the Minimum Bid Price Requirement.

According to the notice, trading in the Company’s Class A common stock on Nasdaq will be suspended at the opening of business on November 25, 2026. Nasdaq will file a Form 25-NSE with the Securities and Exchange Commission to remove the Company’s securities from listing and registration on Nasdaq.

Under the Nasdaq Listing Rule 5800 Series, the Company may request a hearing before a Nasdaq Hearings Panel to appeal the Staff’s determination by 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 25, 2026. A timely hearing request would not stay the suspension of trading in the Company’s Class A common stock. The Company does not intend to request a hearing.

Following the delisting from Nasdaq, it is expected that Company’s common stock will initially trade on the Pink Limited Market operated by OTC Market, under the same trading symbol “SAFX”. However, the Company is working to facilitate quotation of its common stock on the over-the-counter market following the Nasdaq suspension and intends to pursue the highest OTC market tier for which it qualifies, which we expect will be OTCID. The timing of OTC quotation, applicable market tier and trading symbol will be announced when confirmed. There can be no assurance regarding the timing or availability of OTC quotation or qualification for any particular market tier.

XCF Global, Inc. Following its recent combinations with Southern Energy Renewables and DevvStream Corp., XCF is building a vertically integrated platform across the clean fuel sector, employing today’s commercially scalable technologies, future lower cost-reduced carbon technologies and environmental asset management and monetization. text:
One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.

The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.

The UK government has pledged £380m in financial support for the factory because it is seen as crucial to the long-term survival of the British car industry, but the build has suffered several setbacks. The construction specialist contracted by Agratas, TSL, has decided to leave the project after failing to agree terms with the battery company, according to three sources.

Batteries are among the important parts of EVs, but global supply is dominated by China, South Korea and Japan. Successive Conservative and Labour governments have strongly supported efforts to build a British battery supply chain, and it also fits with Andy Burnham’s hopes to “reindustrialise” the UK. Not all of the subsidy has yet been paid out.

Tata announced the gigafactory in 2023, aiming for a 2026 start of production with as many as 4,200 employees, before pushing it back to 2027. Replacing the lead contractor for the second time in five months is likely to add to doubts over whether Agratas can hit its latest target of January 2028 – although the company has not yet pushed back its planned start date.

A spokesperson for Agratas said: “We are on track to meet our customer requirements.

“The Somerset site is a large and complex industrialisation project, and all of our supplier partners are supporting us well as we prepare for the facility’s launch phase.”

The inability to reach an agreement with TSL, formally known as Tonroe Group, stemmed from disagreements over the timeline and cost of the project, two sources said.

TSL is expected to leave the site within two or three months, leaving no other main build contractor lined up. However, it is thought that NG Bailey, the project’s mechanical, electrical and plumbing contractor, could be one option to take over the entire build.

The issues at the heart of the dispute are similar to those with TSL’s predecessor, Sir Robert McAlpine (SRM). Agratas fired SRM at short notice in June, and one source suggested discussions over the terms of its departure remain ongoing.

Morale within Agratas has also been hit by the company’s decision to relocate some workers from Coventry, in a building shared with other Tata Group companies, to Somerset.

Some of those workers are expected to take redundancy rather than uproot families and move 120 miles away. If they did so it would continue a stream of senior staff leaving the business in recent months, two sources said.

The UK’s only operating gigafactory, AESC’s plant in Sunderland, north-east England, has also faced problems as carmakers have scaled back plans for EVs, with governments delaying bans on petrol and diesel cars. The Guardian revealed in August that AESC had shelved expansion plans after it failed to agree a separate deal to supply JLR.

It is understood that JLR has secured batteries from other suppliers, so its plans to increase sales of new electric Land Rovers and Jaguars will not be affected. However, those initial cars will not have British-made batteries, although the manufacturer could also avoid EU tariffs under “rules of origin” if it uses batteries made in Europe.

Agratas has made some progress at the Somerset factory, as well as another site in Sanand, western India. Some Agratas managers have travelled to India this week to share experiences with their counterparts in India and discuss the UK situation.

The shell of the building site in south-west England is mostly complete, and National Grid has started work on the electricity substation that will provide the large amounts of power needed to make batteries.

People close to the project suggest Agratas could still succeed in producing batteries and avoid the fate of an earlier rival project, Britishvolt, which collapsed after failing to secure firm orders. The former Britishvolt site in north-east England is now being turned into a datacentre for artificial intelligence – a potentially attractive prospect for an empty building with a high-capacity connection to the electricity grid.

Agratas was approached for comment. TSL declined to comment. JLR declined to comment. NG Bailey was approached for comment.

text:
As a member of Mesa, Ariz.’s city council, Jennifer Duff knows firsthand just how deep the anger over data centers runs.

“If you say ‘data center’ in public right now, people will just yell at you,” said Duff. “There’s AI, there’s people, and it’s a war.”

Duff was speaking at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR), where top leaders in business, government, and academia gathered on Nov. 12 to examine the potential economic impacts of AI and the steps policymakers should be thinking about now given the uncertainty around what’s to come. One of the discussions at the SIEPR Fall Policy Forum, “Economic Policy in the Age of AI,” focused on the debate over the data centers needed to deliver AI’s computing power and how to ensure that the trillions of dollars expected to pour into their construction are a boon to local communities.

The speed and ferocity of the data center backlash has taken local governments and the AI industry by surprise. During the November midterm elections, voters overwhelmingly opposed the buildout of AI’s physical infrastructure: Voters passed 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives either outright restricting or limiting data center development. As Duff noted, not that long ago, people, including local officials, didn’t know what a data center was. Mesa, with a population of 530,000 across 140 square miles, went from one to 17 data center projects in just five years.

Erika McEntarfer, former commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics who is now a SIEPR senior policy fellow, set the stage for the panel discussion when she noted that voter concerns over rising electricity bills, water consumption, land use, and the generous tax breaks doled out to data center developers are not a partisan issue. “This has united unlikely allies across party lines,” she said.

Jasmine Sun, a writer at The New York Times Opinion and a speaker on the panel who interviewed residents affected by data center construction ahead of the November election, said community distrust goes beyond environmental and quality-of-life issues. People, she said, are angry with local officials for signing non-disclosure agreements before negotiating deals with “hyperscalers” — large-scale data center developers that include Amazon, Meta, and Google — and that secrecy has become a lightning rod for community opposition. The perception that “out of touch Silicon Valley billionaires are shaping the country in their image, extracting resources, doing what they want,” Sun said, “connects to much broader political and cultural concerns over inequality, over corruption, over affordability.”

Another reason why people are wary of data centers: They don’t buy into the narrative that AI is the country’s economic future. “They didn’t find AI necessarily evil, but they did find it pretty useless,” Sun said of her conversations with local communities. And in the Midwest, memories are still fresh of the economic and environmental fallout after car manufacturers abandoned factories.

Learning to coexist

Community concerns, however, could be obscuring a significant economic opportunity. Data centers are potentially key to the state of U.S. manufacturing, said fellow panelist Josh Zoffer, a partner at investment firm CIV and a SIEPR Policy Fellow.

As evidence, Zoffer, along with Ben Sampson, a Stanford PhD student in economics, recently analyzed the effect that rising demand for data center components is having on U.S. manufacturing. Their findings are striking: At today’s investment levels, the data center buildout is creating more than 300,000 American factory jobs in the upstream supply chain.

And those are conservative estimates. In their SIEPR Policy Brief, Zoffer and Sampson argue that significantly more jobs are likely to follow, particularly if data center development continues at its current pace and if the U.S. adopts policies aimed at supporting domestic manufacturing of transformers, switchgears, power equipment and other components.

“[AI] is where the center of gravity in the global economy is headed,” Zoffer said at the policy forum. If the U.S. doesn’t seize the opportunity, he said, the country risks repeating past mistakes when local opposition thwarted rare earth production and nuclear energy development.

Big Tech, Zoffer said, has an opportunity to repair its reputation in local communities. Data centers are hugely profitable, so there’s plenty of wealth to go around, whether it’s by paying higher taxes or investing in clean energy, schools, hospitals, and local jobs, he said.

Duff said budget-constrained communities also would benefit from a general framework for structuring data center deals. At minimum, she said, local governments should adopt laws governing data centers before taking a seat at the negotiating table. It wasn’t until last year, for example, that Mesa passed its first ordinance for data centers.

Developers, too, could start publicly disclosing their water and energy use on websites. The lack of transparency today is one reason people don’t trust Big Tech’s intentions, the panelists said. “If people don’t know [what’s happening],” Duff said, “they just make it up and then it becomes fact in the community.”

When AI starts improving lives in meaningful ways, such as in healthcare, Duff expects community skepticism to fade. Until then, though, developers and local governments need to find common ground.

“We need to come together and figure this out,” Duff said.

title: Here's what's next after climate talks collapse: Reform, individual action, hope and more heat
description:
Just because the U.N. climate talks in Turkey imploded, it doesn't mean that hope for rescuing an ever-warming world is gone, experts say.
The climate talks, called COP31, ended Sunday in division and finger-pointing, without the hoped-for overarching agreement on fighting climate change that the world could follow.
It is a climate and political crisis,” said Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany.
But University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann argues against making too much of these November heat spikes because they were influenced by the El Niño weather pattern, which is a phenomenon separate from climate change.

text:
Just because the U.N. climate talks in Turkey imploded, it doesn't mean that hope for rescuing an ever-warming world is gone, experts say. But the road ahead will be tougher, require changes to negotiations and may be more about individual efforts by nations and companies instead of joint action.

And the planet will just keep getting hotter.

The climate talks, called COP31, ended Sunday in division and finger-pointing, without the hoped-for overarching agreement on fighting climate change that the world could follow. The main reason for the collapse was disagreement over mentioning the need to transition away from fossil fuels, the chief cause of global warming.

“The world cannot afford a repeat of this moment,” United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said as the negotiations fell apart. “The fight continues. We will never give up.”

The Associated Press asked numerous experts to outline what's next for the U.N. climate process, which reconvenes next year in Ethiopia, and the fight to reduce emissions of heat-trapping gases from the burning of fossil fuels.

Most of the experts found positives from the collapse, mostly in how it appears to be galvanizing many countries to do something about phasing out coal, oil and natural gas.

“This leads to a crisis. It is a climate and political crisis,” said Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany. “But it will hopefully result in taking COP reform more seriously as well as ‘truly getting serious’ in delivery of the Paris Agreement.” That 2015 pact requires countries to ratchet up plans to cut carbon emissions and aims to keep global average temperatures out of the danger zone.

The climate doesn't 'care about politics'

The Paris deal set goals of limiting long-term warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably below 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times. Earlier this year the U.N. conceded that it's inevitable that the world will blow past that long-term 1.5 degree mark, probably in a year or two.

Exceeding it over the long term means “danger in terms of billions of people suffering from droughts, floods, fire, heat waves, disease and human-reinforced storms," Rockström warned.

But the temperature climb isn't stopping there.

Six times this month, the average global daily temperature was more than 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, according to the European climate service Copernicus.

“This is yet another sign that the climate doesn't really care about our politics — either in the U.S. or COP,” said Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather. Heat-trapping gases keep increasing in the air. The November temperature spikes show that the world is not only passing the 1.5 mark over the long term, but isn't too far away from the 2 degree threshold, he said.

But University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann argues against making too much of these November heat spikes because they were influenced by the El Niño weather pattern, which is a phenomenon separate from climate change.

What happened after past talks failed

Given the need to address suffering from increasing extreme climate events such as the deadly Nepal flood, environmental advocates Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa and Tasneem Essop of Climate Action Network International called it “the worst COP ever.”

Because expectations were low and there wasn't a big deal needed, this isn't quite the worst climate talk failure, said climate negotiations historian Joanna DePledge of the University of Cambridge. That belongs to 2000 in The Hague — which had to be continued six months later in Germany — and 2009 in Copenhagen, where a hoped-for deal collapsed, she said.

She blamed the joint Turkey-Australia leadership of COP31 — as did many experts — for handling the negotiations poorly. She said there was no need for an overarching final agreement because the purpose of this round of talks was more about implementing past goals. Insisting on something big, and then not delivering it, was a mistake, she said.

Six years after the failure in Copenhagen, the world agreed to the landmark Paris pact.

Climate Analytics CEO Bill Hare said the failure of Copenhagen led the countries of the world to realize just how important it is to work together. And this failure will remind them to “stop running after the fossil fuel producers and companies and begin to deal seriously with the climate change problem,” Hare said.

Experts urge a reform of the climate talks

For years, experts have said the world needs to change the entire process of COP, a giant two-week climate Super Bowl that attracts 100,000 people to a closed-in campus. Many of the outside experts said the key thing is to ditch the requirement for near-unanimous consensus in big final agreements, and make it majority or super-majority rule.

Mann would also like to apply financial penalties such as embargoes and tariffs to countries that fail to fulfill climate commitments. He also thinks the talks should not be located in fossil fuel-exporting states — like four of the last five host countries.

“We can no longer continue with this charade where a small number of bad petrostate actors stand in the way of planetary sustainability,” Mann said. “The U.N. must change the rules now.”

Hope lies in countries' individual actions

While much of the focus in climate talks is on the overarching agreements, side deals that don't require consensus are thriving.

About 80 countries signed on to Turkey's plan to have 35% of the world's energy use — including transportation such as cars and planes — come from electricity. That could reduce emissions by at least 8 billion metric tons, said International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol.

Just before the conference started, Brazil offered countries specific “road maps” for how they could transition away from fossil fuels — and several have already adopted them. Nearly 60 countries are part of a separate conference devoted entirely to phasing out fossil fuels.

“The true test of climate action will be what happens beyond the negotiating halls," U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said.

His message to young people, scientists and those vulnerable to climate disasters is “keep demanding action. Keep turning up the heat,” Guterres said. “Hold governments and companies to account.”

text:
Bioenergy ‘campuses’ in Fresno, San Bernardino counties are feasible, say UC researchers

Imagine a facility that lowers the risk of severe wildfire, makes use of underused materials from forestry and agriculture, helps California reduce carbon emissions – and also generates jobs, regional economic growth and community health benefits, such as better air quality.

A biofuels and wood products campus that transforms woody biomass and agricultural residues into renewable energy can deliver all of the above. While demonstration sites have proven the effectiveness of the technology, California currently lacks commercial-scale facilities of this kind.

Two reports by UC Cooperative Extension scientists – and collaborators from Sierra Resource Conservation District and the Agricultural Technology Innovation Partnership (ATIP) Foundation – offer blueprints for models that can realize such a vision.

“When it comes to biomass utilization, there are not many references in California that can guide industry people, investors and policymakers in making decisions – where they need to invest, how much to invest, what options are appropriate,” said Cindy Chen, a co-author of the reports and UCCE woody biomass and forest products advisor for the Central Sierra.

One report looks at the feasibility of a “wood products innovation campus” that generates renewable diesel in Fresno County (PDF), and the other investigates a possible hydrogen fuel-producing campus in San Bernardino County (PDF). Both campuses would encompass a large biofuel facility, as well as smaller structures that produce other wood products.

“In terms of San Bernardino, the conclusion we reached, based on our techno-economic analysis, is that it is feasible economically to produce hydrogen from woody biomass,” said Haris Gilani, report co-author and principal investigator, and UCCE biomass and bioenergy advisor serving Riverside and San Bernardino counties.

The researchers also found that commercial production of renewable diesel was feasible for Fresno County.

“These scenarios were shown to be economically viable, so I hope that these reports will encourage more investment in these types of projects,” Chen said. “They’re not only useful for companies that could potentially make a profit from them; they also will help California communities reduce wildfires and help achieve California’s climate change goals.”

Gilani and Chen both emphasized that the models presented in the reports are meant to be replicable in other regions of the state with similar access to available woody biomass and agricultural residues.

Fresno County report: Biomass from agricultural lands, forestry, municipal waste can produce renewable diesel

Fresno County was selected for study because it sits at the nexus of multiple streams of biomass (or “feedstocks”) that can be used to produce renewable diesel. The wood product innovation campus could receive agricultural residues from a host of farm-related activities in the region (pruned branches, almond hulls, trees from orchard removal, etc.), municipal solid waste, and – crucially – the woody debris from forest operations in nearby foothills and the Sierra Nevada.

“The business-as-usual scenario is that the debris is left on the forest floor, where it either decomposes, or in the event of a wildfire, adds to the available fuel and can contribute to more intense wildfires,” Gilani said. “By removing that excess woody biomass and moving it to these proposed facilities, we can turn a potential wildfire fuel source into valuable bioenergy products.”

Through a process called gasification, the organic biomass is heated (not burned) to an extremely high temperature, producing a mix of various gases called “syngas” and solid biochar – a carbon-rich byproduct that has a growing number of applications, including as a soil amendment.

The syngas component can then be converted into renewable diesel or hydrogen fuel. Both pathways offer the potential for substantial greenhouse gas emission reduction compared with conventional fossil fuel. Based on the reports’ assessments, renewable diesel produced from biomass has about 93% lower carbon intensity than conventional petroleum diesel, while hydrogen produced from woody biomass is estimated to have approximately 59% lower carbon intensity than conventional hydrogen produced from natural gas.

“When we look at the technology readiness level (TRL), which ranges from 1 (basic research) to 9 (fully commercialized technology), integrated biomass gasification systems for producing renewable fuels are generally around TRL 7 to 8,” Gilani added.

In the Fresno County report, the authors outline a systematic process for identifying potential sites for a wood products campus using multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA). Geographic information systems (GIS) screening was integrated with 23 criteria layers, such as the availability and density of feedstocks and proximity to transportation networks, to determine the suitability of the sites.

After eliminating locations that were near sensitive habitat areas and other protected lands, they identified 77 high-suitability sites across California, including nine in Fresno County. They chose a representative candidate – the Rio Bravo Fresno Biomass Power Plant site – for further analysis.

The researchers then modeled the performance of four feedstock mixes: 1) 100% forest residues; 2) a 50/50 blend of forest and agricultural residues; 3) a mix that introduces 20% municipal solid waste; and 4) a high (50%) municipal solid waste mix.

“Scenario one, which was 100% forest residues, demonstrated the strongest financial and operational performance in terms of the volume of renewable diesel produced and the highest internal rate of return [of investment],” said Gilani. He added that the first scenario also generated the greatest health benefit, as it significantly reduced the risk of wildfires and smoke-related health impacts.

San Bernardino County report: Repurposing existing facilities reduces capital costs by 40%

San Bernardino County was chosen for the second report because of its proximity to high wildfire-risk areas. Currently, there are limited markets and end-uses for woody biomass generated through forest thinning and other fuel-reduction treatments in the national forests across the region. That biomass – which might otherwise remain on landscapes and contribute to wildfire fuel loads – could instead be used as feedstock for a commercially viable hydrogen production facility.

“It’s very important to remove excess woody biomass in areas where it poses a wildfire risk, but it’s costly, unless we create an alternative market for what’s left on the forest floor,” Gilani said. “We won’t be able to remove it without any incentives.”

The researchers also chose San Bernardino County because of the high volume of freight traffic connecting the Port of Los Angeles to distribution centers and warehouses throughout the Inland Empire. The report envisions reducing the reliance on fossil fuels by tapping into a renewable source, hydrogen produced through biomass gasification. Replacing diesel-burning vehicles would also be a boon for a region that historically has had some of the worst air quality in the U.S.

“Heavy-duty transportation is a sector where we need to put more focus on decarbonization, and this is a great opportunity where trucks potentially would be running on a clean fuel,” Gilani said.

Recognizing that infrastructure needs present a major obstacle to creating a biomass innovation campus, the authors also studied the advantages of repurposing an existing facility. Gilani pointed out that California has a large number of idled or abandoned sites that are candidates for reuse, such as old sawmills or biomass power plants.

In the San Bernardino report, the researchers used the idled Desert View power plant in Riverside County as a case study of how “brownfield” development (building on land that was previously used for industrial or commercial purposes) can provide benefits over a “greenfield” pathway (building from scratch).

“We did the repurposing scenario and found that there’s about 40% less capital cost in using the repurposed site; you have existing buildings, infrastructures, permitting and biomass supply chains – all those factors add up,” Gilani explained, noting that reusing an existing site also can reduce risk for potential funders and accelerate project timelines.

Regulatory challenges, hydrogen market, transport of biomass remain obstacles

While a brownfield approach can expedite some aspects of developing a biomass innovation campus, such efforts still face significant regulatory barriers. Chen observes that its backers would need substantial finances to meet an array of environmental criteria, even before it can start operating and generating revenue.

“All of these scenarios face some level of policy regulation, policy restraints, regulatory permitting challenges,” Chen said. “As you know, everything [related to permitting] can take longer in California, especially when it comes to building these types of facilities.”

Another crucial barrier for companies and investors is uncertainty in the hydrogen market.

“The price of hydrogen is unstable, which I think is one of the biggest constraints,” Gilani said. “If you look at the retail price, it’s somewhere between $25 to $30 per kilogram; at that price, it’s not going to be able to compete with diesel and other heavy-duty transport fuels, despite policy incentives in place such as California Low Carbon Fuel Standard.”

According to Gilani, hydrogen currently costs approximately 2.8–3.3 times more than diesel, when purchased at public retail prices, for fueling a truck that covers the same distance.

Then there’s the challenge of moving the feedstocks to the wood product/biomass innovation campuses, which can be cost prohibitive.

“For these facilities to work and ensure the continuous production of hydrogen or renewable diesel, you need a continuous supply of biomass,” Gilani said.

One possible solution is the establishment of strategically located feedstock aggregation yards, where biomass from disparate sources can be collected.

“In this model you have long-term agreements with these ‘middle man’ entities that will receive all this feedstock from different landowners, and then they will supply the biomass facility,” Gilani explained.

If Chen and Gilani secure funding, they hope to continue their study of the biomass innovation campus project. They aim to focus next on workforce development, including a proposal to launch a training pilot program in partnership with community colleges.

The Fresno County and San Bernardino County reports were made possible by funding from the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. In addition to Gilani and Chen, co-authors of the reports were Md Sahadat Hossain, formerly with University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources and now a postdoctoral associate at Virginia Tech; John Heywood, Sierra Resource Conservation District; and Rick Brenner, ATIP Foundation.

title: The collapse of UN climate talks over fossil fuels was years in the making | PBS News

text:
Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

The science has been clear for decades

The burning of these fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases, which go up into the atmosphere and raise global average temperatures, creating havoc on ecosystems and leading to more, and more intense, extreme weather events.

In simple terms, the solution is to burn less of these fuels over time and instead use sources of energy that don't release greenhouse gases, like solar, wind and geothermal. But there is nothing simple about getting countries to agree on a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, particularly major oil producers like Saudi Arabia, Russia and the United States, or major coal users like China and India.

READ MORE: In their own words: Leaders at UN climate talks discuss why negotiations ended without deal

So, even though fossil fuels are the cause of climate change, and the annual climate summits are convened to confront climate change, it's become all but impossible to have even the words "fossil fuels" show up in a final agreement, much less any detailed transition plan.

In the 30 years of climate negotiations, the one exception was the U.N. climate conference three years ago in Dubai, COP28, where the final decision encouraged countries to "transition away from fossil fuels." Fossil fuels were not mentioned in the final agreements in the following two conferences, and the current one, of course, had no final agreement.

Emerging fault lines finally cracked

The backdrop to the climate talks had become a split-screen reality, with the world being hammered by costly and deadly extreme weather events while the top international body set up to deal with the crisis could only nibble around the edges. It ultimately became too much to sustain.

During previous conferences, nations frequently threatened to walk away if there wasn't a strong agreement on fossil fuels. Instead, in the end, they would voice their disagreements in closing plenaries and ultimately get in line, figuring there was always next year and ultimately the overall negotiating process needed to be preserved.

But by the final week of this year's conference, which would go into overtime and become the longest on record, it was clear that many nations, including the European Union bloc, were no longer willing to do that.

Earlier this week, Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister of environment, seemed to encapsulate what many frustrated participants were thinking when he said the COP process was being "held hostage by the petroleum mafia."

Navarro likened the situation to "Stockholm syndrome," when captives, in this case people worried about the future of the planet, were "in love with our kidnappers," or the oil industry.

The "petroleum guys" have convinced us that "they destroy nature to help us," said Navarro.

The mention of carbon removal was also a sticking point

The collapse didn't happen just because the cause of climate change was left out of a final agreement, but also because of what was in it. Draft agreements, including the final text released early Sunday, included language encouraging the world to scale up technologies that remove carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, and store it.

READ MORE: Activists, leaders criticize COP31 climate talks as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft deal

Such technology, heavily supported by the oil industry, is energy intensive, expensive and far from being deployed at scale. To date, it only captures and stores much less than 1% of the estimated 60 billion tons of global greenhouse gases produced each year. For many at the climate talks, including carbon removal in the agreement was at best a misguided attempt to produce a small solution, and at worst a pass for carbon polluters to simply continue with business as usual. After all, why stop spewing carbon pollution when it can just eventually be scooped up?

In the months ahead, there will be many recriminations and reflections about what happened in Turkey, and what it may all mean for the next round of talks, scheduled in Ethiopia next year. Inevitably, long-standing questions about the entire U.N. climate process will be raised and likely get much more attention than in years past.

Has the process run its course, or can major reforms turn it into a credible way to confront climate change? Reforms floated over the years include shortening the conference from its current two weeks, limiting it just to delegates and reducing its overall size. Indeed, in recent years it's ballooned so much that on the ground it feels more like a trade fair than a summit to confront one of humanity's most pressing challenges.

Wherever the process ultimately goes, extreme weather events will continue and intensify as global temperatures rise. Many scientists expect 2026 to be the hottest on record.

"Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high," said United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, reacting to the outcome. "And every delay makes our task harder and more costly."

text:
Flipkart has doubled its last-mile electric vehicle fleet to 42,000 this festive season, from over 20,000 in 2025, the company said on 23 November 2026.

The expansion is part of Flipkart’s commitment to a 100% electric last-mile fleet by 2030 under the Climate Group’s EV100 initiative.

Electric two-wheelers used for Flipkart Minutes, the company’s quick commerce service, account for about 77% of the electric fleet, Flipkart said, with another 20% operating across the rest of its delivery network. The fleet grew most in Bengaluru, Mumbai, Chennai, Pune and Gurugram.

A Flipkart survey of more than 9,400 delivery partners, known as Wishmasters, covering both electric and internal combustion engine (ICE) riders, found that intent to switch to an EV was nearly four times higher among those who had already tried one. Among EV riders, 59% cited cost savings as a key motivation, while charging access remains an operational need, the company said. Among ICE riders, 55% said financial support such as EMI loans, down-payment assistance or a daily EMI option would encourage them to switch. Awareness of government incentives was higher among EV riders (58%) than among non-EV riders (37%).

Flipkart said it supports delivery partners through training, awareness drives, nationwide EV roadshows and digital learning on incentives and financing. It also organised an EV Mela in Bengaluru, bringing together manufacturers including Ampere, Bajaj, Hero Vida and Motovolt, as well as financing institutions.

EV Assist, a platform Flipkart said it launched earlier this year, connects Wishmasters with electric two-wheeler rental providers so they can use an EV without buying a vehicle upfront. The company said the platform has seen strong demand in Delhi NCR, Patna and Bengaluru.

On charging, Flipkart is working with battery-swapping company YUMA and other partners on infrastructure at its hubs and micro-fulfilment centres. Eight battery-swapping stations are operational in Bengaluru, with plans to extend the network to other metro cities, the company said.

Rajneesh Kumar, Chief Corporate Affairs Officer, Flipkart Group, said: “Our delivery partners decide whether electric works, and they tell us it comes down to cost, charging and financing. A rider who has tried an EV is nearly four times more likely to switch, so our job is to make that first try easy. Doubling our fleet this festive season shows riders are ready when the switch is practical, and we will keep building this with our Wishmasters and partners.”

Broader Grounds for Adverse Post-Permit Actions: The September version of the bill prohibited agencies from rescinding, suspending, or otherwise interfering with fully permitted projects.
New Guardrails on Remedies: The November bill also narrows how a developer might recover damages from the government for adverse post-permit actions.
