text:
On November 19, 2026, the Senate voted 62–33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, signaling strong bipartisan support for what would be the most significant permitting reform legislation in decades. This version of the bill preserves many of the streamlining and fast-tracking provisions of the version introduced in September 2026, including the 150-day statute of limitations for many project challenges, remand without vacatur as the default remedy, an enhanced nationwide permit program, and exemptions from the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”) and the National Historic Preservation Act (“NHPA”) for many natural gas infrastructure and transmission projects. But compared to existing law, it also sets more defined sidebars around several of those provisions and weakens protections aimed to provide more certainty for project developers.

As a supplement to our earlier list of ten ways the bill would promote energy infrastructure, we highlight the most consequential changes from the September version of the bill for project developers. They touch on these key topics:

Adjustments to the project certainty provisions, with some narrower protections for permitted projects;

Continued strong support for natural gas infrastructure development;

An essential fix to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”) backstop siting authority for transmission facilities;

New provisions for judicial review and NEPA streamlining;

A new approach to the NHPA overhaul; and

Partial retreat on the limits imposed on states issuing Clean Water Act water quality certifications.

1. Adjustments to the Project Certainty Provisions, with Some Narrower Protections for Permitted Projects

The September version of the bill contained provisions to bolster project certainty by limiting the ways a later administration could undo agency decisions for projects finalized in a preceding administration. The November version of the bill still offers project developers strong protections against agencies backtracking and revoking approvals, but targeted changes make some of these protections materially weaker.

Broader Grounds for Adverse Post-Permit Actions: The September version of the bill prohibited agencies from rescinding, suspending, or otherwise interfering with fully permitted projects. The updated Section 1401 of the bill expands certain exceptions that would allow the government to suspend, terminate, revoke, or otherwise take action to interfere with authorizations in cases where action is necessary to prevent substantial harm or damage to human health or the environment, or when action is “pursuant to any applicable law or regulation.” These changes are significant because they could, in practice, swallow many of the protections. For example, a new administration could claim some resource or impact was not fully considered in a project’s earlier environmental review, and the “pursuant to any applicable law or regulation” provision would make that avenue even easier, since many environmental and natural resources laws contain provisions allowing suspension or termination of permits on broad, vaguely defined grounds that could require only general alleged harm to property or the environment. The revised exceptions weaken the bill’s protections for developers and still leave room for a future administration to retroactively assert its policy preferences on permitted projects.

New Guardrails on Remedies: The November bill also narrows how a developer might recover damages from the government for adverse post-permit actions. In order to recover delay costs plus 25 to 50 percent for a denied project’s development and construction costs incurred to date, developers must now show that the government acted in bad faith. The government retains the burden of proof but would no longer be held to a “clear and convincing evidence” standard. Developers can still receive some relief without a bad-faith showing, including reinstatement, injunctive relief, attorney fees, and delay costs.

Disparate Treatment: The disparate-treatment claims over permit delays and denials allowed under Section 1402 of the bill would now also require a showing of “bad faith” as part of the government’s pattern of disparate treatment. However, developers would benefit from a broadened comparison period—10 years instead of 5—as well as a presumption that a “substantial increase” in the rate of denials for a category of projects is indicative of bad faith.

One-Year Clock: The November bill also slightly adjusts the timeline for federal approval in favor of developers: For permits not requiring an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement under NEPA, federal agencies must now render decisions within one year of an applicant submitting an application—rather than one year of the application being deemed complete. This prevents agencies from pushing out the one-year clock by delaying or withholding completeness determinations.

2. Continued Strong Support for Natural Gas and Transmission Infrastructure Development

The November bill continues to recognize the importance of streamlining approvals for much-needed energy infrastructure, broadly exempting a wide range of interstate natural gas facility and electric transmission activities, including repairs, upgrades, modifications, and capacity enhancements, from NEPA and NHPA review when they take place in existing rights-of-ways or previously reviewed footprints. The September version of the bill would exempt such an activity as long as it was limited to those areas plus “any minimum additional area adjacent to an existing right-of-way that is necessary to complete” the covered activity. Some pipeline expansion projects using looping frequently have loops that depart from the corridor to avoid congested development or natural features, and it was unclear just how far those loops could deviate before flouting the “minimal additional area adjacent to an existing right-of-way” standard. The November bill addresses this uncertainty by capping that distance to one-quarter mile from the right-of-way’s boundary.

The November bill also expands the transmission project exemption to cover installation of grid-enhancing advanced transmission technologies on existing facilities. The expanded exemption, which November version adds to the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) and which allows these upgrades to proceed without NEPA and NHPA review, reflects a bipartisan desire to make necessary transmission upgrades that can alleviate the rate pressure felt by Americans.

3. At Long Last, a Fix to the FERC Backstop Siting Authority for Transmission Facilities

As we have previously reported, the Energy Policy Act of 2005 gave FERC backstop siting authority in the FPA to permit interstate transmission lines when states lack siting authority or fail to act within one year, but it contains a fatal flaw and has never been successfully used. Presently, FPA Section 216(e) prevents the holder of a FERC backstop permit from exercising eminent domain authority over state lands. Thus, a state opposed to a project authorized under FERC’s backstop siting authority can still block a transmission project simply by refusing to grant real estate easements, and it is practically impossible to build a high-voltage transmission line of any significant length without crossing state-owned lands, which include, among other features, the bottoms of all navigable waters, most of the lands used for interstate highways, and other highways and roadways. The November bill removes that state veto.

The November bill expands where FERC can exercise this siting authority. Currently, this authority applies only within designated national interest electric transmission corridors—or NIETCs. Both versions of the bill would remove the corridor requirement but limit the authority to lines of 230 kV or more that, among other requirements, transmit electric energy in interstate or foreign commerce, are consistent with the public interest, and benefit consumers and improve reliability. The November bill extends this authority to include facilities “necessary to safely and reliably interconnect” those lines and removes the simultaneous FERC-state processing track for 345-kV lines found in the September bill. This brings interconnection facilities such as lower voltage tie-ins and substations within FERC’s backstop siting reach, making it less likely that federally permitted lines are stranded due to connecting facilities being unable to get state approval. This will benefit developers serving data centers and other fast-growing loads.

4. New Provisions for Judicial Review and NEPA Streamlining

The November bill maintains measures to reduce delays from judicial review. A new section extends the 150-day statute of limitations for challenges under NEPA, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the NHPA, the Mineral Leasing Act, and more to projects proceeding under the expedited FAST-41 pathway. As such, enrolling a project in FAST-41 can now offer litigation-risk benefits in addition to scheduling benefits.

A new provision also clarifies the venue for review of agency actions under NEPA. The November bill carves out cases governed by Natural Gas Act Section 19(b) and FPA Section 313(b), so appellate litigation over FERC orders will continue to follow those statutes’ existing judicial review venue provisions. However, claims challenging agency rules on the basis of NEPA compliance, as well as challenges to authorizations for projects with no physical location, will go exclusively to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

5. A New Approach to the NHPA Overhaul

The September bill aimed to reform the NHPA Section 106 process. The November bill still does this, but in a different way. The November bill maintains the requirement for federal agencies to prepare reports on undertakings that include a determination of the area of potential effects, identify historic properties, describe any adverse effects, and identify prudent and feasible measures to avoid, minimize, or mitigate those effects, subject to comments from State and Tribal Historic Preservation Offices. It also expands obligations to the courts, mandating that absent extraordinary circumstances, they issue a ruling within 120 days after a plaintiff files suit. In keeping with a narrowed focus on federal agency process, the November bill drops the September version’s sanction on State and Tribal Historic Preservation Offices that miss NHPA deadlines, which would have forced the offices to spend 50 percent of their workweeks on the delayed review; the November bill maintains this sanction for senior federal agency staff.

The Senate also responded to backlash against measures perceived as interfering with Tribal sovereignty. The November bill removed provisions that would have imposed a mandatory federal takeover of Tribal Historic Preservation Offices with programs deemed deficient under the NHPA, replacing it with a corrective-action process. The Senate also removed the earlier, narrower definition of properties of traditional religious or cultural importance that could have excised important Tribal sites from the NHPA’s purview.

6. Partial Retreat on the Limits Imposed on States Issuing Clean Water Act Water Quality Certifications

The November bill adjusts some of the Clean Water Act streamlining provisions seen in September. One change is that certifying authorities (like states, some Tribes, and EPA in some circumstances) would be able to deny certification of a Clean Water Act Section 401 application if it still lacks required information after the certifying authority has requested the missing materials and given the applicant a reasonable opportunity to provide them.

A second change relates to one of the provisions the November bill retains to align Section 401 with the Environmental Protection Agency’s January 2026 proposed rule, where it limits certifying authorities from denying or conditioning certifications only if they show, by clear and convincing evidence, that no modification or reasonable condition would avoid a water quality violation and that any conditions placed on the approval are the least burdensome approach to ensure compliance. The November bill removed a third condition, which would have required that the condition be “consistent with the requirements of the Federal license or permit” that is the subject of the application.

And a third change relates to which agency decides which conditions are necessary. The September bill affirmed that a federal agency could not refuse to include a certifying authority’s conditions that were necessary to ensure compliance with a water quality requirement. That left open who decided which conditions were necessary. The November bill clarifies this, stating that the certifying authority decides.

Next Steps

While the bill is closer to the finish line, it must still pass through the House of Representatives, including committee review, before it can reach the President’s desk. Timelines are tight. The House is expected to adjourn for the year in mid-December, and the bill could face new challenges if it is not passed before the new Congress begins in January. Any changes the House makes would also have to be reconciled with the Senate before the bill can be enacted, and the final bill will depend on bipartisan compromises.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

New Jersey’s four regulated utilities have less than 11 months to implement the state’s new virtual power plant program, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities said on Nov. 12.

Beginning no later than Oct. 1, 2027, Atlantic City Electric, Jersey Central Power & Light, Public Service Electric & Gas and Rockland Electric will operate interim versions of PowerUp NJ for two years while gathering performance data to inform a long-term, open-access VPP tariff, the BPU said.

The utilities began laying the groundwork for PowerUp NJ early this year following Inauguration Day orders from incoming Gov. Mikie Sherrill, D, to accelerate deployment of distributed and utility-scale clean power resources across the easternmost state in the PJM Interconnection. One of those orders directed the BPU to develop a statewide VPP program.

Dive Insight:

PowerUp NJ is a “first-of-its-kind statewide virtual power plant program that will give ratepayers more control to drive down their own energy costs,” Sherrill said in a statement that also referred to the plan as a “voluntary community energy program” that allows customers to “lend power from their homes” to support the grid.

The BPU’s order this month cements the program features and goals outlined in a July straw proposal from the agency.

Among other things, the order envisions a market-based framework that compensates distributed energy resources for grid services, rather than subsidizing their deployment; has standard program design elements across all four regulated utility territories; is technology neutral, with eligibility extended to net-metered solar-plus-storage systems; and requires utilities to test localized dispatch with an eye towards developing grid services that could defer or avoid infrastructure upgrades, according to a program factsheet.

The order also establishes technical working groups on measurement and verification, cost-benefit analysis, and program marketing; and aims to coordinate existing utility and state programs and proceedings involving distribution system planning, net metering, energy efficiency and electric vehicles, according to the factsheet.

The BPU expects smart thermostats, stationary home batteries, internet-connected electric water heaters and vehicle chargers and electric vehicles themselves to be eligible for PowerUp NJ at launch. Participating utilities and manufacturers will notify customers of specific eligible devices and models in mid-2027.

PowerUp NJ will be an opt-in program, meaning customers must affirmatively choose to participate. Once enrolled, customers will be able to “choose which devices and events to include” to avoid inconvenient or uncomfortable situations, like ceding control of a thermostat on a hot day, the BPU said.

Like other state-level VPPs, such as California’s Demand Side Grid Support program, PowerUp NJ aims to reduce grid stress and mitigate power price spikes by shifting load away from demand peaks. It will target both “distribution-level grid stress events” and PJM capacity and transmission coincident peaks, according to the program factsheet.

A preliminary staff analysis found that a 3% cut to peak demand could avoid about $60 million in annual system capacity costs while cutting local and greenhouse gas emissions from fossil-fueled peaker plants in New Jersey, the BPU said.

In a statement, BPU President Ben Hertz-Shargel said his agency would apply lessons from the two-year interim version of PowerUp NJ to the development of a long-term framework for the program.

title: Virtual Power Plants Reach 47 GW: How Commercial Buildings Get Paid for Flexibility
description:
A virtual power plant pools batteries, thermostats, chargers and generators in many buildings and dispatches them as one resource when the grid is short.

Where Commercial Buildings Fit Commercial and industrial aggregators are competing harder for enrollments, and Wood Mackenzie identifies battery ownership and optimization as the main differentiators.

text:
A virtual power plant pools batteries, thermostats, chargers and generators in many buildings and dispatches them as one resource when the grid is short. Wood Mackenzie counts 47.2 GW of that capacity in North America, and new turbines now cost more per kilowatt than battery fleets. Commercial owners can enroll equipment they already operate and earn revenue for reducing load or exporting power at peak.

Key Takeaways

Wood Mackenzie counts 47.2 GW of behind-the-meter flexible capacity in North American virtual power plants (VPPs), up 25.9% in a year.

With heavy-turbine capital costs up more than 80% since 2020, battery-based VPPs now win on cost per kilowatt, the firm says.

VPP providers disclosed a 1 GW pipeline aimed at data center load, and PJM and ERCOT hold the largest VPP offtake.

Puerto Rico’s VPP draws on batteries in nearly 115,000 homes and has prevented or mitigated more than 60 outages since June 1.

Buildings that own batteries, controllable HVAC or generators can earn capacity revenue through utility programs and wholesale markets.

47.2 Gigawatts

47.2 GW. That is the behind-the-meter flexible capacity Wood Mackenzie counts in its 2026 North America virtual power plant market report, released November 18, up 25.9% from a year earlier. The firm says the market “deepened more than it broadened” this year: capacity grew faster than the number of company deployments, buyers and programs, each of which rose less than 15%.

Residential customers drove the biggest gain in wholesale markets, where their VPP capacity rose 155% year over year. Wood Mackenzie credits opt-out enrollment, which “has demonstrated it can shift capacity overnight,” and battery growth led by retail electricity providers. Batteries installed behind the meter do not count as VPP capacity until someone enrolls and dispatches them, which leaves room to grow.

Why Batteries Now Beat Turbines

The economics turned on equipment costs. “Escalating turbine costs, affordability concerns and slow supply response to large loads are driving more interest in VPPs,” said Elham Akhavan, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie. Capital costs for heavy-duty gas turbines have risen more than 80% since 2020, and battery-based VPPs now win on cost per kilowatt in 2026, she said.

Data centers created a new buyer. VPP providers disclosed a 1 GW pipeline of capacity aimed specifically at data center load, a category absent from last year’s report. PJM and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) hold the largest utility commitments to data center capacity and the largest disclosed VPP offtake. Distributed capacity in those two markets can serve the same peak hours that large new loads strain.

Puerto Rico Shows the Model at Scale

Puerto Rico offers the clearest field test. Its VPP draws on batteries in nearly 115,000 homes, part of more than 207,000 rooftop solar systems on the island, and has prevented or mitigated outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to LUMA Energy, the Associated Press reported. The AP calls it the second-largest VPP in the United States by capacity.

The mechanics are simple. When LUMA forecasts a deficit, enrolled customers get a digital alert, and they can opt out or choose how much of their battery to share; most offer about 30%. A typical event lasts about four hours and supports the equivalent of roughly 80,000 residential customers. LUMA pays solar providers three times the residential electricity price for the energy it draws and recovers the cost through rates. One participant received $162 last year.

The program has growing pains. Some participants criticized the payment structure in a 2026 Solar United Neighbors survey, and others hesitated because they feared losing backup power. LUMA’s chief regulatory officer, Alejandro Figueroa, said daily use would require a different design and compensation structure. On the mainland, New Orleans plans a $23 million program to network more than 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses.

Where Commercial Buildings Fit

Commercial and industrial aggregators are competing harder for enrollments, and Wood Mackenzie identifies battery ownership and optimization as the main differentiators. Owners of large buildings bring what aggregators want: concentrated load, controllable HVAC, chargers and, often, standby generators.

Wholesale markets are opening to that equipment. In New York, Strobe Power said on November 12 that it became the first to commission a New York City building as a power plant under the New York Independent System Operator’s (NYISO) program for distributed energy resources. In New Jersey, the Board of Public Utilities (BPU) moved forward this month with a program that would reward residents and businesses for using smart devices to support the grid, ROI-NJ reported. Each program sets its own rules for baselines, performance tests and penalties, and those terms decide what a building earns.

The revenue stacks on savings many owners already capture. A battery that discharges during a building’s monthly peak lowers demand charges, and the same equipment dispatched during a grid event earns program payments. Capacity programs pay for availability during a limited number of event hours, so participation works when the contract sets thermostat limits, battery reserves for backup power and tenant notice periods.

Questions to Ask Before Enrolling

Who controls the equipment? Confirm whether the aggregator, the utility or the building operator issues dispatch commands, and how tenants can override them.

How is performance measured? Baseline methods decide whether a building gets credit for a reduction, especially in buildings with variable occupancy.

What happens on a missed event? Penalties for underperformance can erase a season of payments.

How much battery stays in reserve? Set a floor for backup power, a lesson from Puerto Rico’s enrollment concerns.

Who keeps the revenue? Leases and service agreements should state how payments split among owner, tenant and aggregator.

What It Means for Owners and Managers

Opportunity: Existing equipment earns revenue. Batteries, controllable rooftop units, chilled water plants and EV chargers can qualify for capacity payments in PJM, ERCOT, New York and other markets.

Implication: Leases need control language. Owners should define who controls dispatch of thermostats, batteries and chargers, how tenants are notified and how revenue and comfort limits are shared.

Opportunity: Data center neighbors gain a buyer. Providers now market VPP capacity to serve data center load, which adds demand for flexibility near large new campuses.

Risk: Payment terms vary. Puerto Rico’s experience shows that unclear compensation slows enrollment. Read performance penalties, baseline methods and battery reserve rules before signing.

Implication: Batteries compete with turbines on cost. Storage installed for resilience can also count toward the grid’s peak needs, which supports its value in underwriting.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a virtual power plant?

A network of distributed batteries, thermostats, chargers and other devices that a utility or aggregator dispatches together to cut demand or supply power during peak periods.

How large is the VPP market?

Wood Mackenzie counts 47.2 GW of behind-the-meter flexible capacity in North America in 2026, up 25.9% from 2025.

Why are VPPs growing now?

Gas turbine capital costs have risen more than 80% since 2020, and battery-based VPPs now cost less per kilowatt, according to Wood Mackenzie.

How do commercial buildings participate?

Through utility demand response and VPP programs or wholesale market programs such as NYISO’s distributed energy model, usually with an aggregator that handles enrollment, dispatch and settlement.

title: BMW's iX5 Kept Going 21.8 Miles Past Zero Percent | The Truth About Cars
description:
It covered 8.4 miles past zero percent and pulled nearly 3 kWh from the supposedly empty pack.
At 10.7 miles came the first big cut, with the car refusing throttle inputs and coasting down.
The iX5 drew 7.4 kWh from the reserve before it finally powered off, rolled to a stop, and automatically engaged Park.
As for the headline number buyers care about, the iX5 60 xDrive, currently the sole version on offer, is EPA-rated at 456 miles.
In a comparison against the Lucid Gravity, Porsche Cayenne, and Rivian R1S, it covered 411 miles at 70 mph, beating every rival by at least 43 miles.
text:
The iX5 is the first electric X5, a nameplate that has long been one of BMW's best-sellers, and BMW is building it in the United States, a first for an electric model from the brand. The car is carrying expectations, and it arrives with a 144-kWh usable battery, per BMW.

The test began with 4 percent energy remaining. The displays nagged about recharging, sensible advice for a road trip, but the SUV still drove like nothing was wrong. At 2 percent, output was capped at roughly 350 horsepower, down from about 450 hp, which is still more than enough. At 1 percent, the driver held speeds between 35 and 55 mph.

At zero, those speeds were still possible, now with a turtle icon, a yellow power meter, and a warning to avoid hard acceleration and overtaking. The iX5 did not slow. It covered 8.4 miles past zero percent and pulled nearly 3 kWh from the supposedly empty pack. The pedal softened at roughly 10 miles. At 10.7 miles came the first big cut, with the car refusing throttle inputs and coasting down.

That wasn't the end. A restart got it moving again at up to 55 mph. The iX5 drew 7.4 kWh from the reserve before it finally powered off, rolled to a stop, and automatically engaged Park. A second restart attempt failed. Based on the test, the buffer works out to a total battery capacity around 151 kWh.

As for the headline number buyers care about, the iX5 60 xDrive, currently the sole version on offer, is EPA-rated at 456 miles. In a comparison against the Lucid Gravity, Porsche Cayenne, and Rivian R1S, it covered 411 miles at 70 mph, beating every rival by at least 43 miles. The hidden reserve is a bonus on top of that.

text:
In “Gaslit,” a new documentary about climate change activists, Jane Fonda stands outside one of Formosa Petrochemical’s Texas facilities and looks through a thermal camera. The Oscar-winning actress is brought to tears by what she sees: a tremendous expulsion of methane gas into the air.

“Methane is 80 percent more destructive to the climate, in terms of global warming, than carbon dioxide,” Fonda explained during a recent Zoom interview. “It’s the most destructive chemical that we’re using, and it’s extremely dangerous for people. And yet here it is billowing into the air, and nobody even knows it.”

For years, Fonda has been sounding the alarm about the looming environmental catastrophe that will take place if the world doesn’t wean itself off fossil fuels. She launched a series of climate change protests dubbed “Fire Drill Fridays” in 2019 — a reference to activist Greta Thunberg’s charge that people should “act as if your house is on fire” — and has been arrested multiple times for civil disobedience. Fonda is embracing the cause with the same passion that has led her to speak out on everything from the Vietnam War to feminism to LGBTQ+ rights. But she worries her efforts may not be enough.

“Our emission of global warming chemicals has gone way up since Donald Trump has become president,” Fonda said. “And of course the concern is always: Have we passed too many tipping points or a tipping point? Many climate scientists say if we act fast now, it won’t be too late. But it’s very hard to act fast when Trump is president.”

The political winds are changing. The midterms were a blue wave election that saw Democrats take back the House and the Senate in commanding fashion. They not only performed well in liberal bastions, but also captured the governor’s mansion in Texas and elected James Talarico to a U.S. Senate seat that has been in Republican hands for decades. Much of “Gaslit” focuses on the environmental damage wrought by the oil fields in West Texas’ Permian Basin. Will the change in leadership make a difference?

“It won’t hurt,” Fonda said. “I don’t know how strong Talarico is on these issues. We can’t do too much until our members are seated, and we actually have the majority in the House in January.”

“Renewables are ready,” she added. “They’re cheap. They’re safe. They’re job-intensive. It’s the perfect solution. It’s right there. It makes all the sense in the world. The only thing we lack is political will, and hopefully, with this swath of new people that have been elected to the House and the Senate, we will have the political will when we take power to turn this around.”

Fonda believes average citizens concerned about climate change can’t afford to be passive.

“One of the most important things that people can do is to demand that their elected officials pass legislation that makes these polluters pay for what they’re doing,” Fonda said. “Right now, it’s consumers, it’s us taxpayers that have to pay for the damage. They should pay, and we have to stop the $21 billion annual subsidies that we pay them. They make trillions of dollars of profit. If we cancel those subsidies, it would spell the beginning of the end for fossil fuels.”

Fonda is blunt in her warnings that the chaos and damage that global warming has caused will only accelerate unless the world switches to renewable sources of energy. Her assessment is sober, even terrifying, but one thing that gives her hope is the work that the activists highlighted in “Gaslit” are doing. “Gaslit” was financed and produced by the environmental group Greenpeace USA, and it focuses on people in the Gulf Coast and Texas who are trying to change things across the political spectrum. They range from a Republican cattle rancher, who has seen what the oil and gas business has done to his family’s land, to cancer survivors and community organizers who are hoping to change hearts and minds about fossil fuels.

“What is so moving to me about the film is we’re showing these people who do not give up; they will not,” Fonda said. “All of these activists are so brave and so incredible. They inspire me.”

“Gaslit” was directed by Katie Camosy. It is now available to rent or buy on Amazon Prime and Documentary+. As of November 19, the film can be streamed on the Greenpeace USA YouTube channel, with additional platforms rolling out.

text:
AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, back in New York.

In Turkey, the United Nations climate summit collapsed Sunday after nations failed to reach an agreement on a new climate deal as the Earth warms. The European Union and a number of countries opposed the final draft because it made no mention of fossil fuels. The effort to strip the text of references to coal, oil and gas was led by Saudi Arabia and joined by Russia. The United States did not participate in COP31.

This is Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, the climate envoy for the Marshall Islands.

KATHY JETN̄IL-KIJINER: The Republic of the Marshall Islands objects to the adoption of the CMA text and cannot join consensus. We came to Antalya to honor our commitment to the Paris Agreement and to do what we promised our people back home. We face an inevitable overshoot of 1.5. We came here expecting the world to deliver a comprehensive and urgent response on reducing emissions, on protecting our people and on providing the finance to do this. We have been let down on all sides. We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot: a response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future.

AMY GOODMAN: Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien outlined the European Union’s opposition to the final text.

DARRAGH O’BRIEN: At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous levels of global warming, the draft cover decision falls well short. We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach. We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time. And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel.

AMY GOODMAN: Over the weekend, climate justice activists rallied against the final text. On Friday, a Malaysian climate activist, Amalen Sathananthar, was detained after interrupting the closing plenary. He stood on a table holding a red noose around his neck and wearing a shirt that read, “You are killing the future.”

AMALEN SATHANANTHAR: You are killing the future! You are killing the future! Why don’t you just kill me now? The climate crisis is killing! … There’s no money! Just kill me now! The Global South can’t wait! The Global South can’t wait for this! And yet you just keep doing nothing, nothing at all! Racists! Kill me now! Kill me now! Kill me now! Kill me now! … You are killing the future! You are killing the future! You are killing the future! You are killing the future!

AMY GOODMAN: We are joined now by three leading climate justice activists who just returned to their home countries after attending the U.N. climate summit. Brandon Wu is with us from Washington, D.C., director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA. In Manila, Lidy Nacpil is with us, the longtime Filipina climate activist and coordinator with the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development. And from Cape Town, South Africa, we’re joined by Tasneem Essop, executive director of the Climate Action Network International.

I want to begin with Tasneem, but first let’s play a short video from Turkey of Tasneem Essop trying to interact with Chris Bowen, the COP31 president of negotiations from Australia.

TASNEEM ESSOP: You have an opportunity to save this process. We need decisions that will protect the people of the South. There’s nothing in the text, and corporate interests will be the only ones that benefit. CCUS, carbon dioxide removals are dangerous, dangerous, opens the door for fossil fuels. Please read the letter.

CHRIS BOWEN: I will.

TASNEEM ESSOP: The Global South demands the protection of its people.

AMY GOODMAN: “The Global South demands the protection of its people,” Tasneem Essop said, executive director of the Climate Action Network International, joining us from Cape Town, South Africa.

Tasneem, you must be extremely tired at this point. I just saw you in Antalya, Turkey, and now you’re back home in Cape Town, South Africa. Can you respond to the collapse of the talks, as you tried to question the president of the COP, the Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen?

TASNEEM ESSOP: Thanks, Amy. Yeah, a bit tired from the COP itself, but also, in a sense, very disappointed that it had to come to this.

I wouldn’t characterize the COP as having collapsed. I think it’s important for your viewers to understand that there were two processes, actually, at this COP. The one was the formal negotiation process, and that is where the negotiations on different tracks — on the just transition, on adaptation, on mitigation, on climate finance — was taking place. And then there was the cover decision.

The cover decision was a decision by the COP presidencies, in fact, driven by the COP president for negotiations, Australia, as a way of including political statements, if I can call it that. And it’s really that where there was no agreement reached. The others had — you know, they were largely procedural. They had passed through. There was one or two where there were objections, like the mitigation work program track. But certainly, it was the cover decision that caused the most controversy.

Presidencies do not need to have cover decisions. We were concerned about this cover decision from the start, when they announced this at the pre-COP. And so, we saw that, in fact, this cover decision distracted the entire negotiations. All of the political attention that was needed in the formal negotiations got taken out and into the cover decision negotiations and discussions. So, that is where things collapsed, if you might call it that. It’s disappointing that it had to come.

I think the biggest lesson here is cover decisions just do not work. We need to pay attention and focus on the mandated negotiations. And that is where developed countries, actually, the ones that, you know, had the theater around rejecting a cover decision — that’s where they actually gutted the negotiations. That’s where — and it’s hidden — where the problems arose. The finance for adaptation track didn’t move forward. They kept on resisting the delivery plan for a commitment they made on tripling finance for adaptation. The just transition track didn’t move, because they obstructed the creation of a just transition mechanism.

And so, if you go through all of the formal negotiation tracks, it was developed countries that actually blocked and obstructed, and then came to the cover decision and, you know, decided that they’re going to reject it, and pretended to be the champions, when, in fact, the real negotiations were happening elsewhere, and they actually obstructed this.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to bring Brandon Wu into the conversation, of ActionAid USA. He also just returned from the U.N. climate summit. If you can give your analysis of what took place? A lot of people are saying COP31 collapses as EU rejects texts for being weak on fossil fuels. But when we were at the U.N. climate summit, we were speaking to many, including a young European activist who was saying, in fact, to their shock, the European Union replaced President Trump, who had pulled the U.S. out, in pushing for fossil fuels at the U.N. climate summit. What happened?

BRANDON WU: So, I think this has become the headline. I mean, you read these headlines at the top of the show, right? The COP collapses, and it’s because — and the EU is rejecting the text because of lack of fossil fuels. And I do think that that is actually a dangerous and deeply misleading story, because, as Tasneem said, the EU, you know, try to style themselves as the climate champions: “This is not enough ambition. We need more movement on phasing out fossil fuels,” which, of course, we do. We need more movement on fossil — on phasing out fossil fuels. And it’s got to start in the Global North.

The EU are being quite hypocritical, actually. Their transition plans away from fossil fuels are not at all aligned with the 1.5 degrees Celsius climate target that they claim to be defending so much. And the way these negotiations are structured, the Global North has the responsibility to reduce its emissions first and fastest, and also the responsibility to provide money and support to the Global South, so that the transition can be enabled in those poorer countries.

And what we saw is that the developed countries, across the board, acted more like bullies than champions. They come in demanding more of the Global South, but in every negotiating room blocking any progress on the finance that is going to make that transition possible.

And one thing, like two weeks before the negotiations started, the EU climate commissioner actually said any new climate finance commitments were, quote, “dead in the water.” “Dead in the water.” He actually said that. This was two months after the floods in Nepal that killed 1,500 people, with five over 5,000 people still missing. “Dead in the water.” It was shockingly tasteless and also a shocking way to approach the negotiations. They said out loud two weeks before the negotiations that they were coming in with nothing to offer, with no room for compromise on the one thing that is the major priority for the Global South countries in these negotiations.

AMY GOODMAN: So, talk about what this means. What does it mean for the COP, for the conference of the parties, COP31, the longest, the largest, to collapse? And while I think up to 100,000 people participated, would you also say it’s one of the largest gatherings of fossil fuel lobbyists in the world?

BRANDON WU: So, yes, there are a lot of fossil fuel lobbyists that come up into these spaces. There are a lot of lobbyists for data centers, for, you know, Big Tech, all these things. It’s not a clean space, right? And the reason we have so many intransigent governments is because there’s so many profit-seeking interests that have their ear.

The way forward — I mean, as Tasneem said, the actual negotiations did not fully collapse. There were decisions that moved forward some key things on just transition, which is, you know, making sure communities are supported as we change our economies to more sustainable ones, on finance, on adaptation. Those tracks are not dead. We didn’t get anything we wanted, but it was only the cover decision that was fully rejected.

And so we live to fight another day, but we’re going to face the same problem over and over again. This has been happening for decades, right? The way that these negotiations are structured is the Global North, as I said, has to lead, on cutting emissions, on providing finance. They have the legal obligation to do that. They have the money to do that. We see how the U.S. is throwing trillions of dollars a year for genocide and war. The money is there. They need to provide it to the Global South to make the transition happen, and then the Global South can reduce emissions, their dependence on fossil fuels. And what we’ve seen over the past decades is the Global North are not delivering on any of their responsibilities. That’s what’s causing the deadlock. It’s not new to this COP, but it’s becoming increasingly untenable.

AMY GOODMAN: And, I mean, I think part of the problem, being at the COP for this past week, is the level of jargon that most people just don’t have access to — “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “climate finance.” These may sound obvious to you. The cover decision and the cover letter, explain exactly what you mean.

BRANDON WU: Look, at the end of the day, this is a question of fairness. There are basic principles of fairness, that everyone understands, that are just being blown out of the water in this process. The rich developed countries — the U.S., EU, Australia, Japan, Canada — these are the countries that spewed greenhouse gases into the atmosphere over the last 150, 200 years, and have built their economies on the backs of fossil fuels. These are the countries that created the mess, and these are the countries that have to clean it up.

“Climate finance” is just a fancy term for sending money to poorer countries so that they can make the transition, as well, so that they can help their communities survive in a world in which, you know, we’re breaching the 1.5-degree limit. That’s another piece of jargon, but what that means, of course, is that climate impacts are getting worse. We all know this. They’re getting worse. They’re going to get much worse, much faster, I think. And countries need the support to deal with that. These are countries that have had nothing to do with the problem, and it’s their people whose lives are at stake. They’re basic principles of fairness. I think everybody can understand that.

AMY GOODMAN: And the cover decision?

BRANDON WU: So, the cover decision, I mean, the reason that that’s important is because the rich countries are using what happened with the cover decision as a way to deflect blame. So, they are pointing at —

AMY GOODMAN: And “cover decision” means?

BRANDON WU: So, the cover decision, again, it was a political text, that came out of nowhere. The presidency of the COP wrote it, so Türkiye and Australia. It was not part of the formal negotiating tracks, where you have all the different country blocs talking about issues of substance that they’ve decided should formally be on the agenda for the negotiations. So, it’s a political text that was written by the presidency, and then they tried to, in a top-down way, get buy-in from all the countries so they could include all their little pet projects and all the pet projects of the countries that had their ear.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to bring Lidy Nacpil into this conversation. Lidy Nacpil is a Filipina climate activist, coordinator with the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, with the Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice. Lidy, thanks so much for being with us. You’re joining us, I believe, from Manila. Can you respond to what has taken place? You know, for so many COPs, so many of these U.N. climate summits, in the midst of them, the Philippines is hit with tsunamis, with hurricanes. I think of how many times Yeb Saño, first as a chief climate negotiator for the Philippines, now, as he’s described, as a climate pilgrim, but then he would stand up and talk about how the Philippines was being ravaged by the climate crisis. What this means for the Philippines, and what you think needs to happen now, Lidy?

LIDY NACPIL: Well, first of all, our reaction to COP31 is also amidst the backdrop of the UNEP report saying that the breach of 1.5 degrees is imminent and unavoidable. So we thought that this would at least imbue a sense of urgency for this COP to deliver very concrete and actionable agreements that will actually mean progress in the real world and not just in text language. So, of course, we are so deeply disappointed and enraged that we have not made this progress, and, in fact, backtracked on a number of things. There are, of course, some important gains we have made in terms of securing at least some meager progress on certain things. Tasneem has mentioned, for instance, other negotiating tracks. But this is not what — the progress we needed at this point. We need much, much more.

And in terms of the climate finance that we’re discussing here, I’d like to really make it clear: This is not about the Global South begging for assistance and help. And this is one of the worst things that happen at COPs. They make us feel like, OK, here we come again with our finance demands. But this is a matter of principle, as well as practicality. The principle is that they have created this problem, and they have to contribute to the solutions, including that of providing climate finance as part of the reparations for all the harm that has been caused. And the practicality is that we cannot fully transition away from fossil fuels, which we want to do. We will be one of the first people to be — to want to do that, because the impacts on us are huge and horrifying. But this is not simply possible to succeed in completing that transition if that climate finance is not delivered.

And this is a fact that they continuously leave out in their stories. And when I say “they” here, it’s the Global North. The EU, for instance, we were very appalled that they were, as Brandon said, hypocritically saying they’re going to reject the cover decision because there’s no mention of fossil fuel transition, but they leave out the fact that this is not going to happen unless they deliver on their climate finance, which they have successfully obstructed in all the negotiation tracks, any discussion on finance.

So, this leaves the Global South in a situation where we realize it’s — we really need to fight harder and build our power, because no way are these countries going to, or these governments, are going to negotiate it on the basis — negotiate on the basis of good faith, of good intention for the whole of humanity.

And by the way, it is not just for our sake that we need to complete that transition in our countries for which we need the climate finance. It’s for the entire world’s sake. We’re not going to succeed in solving the climate problem with just actions in the Global North. We know that. We need to act in the Global South, but we need to do more than our fair share. And for that to happen, we definitely need that climate finance.

So, we’re not here to beg. We are here to insist on what is owed us and to insist on what success for the whole of humanity, for the whole of the planet, what success requires.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to bring in Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner. We’ve just spoken with three well-known activists who have attended so many of the climate summits, from the Philippines, from South Africa, from the United States. Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner is also an activist, but now the climate envoy, one of the delegates, the climate envoy for the Marshall Islands. We just played a clip of you speaking. And I wanted to ask you: What was it like from the inside? And how does climate change affect the Marshall Islands, even where they are?

KATHY JETN̄IL-KIJINER: Yeah. Thank you, Amy. I’m so glad to be here, and I’m glad you were able to catch me, actually.

But I would just say that in the — it was incredibly long hours of negotiations. I mean, I didn’t sleep that whole night. I got there to swap out my minister at 7 p.m., and then I was there until we delivered our statement. And so, we were negotiating at 3:00 in the morning, at 1:00 in the morning, and then again at 5:00 in the morning. And it was long hours of discussions between ourselves, our allies within the Pacific Small Island Developing States, within the Alliance of Small Island Developing States, and, of course, other countries, too. And we were really trying to figure out how do we make our way forward and whether or not we needed to sign on to the cover decision or not sign on to the cover decision. So, it was not an easy decision at all.

But I think, ultimately, for us, this deal did not provide on fossil fuel transition that we needed. It did not have the ambition on finance, on adaptation finance. It did not have enough strong language on the ICJ. It did not recognize how incredibly monumental the ICJ was, especially for those of us in the Pacific. And then, of course, it did not have enough on any of the other components that were so important to us, on IPCC.

And so, I think, ultimately, we did decide that we needed to not sign on to the cover decision. It is the first time that Marshall Islands did that, and we did not come to that decision lightly. But I think that I stand by it, you know, and I think that it was the right call to make. I think that the two COP presidencies had an incredibly difficult task of, first of all, working together, but also working with multiple different countries and all the different priorities. But I think the biggest thing of all was that we could not sign on to a decision that had to do with CCUS, the carbon capture, utilization, storage. We did not want this COP to be a CCUS. And, of course, I think also —

AMY GOODMAN: Kathy, if you could explain what CCUS is, what these options are that are being talked about?

KATHY JETN̄IL-KIJINER: Yeah. So, I’m not a climate scientist, so I’ll just say that CCUS is actually a way to capture carbon that actually utilizes fossil fuels. So, it basically would have opened up the way for more fossil fuel usage. And ultimately, we as the Marshall Islands could not agree to a deal that would actually open the path for further fossil fuel usage and actually make the environment worse. So, that was part of the reason why we didn’t sign on.

But it was also because there was extremely weak language on adaptation finance. So, I think that’s really important, because I think what’s coming away is that a lot of countries are saying, “They walked away only because it did not have transition away from fossil fuels.” Yes, definitely, so important, and also it did not have enough on adaptation finance. Countries like mine need both. We cannot survive the climate crisis without the transition away from fossil fuels and without the needed adaptation finance for developing countries, that we’re duly owed.

You know, the Marshall Islands is only two meters above sea level. We are dealing with massive impacts from climate, from climate change, including the worst drought in El Niño, super El Niño that’s about to hit us. And then we’re looking at adaptation at such a large scale, changing the landscape of our islands, that would cost tens of billions of dollars just for two of our urban centers. And we did not cause this problem. So, of course, we are owed that finance. So, I think that’s really important to come away with, too, is that we were betrayed on two fronts: on the transition away from fossil fuels and on adaptation finance.

AMY GOODMAN: I just have to quickly ask: You are — there’s something oddly appropriate about you — I don’t think you’re in your closet. I think you’re in some kind of store. But there are pocket books everywhere, which suggest money. And maybe that’s the most appropriate way to understand what took place.

KATHY JETN̄IL-KIJINER: Yes, yeah. You caught me on my day off right after, and so I’m out actually doing a little bit of sightseeing in Antalya.

AMY GOODMAN: Amazing. I wanted to end back with Brandon Wu. You’ve returned to the United States. President Trump just had his trilateral summit, or, I should say, photograph, with President Xi of China and President Putin of Russia. And one of the deals in their so-called peace declaration was increasing the production of fossil fuels. If you can talk about what it means to come back to the historically largest emitter of carbon, of carbon pollutants in the world, after Trump just met with now the current largest producer of carbon pollutants in the world, China, and their resolution to increase oil, gas production?

BRANDON WU: Yeah, I want to say two things about that. Excuse me. First, the U.S. is actually the country with the largest oil and gas expansion plans of any country in the world. And so, if we want to point a finger at anybody, it should be our own country, you know, and, of course, in addition to being the largest historical polluter.

The second thing is that, you know, I think what this really shows is it actually comes back to the importance of a multilateral democratic process like the COPs. You know, we come away from these COPs every year saying, “Well, that was a disaster.” And then, of course, so we always ask ourselves, “What’s the point? Why are we still fighting in these places that are dominated by countries in the Global North that don’t want to do anything, that have fossil fuel lobbyists roaming the hallways? Like, why are we here? What are we accomplishing?” And I think that trilateral summit really shows us kind of what the alternative is. Right? It is a world that is dominated by autocrats, or wannabe autocrats, and strongmen, who have very little accountability. And that is what we’re up against, right? And the UNFCCC and the U.N. spaces, in general, provide an alternative to that, where everybody, at least in theory, formally has a voice, and we, as civil society, have a space to input and to protest and to advocate.

And we have to preserve that. It’s not delivering the results that we need so far, and we know why. It’s because of the intransigence of many countries, where, as Lidy said, we need to be building power. We need to be pushing these governments to do better. Certainly in the U.S., we need to be doing that. And hopefully, we’ll have that opportunity in the very near future. But, yeah, I think the alternative to these multilateral spaces are places where we have even less power, even less of a say, and have even less of an opportunity to hold leaders accountable.

AMY GOODMAN: Brandan Wu, director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA; Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, climate envoy for the Marshall Islands; Tasneem Essop, executive director of the Climate Action Network International, speaking to us from Cape Town, South Africa; Lidy Nacpil, coordinator with the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and development, speaking to us from the Philippines. We want to thank you all for being with us.

Coming up, as Democrats flip another House seat in North Carolina, we speak to Bishop William Barber. He’s calling for the Third Reconstruction. What does that mean? What is he calling on Democrats to do, who now have the largest majority in the House of Representatives in 30 years? Stay with us.

text:
Northern Michigan saw an uptick in people working in clean energy last year. That's contrary to the rest of the state, as changes to federal policies scaled back jobs in a sector that’s a key part of addressing climate change.

The numbers come from the annual Clean Jobs Midwest report, released last week by the clean energy advocacy group E2. The report uses yearly federal survey data collected by the U.S. Department of Energy.

Northern Michigan added 278 clean energy jobs last year, an increase of nearly 10 percent over 2024. Wexford County saw the most growth, followed by Kalkaska and Grand Traverse counties.

“When people think about clean energy jobs, they often picture large manufacturing facilities around Detroit, or other major population centers. But one of the things that our data shows is that that's only part of the story,” said Micaela Preskill, director of state advocacy at E2.

The majority of clean energy growth in the country is happening in rural areas, according to research. Renewable energy developers are often drawn by access to natural resources like large tracts of land or water, and northern Michigan is no exception.

In Wexford County, 250 jobs were added last year in “microgrids,” small-scale electric grids that can generate, store and provide power to a localized area, even in the event of a broader grid outage.

There are signs that the county’s industry will likely continue to grow, as the City of Cadillac seeks to convert its municipal buildings into a microgrid powered with renewable energy, using $4.4 million from the energy efficiency company Budderfly.

Michigan has ambitious clean energy goals. In counties along the Lake Michigan coastline, the state has already invested millions of dollars to boost the region’s “Blue Economy” through electric boats, which don’t use fossil fuels, and powering ports with clean energy. And a new state siting law curbs local governments’ ability to flat-out reject big solar, wind and battery projects.

Still, large-scale clean energy growth in the region faces backlash from some local residents, many who say the projects take away productive farmland.

Federal policies stall investment

Despite some jobs gains, seven other counties in northern Michigan saw decreases in clean energy jobs, mirroring the rest of the state. Preskill said the drop is a direct result of the federal policy changes that have stalled investment and reversed short-term progress.

Michigan lost about 2,000 jobs in clean energy in 2025, or a 1.5% decrease from the year prior.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025 reversed many of the clean energy policies put in place by the Biden administration — policies that led to gains in clean energy jobs across Michigan and the country.

Rebate programs for electric vehicles, heat pumps and other home energy upgrades went away. According to the report, Michigan was hit hardest by cuts to electric vehicle programs. The transportation sector saw the largest cuts, making up the majority of losses in the state.

text:
A Michigan homeowner was told by a city inspector to move two Enphase IQ 10C home batteries from the basement to an uninsulated garage. The homeowner worries that winter temperatures near minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit could damage the batteries.

Why it matters

The case highlights how battery temperature ratings and home installation rules can conflict in cold climates. Homeowners weighing battery systems may need to consider where units can safely be installed in winter.

Enphase lists full-power discharging at 32 to 122 degrees Fahrenheit and charging at 59 to 113 degrees Fahrenheit, while a commenter reported a insulated garage holding around 30 degrees Fahrenheit. Whether the uninsulated garage will stay within these limits through Michigan winters remains unknown.

The players

Enphase Energy

Enphase Energy is a California-based manufacturer of residential solar microinverters and home battery systems, including the IQ 10C battery model at issue.

The details

The homeowner's two batteries were originally installed in the basement, and a city inspector required them moved to the uninsulated garage, which shares only one wall with the house. Fire-resistant drywall is in place behind and above the batteries, and the homeowner posted on Reddit asking whether others had winterized their garages. A commenter noted that Enphase's operating limits differ from its full-power temperature ranges.

Timeline

Local temperatures have historically reached minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit in the area.

The article about the homeowner's battery relocation concern was published on November 23, 2026.

This case shows how manufacturer temperature ratings, not just local building codes, will shape where residential EV and storage systems can be placed.

Homeowners considering home batteries should check the manufacturer's minimum operating temperature against their garage's winter lows before installing. Uninsulated or poorly insulated garages may require additional planning or a different installation location.

Before installing home batteries, compare the manufacturer's minimum temperature rating with your coldest local conditions. Ask your installer and local inspector where the units can be placed safely through winter.

COP31, the annual U.N. climate conference, concluded chaotically yesterday after going into record overtime, with few meaningful commitments from world leaders even as climate impacts are rapidly worsening and the world verges on breaching 1.5 degrees Celsius of global warming.

The COP Turkish and Australian Presidencies ran a singularly inept process, and many country parties expressed their deep frustration in no uncertain terms during the final plenary. The Presidencies were unable to get agreement on their proposed Antalya Pact. The minimal negotiated outcomes do nothing to advance implementation of previous agreements related to a transition away from fossil fuels and developed countries’ climate finance obligations. Several significant agenda items were left unresolved, including details on implementing a fast, fair, funded transition away from fossil fuels and richer nations’ obligation to ensure delivery of a tripling of adaptation finance to at least $120 billion by 2035. These and other matters will now be punted to the Bonn intersessional meeting in June 2027 and COP32 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia in November 2027.

Below is a statement by Dr. Rachel Cleetus, Climate Program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS). She has been attending the U.N.’s international climate talks and partnering with the international community on climate and clean energy policies for over 20 years. Dr. Cleetus attended COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

“The failure of this COP to deliver ambitious, fair, science-based outcomes falls squarely on the shoulders of richer nations, petrostates, and the disgracefully incompetent duo of the Turkish and Australian COP presidents. This multilateral process is an essential space where all countries have a voice, but richer, more powerful countries have repeatedly abused it to trample on the rights of those on the frontlines of the climate crisis. In Antalya, these longstanding challenges were compounded by the Turkish and Australian COP Presidencies’ thoroughly inept management of the negotiations process and lack of transparency, which will go down in infamy.

“COP31’s disastrous, wholly insufficient outcome has exposed the hypocrisy of rich nations that claim to champion science while refusing to deliver on their climate finance obligations that are essential to achieve global climate goals. People in developing countries reeling from devastating climate impacts don’t need empty words about the gravity of breaching 1.5 degrees Celsius of global warming—they are already living with the harsh injustices of the long-standing failure of wealthy, major polluting countries to rein in their heat-trapping emissions. The EU and other developed countries’ flagrant refusal to agree on a clear pathway for delivering a tripling of adaptation finance or provide meaningful support for loss and damage is an ignominious indictment of their climate action grandstanding.

“Once again, Saudi Arabia, Russia and other fossil fuel enablers shamefully obstructed an ambitious agreement on implementing a fast, fair transition away from fossil fuels. Petrostates also pushed for wholly infeasible and risky Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage targets to excuse prolonging unacceptable fossil fuel expansion. Fossil fuels are the root cause of climate change and there is no plausible pathway to limit overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius without rapidly phasing them out. At the same time, some Global North countries are cynically putting forward national roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels that just reinforce the disastrous status quo. And without public finance to help lower income nations transition to clean energy while also providing energy access for the millions who do not have it today, a much-needed global transition away from fossil fuels will be elusive.

“Meanwhile, the Trump administration has disgracefully abandoned the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, attacked climate and clean energy policies and aggressively undermined global cooperation on multiple fronts while launching an illegal war and triggering a global fossil energy crisis. The newly elected U.S. Congress must hold this reckless administration in check, reverse harms where possible, and demand accountability from fossil fuel corporations that are raking in billions in profits while causing untold damage. The U.S. has a significant task ahead to rebuild trust with the global community after being such a disruptive and unreliable partner.

“The science is unmistakable on the imperative to rapidly make deep cuts in heat-trapping emissions to limit dangerous climate impacts that are already quickly, irreversibly worsening. What people across the world need is also unambiguous—a rapid, fully funded transition to renewable energy and increased climate resilience. We must keep up the pressure on political leaders to deliver real action in these international venues and back home to make a safer, more just world possible for generations to come.”

text:
There’s now a pretty good chance—about three in four, according to prediction markets—that Washington will soon take action to make it faster and cheaper to build infrastructure of all sorts. While the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act has a number of provisions addressing federal permitting rules, reforming the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) is probably the most important part. NEPA is the national environmental review law signed by President Richard Nixon in 1970. It’s often called the “Magna Carta” of environmental regulation.

But whatever the good intentions of lawmakers back then, NEPA quickly became a stunningly Down Wing law that’s made it hard in terms of time and cost to build infrastructure in this country. As I wrote in my 2023 book, The Conservative Futurist: How to Create the Sci-Fi World We Were Promised, “Whether you want to build high-speed rail, clean energy infrastructure (both power plants and transmission lines), new launch facilities for the space economy, or even structures in space, NEPA is a barrier of paperwork raised by government that does little to no good.”

Or as James Coleman, a professor of law at the University of Minnesota and a nonresident fellow here at AEI, tells me in a new Faster, Please! podcast, “We’re spending down our postwar inheritance of all the infrastructure that we built up until 1970.”

Some key points from Coleman, assuming the bill does get passed:

First, courts can no longer stop a project over a flawed environmental review: “The biggest single fix is saying that the remedy for this [a court finding that a federal agency’s NEPA review was inadequate] is just that you ask the government to go back and improve its review. In the meantime, the project can go forward.”

Second, builders and investors get some much-needed certainty: “If the federal government supports your project and brings it forward, you won’t have the courts coming in for years after the fact holding up the project. And so eliminating that uncertainty, I think, will be transformative for a number of industries.”

Third, NEPA heads back to its original purpose without undermining environmental protections: “This is not a rolling back of substantive environmental protections. It’s basically trying to speed up the [permitting] process so these [infrastructure] projects get built faster.”

Fourth, clean energy—from whatever the source—needs transmission built about 10 times faster, which requires massive reform: “That kind of change is only possible by fundamental changes to the permitting system, and that’s what this [bill] attempts to provide.”

Fifth, making it easier and cheaper to build should boost affordability without the Federal Reserve having to slow the economy: “Supply-side reforms can be transformative because that is the only way you really achieve affordability . . . and this [bill] is your classic supply-side reform that can help us lower energy prices.”

And Coleman’s bottom line: “I’m very impressed with the bill. There’s very little of it that I can say is just fundamentally a bad idea.”

text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, today released a statement urging the House to swiftly pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), legislation that would lower costs for American families and crack down on data centers that are raising utility costs for consumers and small businesses:

“For the last year, I’ve investigated AI companies for pursuing massive off-grid, emissions-heavy gas turbines to power their new data centers. And last month, the American people loudly asked Democrats to bring down their energy costs and end the free ride for data centers.

“BAAJA would end data center free-loading and require current and future data centers to pay for the upgrades to the grid that their huge electricity consumption requires, without passing off any of their costs to consumers, which they are currently doing. It’s a strong, bipartisan whack against an industry run amok.

“Democrats should not deny Americans the data center accountability they have demanded over ghost stories being told to try to deliberately mislead people.”

The Senate voted to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 by a vote of 62-33 late last week.

BAAJA would ensure that data centers pay the full cost of their associated transmission needs plus upgrades to the larger transmission network, rather than passing those costs on to families and small businesses. Grid Strategies estimates $55 billion in transmission costs could be collected from data centers over ten years due to BAAJA’s data center accountability language, which would represent $35 billion in additional costs to data centers from baseline policy.

The Institute for Progress on Friday released a timely report pushing back on misinformed speculation that the permitting reform legislation could spur the buildout of data centers on public lands. The report finds, “BAAJA has no direct effect on the laws that could authorize data centers on public lands, such as the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA). Nor does the bill prohibit any FLPMA permit from being revised pursuant to applicable law or regulation, or set aside if it illegally permitted a data center on public lands.”

In March, Senators Whitehouse, Martin Heinrich (D-NM), and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) launched an investigation into eight AI companies, including xAI, OpenAI, and Meta, regarding twelve planned data center projects that would be powered by massive new off-grid gas plants. The off-grid gas plants—many of which are ten or more times the size of the average gas plant currently powering the U.S. electric grid—would emit millions of tons of greenhouse gases and tens of thousands of tons of health-harming pollutants every year. In October, Whitehouse launched a bicameral investigation into the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) guidance exempting data center power plants from the Acid Rain Program (ARP).

BAAJA will deliver cheaper, cleaner energy, more well-paying jobs, lower electric bills, and responsible growth by accelerating the permitting and construction of critical energy and infrastructure projects while maintaining key environmental and historic preservation safeguards. The legislation provides greater certainty for projects that have already been permitted and financed, including by preventing the current and future administrations from arbitrarily revoking permits, while establishing clear timelines for environmental reviews and legal challenges. It also includes major reforms to expand and modernize the electric grid, and speed the development of geothermal, nuclear, and other energy projects. The legislation reflects input from members of both houses of Congress on both sides of the aisle and a diverse group of stakeholders.

The legislation has been endorsed by the AFL-CIO, North America’s Building Trades Unions, Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA), Evergreen Action, and Citizens’ Climate Lobby. The New York Times editorial board has urged Democrats to “take the deal” and pass the legislation, highlighting its capacity to deliver lower electricity costs and reduce emissions.
