text:
Actor and progressive activist Mark Ruffalo warned his social media followers about the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act being considered in Congress, saying the bill to loosen the permitting process for major energy projects, including data centers, would harm the environment.

This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.

In the Nov. 18 video that’s been viewed 22 million times, Ruffalo said, “Democrats in the United States Senate are on the verge of handing Trump, Republicans and the fossil fuel industry a major legislative win by passing a bill that would fast-track AI data centers, pipelines, mines, power plants, and ICE camps, while sacrificing our clean water, tribal rights, public lands, and endangered species. If it passed, it would be the most severe and devastating rollback of environmental laws in American history.”

A day after Ruffalo’s post, the bill cleared the Senate, 62-33, with 14 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent joining most Republicans in support. The vote sharply divided Senate Democrats: 30 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent voted against it.

The legislation, which President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance vouched for in a Nov. 20 news conference, must win approval in the House to advance. The House could amend the bill, which would require the Senate to approve the new text.

The uncertainty over the bill’s fate, the potential for updated language and the difficulty of predicting how courts would interpret its provisions make it difficult to know with any certainty whether the scenario Ruffalo predicts will come to pass.

As written, the bill would ease the process of building major infrastructure — including data centers — by limiting laws historically used to block such projects.

It would also accelerate the adoption of low-emission renewable energy and require data centers to pay for their increased energy use.

“There are priorities that both sides want — it is not perfect,” said Juniper Katz, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst assistant professor of public policy.

Ruffalo’s representative did not respond to an inquiry for this article.

What does the bill do, and who supports and opposes it?

The bill’s sponsors — Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia — designed it to speed up the process of securing approval for major infrastructure projects, particularly those for energy production and transmission.

The bill grew out of concerns from both fossil fuel backers and renewable energy supporters that opponents could stymie projects for years in the courts. With energy demand growing and electricity prices rising, supporters said a failure to build new infrastructure would consign the United States to a spiral of insufficient energy supplies and higher costs.

Rising electricity costs made it harder for many households to afford safe cooling during the hottest months of 2026, according to the Union of Concerned Scientists.

Nearly 95% of people in the lower 48 states faced major or extreme heat risk at least once during that six-month period.

Here's what to know

Moderate or greater heat risk covered as much as 63% of the contiguous United States during the May-through-October "Danger Season," the UCS reported on its blog, The Equation.

Seven episodes, each lasting several days, affected at least 30% of the region.

People without access to cooling or hydration face particular danger from major or extreme heat risk, the National Weather Service warns. Archived records from the agency's Heat Risk Tool put the share of the population exposed to those conditions at 94.6%.

An analysis by Climate Central found that 233 of 241 major U.S. cities had cooling degree days averaging 37% above their 1970s levels. The measure tracks temperatures above 65 degrees Fahrenheit to gauge cooling demand.

Meanwhile, the U.S. Energy Information Administration estimated that residential electricity consumption in July through September exceeded the corresponding 2025 figure by 6%, partly because of hotter weather.

More background

Millions of households reported uncomfortably hot homes despite having cooling equipment.

The UCS cited census figures showing that roughly 9.2 million American households lacked air conditioning in 2023. Spending at least 6% of household income on home energy is considered a high energy burden.

A UCS analysis using 2022 figures that the Energy Equity Project prepared with the Department of Energy's Low-Income Energy Affordability Data tool found substantially greater average burdens among lower-income households.

Power failures compound the danger.

After an August 2026 derecho — a widespread storm with powerful straight-line winds — some residents of the predominantly Black city of Gary, Indiana, went without electricity for two to three weeks.

Without air conditioning, residents faced borderline-dangerous indoor temperatures nearing 85 degrees.

The EIA projects that average residential electricity prices will rise another 2.6% in 2027, bringing them nearly 8% above 2025 levels.

What can be done?

The Union of Concerned Scientists highlighted two existing federal programs that, if strengthened, could help more households.

The Weatherization Assistance Program helps lower-income households improve home efficiency and reduce energy costs, while the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program helps households manage energy expenses.

The UCS also calls for expanded access to affordable cooling and community solar.

Combining renewable generation with energy storage can maintain essential electricity supplies for homes, community facilities, and microgrids during wider outages.

Stronger utility-disconnection protections could also help prevent households from losing power when a shutoff poses a health risk. Investment in the power grid is particularly important in communities that have received fewer infrastructure improvements.

UCS research points to carefully planned, climate-resilient electricity systems as a way to reduce disparities in energy burdens, with affected communities helping determine where investments go.

For housing and energy advocate Mary Wambui, the benefits of these investments extend beyond the households facing the steepest bills.

In a conversation recounted by UCS, she said, "Equity is for everyone."

November 23, 2026

SAN FRANCISCO (Nov. 23, 2026) – Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced eight settlements with eight companies operating California and Arizona facilities, resolving alleged violations of chemical safety requirements under the Clean Air Act. The settlements involve the companies’ anhydrous ammonia and chlorine gas handling at various facilities, all of which will come into compliance with the safety regulations.

“Too many companies handling large quantities of dangerous chemicals are not fully aware of federal safety requirements and the serious consequences of accidental releases,” said EPA Pacific Southwest Regional Administrator Mike Martucci. “These EPA actions will ensure facilities are working to keep our communities safe by meeting standards required by law.”

EPA’s action is enforcing the Risk Management Plan (RMP) chemical safety requirements of the Clean Air Act’s Section 112(r). In addition to returning to compliance, the companies have collectively agreed to pay penalties totaling over $1.3 million.

Background

The goal of Section 112(r) of the Clean Air Act is to reduce the risk of chemical accidents. Facilities that house over 10,000 lbs of anhydrous ammonia or over 2,500 lbs of chlorine gas must comply with RMP requirements designed to prevent and prepare for accidental chemical releases.

Anhydrous ammonia presents significant health and safety hazards as it is corrosive to the skin, eyes, and lungs. Exposure to 300 parts per million is immediately dangerous to life and health. Ammonia is also flammable at concentrations of approximately 16% to 25% by volume in air and can explode if released in an enclosed space with a source of ignition present, or if a vessel containing anhydrous ammonia is exposed to fire.

Chlorine is a gas used in the production of thousands of products and for water disinfection. Exposure to 10 parts per million is immediately dangerous to life and health and can result in changes in breathing rate, coughing, and lung damage.

Ohio regulators just greenlit construction of a big gas plant to power a data center complex, despite local residents’ overwhelming rejection of the projects in this month’s elections.

The permit approval itself is not unique: Around the U.S., energy-hungry data center developers are racing ahead with controversial plans to build natural gas–fired generation. But critics of the recent Ohio ruling say it highlights the state’s leniency toward fossil-fuel projects compared with its tight restrictions on solar and wind farms, which are often denied permits due to local opposition.

“There’s a huge double standard for fossil fuels and renewables in the state of Ohio,” said state Rep. Tristan Rader, a Democrat who serves as ranking minority member on the Ohio House Energy Committee and took part in the case as a nonvoting member of the Ohio Power Siting Board.

The gas plant in question is an 800-megawatt facility to be built at a data center complex under development in the central Ohio village of Ashville. As of now, the plant won’t be connected to the grid at large and will serve just the computing warehouses. The project site is close to homes, as well as a playground, park, and soccer field, Rader noted.

“This plant is literally going to be throwing a shadow on these communities,” while spewing health-harming pollution, Rader said during the Power Siting Board’s Nov. 19 meeting. Yet Ohio has more stringent requirements for wind and solar, which emit zero air pollution.

Ashville’s Village Council passed a resolution in April to back the data center and gas plant project, after its developer, EdgeConneX, agreed to pay up to $102 million to support municipal, school, and community work. But the deal didn’t sit well with some residents, who gathered enough signatures for a referendum on whether to overturn the resolution.

On Election Day, Ashville was one of dozens of U.S. communities to reject data centers, with 81% of the village’s voters opposing the local government’s agreement with EdgeConneX.

Even so, the Power Siting Board’s decision OK’ing the gas plant finds that the developer met a statutory requirement that the project is in the public interest. Regulators pointed to factors like the project’s economic benefits, backing from the Village Council and local school district, and the developer’s promises to limit noise and construction hours.

That’s sparked frustration from clean energy advocates in the state. The board has denied multiple solar projects on the basis that local opposition outweighs economic benefits or has proposed permit conditions aimed at addressing community concerns, said Chris Tavenor, general counsel for the Ohio Environmental Council, which was not a party to the case.

“In this case, the Board does the exact opposite, using those community benefits and conditions to justify ignoring local concerns,” he said in an email.

In this decision and those pertaining to renewable energy, critics take issue with the Power Siting Board’s deference to local governments, even when evidence shows they are not necessarily reflecting the wishes of the broader public.

In 2025, for example, the Power Siting Board’s staff recommended against the Grange Solar project in Logan County on the basis of pushback from local governments. But a majority of individuals who submitted comments wanted the solar farm. The developer ultimately withdrew its plan and opted to pursue projects elsewhere.

And earlier this year, regulators nixed the Crossroads Solar farm in Morrow County because all nearby local governments opposed the project. Although that ruling noted the ​“presence of strong, united opposition” among the local population, dozens of comments were apparently fake, and an analysis by the developer found that the number of verifiable individuals against the project was not overwhelming in comparison with its supporters.

The board’s staff also did an about-face from supporting Crossroads Solar to opposing it after one township changed its position from neutral to opposed.

“Ultimately, the Ohio Power Siting Board has demonstrated its hypocrisy,” Tavenor said, ​“by approving a natural gas facility for a data center where it has denied renewable energy projects with less significant opposition.”

Regulators, for their part, acknowledged the Ashville vote in their decision but asserted that they have authority to issue the permit regardless of the outcome of the election. The 108-page opinion also says that conditions agreed to by the village, the developer, and the board staff were enough to deal with public concerns.

The board also gave short shrift to opponents’ argument that the gas plant proposal fails to meet a separate legal requirement that projects have minimal environmental impact. Its take stems from the fact that the developer opted for reciprocating internal combustion engines and simple-cycle natural gas turbines over less-polluting combined-cycle turbines or fuel cells, which are more expensive right now.

Regulatory staff argued that ​“minimum” doesn’t demand the lowest environmental impact but depends on a plant’s purpose, available technology, and economics. The board decided that the project meets the requirement, basically punting to the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency’s expected issuance of air permits for the facility.

Project opponents have 30 days to ask for reconsideration of the ruling. Unless the Power Siting Board changes its mind, an appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court could follow.

A day after Ruffalo’s post, the bill cleared the Senate, 62-33, with 14 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent joining most Republicans in support. The vote sharply divided Senate Democrats: 30 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent voted against it.

The legislation, which President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance vouched for in a Nov. 20 news conference, must win approval in the House to advance. The House could amend the bill, which would require the Senate to approve the new text.

The uncertainty over the bill’s fate, the potential for updated language and the difficulty of predicting how courts would interpret its provisions make it difficult to know with any certainty whether the scenario Ruffalo predicts will come to pass.

As written, the bill would ease the process of building major infrastructure — including data centers — by limiting laws historically used to block such projects.

It would also accelerate the adoption of low-emission renewable energy and require data centers to pay for their increased energy use.

“There are priorities that both sides want — it is not perfect,” said Juniper Katz, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst assistant professor of public policy.

Ruffalo’s representative did not respond to an inquiry for this article.

What does the bill do, and who supports and opposes it?

The bill’s sponsors — Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia — designed it to speed up the process of securing approval for major infrastructure projects, particularly those for energy production and transmission.

The bill grew out of concerns from both fossil fuel backers and renewable energy supporters that opponents could stymie projects for years in the courts. With energy demand growing and electricity prices rising, supporters said a failure to build new infrastructure would consign the United States to a spiral of insufficient energy supplies and higher costs.

Critics of the bill say it effectively guts tools to prevent local governments and citizens, Native American tribes, and other local interests from blocking the harms caused by such projects. They also say the Trump administration, which refuses to acknowledge the possibility of emissions-driven climate change, could wield the law to advance fossil fuel projects over renewable energy infrastructure.

It has the support of some renewable energy groups such as the Solar Energy Industries Association and the AFL-CIO labor union, the American Petroleum Institute and the Edison Electric Institute, which represents utilities.

Groups opposing the bill include the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Climate Justice Alliance, a range of tribal organizations, the NAACP and the American Civil Liberties Union.

Why are environmentalists concerned?

Certain laws that have long been used to oppose big projects — including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act — would be pared back if the new law is enacted.

The Natural Resources Defense Council’s analysis concluded that under the bill, a court “can never invalidate a permit” based on a violation of the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act, “no matter how severe it finds a legal violation to be.” It also found that the bill would exclude certain types of environmentally harmful activities from review and limit who can bring a case.

In most cases, the bill would prevent federal agencies from canceling, suspending or changing federal permits for projects that have received all necessary permits.

“It is reasonable to be concerned that the development of each of the kinds of projects (Ruffalo) mentioned could be facilitated by this bill,” said Geoffrey Henderson, a University of Michigan assistant professor of environmental policy and planning.

Opponents also worry the bill could allow the Trump administration to lock in fossil fuel projects or data centers without enough opportunity for opponents to challenge them.

“If the Trump administration issued a blanket grant of all permits for oil and gas infrastructure without any environmental review, the bill provides no clear mechanism for a future administration to revoke those permits,” the NRDC analysis says.

As for Ruffalo’s reference to detention facilities for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the bill does not directly address those, but opponents of the bill say their concerns stem from the use of the National Environmental Policy Act to oppose ICE facilities in court in Maryland, Arizona and Florida.

How does the bill advance environmentalists’ goals?

Although the Natural Resources Defense Council opposes the bill in its current form, its analysis devotes almost 1,000 words to describing what it considers the bill’s positive features, including:

The bill would improve the nation’s electric capacity in two ways: by increasing how much power existing transmission lines can carry and by enabling construction of new lines. The bill could cut the time to build a major new transmission line from 10-plus years to five or six.

While fossil fuels and data centers could benefit from the bill’s changes, renewable energy — including solar, wind and geothermal energy — would benefit more. “Approximately 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage.”

The bill includes a provision that requires data centers to pay for their impact on electricity supply rather than shifting those costs to ratepayers. (Critics say this response is insufficient if the new rules promote data centers being built in the first place.)

One of the bill’s highest-profile supporters is The New York Times columnist Ezra Klein, who is considered left of center politically.

In a recent column, Klein said he was “unnerved” by conflicting interpretations over what certain provisions of the bill mean, but still supported it.

“The problem, right now, is that we cannot meet enough new demand — whether from data centers or electric vehicles or heat pumps or anything else — with renewables,” Klein wrote. “What the act might make possible is the construction of an energy grid where there is enough renewable power to meet new demand. In the absence of that energy system, new demand would be met by fossil fuels. And the absence of that system describes our reality today.”

The bill could also boost non-energy projects that have faced long-running challenges in the courts, Klein wrote, including rail and transit, affordable housing and broadband access.

Ultimately, Henderson said, the bill’s impacts “are highly uncertain, depending on a mix of political outcomes (who controls the federal government and what decisions they make), market outcomes (competition between electricity sources domestically), geopolitical outcomes (such as global demand for the United States’ oil and gas exports), and legal outcomes (courts’ interpretation of the law).”

title: COP31 ends with no deal after negotiators fail to reach an agreement on fossil fuels - WVXU
authors: Rachel Waldholz, Steve Inskeep, www.wvxu.org, steve-inskeep
description:
Nearly 200 nations typically commit to some statement on the next steps to address climate change.
But oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia blocked any mention of fossil fuels in the final agreement.
Ultimately, the EU decided that getting no deal at this summit was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels at all.
And wealthy countries, who are most responsible for climate change, agreed to provide funding as part of the Paris Climate Agreement.
But given how key fossil fuels are still to most economies, that's a big shift.
text:
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:

Delegates from around the world walked away from a climate summit over the weekend after failing to agree on a plan.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

Yes, this annual meeting has taken place since 1995. Nearly 200 nations typically commit to some statement on the next steps to address climate change. This time, even going overtime did not lead to an agreement.

INSKEEP: NPR's Rachel Waldholz also went into overtime. Is that right, Rachel?

RACHEL WALDHOLZ, BYLINE: Yes, indeed, Steve.

INSKEEP: OK. She's still in Turkey. What caused the talks there to break down?

WALDHOLZ: Well, countries came into these talks with a lot of disagreements, but the issue that really pushed this conference over the edge was the question of how to address fossil fuels. Many countries wanted a final agreement that explicitly called for a global transition away from coal and oil and natural gas as the primary drivers of climate change. And that included especially many small island states - Panama, the European Union. But oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia blocked any mention of fossil fuels in the final agreement. Ultimately, the EU decided that getting no deal at this summit was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels at all. Darragh O'Brien is Ireland's environment minister.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

DARRAGH O'BRIEN: It fails to meet the moment. The moment that our world faces, the crisis that our world faces.

WALDHOLZ: And he said that's especially true in a year that has seen climate-fueled disasters all over the globe, from heat waves and wildfires in Europe to the massive flooding in Nepal.

INSKEEP: Was the mention of fossil fuels the only thing they disagreed about?

WALDHOLZ: Oh, it is never only one thing, Steve. And the other big sticking point at the summit was money. Developing countries want more help dealing with climate change. They point out that they've contributed very little to global warming but are often dealing with some of the worst impacts. And wealthy countries, who are most responsible for climate change, agreed to provide funding as part of the Paris Climate Agreement. Kathy Jetnil-Kijiner - she represents the Pacific Island nation of the Marshall Islands, and she called on rich countries to follow through on their promises.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KATHY JETNIL-KIJINER: We cannot do this on our own. We cannot survive on empty promises. People are dying. Seas are rising. Ecosystems are collapsing.

WALDHOLZ: And, of course, one big, wealthy country that wasn't at the climate talks is the U.S. The Trump administration has withdrawn from the international climate negotiations.

INSKEEP: OK. So what does it mean when the various countries of the world can't seem to agree on anything big, even if the U.S. - which has its own issues - is not there?

WALDHOLZ: Yeah. It certainly raises questions about how effective the U.N. process can be for dealing with an issue like climate change. But actually, you know, what's interesting is that some of the biggest defenders of this COP system are the smaller countries and developing countries. They see it as one of the places where they can have a say and be heard. Mohamed Adow leads the nonprofit Power Shift Africa, which is based in Nairobi.

MOHAMED ADOW: It's the only process we have where the least developed countries, the small island states, have a voice and are able to provide that much-needed moral leadership.

WALDHOLZ: You know, one interesting development at these climate talks is that countries have begun forming these side deals, these kinds of coalitions of the willing. Countries including France and Germany and Spain have rolled out these roadmaps to leave behind fossil fuels entirely. These are voluntary. A lot of them are pretty squishy. They don't have that many specifics. But given how key fossil fuels are still to most economies, that's a big shift.

INSKEEP: OK. NPR's Rachel Waldholz in Turkey. Thanks so much.

WALDHOLZ: Thank you. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

title: California Needs Science And Politics Free From Corporate Influence
description:
Leading up to the 2026 midterms, a small number of powerful people spent staggering amounts of money to influence the election.
Industrial agribusinesses are more concerned with protecting their bottom lines and maintaining California’s resource-intensive and unsustainable agricultural system, while communities, public health, and local economies pay the price.
What must come next: science-based policymaking free from corporate influence To help see past the disinformation and deliberate deception on such complex issues, UCS works to ensure that independent science, free from corporate or political bias, can guide decision-making.
Even with these new opportunities, issues like climate change, energy affordability, and sustainable land use remain complex.
When we put science at the center of the policy process, we can build a California that is more affordable, healthier, and fairer.
text:
My daughter, 6 years old, likes to sit with me as I fill in my mail-in ballots. Maybe she’s motivated by the beautifully designed “I voted” sticker from the City and County of San Francisco’s Department of Elections. Maybe filling out the circles on the ballot looks like the worksheets that she’s used to doing at school. But I also hope she’s curious about what the adults are doing around Election Day.

I try to bring her into why we vote, understanding who the candidates are, what the issues are, and how we vote. Living in San Francisco, I start with an issue that is local and easy to explain to a 1st grader. I explain how some people want to use an area next to the ocean as a highway for driving cars, some people want to use it as a park for playing, and San Franciscans choose between the two options by voting.

Which has happened three times in her lifetime, in 2022, 2024, and 2026.

Many San Francisco voters are probably exhausted by this issue coming back again and again on our ballots, but I have some appreciation that a lesson is easier to teach to your kid when you can repeat it a few times.

Who else showed up?

But my explanation of how we vote left out who else showed up in the election.

Leading up to the 2026 midterms, a small number of powerful people spent staggering amounts of money to influence the election. The top 20 megadonors spent $2 billion on federal races in this year’s election. In California, ultra-wealthy donors spent $378 million to defeat a proposition that would have taxed the state’s few hundred billionaires to fill the gap left by federal Medi-Cal cuts. There’s no sticker to record their participation in the election. If there were, it would say, “We spent billions to influence votes.”

The influence extends beyond elections, as those with extreme wealth and power are using disinformation to influence the policy fights. Oil companies try to shift the blame for the affordability crisis away from their own sky-high markups to California regulations designed to keep people safe and preserve a healthy environment. After decades of fossil fuel companies misleading the public about their products’ contributions to climate change and blocking climate action, we now know that 94% of industrial CO2 emissions since 1959 trace to just 122 oil, gas, coal, and cement companies.

Tech companies are resisting protections for children and consumers, while forcing data centers on communities where the pollution, noise, and energy costs are not welcome. Industrial agribusinesses are more concerned with protecting their bottom lines and maintaining California’s resource-intensive and unsustainable agricultural system, while communities, public health, and local economies pay the price.

What must come next: science-based policymaking free from corporate influence

To help see past the disinformation and deliberate deception on such complex issues, UCS works to ensure that independent science, free from corporate or political bias, can guide decision-making. The midterm elections opened up opportunities with the 120th Congress and with states to prioritize the public good over distortion of facts and to continue the work to protect democracy, science and public institutions.

Even with these new opportunities, issues like climate change, energy affordability, and sustainable land use remain complex. In California, leaders including the newly elected Governor Becerra will have to tackle challenging questions.

Addressing energy affordability in California needs to include reducing risk of future wildfires, paying for the costs of wildfires that have already ravaged communities, and transitioning to an electricity system that no longer exacerbates climate change. Read my colleague Mark Specht’s piece on the seven energy priorities for our Governor-Elect.

We can—and must—tackle unfair gas prices without sacrificing environmental progress. Read my colleague Jeremy Martin’s piece outlining a path to taking on the oil monopoly and restoring fair competition.

Despite federal attacks on California’s authority to regulate air pollution, we have effective options to transition to clean transportation to save Californians money at the pump, while avoiding the worst public health and climate impacts. My colleague Don Anair lays out a bold agenda for California’s new governor to target the most polluting vehicles on the road and make electric cars more affordable for more people.

As California transitions away from unsustainable agricultural practices, communities need to be in the driver’s seat, leading a coordinated transition towards thriving and resilient local economies. Read my colleague Erin Wooolley’s piece to hear more about the multiple benefits that can be achieved with a just cropland transition and how to focus resources and coordinate planning to achieve transformational change.

These are all hard problems with no easy solutions. In each of these linked posts, my colleagues at UCS sift through the noise of unfounded claims to understand real trade-offs and feasible solutions. When we put science at the center of the policy process, we can build a California that is more affordable, healthier, and fairer. Whether in Sacramento or Washington, DC, decisions should be grounded in evidence, not in the interest of the biggest donors.

title: Statement by Elizabeth Yee, Executive Vice President of Programs, on Outcome of COP31 Talks
description:
Like many, The Rockefeller Foundation is disappointed that countries were unable to reach consensus at COP31.
Global consensus matters, especially when people around the world are feeling the effects of extreme weather, pollution, and rising food and energy costs.
But the outcome shouldn’t obscure an important point of consensus: Nations are not divided on the need to electrify.

text:
Like many, The Rockefeller Foundation is disappointed that countries were unable to reach consensus at COP31. Global consensus matters, especially when people around the world are feeling the effects of extreme weather, pollution, and rising food and energy costs. But the outcome shouldn’t obscure an important point of consensus: Nations are not divided on the need to electrify. The disagreement lies in how, and how quickly, economies move away from fossil fuels.

That distinction is important. Climate negotiations at COP have historically focused on subtraction — which emissions are cut, by whom and how much. That is a difficult conversation to resolve amongst 200 nations. Building clean power for people is different because it’s additive. It means new grids, new jobs, and new businesses–as well as lower emissions. It is a policy of economic growth, and growth is a goal that communities and leaders can align behind.

Today, 655 million people still live without access to reliable electricity. Energy poverty rarely exists on its own — most energy-insecure people experience another form of poverty, such as in health, education, or food security. Our research shows that if today’s energy-poor countries are left behind, their share of global emissions could rise from 25% in 2020 to 75% by 2050. How the world brings electricity to these communities is not a side issue in the climate debate; it is central to it.

Progress on electrification will not come from negotiated text alone. It will come from capital, most importantly from lowering its cost and increasing accessibility. Clean energy projects in emerging economies often cost more to finance than in wealthier countries. Closing that gap will unlock investment at the scale that electrification goals require.

The Rockefeller Foundation will continue to deploy grants and catalytic finance that take on early risk so others can follow, in particular supporting grid finance that makes larger-scale investment possible. Philanthropy cannot fund the energy transition alone, but it can help make it investible.

We are grateful to everyone who worked toward an agreement at COP31. The consensus on electrification is strong, and the task is now to finance it.

text:
The first cells are being shipped to Louisville Assembly Plant for use in Ford Fathom prototypes. Ford said the milestone makes it the first company to manufacture LFP batteries in the US for mainstream consumer automotive applications while also building expertise that can be applied to its growing energy storage activities.

LFP Focus for Lower-Cost EVs

According to Ford, the development programme centred on identifying an LFP prismatic battery technology that could help reduce EV costs while supporting large-scale manufacturing.

The company selected technology from CATL, whose batteries are used in millions of vehicles globally. Ford highlighted LFP chemistry’s lack of nickel and cobalt as a key factor in lowering costs, while also pointing to the chemistry’s durability through years of charging and use.

Battery durability is expected to play a role in vehicle-to-home energy applications. Ford noted that AC bidirectional power can enable a vehicle to receive electricity from a suitably equipped home and supply power back when required.

Prismatic Cells and Structural Pack Design

Ford engineered the Fathom platform around battery efficiency, using prismatic cells and incorporating the battery pack as a structural part of the vehicle. Rather than acting solely as an enclosure, the pack contributes to the vehicle chassis.

The company said the rectangular cell format allows cells to fit directly into the structure, helping to reduce structural costs. Electrical and sensing connections have also been combined into a flexible circuit board, while compact power electronics have been integrated into the pack.

Scaling Battery Manufacturing

Beyond cell design, Ford is focusing on high-volume production. The assembly lines at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan are capable of producing 40 cells per minute, making the facility one of the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly operations outside China.

To support quality control, employees use AI-powered image recognition and other inspection tools to identify defects during production.

Ford said the experience gained in Michigan is also being applied to preparations for battery energy storage production in Glendale, Kentucky. While the end products and customer base will differ from the automotive sector, the company believes the manufacturing expertise, controls and battery know-how developed through the programme will support both businesses in the future.

text:
Although the NRC issued the project’s initial license in 1998, facility construction never began. The project has faced opposition since the license approval; most recently, in July of this year, the New Mexico Department of Justice filed a petition to intervene in the CUP license renewal process with the NRC, noting that the project sites extend into Navajo Nation land and calling for assurances that the project will meet the state’s standards for groundwater protection. That petition is still being adjudicated as of this writing.

History of the CUP: The license for the CUP was initially held by another company, Hydro Resources, which filed its application with the NRC in 1988. The NRC issued the construction and operation license for the CUP a decade later, after which, according to NRC documentation, the project stalled because of ongoing litigation, fluctuations in the market for uranium, and negotiations regarding the facility between Hydro Resources and the Navajo Nation.

Hydro Resources submitted its first license renewal request for the project in 2002; however, delays persisted for similar reasons. The CUP license was transferred to NuFuels in 2018, and in 2024, the NRC requested a revised license renewal application from the current license holder.

Recent regulatory actions: NuFuels submitted the revised renewal application for the CUP in January 2025. Along with providing an updated environmental report, it also incorporated parts of the previous licensing history into its application as allowed by 10 CFR Part 51. The NRC published its notice of the application on May 27, 2026.

Two months later, the NMDOJ filed its petition to intervene, listing 10 environmental contentions and three safety contentions. Among its environmental contentions, the state claimed that NuFuels’ environmental report failed to demonstrate the feasibility of restoring the Westwater Canyon aquifer below the project areas, relied on outdated hydrogeological models, and lacked any references to the Navajo Nation’s legal prohibitions. In its safety contentions, the state claimed that NuFuels’ mine design and characterization, assessments of existing boreholes, and financial guarantees were inadequate.

NuFuels and the NRC both submitted their responses to New Mexico’s petition on August 21. While NuFuels argued that none of the state’s contentions were admissible, the NRC stated that it found six of the environmental contentions and two of the safety contentions admissible and recommended that the Atomic Safety and Licensing Board grant the petition in part.

A panel from the board held a hearing with representatives from NuFuels and the NMDOJ as well as NRC staff on October 5. During the session, it was noted that the NRC had amended its position on one of the safety contentions and no longer considered the claim regarding NuFuels’ financial guarantees admissible.

This was not the only change potentially made regarding the contentions in New Mexico’s petition. At the end of the hearing, panel chair Michael Gibson confirmed that the November publication of the draft EA would give the NMDOJ 30 days to submit new and amended contentions. The state has yet to file such contentions as of this writing.

A ban and a moratorium: NuFuels’ license renewal application comes as New Mexico and the Navajo Nation continue to deal with the legacy of uranium mining in the Southwest, going back to the first such activity on Navajo land in 1944.

In August of this year, New Mexico land commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard issued a ban on new uranium mining projects and related activities on state lands, calling on the State Land Office to direct its attention instead to cleaning up and restoring the state’s legacy uranium mine sites, which total more than 1,000.

More recently, at the 2026 ANS Winter Conference & Expo, the panel “Uranium Mine Remediation: Past, Present, and Future” examined the history of uranium mining on Navajo land in New Mexico and Arizona, which saw approximately 30 million tons of uranium ore extracted between 1944 and 1986. As a result of this activity, Navajo land now contains 523 abandoned uranium mines, where uranium waste rock sits on the surface; 230 of these sites have not been provided funding for cleanup.

The Diné Natural Resources Protection Act, which the Navajo Nation Council passed in 2005, stands as a response to this history. The act established a moratorium that prohibits uranium mining and milling on Navajo land—including land where NuFuels seeks to establish the CUP.

text:
The $7,500 federal tax credit for electric vehicles expired on September 30, 2025, after U.S. EV market share peaked at nearly 12% that month. Market share has since fallen to under 6%, and EV sales dropped 20% in January compared with December.

Why it matters

Without the credit, EVs cost roughly $5,000 more than comparable petrol cars, pricing out many buyers. Automakers that invested heavily in EV factories and technology are absorbing billions in write-offs as demand softens.

U.S. EV market share peaked near 12% in September 2025 and later fell below 6%, while the federal credit was $7,500 per vehicle. Analysts expect 2026 EV sales to be flat, and it remains unclear how much of the drop is tied to the credit's expiry alone.

The players

Tesla

Tesla is an American electric vehicle and clean energy company, and a leading EV maker that is offering 0% financing on its Model Y.

General Motors

General Motors is a Detroit-based automaker that has continued to prioritize hybrid vehicles as its EV demand softens.

Ford

Ford Motor Company is a Detroit-based automaker that remains committed to hybrids and plans a smaller electric truck.

The details

The Biden-era goal of having half of new vehicles be electric by 2030 was revoked under a tax-and-spending bill signed by President Trump. Tesla is offering 0% financing on its Model Y, while General Motors and Ford remain committed to hybrids.

Timeline

September 30, 2025: The federal $7,500 EV tax credit expired.

September 2025: EV market share peaked near 12%.

January 2026: EV sales dropped 20% from December.

2026: Analysts expect EV sales to remain flat for the year.

2028: Ford plans a smaller electric truck reportedly priced around $30,000.

Roadmap

The expiration of the $7,500 federal credit, once a central pillar of U.S. EV adoption under the Inflation Reduction Act, has exposed how dependent demand was on subsidies. The shift marks a sharp reversal from the Biden-era goal of electric vehicles making up half of new vehicle sales by 2030.

Without the $7,500 credit, buyers face roughly $5,000 more in upfront cost compared with petrol cars, making EVs harder to afford. Shoppers weighing a purchase may find deals such as Tesla's 0% Model Y financing more relevant than the removed federal incentive.

The takeaway

Buyers considering an EV should compare total cost after the credit's expiration, including financing offers, rather than relying on pre-September 2025 pricing.

text:
Nevada’s Democratic US Senators were split on a controversial bill that would make it easier to build large-scale infrastructure projects on public land.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act passed the Senate on November 19, 62–33.

The federal permitting reform bill is designed to speed up environmental reviews and approvals for energy, transmission, and infrastructure projects across the United States by changing the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and preservation laws meant to protect the country's natural and tribal history.

The bill is more than 400 pages long and drastically modifies the process for approving large-scale development on federally owned land across the country.

According to one of the bill's sponsors, Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from New Mexico, all of it is part of an effort to make energy development cheaper.

"[Voters] want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable," said Heinrich. "And that's precisely what this permitting reform bill will do. BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, so families have money in their pockets for more than just keeping the lights on and their homes warm. This bill directly holds data centers accountable, forcing big corporations to pay their full share instead of pushing costs on the consumers. That one provision is worth $35 billion to American households. That's pretty remarkable. BAAJA will create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, good-paying jobs that workers can be certain will be around to support their families through a project's completion. BAAJA will cut emissions in the power sector by up to 20% over the next decade, meaning cleaner air, healthier communities, and lower healthcare costs.

Nevada’s Senior Senator Catherine Cortez Masto voted against the bill. In a statement, she said it contains harmful changes to the National Historic Preservation Act that undermine Tribal sovereignty and fail to protect government-to-government Tribal consultation.

Senator Jacky Rosen, on the other hand, voted for the legislation. She says it will, among other things, strengthen American energy independence.

“As the state with the most solar jobs per capita and an abundance of geothermal and other clean energy sources, Nevada stands to greatly benefit from increased investments in renewable energy projects that create good-paying jobs and lower energy costs, all while reducing carbon emissions," said Rosen in a statement. "Unfortunately, current government red tape has made it nearly impossible to bring these clean energy projects online, which is why sensible reforms like this bipartisan bill are needed. While further improvements can and should be made to strengthen this bill, we cannot squander the opportunity to deliver results and lower costs for families.”

But what do conservation and environmental groups make of the legislation?

"This kind of eliminates many of the options we have to weigh as a public on whether that's the right place for a transmission line or a data center," said Jocelyn Torres, chief Conservation officer, Conservation Lands Foundation. "All of those right decisions that our community really has been facing here in the last couple of months, [this bill is] just eliminating the processes to have that science-based information to make those decisions, weakening or removing options for public engagement within that, and really eliminating that tribal consultation piece."

The bill now heads to the U.S. House of Representatives.

text:
The clearest message from the recent United Nations annual climate change conference was that the world must increase its use of electricity in global energy consumption from its current level of 23 percent to 35 percent by 2035, under a “35 by 35 Global Electrification Pledge.”

The 31st Conference of the Parties, or COP31, officially wrapped up in the southern city of Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 20, but the negotiations ran two extra nights, making it the longest COP ever. The conference ended without a mutual agreement to meet the electrification pledge, among other issues.

In the early hours of Nov. 22, the Turkish climate minister and COP31 co-president, Murat Kurum, announced that COP31 had failed to reach a final “cover decision,” the overarching political statement adopted at the end of every COP. COPs meet annually to focus the world on implementing the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

In Antalya, Australia’s climate minister and COP31 co-president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, pointed to “unbridgeable red lines” and called the geopolitical environment around this COP “the most complicated and fraught in living memory.”

He said, “Things that were manageable in the past, in previous COPs like the last two where people wanted certain words mentioned but didn’t get them, it became a red line this time.”

During the 12-day gathering, negotiations on the electrification goal were deadlocked mainly over omission of references to fossil fuels and climate finance obligations.

A third and 94-paragraph draft deal, technically the final version, was published in the early hours of Nov. 22. It was rejected by the European Union, Panama and highly vulnerable nations like the Marshall Islands, on the grounds of being “‘unconscionable” and failing to especially address fossil fuels. Although the co-presidents attributed the omission of the language “transition from fossil fuels” to and that the global commitment to it was established in the COP28 Dubai agreement, Saudi Arabia and other large oil producers reportedly blocked any mention of phasing out coal, oil and gas in the final COP31 draft.

Every COP decision requires consensus from the nearly 200 participating nations and territories, meaning they can abstain from active support without blocking the decision, provided they do not formally object. The omission of fossil fuels in draft agreements became common practice in COP talks until just a few years ago. The omission this year, which led to the breakdown of talks, laid bare a basic impediment to UN climate negotiations, which rely on decision-making by consensus, according to the Washington-based Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL).

While acknowledging the need for COPs and their multilateral nature to manage global warming, Nikki Reisch, the director of the climate and energy program at CIEL, said in a statement that “because those with the money won’t pay, those with the oil won’t give it up, and those most responsible refuse to answer for the harm they’ve caused.

The fact that any one of them can hold collective action hostage is part of the problem. . . . Decision-making that requires every country to agree on every comma is not fit for a climate emergency.”

Pushing an electric future

Backed by analysis from the International Energy Agency (IEA), a Paris-based intergovernmental organization established in 1974 after the 1973 oil crisis, and the Abu Dhabi-based intergovernmental organization International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), which supports countries to transition to sustainable and renewable energy, the pledge on electrification was seen as much-needed progress and glimmer of hope for the Antalya COP.

As of Nov. 22, around 90 countries and 180 business and civil society organizations had taken the voluntary 35 by 35 electrification pledge regardless of a final agreement.

The UN says the pledge’s implementation initiative, COP31 Electrification Delivery Package, announced on Nov. 19, covers action by 150-plus countries and the European Union, 37 cities and over 260 businesses. Electricity grids of 21,000-plus kilometers were deployed in 2025 by members of the Utilities for Net Zero Alliance. Annual investment plans totaling $156 billion were announced for grids, renewables and energy storage by the alliance.

In some rural parts of Africa, cooking with fossil fuels, such as coal, firewood and dung, emit as much carbon yearly as the world’s entire airline and shipping industry combined, according to the IEA, leading to 2.5 million premature deaths worldwide of mostly women and children.

Electrification initiatives such as Clean Cooking Africa use renewable-powered high-efficiency appliances like induction stoves, electric pressure cookers, hot plates powered by national grids, solar mini-grids and rooftop solars. Pairing smart electrification directly with new clean power would nearly double global greenhouse gas cuts — jumping from roughly seven to nearly 14 percent (7.9 billion tons annually) — at 20th the cost, according to Climate TRACE, an independent greenhouse emissions tracking platform.

Language on ‘fossil fuels’

A major controversy from the onset of the COP31 negotiations was whether global electrification could deliver genuine climate progress without any binding commitments to clean, renewable electricity and a meaningful reduction in fossil fuel dependence.

The COP31 co-presidents Türkiye and Australia released an 18-page, 144-paragraph first draft of the cover decision on Nov. 16, which didn’t mention a “clean electricity” obligation but instead used the phrase “electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix.” The draft mentioned “fossil fuel(s)” six times.

A second, nine-page draft was unveiled three days later. After pushback from Saudi Arabia, the Arab Group and Russia, all mention of fossil fuels were removed. The omissions raised concerns that fossil-fuel-generated electricity could still count toward the 35 by 35 electrification goal without a corresponding roadmap to phasing out fossil fuels.

The text also positioned COP31 as the first climate summit to formally acknowledge that the world is overshooting the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold established in the Paris climate agreement.

Despite the voluntary nature of the electrification proposal, the broader issue still needed to clear significant political friction during the decisive second week of negotiations due to the fossil fuels loophole behind it.

The fact that the 35 by 35 target concerns electricity’s share of energy consumption rather than renewables’ share of electricity generation means countries can expand gas- and coal-fired power plants while still claiming progress toward the 35 percent goal.

Voluntary electricity pledge

To reach an overall agreement, the so-called COP31 Divan, an informal ministerial gathering based on the old Turkish “divan,” a council of deliberation and collective judgment, was held on Nov. 18.

To avoid setting an unachievable COP target, the conference co-presidents had noted at the opening of the summit, on Nov. 10, that the electricity pledge was voluntary. They also did not specifically describe whether low-carbon renewables (solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal and nuclear) or high-carbon fossil fuels (oil, gas and coal), were required to power the additional electricity production.

Faith Birol, the head of the IEA, described during a Nov. 13 press conference at COP31 how further electrification would reduce carbon emissions even under countries’ current national energy policies. Birol also hinted that the IEA was being pragmatic by recommending that the COP31 presidency not attach a rigid clean energy condition to the 35 by 35 pledge.

“To have as many countries as possible signing this pledge is extremely important,” Birol said. “It is high time that we see that many countries come together behind an international target, which could have a reflection on the market trends.”

Yet the clean route to electrification was repeatedly noted as a requirement throughout the conference by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, whose term ends on Dec. 31, 2026, and by countries like Portugal, Spain and Denmark through the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance (BOGA) initiative.

Hard red lines

Although the tendency during COP31 was to push for faster phaseout of fossil fuels, both the first and the second draft proposals generated major political divisions.

Panama said after the second draft that it would block any outcome that failed to meet its demands, including a cap on oil production. The Arab Group and Russia rejected the first draft text almost entirely over its fossil fuel phase-out language and the electrification targets or anything they argued would interfere with their national priorities.

Similarly, the Like-Minded Developing Countries bloc — a subset of the G77-plus China coalition, including India and Saudi Arabia and representing over 50 percent of the world’s population with low economic development — stated that setting a 35 percent electrification goal and fossil fuel roadmaps as well as singling out methane, which has a warming impact 80 times stronger than CO2, crossed their red lines.

Rich countries, including those in Europe, as well as Switzerland, generally embraced the 35 by 35 initiative but criticized its broad approach. The European Union’s climate envoy, Wopke Hoekstra, described the first draft as “a shopping list” that reopened issues such as climate finance.

As the only G7 leader participating in Antalya, Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain, which officially endorsed 35 by 35, was the front-runner European leader to back it.

Small island states and developing nations, led by Pacific Island nations and Brazil, insisted that the global electrification target sources be strictly tied to renewable energy and explicitly exclude fossil fuels to ensure a genuine climate impact rather than just shifting emissions elsewhere.

China stayed out of the heated battle over fossil fuel wording — saying it had decided on its own clean energy transition to dominate green energy manufacturing and deployment in the world — and focused instead on pushing against green tariffs.

Civil society objections

Guterres of the UN expressed disappointment over the collapse of the COP31 talks but was adamant in his message to civil society: “The climate crisis will not wait for governments to find common ground. Neither can we. Keep spreading the facts. Keep demanding action. Keep turning up the heat.”

Climate advocacy organizations also criticized the COP31 drafts, which they feared would give the fossil fuel industry cover to carry on as usual, raking in profits.

Climate Analytics, a global science and policy institute based in Berlin, warned that electrification without binding clean-power conditions could add at least 0.1°C to global warming by midcentury. Its research found that under current policies, gas-fired electricity generation could increase, while energy-related carbon-dioxide emissions would decline by only 20 to 25 percent from 2025 to 2035.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the grassroots environmental movement 350.org, said in a statement: “They have reduced one of the defining challenges of our time to an inconvenient paragraph they would rather delete, while leaving the door open for fossil fuels to masquerade as clean electrification.”

Meanwhile, the world has produced 38 billion tons of emissions so far this year. Based on the same IEA modeling of energy production, of all the new power plants installed in 2026, 79 percent came from renewable sources, according to the IEA.

“With the current settings, which means, if we don’t put a [clean energy] condition to the ‘35 by 35’ . . . [the figure] will go down to 30 billion tons of emissions. So there’ll be a strong decline in the emissions coming from the energy circle,” Birol said.

US no-show

As the world’s historically largest polluter, and now the second-largest after China, US government officials were notably absent from COP31, the biggest UN event of the year, drawing more than 100,000 attendees. The Trump administration withdrew from the Paris climate agreement in its first presidency and again last year as it continues to boycott UN climate summits. (The Biden administration rejoined the Paris agreement in 2021.)

Instead, a 120-member “observer” delegation, mostly Democrats and headed by Gavin Newsom, the governor of California and the highest-profile American official to participate in COP31, showed up to support international allies of mitigating climate change and save America’s face at Antalya with the motto “America Is All In.”

Newson reminded the COP31 participants that as the world’s fourth-largest economy, California had achieved climate goals at scale, cutting greenhouse gas emissions by over 20 percent since 2000, while growing its economy by more than 80 percent.

Meanwhile, in Shenzen, China, around 4,956 miles and a 900-metric-ton flight away from Antalya, the world’s biggest polluters, the US, China and Russia, met on Nov. 18-19, where they agreed to pump more oil into the world, among other matters.

As to the three powers’ pledge to boost oil production at the trilateral summit in China, Kurum, the COP31 co-president, said that countries could not be forced to do anything unless voluntarily, using a Turkish proverb, “You cannot force beauty.”

text:
I love my Tesla Model Y.

And apparently a lot of my readers do too. Like Bruce C. who messaged me: “I own a 2026 Tesla Model Y. I LOVE IT! Every owner that I’ve talked to absolutely LOVES their Tesla.”

There’s just one thing I wish I could change about owning an electric vehicle (EV).

Charging.

If you’re driving around town and can plug in at home every night, charging isn’t usually much of an issue.

But what happens when you want to take a long road trip?

You have to think about how far your battery will take you, where you’ll stop to recharge and how long you’ll have to wait before getting back on the road.

And if you’re driving an electric truck carrying thousands of pounds of cargo across the country, those problems compound exponentially.

I always thought it would be amazing if you could charge your electric vehicle without ever having to stop driving.

And today, Honda is developing a technology that could make this dream possible.

The Road Charger

Last month, Honda announced it’s developing a technology that could fundamentally change how electric vehicles get their power.

And it’s based on something we use every day.

The roads we drive on.

Working with Japanese construction companies Taisei and Taisei Rotec, Honda has developed a system that can wirelessly transfer electricity from equipment buried beneath the pavement to vehicles driving overhead.

The technology uses electromagnetic induction, the same basic principle behind the wireless charging pads you can use for your smartphone.

Coils embedded in the pavement create a magnetic field that transfers electricity to a receiver mounted underneath a vehicle.

And the vehicle doesn’t have to stop for any of this to happen. It can keep driving while its battery receives electricity.

Honda plans to begin testing the technology on a public highway during Japan’s fiscal year 2027. The company wants to demonstrate that it can deliver up to 150 kilowatts of power to moving vehicles.

That’s roughly as much power as you can get from a typical highway fast-charging station, without ever having to stop to use it.

But this technology isn’t unique. Engineers around the world have already demonstrated that charging vehicles while they drive is possible.

And some of the most impressive work is happening right here in America.

Earlier this year, researchers at Purdue University revealed they’d successfully charged an electric semi-truck while it was traveling down a public highway at 65 miles per hour.

Working with the Indiana Department of Transportation and commercial vehicle manufacturer Cummins, the researchers installed wireless charging equipment beneath a quarter-mile stretch of highway in West Lafayette, Indiana.

As the specially equipped truck drove over the pavement, the system transferred electricity directly to its battery.

And we’re not talking about a mere trickle of power.

It delivered between 50 and 190 kilowatts of electricity while the truck was moving, with power-transfer efficiency approaching 85%. In other words, it received enough electricity to significantly extend its driving range, with very little energy lost in the process.

Other entities are also working on this technology.

In Detroit, Israeli technology company Electreon helped build America’s first public wireless charging roadway in 2023. The quarter-mile installation uses coils embedded beneath the pavement to charge specially equipped vehicles as they drive over it.

Meanwhile, Florida is developing a three-quarter-mile wireless charging section of State Road 516, a new highway being built near Orlando. That project is designed to deliver up to 200 kilowatts of power to compatible vehicles, roughly as much as a powerful public fast-charging station.

And overseas, a company called Electreon has already demonstrated even greater charging power on France’s A10 motorway. During testing, its system delivered more than 200 kilowatts on average to a heavy-duty truck, with peak power exceeding 300 kilowatts.

Of course, these are still small-scale tests. But they prove that the technology can work on real roads.

Even the federal government is getting involved.

The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) is supporting research into wireless charging roads, including the project in Indiana.

But the reality is that installing charging equipment beneath existing highways is expensive. One Indiana feasibility study estimated that a wireless charging lane could cost more than $6 million per mile.

Still, there may be a practical way to introduce the technology without rebuilding the entire highway system.

And it starts with America’s trucking industry.

Electric semi-trucks need enormous batteries to haul heavy loads over long distances. These batteries are expensive, heavy and take up valuable space.

But if trucks could recharge while driving, they wouldn’t need nearly as much battery power onboard.

That could mean smaller, lighter and cheaper batteries, more room for cargo and a much more practical way to power long-distance trucking.

Commercial trucking could also make the technology more affordable to roll out.

Unlike passenger vehicles, which travel all over the place, commercial trucks often follow the same shipping routes. That means we wouldn’t need to electrify every highway.

We could simply start with the busy trucking routes where thousands of vehicles travel the same roads every day.

Here’s My Take

What excites me the most about Honda’s announcement is that it offers a potential solution to one of the biggest headaches of owning an electric vehicle.

Instead of building bigger batteries or faster charging stations, we could make charging part of the driving experience.

It’s the kind of breakthrough that could give the EV market a much-needed jolt.

Regards,

Ian King

Chief Strategist, Banyan Hill Publishing

text:
Washington, D.C. — U.S. Congressman Sean Casten (IL-06) released the following statement regarding the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act:

“America desperately needs permitting reform to spur the deployment of clean, affordable, and reliable energy that fuels the American economy. I have worked extensively on this issue, most notably with Congressman Mike Levin on the Energy Bills Relief Act (EBRA, H.R. 7977). While the Senate’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) includes many provisions from EBRA, I cannot support BAAJA in its current form. The House must be given the opportunity to improve the legislation.

“The United States does not struggle to build data centers, LNG export facilities, natural gas pipelines, or electricity assets that are owned, operated, and controlled by regulated utilities. Instead, we consistently struggle to build cheaper, cleaner energy sources that would successfully compete against existing fossil fuel assets but are blocked by the incumbent interests. BAAJA fails to eliminate the economic disincentives stacked against cheaper energy and weakens critical environmental laws that keep dirtier energy sources offline.

“Those problems in BAAJA can be fixed, specifically by overhauling sections 1401 and 1402, which make it impossible for a future administration to undo the damage being done by the Trump Administration’s willful disregard of current environmental law and judicial precedent, and by adding provisions to create incentives for utilities to deploy lower-cost, cleaner energy sources. While the manager’s amendment improved BAAJA in these areas, it still falls far short of what’s necessary.

“Climate change and permitting reform are too important to settle for anything less than a deal that unleashes our economy and protects our communities. If we are compelled to vote only on the Senate-passed text, I will vote No, with confidence in our ability to craft a better version in the 120th Congress.”

text:
Despite the recent attention on new electric demand created by data centers, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries sees greater potential for long-term growth in the utilities sector, MHI President and CEO Eisaku Ito said earlier this month.

Utilities and independent power producers accounted for 94% of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ new gas turbine orders in 2024 and 2025, Ito said.

Although many U.S. data center operators say they intend to install their own off-grid generation, Ito argued that these plans rely on smaller gas-fired power plants that cost more to run than the larger plants utilities and IPPs are pursuing.

In the long-term, Ito said, the cost differential will push data centers to connect to the grid, ultimately supporting utilities’ expansion plans.

His comments, made during a call with analysts on Nov. 6, according to a translated transcript, come as fallout from the U.S. midterm elections and stock market volatility raise questions about the future of the artificial intelligence buildout in North America. Ito expressed confidence in utilities’ long-term expansion plans, arguing that growing demand for electricity does not rely solely on data centers.

“Electricity demand from data centers is expected to grow rapidly in the United States, but data centers still account for only around 10% of the country’s total electricity demand,” Ito said. “If some of the anticipated growth in demand does not materialize, there will be some impact, but we believe the effect on our overall GTCC business would be limited.”

MHI booked 8 GW in orders for large frame gas turbines in the first half of its 2026 fiscal year, compared to 16 GW of orders in all of FY 2025. Profit for the company’s Energy Systems segment rose 80% on account of increased orders and shifts in the value of the yen, according to the company’s financial statements.

“We are also beginning to see the benefits of improved pricing on new unit projects, lower loss-related costs and greater production efficiency,” MHI CFO Hiroshi Nishio said.

Company executives said they continue to take a conservative approach to forecasting demand and expanding manufacturing capacity. The company expects global demand for gas turbines at all manufacturers and makers to average about 70 GW per year over the next five years — somewhat lower than the 100 GW MHI expects will sell across all manufactuers this year amid what Ito characterized as “exceptionally strong” demand he does not anticipate will continue.

But Ito said he remains confident in MHI’s company backlog, noting that the company vets new orders carefully and hasn’t had any order cancellations in the past two years.

The company plans to double its gas turbine production capacity by 2030, though most of the additional capacity will come from improved processes and automation at existing plants in the U.S. and Japan.

“We are improving productivity and driving other initiatives at a pace that outstrips the growth in orders,” he said.

MHI also signaled that it’s exploring opportunities to expand into other infrastructure-related markets.

Ito said MHI will release additional details in May, but suggested the company is interested in expanding its gas turbine service and repair capabilities, as well as investing in unmanned systems that can operate in harsh environments. At the same time, MHI plans to divest some of its aerospace business, he said.

“These examples may seem quite different, but they all share a common theme: resilience,” Ito said. “We aim to identify new business opportunities in infrastructure and industrial machinery through the lens of resilience and turn them into future growth.”

text:
The City Council is nonpartisan and comprises eight district representatives who annually set a tax rate, adopt a budget, make wide-ranging policy decisions and appoint a city manager and city attorney. They serve four-year terms and are paid $72,800 a year. District 8 represents South El Paso, Downtown and neighborhoods around the University of Texas at El Paso.

Who’s running for this seat?

Candidate Questionnaires

Candidates were asked to limit their responses to 100 words. Responses have been lightly edited for grammar. (These Q&As are from the November general election responses and republished here.)

Looking ahead 10 years, what do you want El Paso to look and feel like, and what are the most important decisions the city needs to make now to get there?

Chris Canales: I want El Paso to be an affordable and welcoming city where people of all backgrounds can build a good life. That means investing in the city we already have: expanding housing choices, strengthening neighborhoods, creating good paying jobs, managing finances responsibly, and maintaining streets, infrastructure and public facilities. We also need to grow sustainably, directing development where existing infrastructure can support it and protecting our clean air, water and natural resources.

Matthew Guzman: I want El Paso to be ripe with job opportunities for young professionals seeking a city on the rise. I want the region to recognize El Paso as a destination for the arts, food and culture. And I want residents to be proud of where they live and happy with their quality of life. To get there we have to capitalize and execute on the economic development opportunities ahead of us. Namely the buildout of the Advanced Manufacturing District and creating sustainable energy capacity to support growth.

El Paso relies heavily on residential property taxpayers to fund city services. What specifically should the city do to attract more commercial and industrial development and broaden the tax base?

Chris Canales: We should diversify our economy by targeting industries that fit our strengths, including renewable energy and advanced manufacturing. I supported creating the new Business One Stop Shop to help local businesses and entrepreneurs access resources and assistance. We must also streamline permitting and inspections, invest in infrastructure, infill, and redevelopment, and focus resources on projects that create quality jobs, substantial taxable value and lasting benefits for El Pasoans.

Matthew Guzman: We need to align educational institutions and workforce development with high wage sectors like aerospace, advanced manufacturing, robotics and skilled trades so we can provide the workers these companies need when they look to relocate. We need to create shovel-ready sites to lure companies looking to expand. And, as companies begin to recognize the benefits of our location and the quality of our workforce, incentive packages should be based on performance and job creation.

Police and fire make up a significant share of the city’s budget. How should the city balance competitive compensation and staffing with the need to control public safety costs and fund other city priorities?

Chris Canales: We must provide competitive compensation and adequate staffing to keep up with public safety needs. I have supported funding three police academies annually to address vacancies while investing in programs like the Crisis Intervention Team for mental health that best match resources to community needs. Public safety spending must also receive the same scrutiny as every part of the budget, including efficient use of personnel and overtime, so we can adequately fund other essential City services.

Matthew Guzman: We have been training recruits with our tax dollars then watching them leave for other cities. We need to take a look at contract minimums for new fire and police recruits to ensure they have a stable workforce and aren’t forced to go over budget on overtime hours that eventually burnout their existing workforce. Safety services are an increasing part of the overall budget, which brings us back to our need to grow the commercial and industrial tax base to fund these expanding services.

El Paso is attracting interest from data centers and related developments. What standards or conditions should the city require of these projects regarding infrastructure and economic benefits to the community?

Chris Canales: I don’t want hyperscale data centers, particularly those supporting AI, in El Paso. They require huge amounts of scarce land, energy, water and infrastructure. I led council action to not incentivize them moving forward. If private projects go ahead anyway, they must be made to pay their full infrastructure costs, protect ratepayers from higher utility rates, meet strict water and energy standards and provide enforceable community benefits commensurate with their enormous resource demands.

Matthew Guzman: We need to ensure these companies are creating jobs, attracting industry, and growing our commercial/industrial tax revenue. There needs to be contract language in place that ensures the responsible use of our resources, and investment from these companies into our energy and water infrastructure that creates new capacity, or improves efficiencies. Legally binding community benefit agreements need to be executed that ensure El Paso extracts as much from these companies as they extract from us.

When the city offers tax breaks, grants or other incentives to attract businesses and development, what should taxpayers expect in return, and how should the city determine whether those incentives are worth the cost?

Chris Canales: Taxpayers should receive a clear, measurable return for economic development incentives. During my term, I have approved stronger requirements for projects receiving city incentives, including performance standards and clawbacks. We should prioritize projects that create quality jobs, expand the tax base and produce lasting benefits that justify the public investment, while accounting for infrastructure and resource needs and publicly tracking whether promised benefits are actually delivered.

Matthew Guzman: Taxpayers should expect that the revenue derived from these deals will have a real effect on their tax bills. Transparency is paramount, and when a deal is finalized we should be able to provide a visual projection showing what was given up in incentives versus the tax revenue expected, the new jobs created, and the services the new tax revenue can cover. Taxpayers want to know where their money is being spent and spared.
