text:
Discussions to add electric vehicles to the domestic production tax credit, known as the Korean version of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), have intensified. As Chinese-made electric vehicles rapidly invade the domestic market, the National Assembly is forming a consensus on including electric vehicles in the tax credit, raising interest in whether support for the domestic automotive industry will be expanded.

According to the National Assembly and the automotive industry, the National Assembly's Finance and Economy Committee held a subcommittee meeting on the 23rd to address a revision bill for the Tax Exemption and Restriction Act that includes electric vehicles in the domestic production tax credit.

On this day, lawmakers reportedly formed a consensus on including electric vehicles in the tax credit but could not narrow the differences with the government. Consequently, it appears that a separate consultation involving committee secretaries and government officials will be held to coordinate related matters.

One legislative official stated, "Contrary to expectations, it seems that reaching a conclusion on including electric vehicles will not be easy," adding, "It does not seem that the Ministry of Finance will change its stance on reviewing the inclusion of electric vehicles in the tax credit."

The revision bill for the Tax Exemption and Restriction Act, jointly proposed by 19 lawmakers from both the ruling People Power Party (PPP) and the opposition Democratic Party (DP), aims to add electric vehicles to the domestic production tax credit to enhance the production competitiveness of the automotive industry.

Since electric vehicles were excluded from the domestic production tax credit in August, the industry has continued to raise concerns about fairness. The government selected six sectors, including secondary batteries and semiconductors, as support targets for the domestic production tax credit. In response, the industry has voiced the need to consider the conditions of the domestic automotive industry, which is threatened by the onslaught of Chinese-made electric vehicles.

The growing demand for tax support for electric vehicles is rooted in the encroachment of Chinese-made electric vehicles in the domestic market. Chinese electric vehicles are expanding their influence in the domestic market by leveraging lower prices compared to their counterparts. According to the Korea Automobile Mobility Industry Association (KAMA), the share of Chinese-made vehicles in the domestic electric vehicle market rose from 1.1% in 2021 to 33.9% last year, marking the third most significant growth among major global automobile-producing countries, following Mexico and Brazil.

Chinese automakers are entering the market by bypassing low export thresholds and domestic tariff barriers. The basic tariff applied to Chinese automobiles in Korea is only 8%. This contrasts sharply with the tariffs of 127.5% and 110% imposed on Chinese electric vehicles by the United States and India, respectively. The European Union, which is also trying to curb the entry of Chinese electric vehicles, has raised tariffs to as high as 45.3%.

The government has acknowledged the need for support for the domestic electric vehicle industry. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyung-il stated during a press conference at the Government Sejong Center that the government understands that the next two to three years represent a golden time for the transition of the electric vehicle market and that it will make a comprehensive decision.

The government is expected to announce its position on the electric vehicle tax credit through a 'plan to strengthen electric vehicle competitiveness' later this month.

The automotive industry is calling for tax support at a level similar to that of Japan. Japan provides a subsidy of 400,000 yen (approximately 3.8 million won (KRW)) per electric vehicle to differentiate itself from foreign brands. The industry anticipates that the introduction of a tax credit will help induce domestic facility investment by automakers and secure production volumes for suppliers.

Kim Joo-hong, executive director of the Korea Automobile Mobility Industry Association, stated, "Chinese-made electric vehicles are entering the domestic market with price competitiveness based on massive support from their government, making it difficult to respond. It is urgent to reflect electric vehicles in the tax credit to enhance the competitiveness of domestic electric vehicles."

text:
GET THIS IN YOUR INBOX FIRST: Subscribe to CNBC’s “Power Insider” newsletter.

POWER POINT

What I’m hearing from energy insiders

Is one of the greatest money-making trades of the last few years coming to an end?

No, I’m not talking about Nvidia or any of the data center- or AI-related power companies (although they have been crushed lately too… more on that on CNBC TV. Tune in!).

I’m talking about whether the epic boom in refinery-related stocks is unwinding. Over the last year, the jump in some of these companies has been nothing short of remarkable.

That jump is largely due to massive increases in margins, earnings, and cash flow. Those have occurred because of a big jump in what is called a crack spread. That is the difference between the price of oil and the finished price of refined products such as diesel and jet fuel. For most of this year, spreads have been soaring as disruptions and attacks on facilities and shipping in the Arabian Gulf, Hormuz, and deep inside Russia have played havoc with the market. In the last week or so, however, something big has changed: many of those spreads have started to tighten.

This seismic drop in spreads is causing a selloff in the aforementioned refinery companies.

If spreads continue to fall, these stocks may well keep selling off from recent highs. The upshot for investors may be that, as the shares come down, analysts see more upside. The median price target for Phillips 66 (PSX) now indicates a 20% gain from here, while smaller-cap Par Pacific (PARR) is double that.

Here are a few other key points to focus on heading into the Thanksgiving-shortened week.

I like to keep politics as much at arm’s length as possible — we all know that energy and politics (sadly) often go hand in hand. Energy policies coming from Washington, D.C., can drive — or destroy — investment dollars. With all the big shifts in the White House over the last 10 years (four years of Trump, four years of Biden, and now 2 years into Trump #2), energy policies can blow through Washington faster than a summer squall hits a wind turbine. But because federal policies can mean so much for specific companies, sectors, and investments, it’s important to follow the news flow.

That said, I’d like to take a moment to introduce you to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA (and pronounced like the state in Mexico). Like much legislation, BAAJA is an obscure but important bill working its way through the American Congress. BAAJA does a lot of things, but what Power Insider readers care about is its focus on energy permitting reform. In a nutshell, BAAJA would help speed up the building of new electricity infrastructure. Again, that’s an overly simplistic view of a big bill, but it needs to be on your radar. The utility trade group Edison Electric Institute came out in favor of the legislation this month after the industry received some 11th-hour changes. See more about it in our recent interview with EEI President Drew Maloney here.

The bill passed the U.S. Senate in a vote late Thursday night. Now it moves to the House. Support for its final passage is also coming from the big LNG trade group, whose executive director said he “applauds the Senate for its bipartisan effort to pass meaningful, bipartisan, and durable permitting reforms aimed at delivering greater predictability, consistency, and certainty in the permitting, production, and export process for U.S. LNG. This legislation moves us closer to untangling red tape and eliminating overlapping agency reviews that can keep U.S. energy projects delayed for years.”

The Natural Gas Supply Association also chimed in, saying it urges Congress to see the bill as “a resource-agnostic and balanced reform agenda for boosting American energy security. It keeps strong environmental reviews in place, but it draws a firm line against the endless procedural delays that tie critical energy projects in knots for a decade.”

In my view, passing BAAJA is an important test of Congress’s appetite for helping the energy and electrical power industry, lowering costs, and speeding time to market. The old adage was correct: time is money. Literally. If BAAJA moves on through the House, we could see an upside move in some utility stocks and any company related to energy infrastructure.

Speaking of politics, the news is getting lost in the massive Anthropic (ANT) IPO, but the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) — whose importance I wrote about in the last edition — just decided to resume permitting for data centers. The Texas Tribune did a nice write-up on it, and you can read it here.

Remember: energy is politics.

It’s tough to say, but it’s true. The two are inextricably linked by policies created at both the federal and state levels. As I wrote in the last edition, some federally elected officials may have less impact on state-level issues — like the data center buildout — but they certainly have power over national laws. While many of you are enthralled, disgusted, or confused by sordid tales of Nvidia and Jensen-gate, keep one eye open on what happens in Washington, D.C.

Have a great week, and have a wonderful Thanksgiving, everyone.

Brian

THE ACTIONABLE INSIDER

Perhaps the big investor story — which is, like most things lately, related to Jensen-gate and Nvidia—is the sizable selloff in many AI, neocloud, and data center power-related stocks.

Painful for current shareholders, but big drops can also bring big opportunities. Wall Street believes that’s the case, at least right now. Look at some of the potential upside based on the stocks’ prices versus their price targets.

We spoke with the CEO of Applied Digital (APLD) about all of this on CNBC last week, and you can watch it here. He highlighted how the market may be getting these stock stories wrong because, at least with his company, he has long-term contracts with solid-credit companies. In that way, Applied Digital is more like a landlord than a “pure-play” AI company.

My take → While I’m not going to recommend a specific stock, I would add that it is critical for investors to understand the differences between these companies. While they may have some things in common, they are also different, with different business models, customers, leases, and sources of revenue.

Speaking of recommendations… here are two ideas for you:

A recent decline presents a nice opportunity in SOLV Energy (MWH). UBS analyst Jon Windham upgrades SOLV to buy from neutral, believing the market is “underappreciating several key tailwinds for SOLV given uncertainty around data center demand and higher interest rates.” UBS highlights how the stock has fallen lately despite making two deals and beating and raising recent guidance. UBS says now is an “attractive entry point” for SOLV. (Side note: MWH is a great stock ticker.)

While markets overall fall, BMO remains bullish on Bloom Energy (BE). After speaking with the company, the analyst is upgrading Bloom to outperform, saying he remains “increasingly confident of BE’s commercial traction” and that he still has conviction even with the recent drop in shares. While analyst Ameet Thakkar did cut his target to $230 from $260, that’s still 50% upside from the current price. Bloom shares have tumbled 45% since October 1.

Also…

I was recently asked for my opinion on the price of oil. Here’s my take. The market clearly wants to push oil contract prices lower and has for a few months. But, as I’ve said and reported for a while, don’t confuse the futures (paper) price with the actual price. Yes, shipping rates and insurance rates have come down from recent highs — and there is a good amount of oil now flowing through Hormuz — but the cost of a physical barrel of crude is still well above the futures contract. If we get real, longer-lasting peace around Iran, oil prices will fall. There is plenty of oil in the world. That said, if bombs and missiles start firing again, oil prices will firm. I know that’s a non-answer answer, but the oil market is truly headline-driven right now. My late good friend Boone Pickens (later in life, he didn’t like being called by the “T” in his first name) used to avoid giving a set price target and instead give a directional quote, so I’ll do the same: the odds of oil being lower in two months than it is today are 75%.

Also, part #2…

Last week, I had a one-on-one with Vimal Kapur, chair and CEO of Honeywell International (HON), at an RBC conference in New York City. While the conversation wasn’t filmed, I can tell you that Kapur offered investors reassurance that his order book is doing very, very well. This is important because Honeywell is huge in the things that make other things work. Its sensors go into a ton of energy facilities, from refineries to LNG facilities. Honeywell is a leading indicator of spending and buildouts, so if it keeps getting orders, it’s a good sign for macro energy.

Bottom line: Watch Honeywell stock as a potential “tell.”

title: A Data Center's Broken Promise Leaves a Historic Black Town Waiting - Capital B News
description:
For many Black communities, it is also a question of whether land that sustained generations can remain a foundation for their futures.
“We don’t have anybody to stand for us,” resident Chad McKendrick said at a recent town council meeting about the data center.
Green said this disparity in wealth is seen in data center placement.
“Black communities deserve to be spoken about through the lens of our diversity.
Across the country, local officials have signed nondisclosure agreements with data center developers, restricting access to information as projects move toward approval.
text:
In Eatonville, Florida, America’s first all-Black municipality, the Hungerford School taught generations of Black students how to build a life in a country determined to limit their futures.

The Florida boarding school for Black students built in 1897 paired academics with skilled trades, making it an engine of Black self-sufficiency. Now, 17 years after the school was shuttered, part of its former property holds a project that some residents and advocates argue could limit the futures of its Black children: a data center.

The facility, which began construction in 2019, came with grand promises that have only shrunk as time goes on.

In the early stages, HostDime, the developer, pledged to set up the town’s residents with free at-home Wi-Fi. As construction costs have nearly doubled and the open date keeps being delayed, the company’s CEO, Manny Vivar, said its original promise of free at-home wifi is “not sustainable.”

The company also said it would provide scholarships, programs, and STEM training for Eatonville students and residents upon completion of the facility. It is not clear if that will move forward. HostDime has now said it will offer “public” Wi-Fi through an antenna atop the building.

Without any binding agreements or clear enforcement from local officials, those commitments have faded.

Meanwhile, residents are left without access to the land and the memory of their self-reliance, and now, potential pollution from the data center.

“That’s just been the story of Eatonville,” said Julian Johnson, an Eatonville resident. “It’s almost like the norm to be on defense and fighting because of the valuable land.”

The fight in Eatonville reaches far beyond the 5 acres where HostDime is building its data center. Across the country, the artificial intelligence race is raising questions about who makes the deals, controls the land, and must live with the demands for electricity and the threat of pollution.

For many Black communities, it is also a question of whether land that sustained generations can remain a foundation for their futures.

“We don’t have anybody to stand for us,” resident Chad McKendrick said at a recent town council meeting about the data center.

The situation in Eatonville is “another example of data centers making these promises and offering community benefits, but then failing to deliver on those benefits,” said Shelby Green, the research and communications manager at the Energy and Policy Institute.

In Eatonville, the average household income is less than $33,000. It is located in Orange County, where the average income is roughly 2.5 times higher than that at $80,000.

Green said this disparity in wealth is seen in data center placement.

“This data center expansion is almost replicating the failures of urban renewal back when the federal government through state governments was acquiring land from Black communities and building highways over them in service of white or wealthier communities,” she said.

At a recent town council meeting, Vivar said that offering Wi-Fi to the community “came from a pure heart.”

“Do I regret saying it the way I said?” he added, “Probably, because there was no technicality behind it.”

A century-long fight over Black land

At one point, the land in question was owned collectively by the town’s residents before being donated for the school through a trust. Nearly 50 years after the school was built, Orange County Public Schools acquired the property from the trust following a court battle. In its 1951 order, the Florida Supreme Court required the school board to only use the land to educate Black children.

But over the next half century until the school was closed, the school district had regularly tried to sell the property, prompting continued backlash from Eatonville’s Black community.

“You see, somebody is going to make money off Eatonville and that’s because Eatonville is such a precious commodity. The people of Eatonville are the ones who should be able to benefit and build a lasting legacy and lasting economic legacy,” said N.Y. Nathiri, the executive director of the Association to Preserve the Eatonville Community, or PEC.

HostDime’s 5 acres are only one part of a broader dispute over the former school property, where residents are also contesting how the remaining 100-plus acres of land should be developed.

For years, residents called on the city government to buy the land from the school district. Instead, former Mayor Angie Gardner supported selling land to the data center developer and to Sovereign Land Co., which attempted to build a shopping and entertainment district.

Eatonville’s need for investment is urgent. The town has remained under a state financial-emergency designation for more than two decades and is at threat of running out of money because of a dwindling tax base.

Residents and town council members understand this, but want more say in how to address the crisis. Some accused Gardner of advancing these projects without proper council approval and public input, raising concerns about a lack of transparency and oversight.

Gardner “sat out there and essentially sold this town out,” said Councilman Tarus Mack. “I have always been saying give us the property or let us buy it back.”

Gardner did not respond to Capital B’s request for comment before publication. Following the accusations made during a town council meeting, Gardner said there were several constituents and officials who supported the sale and development of the former school property, and others could have voiced concerns but did not.

In 2023, PEC challenged the effort by Orange County Public Schools to sell roughly 100 acres to Sovereign Land Co. The lawsuit argued that the proposed sale violated restrictions intended to preserve the land’s educational purpose. Sovereign Land Co. subsequently withdrew from the deal.

Now, PEC is suing again, challenging the process behind a new agreement to transfer the property to Dr. Phillips Charities. Plans by the charity include an early learning center, a community and health hub, housing, green space, and a new museum about the town.

But the complaint alleges that the school board improperly discussed the land’s sale and use during three closed-door attorney-client sessions in 2024, including meetings attended by people the organization says were not authorized to participate.

A spokesperson for Orange County Public Schools told Capital B that the district considers the lawsuit “without merit” and will vigorously defend its position in court.

In March, fifth-generation Eatonville resident Ruthi Critton won a three-way mayoral race. Gardner did not seek reelection, instead running for a seat on the Orange County Commission.

The leadership change did not amount to a rejection of the Dr. Phillips project. In an interview after taking office, Critton praised the charity’s efforts to involve residents in planning the property’s future. Critton’s office did not respond to Capital B’s request for comment.

Millard Livatt, a longtime resident and civil rights advocate, said there have been meetings, but there’s been no conversation about updates on the project.

“We’ve been over here in Eatonville and we ain’t heard nothing about no Dr. Phillips coming over here looking out for our interest,” he said.

The project’s supporters describe an opportunity to restore services and activity to the former school property. Bahiyyah Maroon, a resident who chairs the Eatonville Initiative Advisory Committee, said the effort has involved two years of community engagement.

Maroon said a disagreement over the plan does not mean the community has been absent from shaping it.

“Black communities deserve to be spoken about through the lens of our diversity. We’re not required to agree with one another because we’re all Black and we live in a certain geography,” she said.

A data center doesn’t mean internet access

For residents still waiting on HostDime’s promised internet service, the question of who can hold developers to their commitments is already tangible.

“They promised us that they were able to build that building there so that all Eatonville residents would get free internet,” Livatt said. “I can tell you right now, the only internet I got in my house right now is through my cellphone.”

The disconnect extends beyond Eatonville. Data center developers are looking to rural areas for cheap land and available power. These are the very places where at-home internet remains spotty or nonexistent at all. About 25% of rural households lack internet access, compared to 1.5% of urban ones. As billions are spent to introduce new technologies for data centers in these places, they are not automatically bringing affordable broadband to the communities.

“This is a tactic that not just data center companies and big tech use, but also large developers who come into Black communities and try to entice some type of urban renewal or revitalization project,” Green said. “But they really often just lead to displacement and high costs.”

HostDime did not respond to Capital B’s request for comment.

In some communities near data centers, utility bills have tripled because of the costs to build new power plants and transmission infrastructure for the facilities. Rents and housing values have jumped by as much as 40% in some places as well.

Residents in communities where data centers are popping up face several barriers that limit their ability to not only have a say but hold elected officials accountable.

Across the country, local officials have signed nondisclosure agreements with data center developers, restricting access to information as projects move toward approval. At the same time, the federal government has proposed rolling back requirements for public notice and comment on certain air-pollution permits, allowing some projects to advance without a required opportunity for neighbors to weigh in.

Ultimately, this fight is simply about access to land and Black ownership, some residents said.

“You’re not getting any more land, and everybody wants the land,” Johnson said.

Nathiri favors placing the property in a community land trust, an approach she says could accommodate development while protecting the community’s long-term interests.

Her concern, she said, is that “a certain small group of people can take an action that can have an impact for 100 years, for generations to come, and it can be done without full and open discussion.”

title: Report: 3 Wisconsin data centers account for 70% of growth in peak electricity demand
description:
Wisconsin’s peak electricity demand is expected to grow by more than 40 percent by 2032, driven by data centers.
The assessment provides a snapshot of current and future electricity supply, including the types of generation utilities are planning and their projected carbon emissions.
Summer Strand, chair of the Public Service Commission, said the projected rise in peak demand is unprecedented after years of relatively stagnant growth.
And while the state has set a goal of reaching 100 percent carbon-free electricity generation by 2050, there’s no legal mechanism requiring utilities to meet that goal.
Wisconsin utilities are planning to meet surging demand by adding 14.4 gigawatts, or GW, of electricity generation to the grid, the report shows.
text:
Wisconsin’s peak electricity demand is expected to grow by more than 40 percent by 2032, driven by data centers. That’s according to a newly finalized report by state regulators.

Environmental groups worry the rush to meet that growth will derail the state’s climate goals.

The Public Service Commission of Wisconsin on Thursday approved the state’s strategic energy assessment for 2026 through 2032, showing more than 70 percent of the growth in peak demand is tied to data center projects in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington and Beaver Dam.

The assessment provides a snapshot of current and future electricity supply, including the types of generation utilities are planning and their projected carbon emissions.

Summer Strand, chair of the Public Service Commission, said the projected rise in peak demand is unprecedented after years of relatively stagnant growth.

“Prior to the data center, or hyperscaler, situation taking off in Wisconsin, there was electrification and some energy transition things happening, and that was maybe creating a little more demand,” she said. “But nothing like 40 percent — 40 percent is a massive number.”

Strand also raised concerns that regulators may not have enough tools under state law to plan for that spike while protecting the environment and ratepayers.

And while the state has set a goal of reaching 100 percent carbon-free electricity generation by 2050, there’s no legal mechanism requiring utilities to meet that goal.

Wisconsin utilities are planning to meet surging demand by adding 14.4 gigawatts, or GW, of electricity generation to the grid, the report shows. The biggest chunks of that come from solar and natural gas, which account for 5.8 GW and 5.2 GW, respectively. The rest is split between wind and battery storage.

Utilities have said natural gas projects are needed because the North American Reliability Corporation, a nonprofit that monitors risks to the electric grid, warns the Midwest faces an “elevated risk” for electricity shortages beginning in 2028.

Concerns about powering the data center boom aren’t exclusive to Wisconsin.

New research from Harvard shows that more than half of the electricity powering hyperscale data centers nationally comes from fossil fuels, like gas and coal. The study also found U.S. data centers consume as much electricity annually as some states.

The report found that 403 hyperscale data centers accounted for 1.8 percent of total U.S. electricity consumption, and were associated with about 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions.

“We shouldn’t be solving tomorrow’s technological challenges by creating decades of environmental problems,” said Gianluca Guidi. “How we power this expansion really matters just as much how fast we build it.”

Guidi told WPR that the report’s findings are already outdated.

“The study and the numbers that we provided are already a year and a half old, which is basically ancient history in the AI world,” he said. “We have preliminary studies showing that the number of hyperscalers have almost actually more than doubled.”

Guidi called a 40 percent increase in peak electricity demand in Wisconsin “terrifying.”

He also said the energy infrastructure supporting data centers across the country is being built “faster than we can independently measure its consequences.”

Environmental groups warn new gas plants risk climate progress

Environmental groups say building new fossil fuel plants to meet data center demand could undermine efforts to reduce carbon emissions.

A new report from the Sierra Club argues the rush to build natural gas plants across the country could erase pollution reductions over the last 15 years that have come primarily from retiring coal-fired power plants.

By 2030, the report warns the United States’ electric sector could emit more carbon dioxide —2,317 million tons — than it has since 2011.

With Wisconsin utilities planning more than 5 GW of natural gas generation in the coming years, Cassie Steiner, campaign coordinator for the Sierra Club’s Wisconsin Chapter, said the trends in the national report are being “echoed in Wisconsin.”

“Even if the data centers pay for the infrastructure and the fuel, we all will be paying for this in the severe climate impacts and the health impacts that are going to come from all of this new fossil fuel generation,” Steiner said.

Utilities plan ‘all of the above’ approach to energy generation

Wisconsin utilities are planning to invest in a mix of natural gas and renewable energy in the coming years, the PSC’s draft report shows.

Anna Haensch, an associate research professor in UW-Madison’s Data Science Institute, said utilities spent the early part of the decade investing in renewable energy and promoting their climate goals, before turning back to fossil fuel projects as demand projections surged.

“The reason we are getting so much natural gas right now is because we need what’s called ‘firm power,’” she said. “Data centers need power that’s going to show up 24/7, around the clock, super reliable in rain, sleet or snow. And that’s fossil fuels.”

The state’s largest utility, We Energies, plans to add nearly 4.6 GW of natural gas capacity in the coming years, as well as 4.1 GW of solar, the PSC report showed. Wind and energy storage combined for nearly 1.9 GW.

Both the Port Washington and Mount Pleasant data center campuses are located in We Energies’ service territory.

The utility’s parent company did not report its expected CO2 emissions for 2032. In a regulatory filing, the company said that information was not available.

We Energies has paused its near-term carbon emissions reduction goals, but maintains it remains committed to achieving net carbon-neutral electric generation by 2050.

“Our ‘all of the above’ plan includes major investments in solar, wind and battery storage, supported by state-of-the-art natural gas generation that can operate when the sun is not shining or the wind is not blowing,” We Energies spokesperson Brendan Conway said in a statement. “This approach allows us to retire older, less-efficient fossil-fueled generation while keeping customers’ lights on all year-round.”

Alliant Energy, the utility that will serve the data center being built in Beaver Dam, plans to add 356 megawatts of upgraded natural gas capacity at three existing sites by 2032, the PSC report shows. The company also plans to add 790 MW of renewable energy.

The company expects its CO2 emissions in 2032 will be down 49 percent from 2009 levels, according to the PSC report.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Alliant Energy said the company remains committed to its goal of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050.

“While our journey may require the use of several different types of generation resources for the time being, we are also participating in research activities to find lesser carbon emitting generating fuels and technologies,” the statement read.

But in order for utilities to actually hit their long-term climate targets, Haenesch said they need to retire old fossil fuel plants and bring “tons and tons of new renewable energy” online.

“Wisconsin is looking to almost double its wind and solar capacity by 2032, which is fantastic,” she said. “But then at the same time (utilities are) not retiring fossil fuel plants, and they’re actually bringing new ones online.”

“It’s not enough to just stop making a mess in your room,” she added. “You have to clean it up as well.”

PSC chair renews call for Legislature to give agency more planning authority

Strand, the PSC chair, said she’s concerned that regulators may not have enough tools to adequately plan for the spike in energy demand.

Under current state law, she said the commission approves generation projects on a case-by-case basis as utilities or developers file applications to build them. She said the primary planning tool the commission has is its strategic energy assessment, or SEA.

“The SEA has no teeth. It’s more of a report,” she said. “We’re not really opining or editorializing, and we’re definitely not saying yea or nay on a comprehensive plan. We’re gathering data and information, analyzing that and then publishing information.”

Instead of an SEA, she said many states use a process known as integrated resource planning to review and analyze utilities’ capital plans, and exercise authority over planned generation additions or retirements.

Strand said integrated resource planning, or a similar process, would allow regulators to respond to the challenges spiking energy demand creates, such as pressure on energy bills and climate concerns.

“If ever there was going to be a time to help kind of restore the commission’s proper oversight role in generation and resource planning, now is the time,” Strand said.

text:
Electric vehicle company chief executives voiced modest expectations for expanded federal support after the Trump administration rolled back the up-to-$7,500 federal consumer EV incentive. Scout Motors, Rivian and Lucid Group said they are positioned to operate without relying on new legislation.

Why it matters

The removal of the consumer incentive shifts the cost burden of electric vehicles toward buyers at a time when EV prices already run well above the industry average. Executives' comments suggest manufacturers may pursue production-side measures rather than consumer subsidies.

The maximum federal consumer EV incentive of $7,500 has been rolled back, while the average new EV price stood above $54,800 as of September, compared with an industry average of just over $51,100. Whether any replacement incentive will be enacted has not been determined.

The players

Scout Motors

Scout Motors is an electric vehicle manufacturer planning to build vehicles in the United States.

Rivian

Rivian is an electric vehicle manufacturer known for its electric pickup trucks and delivery vans.

Lucid Group

Lucid Group is an electric vehicle maker known for its luxury electric sedans.

The details

Scout Motors chief executive Scott Keogh said the company was built without relying on potential legislation or programs and indicated a preference for production-side incentives that could lower manufacturing costs. Rivian chief executive RJ Scaringe expressed hope that Democratic lawmakers and President Donald Trump might find common ground on the sector, while Lucid Group chief executive Silvio Napoli said the company would accept any positive developments while preparing for less favorable scenarios. House Democrats' current legislative priorities center on healthcare and data centers rather than climate initiatives.

Timeline

January: Democrats assume control of Congress.

September: Average new EV price reported at more than $54,800.

The rollback reverses the consumer incentive framework established under the Inflation Reduction Act, which had been a central federal tool for narrowing the price gap between electric and gasoline vehicles. Manufacturers now appear to be planning around a market in which federal demand-side support is no longer assumed.

Buyers who had planned around the $7,500 federal credit will now face the full sticker price of an electric vehicle, which averaged above $54,800 as of September. Shoppers comparing EVs to gasoline models should factor in that the federal incentive is no longer available when weighing purchase costs.

Electric vehicle affordability is likely to depend more on manufacturing costs and pricing strategies than on federal purchase incentives in the near term. Buyers should compare total ownership costs, including available state programs, before deciding.

title: New rules require Front Range lawn care companies to trim summer use of gas-powered equipment
description:
Colorado’s latest move to trim unhealthy ozone in nine northern Front Range counties mandates the summer phaseout of gas-powered lawn care equipment by commercial operators in favor of clean electric starting next year, after a Friday vote.
“Air pollution emissions from the lawn and garden sector contribute to approximately 13% of all ground-level ozone pollution in Colorado’s nonattainment area,” state health officials say.
Environmental and consumer groups that have worked on lawn equipment changes praised the AQCC’s unanimous vote Friday.

text:
Colorado’s latest move to trim unhealthy ozone in nine northern Front Range counties mandates the summer phaseout of gas-powered lawn care equipment by commercial operators in favor of clean electric starting next year, after a Friday vote.

The Air Quality Control Commission approved the gradual changeover for private lawn care companies after one of the worst ozone seasons in recent years, with the clock ticking on reaching Environmental Protection Agency caps on the lung-searing toxic gas. New restrictions on commercial providers during the summer high-ozone months come on top of existing rules barring use of gas-powered machines by government parks and landscaping departments.

Toxic ground-level ozone is created by emissions from fossil fuel combustion and other activity combining with wildfire smoke and other substances, then baking under the hot Colorado sun. This past summer, sensors recorded Front Range ozone violations on 66 days, just under the record high of 67, and years of policy changes have failed to achieve cuts below the federal limits.

Fossil-fuel powered lawn equipment like mowers, trimmers and leaf blowers are a small contribution, a couple of parts per billion of ozone toward the current federal limit of 70 parts per billion. But they are also one of the last pieces of relatively low-hanging fruit in the policy battles against stubborn ozone, since most drivers and lawmakers resist restrictions on major contributors like passenger vehicles.

“Air pollution emissions from the lawn and garden sector contribute to approximately 13% of all ground-level ozone pollution in Colorado’s nonattainment area,” state health officials say.

Colorado commissions and lawmakers have passed rules meant to cut emissions from other major contributors, like the oil and gas drilling and production industry, but those trims have in part been overwhelmed by increases in summer temperatures and local and blown-in wildfire smoke. Environmental and health groups have proposed a summertime ban on new oil and gas exploration, but have been rebuffed.

Environmental and consumer groups that have worked on lawn equipment changes praised the AQCC’s unanimous vote Friday.

“We should not tolerate harmful pollution from cutting grass and blowing leaves around, especially when cleaner, quieter technology is available,” said nonprofit CoPIRG’s clean air advocate, Kirsten Schatz. “With this vote, our state leaders have taken another big step toward cleaning up the air pollution that is harming our health and quality of life.”

Nonprofit groups note Colorado law extends a 30% discount on clean electric lawn equipment at qualified retailers, and the Regional Air Quality Council also offers grant help to commercial operators looking to switch out equipment.

“These rules will benefit the communities that face some of our state’s worst air quality,” said Routt County Commissioner Sonja Macys, current president of Colorado Communities for Climate Action, a coalition of 49 local governments. “Gasoline-powered equipment plays an outsized role in contributing to ozone pollution, climate pollution, and localized fumes.”

“Switching to electric alternatives over the next few years will bring meaningful reductions in emissions leading to ozone pollution, so it’s a big win for public health in the region,” said Mike Silverstein, executive director of RAQC, whose representatives from Front Range governments make policy recommendations on air cleanup measures. “It also comes with significant health benefits for the workers who use this equipment all day.”

The new rule sets limits on gas-powered machines from June 1 to Aug. 31, including “push and hand-held string trimmers, hedge trimmers, blowers, edgers, pole saws, and push or walk-behind lawn mowers. Individuals who do their own yard work will not be expected to comply,” the state health department said in a statement after the vote. The state and local incentives do apply, though, to individuals wanting new clean equipment.

The largest ride-on mowers were left out of the new rules because there are not as many viable, affordable options for commercial operators to switch to electric.

Commercial operators must inventory their existing equipment with the state. Beginning in 2027, they may use 85% of their gas-powered equipment during summer months. In 2028, that portion drops to 65% of gas equipment, then 25% in 2030, and finally 10% in 2032.

title: As Washington weakens environmental protections, New Jersey must build a green wall
description:
The Trump administration is taking a wrecking ball to environmental protections, and New Jersey cannot afford to stand underneath it.
New Jersey needs a green wall built from enforceable laws, independent state standards, strong environmental enforcement, and science-based decision-making.
Oregon shows how to build an environmental firewall New Jersey should look to Oregon, which has enacted a law specifically designed to preserve environmental protections when Washington weakens them.
Washington State proves climate protection does not have to depend on Trump Washington State offers another important example of how states can establish independent climate protections.
New Jersey can’t build a green wall by raiding its own Environmental programs Issuing press releases will not protect New Jersey from Trump’s environmental rollbacks while weakening its own environmental protections.
text:
New Jersey must strengthen its environmental laws, protect clean energy funding, and resist efforts to fast-track development as the Trump administration rolls back federal safeguards.

Trump’s environmental war is attacking our air, water, climate, wetlands, forests, endangered species, toxic-site cleanups, public lands, and scientific research. New Jersey cannot fight back with press releases while weakening its own protections. It needs a legal firewall, and it needs to build it now.

After the election, Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Congress needs to stand up to Trump and hold him accountable. I completely agree. Congress could pass new environmental laws, overturn rules that exempt data centers from the Clean Air Act, or reverse rules that weaken standards for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). But even if those measures survive a filibuster and pass, Trump will veto them. The governor and Legislature need to stand up to Trump to protect the environment and build a green wall around New Jersey.

The Trump administration is taking a wrecking ball to environmental protections, and New Jersey cannot afford to stand underneath it.

This is not one regulation disappearing here or one program being cut there. It is death by a thousand cuts. The administration is dismantling safeguards for clean air, clean water, climate, wildlife and public health while cutting the scientists, inspectors and enforcement personnel needed to protect them.

A Brookings regulatory tracker updated October 7, 2026, documents the administration’s sweeping deregulatory actions across multiple policy areas. Other environmental trackers count well over 100 actions, including proposed, completed, and ongoing rollbacks. The numbers vary depending on what is counted, but the direction is unmistakable: Washington is systematically dismantling environmental safeguards.

The damage reaches virtually every part of environmental protection. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is eliminating federal limits on greenhouse-gas pollution from power plants. The administration is moving to strip federal protections from millions of acres of wetlands, weakening environmental review, opening public lands to greater extraction and undermining wildlife protections. Toxic-chemical safeguards are being reconsidered as scientific research and agency staffing are cut.

The administration is turning the Environmental Protection Agency into the “Every Polluter’s Agency,” putting the interests of corporate polluters and the fossil-fuel industry ahead of science and public health.

But the question is not simply what Trump is doing. It is what New Jersey is going to do about it.

When Washington tears down the environmental floor, what keeps New Jersey from falling through it?

New Jersey needs a green wall built from enforceable laws, independent state standards, strong environmental enforcement, and science-based decision-making. And it must stop undermining its own climate programs, fast-tracking environmentally damaging development and waiving protections in the name of affordability or economic growth.

We cannot fight Trump’s environmental war with one hand while helping carry his wrecking ball with the other.

Oregon shows how to build an environmental firewall

New Jersey should look to Oregon, which has enacted a law specifically designed to preserve environmental protections when Washington weakens them.

In 2019, Oregon adopted sections 468.148 and 468.149 of the Oregon Revised Statutes, establishing a baseline of federal environmental standards as they existed on January 19, 2017, for specified provisions of the Clean Air Act, Safe Drinking Water Act and Clean Water Act.

The law requires state agencies to assess federal changes and take or recommend action when those changes significantly weaken protections. It also preserves Oregon’s authority to adopt even stronger standards.

New Jersey needs an environmental backstop act modeled on that approach.

The law should establish a clear statutory baseline for environmental protections, require the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) to evaluate federal rollbacks and maintain at least the baseline level of protection through enforceable state standards. It should cover air pollution, drinking water, water pollution, toxic chemicals, and other areas where the state has legal authority to act.

The Legislature should also authorize the DEP to adopt stronger standards when science demonstrates they are necessary to protect New Jersey residents. This must be more than a promise to study federal actions or issue recommendations. It needs enforceable standards, deadlines, and accountability.

The principle is simple: When Washington weakens a protection, New Jersey should not automatically weaken with it. We should not have to reinvent the wheel every time Trump decides to throw one into the ditch.

Washington State proves climate protection does not have to depend on Trump

Washington State offers another important example of how states can establish independent climate protections.

Washington enacted its Climate Commitment Act in 2021, creating a cap-and-invest program that requires covered businesses to obtain allowances for their greenhouse-gas emissions. The law supports statewide emissions-reduction targets of 45 percent below 1990 levels by 2030, 70 percent by 2040 and 95 percent by 2050, with net-zero carbon emissions targeted for 2050.

The state also enacted the Clean Energy Transformation Act, requiring utilities to eliminate coal-fired resources serving state customers, achieve greenhouse-gas-neutral electricity sales by 2030 and transition to 100 percent renewable or non-emitting electricity by 2045.

New Jersey can’t build a green wall by raiding its own Environmental programs

Issuing press releases will not protect New Jersey from Trump’s environmental rollbacks while weakening its own environmental protections. The Sherrill administration has diverted $155 million from the Clean Energy Fund and redirected or considered redirecting up to $510 million in Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) proceeds for ratepayer relief and other purposes. More than $1.47 billion in RGGI proceeds has accumulated since 2020. These funds should be advancing emissions reductions, clean energy and energy efficiency—not becoming another pot of money for plugging budget holes.

The administration has cut $150 million from the DEP budget, eliminated $8 million for urban parks through Green Acres, and diverted $140 million from the Clean Energy Fund to New Jersey Transit. Cutting environmental programs while claiming to defend New Jersey from Washington’s environmental assault is no firewall. It is like selling the roof shingles to pay the heating bill, then wondering why the house is leaking.

RGGI is not a piggy bank, and the Clean Energy Fund cannot become Trenton’s ATM. If New Jersey wants to stand up to federal rollbacks, it must protect these funds, strengthen environmental enforcement and adopt binding standards—not fast-track permits, weaken safeguards or substitute announcements for action. RGGI is not a comprehensive climate policy, and it cannot substitute for enforceable state requirements covering other major sources of greenhouse gases.

New Jersey should establish binding emissions-reduction requirements for major sources, strengthen methane controls and use its authority under state air-pollution law to address climate pollution.

Washington state is building a climate framework. New Jersey must stop hollowing out its own.

The federal retreat from environmental review creates another major gap

The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) was designed to make federal agencies examine environmental consequences before making major decisions. The Trump administration has eliminated the Council on Environmental Quality’s government-wide NEPA regulations, while federal agencies have revised their own procedures.

New Jersey should enact a State Environmental Quality Act—a state version of the National Environmental Policy Act—requiring comprehensive review of major projects and their cumulative impacts.

The review must examine greenhouse-gas emissions, flooding, stormwater, wetlands, habitat loss, air and water pollution, toxic contamination, environmental-justice impacts, and reasonable alternatives, including not building the project.

One warehouse may not flood a community. Twenty warehouses can.

One data center may not overwhelm the electric grid. A cluster of them can.

One gas pipeline may appear manageable in isolation. A network of pipelines, compressor stations, and associated infrastructure can lock communities into decades of additional fossil-fuel pollution.

Environmental laws that examine every project through a straw instead of looking at the whole landscape are how we pave over the Garden State one permit at a time.

Massachusetts, California and New York have established state environmental-review frameworks that offer useful models. New Jersey should create its own system with enforceable requirements, meaningful public participation and independent scientific review.

Protect wetlands and water even when Washington won’t

The Trump administration is moving to narrow the definition of waters protected under the Clean Water Act. Its September 2026 proposal could strip federal protections from millions of acres of wetlands.

New Jersey has its own Freshwater Wetlands Protection Act. That gives us an important foundation, but the state allowed some weakening under the Christie administration and needs to ensure its protections remain strong and independent of changes in federal jurisdiction.

Wetlands are not vacant lots waiting for a bulldozer. They are nature’s stormwater infrastructure. They store floodwater, recharge groundwater, filter pollution and provide essential habitat.

In a state increasingly threatened by destructive flooding, paving over wetlands and then complaining about flooding is like smashing your umbrella and blaming the rain.

New Jersey should strengthen protections for seasonal wetlands, headwaters, streams and other vulnerable waters. It should also prevent exemptions and waivers from becoming back doors for destruction.

The same principle must apply to stormwater standards, flood protections and development on environmentally sensitive land. The state cannot claim to be preparing for climate change while allowing development practices that increase runoff and put people in harm’s way.

Data centers need real environmental regulation

New Jersey cannot leave data centers to be regulated through piecemeal permits and voluntary promises.

These facilities can create substantial demands on the electric grid and water supplies. Backup generators can emit air pollutants; cooling systems can consume water; and construction can destroy habitat and increase stormwater runoff. When data centers cluster in one region, their combined impacts can be much greater than those of a single facility.

New Jersey needs specific, enforceable standards for data centers, including mandatory reporting of electricity and water use, emissions limits, water-conservation requirements, noise controls and comprehensive stormwater protections. Developers should have to demonstrate how their projects will affect grid capacity, utility bills and nearby communities.

Lawmakers in New Jersey have already recognized concerns about data-center impacts. For example, legislation introduced in September 2026 proposed a temporary moratorium on certain artificial intelligence data-center approvals, construction, expansion, and subsidies while a commission studies their effects.

But a study or temporary pause is not a substitute for permanent standards.

We cannot let the AI boom become another excuse to fast-track development, build new fossil-fuel infrastructure and socialize the costs while private companies collect the profits.

Toxic chemicals: Don’t wait for Washington to protect public health

PFAS, often called forever chemicals, are particularly troubling because they persist in the environment and can contaminate drinking water. Federal policy changes have put several PFAS drinking-water requirements and compliance timelines under reconsideration.

Other chemicals also demand close scrutiny. Trichloroethylene (TCE) is associated with cancer and other serious health risks. Methylene chloride has caused fatal poisonings, particularly when used in poorly ventilated spaces. Chlorpyrifos is a neurotoxic pesticide whose permitted uses have been subject to years of regulatory and legal disputes. The risks vary by chemical, dose, route, and duration of exposure, but weakening safeguards without sound scientific justification can leave workers, children and communities more vulnerable.

The state has already established its own groundwater standards for several PFAS compounds, including perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS), perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA) and hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid (GenX). It should continue updating standards based on the best available science, strengthen monitoring, and ensure contaminated drinking-water supplies are addressed promptly.

New Jersey should also strengthen independent state review of pesticides and industrial chemicals, maintain transparent public reporting of toxic exposures and require polluters to pay for investigation and remediation.

We cannot protect public health by weakening the rules and hoping the chemicals behave themselves.

New Jersey needs a real Endangered Species Act

Federal wildlife protections are also under attack. Changes to the Endangered Species Act and its implementing rules threaten to weaken protections for habitat and make it easier for development and extraction to proceed.

New Jersey has its own Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act, but it needs to do more to protect habitat.

A law focused primarily on unauthorized harm to individual animals is not enough if their nests, dens, breeding grounds, and feeding areas can be destroyed. A species cannot survive if its habitat disappears.

New Jersey should strengthen its law to provide enforceable protection for critical nesting and breeding areas, migration corridors, feeding grounds, and other essential habitat. It should ensure that state land-use and permitting decisions account for these areas before development is approved.

You cannot save the bird by protecting it after you bulldoze its nest.

The state should also maintain funding for wildlife surveys, habitat mapping, and biological research. Without reliable data, officials cannot identify what needs protection or determine whether existing safeguards are working.

Superfund: Polluters must pay, not taxpayers

New Jersey has a long legacy of industrial contamination, from abandoned factories and landfills to sites polluted by toxic chemicals. Federal Superfund enforcement and cleanup funding are critical to addressing many of these sites.

The state should strengthen its polluter-pays laws, protect dedicated cleanup funding, and ensure that responsible companies—not taxpayers—pay for investigating and remediating the contamination they caused.

New Jersey should also establish a state climate-superfund program, designed within the limits of applicable law, to make major fossil-fuel polluters contribute to the costs of climate-related damage and resilience.

A contaminated site should not become a permanent monument to corporate accounting.

The company makes the pollution. The public should not get stuck with the cleanup bill.

Stop fighting Washington with one hand while weakening New Jersey with the other

Gov. Sherrill has emphasized affordability, faster permitting, and expedited development. Her administration has defended efforts to accelerate reviews and reconsider certain environmental requirements. But efficiency cannot mean weakening the safeguards designed to protect residents.

The Department of Environmental Protection’s Operation FAST, for example, has emphasized reducing permitting backlogs. Reducing unnecessary delays is reasonable. But a faster decision is not automatically a better decision, and processing permits more quickly does not justify lowering environmental standards.

The proposed extension of the legacy period for the Resilient Environments and Landscapes (REAL) climate-resilience rules until July 20, 2027, while the administration reviews potential changes, raises the same concern: New Jersey must not postpone necessary protections while climate risks continue to grow.

Natural-gas pipelines and related infrastructure can create long-term emissions, air-quality and land-use impacts. Nuclear projects require rigorous review of costs, safety, waste, water use, and site-specific environmental risks. Neither should receive a free pass because officials say energy demand is growing.

A permit approved quickly that results in flooding, contamination or habitat destruction is not efficient. It is simply a faster way to create the next environmental crisis.

The Department of Environmental Protection must not become the Department of Expedited Permits. The DEP needs the scientists, toxicologists, engineers, inspectors, enforcement officers, and analysts required to protect the public. It needs strong standards and the authority to enforce them—not pressure to clear projects regardless of their environmental consequences.

Protect the science that protects us

Cuts to environmental agencies, climate research, and monitoring programs threaten the data that communities rely on to prepare for floods, identify toxic contamination, track wildlife, and understand changing weather patterns.

Data is environmental infrastructure.

You cannot prepare for flooding if you eliminate the people who model storms. You cannot protect drinking water if you stop monitoring contaminants. You cannot protect wildlife if you stop collecting biological data. And you cannot plan for sea-level rise if you dismantle the science that tells communities how high the water could get.

New Jersey should invest in independent climate modeling, flood mapping, water-quality monitoring, toxic-site investigations and wildlife surveys. It should make environmental data accessible to the public and use it to guide permitting, land-use planning and infrastructure decisions.

Science is not a luxury item to be cut when budgets get tight. It is the smoke alarm. Turning off the smoke alarm does not put out the fire.

Build the green wall now

First, pass an Environmental Backstop Act. Establish a statutory baseline for federal environmental standards, modeled on Oregon’s law, and require the state to preserve at least that level of protection when federal rules are weakened.

Second, enact a State Environmental Quality Act. Create a state environmental-review law requiring cumulative-impact, climate, environmental-justice, and alternatives analysis for major projects.

Third, strengthen wetlands and water protections. Protect seasonal wetlands, headwaters, streams, and other vulnerable waters regardless of changes in federal jurisdiction. Do not allow waivers to undermine flood prevention and water quality.

Fourth, establish enforceable statewide climate requirements. Strengthen greenhouse-gas and methane controls, expand emissions reductions beyond RGGI’s covered power plants and protect the integrity of climate programs.

Fifth, stop raiding climate and clean-energy funds. Keep RGGI proceeds and Clean Energy Fund resources focused on emissions reduction, energy efficiency, electrification and climate resilience.

Sixth, regulate data centers. Require enforceable standards for energy and water use, emissions, noise, stormwater and cumulative impacts. Make developers demonstrate that their projects will not shift environmental and infrastructure costs onto residents.

Seventh, strengthen toxic-chemical protections. Maintain independent PFAS standards, expand monitoring, evaluate pesticides and industrial chemicals using the best available science, and accelerate the cleanup of contaminated sites.

Eighth, strengthen endangered-species protections. Protect critical habitat, nesting and breeding areas, migration corridors and feeding grounds—not just individual animals after they are harmed.

Ninth, establish stronger polluter-pays and cleanup programs. Ensure responsible companies finance toxic-site remediation and develop lawful state mechanisms to address climate-related damage.

Tenth, fully fund DEP and protect environmental science. Provide the staff and resources necessary for independent review, inspections, enforcement, climate modeling and public-health protection.

Eleventh, end the practice of treating environmental standards as negotiable. No fast-tracking, waivers or exemptions that sacrifice public safety and environmental protection for a developer’s convenience. Energy and infrastructure projects must meet enforceable standards and undergo meaningful review.

Don’t wait for Washington to save New Jersey from Washington

That is the point of federalism: states have substantial authority to protect public health and the environment when federal safeguards are inadequate, subject to federal law and constitutional limits.

New Jersey has a choice. It can wait for the next federal rollback, hold another press conference, issue another statement, and then scramble to figure out what disappeared.

Or it can build a green wall now.

But the state must practice what it preaches.

If Washington dismantles the environmental floor, New Jersey must build its own foundation.

If Washington removes the guardrails, New Jersey must put up its own.

And if Trump turns the Environmental Protection Agency into “Every Polluter’s Agency,” New Jersey must ensure its Department of Environmental Protection remains an agency whose first responsibility is to the public—not the next developer standing in line for a permit.

Clean air, clean water, safe drinking water, healthy forests, functioning wetlands, protected wildlife, and a stable climate are not federal favors. They are part of the public’s natural inheritance.

The time for symbolic outrage is over. New Jersey needs to stand up to Trump’s environmental war in practice, not just in words. Build the green wall, strengthen the laws, and act now—before the wrecking ball reaches the Garden State.

title: Inside the Louisiana Town Next to Meta's Largest-Ever Data Center
description:
The tech giant is building its largest-ever data center near Holly Ridge, a small unincorporated town tucked away in Richland Parish.

text:
For years, Susan Lee loved standing in the front yard of her Louisiana home and taking photos as a radiant, bright sun set over a nearby field.

Now that field is a sprawling construction site.

"Our sunset is done," Rikki Goodwin, her 42-year-old daughter, told me during a conversation in September. "Now, you got two beautiful water tanks, an orange building, a gray one, and some big poles."

Lee and Goodwin are among the residents of this rural community who are adjusting to a new neighbor: Meta.

The tech giant is building its largest-ever data center near Holly Ridge, a small unincorporated town tucked away in Richland Parish. The project is set to span nearly 10 million square feet, or around 229 acres. That's huge. For context, Magic Kingdom at Walt Disney World spans 142 acres, and Vatican City is 108 acres.

"It looks like a city back there at night," Buddy McCartney, a 75-year-old Richland Parish resident, told me.

It's difficult to grasp the sheer scope of the data center from grainy, slightly outdated Google Maps images, so I traveled to Richland Parish to see the mammoth construction site myself. I also spoke to residents about what it's like living near the work of a trillion-dollar company.

For some, Meta's arrival has created an economic landscape ripe for new business ventures and entrepreneurship. For others, issues like noise, traffic, and dust have caused growing pains.

A Meta spokesperson said it takes their neighbors' concerns "very seriously."

"We're investing more than $270 million in local road improvements and have installed new traffic signals near the site," the spokesperson said. "Our contractors enforce strict traffic-safety rules and use dust-suppression measures to reduce construction impacts. We hold weekly calls with community partners and contractors and work with local authorities to address concerns."

Booming businesses

Temperatures were nearing 99° Fahrenheit as my colleagues and I drove down Highway 183 in search of the data center. The first few yards were, in a word, uneventful. An elementary school. A Dollar General. A few homes scattered on large plots of land. Trees.

Then, like a mirage, the construction site began to take shape under the sweltering sun. Fields that had been filled with crops were now lined with long orange cones, excavators, newly erected buildings, and hordes of construction workers in high-visibility vests. We drove for nearly three miles before pulling over at an entrance to the sprawling campus, but the construction site continued for at least another mile.

As dump trucks and work crew vehicles zoomed around the site, we visited HeBrews Coffee & Eats in Holly Ridge, one of several businesses that have benefited from the data center.

Since Meta broke ground in 2024, some residents have decided to leverage the opportunity and make some money. The food truck is located across the street from a construction site entrance, making it an easy option for the crews.

TJ and Kaycie Weed first opened HeBrews Coffee & Eats café five years ago in the nearby town of Rayville, but the Holly Ridge location opened in 2025 specifically because of Meta's data center.

"Holly Ridge does most of the catering. If it's any of the businesses under the umbrella of Meta, I send it to Holly Ridge," TJ said.

Shelbie Stephenson, owner of the Holly Ridge location, said they deliver 450 lunch plates to the Meta work site twice a month. They also do coffee and breakfast catering several times a month.

"We have done 900 burritos and 2,500 cups of coffee during safety week," she said.

Ice Queen, cofounded by David Rodgers, is another business that materialized in 2025 because of the data center project. Ice Queen began by selling $3 bags of ice to subcontractors and companies working on the Meta project, but has since expanded its offerings to include a wide range of items.

"Pallets of water are where we make most of our money because it's a safety issue out here. The heat and all that," Rodgers told me. "I buy truckloads of water and deliver probably 30 to 40 pallets of water a week to these guys."

Ice Queen sells a pallet of water for about $600. Another popular item, Liquid I.V., an electrolyte drink that helps with hydration, costs about $1 a pouch.

Similarly, the Allen family of Rayville has found success since opening their restaurant, Holy Tacos, last year. Owner Tim Allen said the construction crews order catering from Holy Tacos one to four times a month.

"Catering costs anywhere from $4,000 to $7,000, depending on the size," Allen said. "We have a good local following, but when you add the catering, probably 40% of our monthly business is directly related to Meta."

The cost of doing business

Lee, 68, has also launched a business. She owns and operates a food truck park near the AI data center campus that charges $1,000 a month for each vehicle.

Despite the new opportunity to make some money, Lee said the changes Meta's arrival has brought have not all been positive. During our conversation, Lee recalled life before Meta arrived, a time she described as quiet and easygoing.

"It was a really pleasant place to live. I've always loved where I live," Lee said. "All that changed. I retired in December of last year, and now I'm at home all day. It's a different ballgame."

She's referring to the ripple effects of the project, including clouds of dust kicked up by the construction crews. Lee said she's dealt with respiratory issues since construction began. She has also contended with bright lights placed at the construction site's entrance at night.

"You don't have to worry about nobody walking up and trying to steal anything because it's lit up like a Christmas tree out here," Goodwin said.

Noise from the construction site is another issue. In all my conversations with residents in Richland Parish, however, one complaint came up more than any other: traffic.

Lee and Goodwin said the influx of contractors and construction workers has overwhelmed local roadways, extending residents' daily commutes and raising safety concerns. The construction site is down the street from Holly Ridge Elementary School.

"It scares me knowing the dump trucks don't stop on a dime," Goodwin said. "I used to be a firefighter, so I've worked too many wrecks."

During our conversation, McCartney agreed that traffic had become a real challenge. He's a former farmer who retired about two years ago.

"You feel like you're being pushed out," McCartney said.

McCartney said he initially planned to spend the rest of his life at that home. Not anymore. He's listed his land for sale, and his agent has advertised it as a commercial property. McCartney said traffic played a part in the decision.

"I didn't sign on for this. When we go to church on Wednesday night, it takes us 30 minutes to get there because you're dealing with all this traffic," he said. "If you had an emergency and need to get to town, you're just going to have to wait."

McCartney isn't against residents leveraging the economic benefits of the data center, though. He told me he's "proud" of them for capitalizing on the moment.

While McCartney has chosen to sell his property, Lee is still figuring out her next steps. Lee, Goodwin, and McCartney have not raised the concerns with authorities or Meta. In a text, Lee said she doubts Meta will take meaningful action on the concerns, since the project is already underway and growing by the day.

As Richland Parish gradually transforms into an AI hub, Goodwin can't help but remember when the area was mostly farmers and agriculture.

"I don't know if people understand this," Goodwin said. "This is not going to feed you."

She added, "You can't eat an AI algorithm, can you?"

text:
LAS VEGAS, NV, UNITED STATES, November 23, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Advanced Global Manufacturing （AGM） Makes North American Debut at RE+ 26, Showcasing New Solar-Storage Technologies to Strong Reception

Three Technology Areas Draw Focused Attention from North American Clients; Multiple Cooperation Intents Reached

RE+ 2026, one of the largest clean energy industry events in North America, was held in Las Vegas from November 16 to 19, 2026. The exhibition brought together manufacturers and buyers across the solar photovoltaic, energy storage, and charging infrastructure sectors. During the show, Advanced Global Manufacturing presented its new photovoltaic and energy storage technologies at Booth N3554. According to on-site observations, visitors came from the United States, Mexico, and Europe, including developers, EPC contractors, data center operators, and investment institutions, with several companies expressing cooperation intent on-site.

text:
Nova Scotia Power project combines ambient-adjusted ratings monitoring across more than 165 transmission lines with 129 DLR sensors on six critical circuits

LIèGE, BELGIUM, November 23, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Ampacimon, a global leader in dynamic line rating (DLR) solutions, today announced the successful completion of its largest DLR deployment in North America, marking a major milestone in grid modernization and operational intelligence.

The deployment was completed for Nova Scotia Power, which serves more than 550,000 customers and operates an extensive transmission and distribution network across the province. This project underscores the utility’s commitment to reliability for its customers and maximizing the performance of existing infrastructure.

Through this collaboration, Ampacimon deployed Ambient Adjusted Ratings (AAR) monitoring across more than 165 transmission lines ranging from 69 kV to 345 kV. The project also included comprehensive ratings for over 165 facilities, enabling enhanced system-wide visibility and more informed operational decision-making.

“This project demonstrates what DLR can look like when utilities move beyond individual pilots and begin applying dynamic ratings at scale. Nova Scotia Power now has greater visibility into the real-time capability of its transmission system, helping them safely maximize existing infrastructure while supporting reliability, future growth, and renewable integration. We’re incredibly proud to be their partner on this milestone deployment,” said Luke Howell, VP of Sales for North America at Ampacimon.

A total of 129 Ampacimon Sense DLR units were installed across six critical circuits, with all sensors deployed via helicopter to efficiently access remote and complex terrain. The system now delivers real-time data that enhances situational awareness and unlocks additional transmission capacity across the network.

Delivered through a secure, cloud-based platform, the solution is fully integrated into Nova Scotia Power’s operational systems. By enabling more dynamic and accurate line ratings, the project is intended to strengthen operational flexibility and improve reliability across the region, including interconnected systems with neighboring utilities.

This deployment represents an important step forward in leveraging grid-enhancing technologies to meet growing energy demand while accelerating the transition to a more resilient and efficient power system.
